The backlash against screens in schools is escalating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:36:37 UTC
23:36:37 KST

In New York City, teachers have two more weeks to prepare for the start of school—and no access to the educational technology software they typically use to teach. City officials have issued a tech freeze while they deliberate over how artificial intelligence (AI) will be allowed in classrooms, amid public pressure to place a two-year moratorium on the technology.
Across the country, parents, teachers, school districts and state legislatures are currently grappling with similar questions revolving around how much technology should be allowed in the classroom. Just this week, as part of a massive settlement, Meta agreed to institute “school mode” so that kids can’t access Instagram during school hours. Most states now ban student cell phone use in schools, and a broader movement to limit educational screen use is gaining momentum. In March Utah and Alabama became the first states to limit the use of screens in classrooms.
Educational technology companies claim their apps and tools can make learning fun and boost student achievement. Schools also want to prepare students for a future where technology is ubiquitous. But many parents and educators see screens as an expensive distraction providing little additional benefit over analog learning with pencils and paper. And while the financial and educational stakes of these debates are high, the scientific research on the subject is highly nuanced: the effectiveness of these platforms can vary widely, researchers have found. Broadly speaking, digital tools that merely require students to drill new skills don’t promote learning, whereas platforms that are interactive and creatively engaging and provide real-time feedback show benefits.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Tech in schools “is like a lightning rod,” says Christopher Saldaña, a K–12 education policy researcher at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “In some ways, the backlash is a long time coming because we’ve had all these claims about what education technology can do that haven’t always panned out.”
The educational technology (or “ed tech”) industry generated $48 billion in revenue in 2024 and is projected to grow to $90 billion by 2030. The U.S. has some 13,000 public school districts but no central authority that vets marketing claims and provides guidance on which platforms schools should adopt, Saldaña explains.
Individual districts “don’t have the money to be able to vet any of these claims or verify them themselves,” he adds. “They’re often at the mercy of whatever vendors are telling them.”
Data privacy has also emerged as a key concern among grassroots parent groups advocating for screen-free schools. A Utah State Board of Education investigation surveyed educational software with data privacy agreements and found that 61 percent shared student data with third parties and 36 percent shared data with advertisers.
Under Alabama’s new rules, the state’s Department of Education will be required to institute limits on screen time in early childhood education. Utah’s new law bans screens in classrooms for K–3 students, except for computer science lessons and testing. It also bans sending devices home with K–3 students. The Los Angeles Unified School District, the second largest school district in the country, passed a resolution limiting screen use in classrooms in April.
Still, those rules are the exception. Most school districts are forging ahead with technology in classrooms. In a survey of teachers and school leaders conducted this year by the EdWeek Research Center, 74 percent of respondents said that their schools haven’t reduced their investment in education technology as a result of parent pushback and have no plans to do so in the near future. Teachers reported an overall positive effect of educational technology on students’ engagement in learning and mastery of skills but an overall negative effect on their social-emotional skills, overall well-being and behavior in the classroom.
Though digital learning tools are still widely used, bans on noneducational tech in school are now commonplace. At least 39 states and Washington, D.C., have prohibited cell phone use in public schools. Some of these laws only ban devices in class, while others ban them for the entire school day, including lunch and recess. These measures have become increasingly popular among the general public; a Pew survey conducted this spring found that support has risen across all age groups of U.S. adults since 2024.
Research on the impact of these phone bans is mixed. A study of schools that used lockable phone pouches from the company Yondr found that disciplinary incidents rose and student well-being fell in the first year of the phone ban. But in the ensuing years, disciplinary incident rates reduced and student well-being increased. There was no meaningful effect on test scores or attendance throughout the study period, however.
“Bans are just a starting line. They are never a whole comprehensive solution,” says Larz May, founder of #HalftheStory, a digital wellness nonprofit focused on teens. “What we’ve seen on the ground is that alongside phone bans, there are other cuts and issues that are impacting [kids]”—such as funding cuts to art programs and extracurriculars.
Phone ban policies restrict how teens can interact without providing further resources for connection and flourishing, May says. “What we’re hearing is, ‘You’re taking these things away, but what else do you have to offer?’”
Students’ main concerns around technology in schools now revolve around AI, May says. Research conducted by the College Board in 2025 found that high school students are “on the fence” about the risks and benefits of AI in their schooling, even as 84 percent reported using it to help with schoolwork. The study also found that one in five high schools allow generative AI but have no formal policy on what kind of use is acceptable.
The uncertainty is breeding anxiety among students, May reports. “One kid told me ... that he actually videos himself while he’s doing his homework, just in case he gets accused of using AI,” she says. “Kids are going to extreme measures out of fear.”
Meanwhile, ed tech platforms are integrating AI further into their products, says Silvia Noguerón-Liu, a literacy studies researcher at the University of Colorado Boulder. While she stresses that the educational technology platforms used in classrooms are typically well-vetted by districts, the offerings of ed tech companies are expanding and are often marketed as time-saving measures to teachers.
“The last ed tech conference I attended had the big names [in ed tech], and they all had an AI exploration room that felt a little bit dystopian,” Noguerón-Liu says. “Now where this gets very, very problematic is when you rely on it for content,” she says, because charts, information and lesson plans created with AI can often be inaccurate.
And whether technology in a classroom is helping or hurting depends a lot on the teacher, experts say. Educators need training and resources to use technology effectively, and they don’t always get it. “In my mind, teachers’ knowledge and teachers’ actions,” Noguerón-Liu says, “that’s the most impactful component.”

British Jewish community leaders have raised strong concerns on Sunday with the UK government over potential plans to ban or restrict trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after recent high-level meetings between community representatives and government officials, including a meeting on Friday between Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
The diplomatic friction follows UK warnings of upcoming measures targeting settlement expansion, prompted by the Israeli government's publication of tenders for the E1 construction project. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar responded sharply to the UK's position, arguing that blaming only Israel while ignoring Palestinian extremism has fueled antisemitic hatred against the British Jewish community.
Major British Jewish organizations issue coordinated statement
In response to the looming trade restrictions, major British Jewish organizations issued coordinated statements. Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis detailed his discussions following his meeting with the Foreign Secretary, stating, "I welcomed the opportunity on Friday to meet with the Foreign Secretary, the Rt Hon. Ed Miliband. While we share fervent hopes for a future of peace and security in the Middle East, I explained why I believe the UK Government’s intended sanctions will be counter-productive and even endanger such a vision of peace."
The Chief Rabbi added that many in the community view the measures with deep dismay, warning they risk spiraling into a de facto boycott of Israel and threatening the livelihoods of tens of thousands of Palestinian workers.
Mirvis also noted that "these measures will also disproportionately affect British Jews because of our close religious, family, charitable and educational ties to Israel," and cautioned that domestic political considerations are driving foreign policy at the expense of regional peace and community safety. He further stated that the policy will not influence Israeli decision-making as intended, but will instead embolden the tiny minority who support criminality while penalizing countless others.
Board of Deputies President Phil Rosenberg stated, "We have engaged with the government in recent days, alongside community partners, regarding potential steps by government in relation to settlement activity."
"We have urged the government to avoid irreversible steps that could further damage the UK-Israel relationship and have a harmful impact on the UK Jewish community, especially in the run-up to an Israeli election that has the potential to bring significant political change," he added.
Rosenberg emphasized that while the community overwhelmingly condemns violence by extremist settlers, the proposed policies risk harming legitimate religious connections and encouraging a wider boycott movement that rejects Israel's existence and marginalizes British Jews.
JLC: 'Why is Israel being singled out?'
Similarly, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) released a statement questioning why Israel is being singled out for economic action while previous punitive measures have failed to influence conditions on the ground.
The JLC warned that as Israel approaches pivotal elections on October 27, further interventions will only embolden extremist factions. The organization further cautioned that broad, untargeted measures "may inadvertently become a wider boycott of Israel, giving legitimacy to those who reject Israel's very existence, and placing increased scrutiny on British Jews at a time when antisemitism in the UK is more prevalent and more violent than ever."

Sacha Baron Cohen's Ali G to return in new film amid character's 'racist stereotypes' controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:28:24 UTC
23:28:24 KST

Ali G’s comeback has already sparked controversy. After nearly 20 years away, actor and comedian Sacha Baron Cohen is bringing one of his most controversial satirical characters back to the screen in a new film. He now faces a global campaign calling for a boycott over the character’s use of “racist stereotypes.”
The new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, was filmed in complete secrecy over the past year, according to the British newspaper the Daily Mail. The movie marks Baron Cohen’s directorial debut.
The mockumentary follows the character’s life since “the world went to hell,” alongside his pregnant girlfriend, played by actress Morgana Robinson. The film is scheduled to open in theaters on October 23 through Amazon MGM Studios, but it has already triggered a storm of criticism.
NewsCord, a British media monitoring platform, launched a campaign just one day after the trailer was released, urging movie theaters worldwide to refuse to screen the film. As of Sunday, campaign organizers said more than 41,000 emails had been sent to 15 major movie theater chains.
The activists accuse Baron Cohen of using satire as a cover to promote racism. “Ali G is a cover to laugh at Jamaican culture," the campaign wrote on X/Twitter. "The character enforces harmful stereotypes of how a Jamaican man behaves in society."
"Ali G smokes weed, is a misogynist, and does nothing meaningful in life," the campaign added. "He does this because he thinks this is what a Jamaican does. The world laughs at Ali G, but the real butt of the joke is Black people, and specifically Jamaicans."
The campaign also cited previous criticism of the character, including comments by Black comedians who called Ali G “an alibi for racism” in 2000. It also referenced author Jeanette Winterson, who questioned how the character differed from racist minstrel shows.
Sony Pictures UK’s slogan for the film, “He’s back. We’re not responsible,” only added fuel to the controversy.
Baron Cohen's sarcastic response to Ali G controversy
Baron Cohen, 54, responded defiantly on X with his characteristic sarcasm, writing, “In an age where a comedian’s career can be ended by a single un-PC joke, I thought I’d play it safe and bring this guy back.”
UK Cinema Association CEO Phil Clapp addressed the boycott campaign in an interview with Variety, stressing that movie theaters do not serve as censors. “They are there to entertain the widest possible audience, not to determine the audience’s taste,” he said.
Variety: Picturehouse has not agreed to boycott Ali G film
Variety also debunked reports that the Picturehouse cinema chain had already agreed to boycott the film. The reports were based on an automated customer service response to requests for screenings that had not yet been scheduled.
Ali G first appeared on the UK’s Channel 4 in the late 1990s before becoming a cultural phenomenon. Baron Cohen retired the character in 2007 after becoming too recognizable. It remains to be seen whether audiences and critics will be as forgiving of Ali G’s return.

Senior US military influencers were discreetly placed in government positions as part of a covert Pentagon operation, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter and corroborating material.
According to the report, the influencers in question have worked to push against criticism of the Trump administration while advancing the positions of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, being assigned as “special government employees (SGE)” or “highly qualified experts (HQE)."
The report noted that HQEs are permitted to work either part-time or full-time with no compensation limitations, whereas SGEs may work up to 130 days per year.
The sources, which named two of the influencers as US Air Force Col. (ret.) Rob Maness and US Army Col. (ret.) Kurt Schlichter, told the Washington Post that several of the veterans are in positions powerful enough to potentially influence policy changes.
Both Maness and Schlichter, as well as US Army Col. (ret.) Thomas Anderson, have active government email addresses with a ".civ" suffix, indicating they are civilian rather than military employees, according to Pentagon records reviewed by the Washington Post.
Retired US military officers with thousands of online followers
In terms of online influence, Schlichter has over 620,000 followers on X/Twitter; Maness has over 135,000; and Anderson, now an attorney, retains over 323,000 under the pen name Cynical Publius, the report noted.
The records further showed that the retired officers, who served for several decades prior to their online presence, are employed in the office of Defense Under Secretary for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata.
According to the Washington Post, Tata's office has been tasked with tackling several issues central to conservative politics, including "woke" college ideology and COVID vaccine policies for American soldiers under former US president Joe Biden.
Anderson and Pentagon spokesperson Joel Valdez declined to comment to the Washington Post, while Maness and Schlichter did not respond to requests for comment.

Germany’s far right eyes small eastern state as springboard to national power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:25:39 UTC
23:25:39 KST

Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), speaks at the presentation of the AfD campaign for state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on June 04, 2026 in Magdeburg, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
MERSEBURG, Germany — It’s here in this small, mostly rural eastern state of just two million people that Germany’s far right is laying the groundwork for an eventual bid for power in Berlin.
Within striking distance of what could become a historic victory for their party in Saxony-Anhalt — one that would give a far-right party governing power in the country for the first time since World War II — leaders of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party see an opportunity too rare and valuable to squander.
And so they’ve devised a detailed, if difficult-to-execute, strategy for using their party’s first real taste of power to dismantle the firewall that mainstream parties have erected to keep the AfD out of government in Berlin.
Advertisement
“Every single one of you is making history right now!” Ulrich Siegmund, the charismatic face of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt set to become state premier should the party win big in a vote on Sept. 6, told a cheering crowd of thousands of supporters at an AfD campaign event in the former industrial town of Merseburg. “Someday, in 20 or 30 years, you’ll look in the history books and say: ‘It began here. It began in 2026 in Saxony-Anhalt!’”
Should the AfD win an absolute parliamentary majority in the state — current polls show them a few seats away from that goal — the party’s strategy for governing strikes a delicate balance: pursuing radical change that distinguishes the party from the establishment — delivering the political revolution it has long promised — without going so far as to alienate ordinary Bürger, middle-of-the-road citizens who don’t want the boat rocked too hard.
Ulrich Siegmund’s voters wearing campaign merch at an event in Querfurt on August 21, 2026. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO
To strike the balance the party seeks, the AfD in the state, for instance, intends to set up a “deportation task force” made up of key state ministers and police while seeking to avoid the scenes of chaos and violence evident in the U.S. when the Trump administration imposed similar measures. The party wants to blend extreme proposals — like redoing school history classes to teach less about Nazi crimes and slash funding for art deemed “anti-German” —with mundane policies that few would protest: like increasing funding for fire departments with response areas that include highways.
“We have to legitimize AfD policies through a practical example. That is our task,” said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the brainchild of the AfD’s program for governing in Saxony-Anhalt, at a regional party conference in Magdeburg in July.
To pull it off, the party has identified up to 200 positions in the state’s civil service that are to be filled with a cadre of party loyalists, some of whom have been pre-selected throughout Germany or specifically trained by the party in Berlin — an unprecedented move in postwar Germany, where the civil service is meant to be apolitical —to speed the execution of the AfD’s agenda while keeping things running smoothly. They’ve also come prepared with concrete plans to thwart expected efforts by mainstream opposition parties to block their agenda in courts.
Advertisement
AfD leaders hope the approach — stable but swift change — will destigmatize the party and pave the way for its further advance nationally, and eventually make it impossible for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to maintain its refusal to govern in coalition with the far right.
“If we can achieve this in Saxony-Anhalt and make it work in Saxony-Anhalt, then citizens will naturally see that the world won’t come to an end, but that things might even get better,” said Götz Frömming, one of the leaders of the AfD’s election programming division in Berlin. “And that will likely persuade many citizens who currently still have reservations or who perhaps don’t yet dare to vote for the AfD to give us a chance.”
‘Restructuring’ the state
If it can take power in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD aims to show it can implement its agenda without major debacles.
The crowd listening to Siegmund’s speech in Merseburg on August 22, 2026. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO
Some of the policies in their 100-day program — slashing public money for state broadcasters, detaining asylum-seekers in large numbers — are certain to face legal challenges and resistance from opposition parties.
To avoid governing chaos, national party leaders established the “Black-Red-Gold Academy” last year — named for the colors of the German flag — to help fill administrative positions with AfD loyalists in the Saxony-Anhalt civil service and prevent expected internal resistance. As part of the effort, the party pre-selected qualified candidates from around Germany who would be willing to relocate to Magdeburg and trained others, with a particular focus on filling positions in the interior and finance ministries.
The AfD cannot fire existing civil servants, and there are legal limitations to its influence over the administration, but the intent is to push aside those who would attempt to block the party’s agenda or leak sensitive information.
Advertisement
It’s not uncommon for an incoming government to appoint new state secretaries and leaders of specific key administrative departments, but a remaking of the civil service on such a scale is unparalleled.
Andreas Lichert, an AfD lawmaker from the state of Hesse with knowledge of the party’s plans nationally, called it a “restructuring process.”
“If there are people whom we know we cannot work with, for example because of political statements they have made in the past, then we obviously cannot fire them,” Lichert said. “They remain career civil servants, but of course, by allocating resources appropriately, you can ensure they — to put it bluntly — can no longer cause any harm.”
Siegmund with voters at an campaign event in Querfurt on August 21, 2026. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO
The AfD’s focus on “restructuring” the civil service stems at least in part from lessons imparted to the party from their Austrian sister-party — the far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) — which, unlike their German counterparts, have governed nationally on-and-off since the 1980s, and currently govern in five regions.
Merz’s conservatives in Saxony-Anhalt say they won’t govern in coalition with the AfD — and are pushing back against the AfD’s plans to “restructure” the civil service, depicting them as a danger to the very Bürger the far-right party wishes not to alienate.
Advertisement
Sven Schulze, the current premier of Saxony-Anhalt and the CDU’s lead candidate in the state, said the AfD’s plans were a dangerous “sham,” creating many new positions that will cost taxpayers and endanger dedicated civil servants.
“One thing is clear,” he said. “If they were to govern here, everyone — truly everyone — from the school principal to the teachers, to the division heads, all the way up to the department heads in ministries and subordinate agencies — everyone who doesn’t even come close to doing what the AfD dictates will have to fear for their job. Then you’ll be transferred, you’ll be harassed, you’ll be worn down until you give up on your own.”
Siegmund taking a selfie with a voter in Teicha at a campaign event on August 22, 2026. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO
Schulze also suggested the AfD didn’t genuinely care about the people of the state — and simply wants to use Saxony-Anhalt as launchpad for bigger ambitions, calling top AfD candidate Siegmund “a puppet” of national party leader Alice Weidel.
“Weidel is exploiting him and the state of Saxony-Anhalt to gain more power in Berlin,” he said last week.
National mainstream leaders have also weighed proposals to potentially cut off federal funding to Saxony-Anhalt that would be part of the so-called fiscal equalization system, which moves money to poorer states from wealthier ones. That funding, which for Saxony-Anhalt amounted to €2.8 billion in 2025, could theoretically be cut for rule-of-law concerns, although legal hurdles are high.
But the AfD says it is prepared to take action against such efforts.
The AfD’s national party leaders created a “Working Group on Government Participation” to begin drafting bills that could be passed in the state legislature and to weigh how the party, both federally and on state level, could work to block possible attempts to obstruct an AfD-led state government using the courts.
AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund giving a speech at a campaign event in Merseburg on August 22, 2026. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO
“We have received significant support from the party leadership,” said Martin Reichardt, the leader of the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch. “We also have the legal department, which is, of course, active as well. And it has prepared for situations where our political opponents might, for example, try to obstruct our work in government,” he added. “We will defend ourselves against this through appropriate legal means.”
Despite such plans, Gordon Köhler, an AfD politician from Saxony-Anhalt who was present at the Salzburg meeting with FPÖ officials, said his party wanted to avoid the kind of fever-pitch polarization that followed President Donald Trump’s return to power for a second term in the U.S.
While the AfD wants a crackdown on asylum-seekers, he said, the party doesn’t want the kind of images of chaos and violence that have occurred with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations on American streets.
“I’d like to call this a tension — on the one hand, taking swift action, but on the other hand, of course, governing well and building bridges,” Köhler said. “We won’t reach everyone — you’ll never succeed in that — but the point is for things to be a bit less tense and not as highly emotional as they are right now.”
After all, he added, “a society must function somehow. And if everyone’s always on edge, that’s obviously not healthy for anyone.”

TRNC suspends port officials after deadly ferry accident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:24:07 UTC
23:24:07 KST

Authorities in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) have suspended port officials who authorised the departure of a passenger ferry that capsized off the coastal city of Girne, Prime Minister Unal Ustel said, as search teams continued looking for 18 missing people.
Ustel said on Monday that the government had launched a full investigation into the disaster and would not allow any negligence or wrongdoing to be concealed.
“The relevant port officials who authorised the ship's departure have also been suspended from duty, an investigation has been launched against them, and new officials have been appointed in their place,” he said.
A Turkish Navy Underwater Offense (SAT) team dispatched from Türkiye has joined the ongoing search and rescue operation, Ustel said, adding that finding the missing passengers remains the government’s top priority.
14 suspects appear in court
Fourteen people were brought before the Girne District Court on Monday as investigators examined the circumstances surrounding the capsizing.
The suspects include the ferry’s captain, seven crew members, a company employee and two Girne Port officials. Police are also searching for two additional people under a court order.
The captain and crew told the court that the vessel overturned after its bow broke off amid rough waves. They said weather conditions appeared suitable when the ferry departed and that the vessel had valid navigational and administrative certificates.
The court ordered police to examine passenger-recorded videos and investigate the ferry’s previous accident and repair history as part of a technical inquiry.
Nine suspects, including the captain, first officer, a company employee and several crew members, were ordered held for another three days. Five others, including two port officials, were released pending trial.
The next hearing is scheduled for Thursday, when investigators are expected to present additional statements, documents and other evidence.
Search continues after eight deaths
The Filo Jet capsized while attempting to return to Girne Port after taking on water through its bow shortly after departure.
The ferry was carrying 267 people — 259 passengers and eight crew members. Authorities said 241 people were rescued, eight died and 18 remain missing.
Relatives of some passengers gathered outside the court and protested as the suspects were brought before the judge.
Ustel pledged that any negligence, fault or responsibility uncovered by the investigation would be addressed under the law.

Property downturn worsens with buyer activity 'particularly low'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:23:42 UTC
23:23:42 KST

Property downturn spreads to 93pc of suburbs in Australia's capital cities
Property data firm Cotality has released its monthly national Home Value Index (HVI) showing a 0.9 per cent fall in August.
This marks the fifth straight month that Australian property prices have slipped.
The data also shows the nation's housing downturn has accelerated, as most suburbs recorded weaker auction results in the final month of winter.
The country's median property value is now 3.6 per cent below the record high recorded in March.
Sydney continued to lead the pace of declines, with home values down 1.4 per cent in August to be 7.1 per cent below peak levels recorded in February.
"The combination of a sharp drop in demand and higher than average advertised stock levels are weighing more heavily on Australia's largest housing market,"
Prices in Melbourne and Canberra both fell 1.1 per cent, while Brisbane dropped 1 per cent.
The other mid-sized capitals were not far behind, with Adelaide and Perth home values dropping 0.8 per cent in August.
Trend expected to continue
Independent economist Alan Oster pointed to some large geographical differences across the national housing market.
"If you go to Perth, they're still going at an annualised rate of 20 per cent," Mr Oster said.
"If you're in Sydney and Melbourne, they're sort of going backwards at around 7 to 8 per cent.
"I suspect those sorts of trends will continue for a while."
The national property market has been hit by several headwinds in recent months, including three Reserve Bank interest rate hikes, and the federal government's decision to restrict negative gearing and increase capital gains tax.
Cotality said more expensive houses continue to record larger declines.
Mr Lawless said the latest figures show the downturn was no longer confined to select markets or higher-value segments.
"What started as a more concentrated easing across higher-value segments has now become a much more generalised softening, with the vast majority of capital city suburbs recording some level of decline,"
The proportion of capital city suburbs recording a fall in home values more than doubled through winter, rising from 45.8 per cent in autumn to 93 per cent, highlighting a much broader weakening in housing conditions.
Cotality data shows this weaker phase of the housing downturn has been largely driven by falling demand, with the firm's quarterly estimate of home sales tracking 15.5 per cent lower than at the same time last year and 11.5 per cent below the five-year average.
Brisbane, Perth, and Sydney have recorded the largest declines in transaction activity, with estimated sales volumes down more than 20 per cent compared with a year ago.
Fewer people inspecting houses
Ray White chief economist Nerida Conisbee said "uncertainty" was the dominant theme in the housing market.
The real estate agency tracks about 13,000 open homes each week.
"We can see that buyer activity is particularly low," she said.
"Last year, we were seeing on average around four people attending open homes. This year, it's sitting at around two people."
Ms Conisbee said fewer properties were coming to market.
"Even though buyer activity is slow, it's leading to very few sellers coming out," she said.
"It may sound like bad news, but it does show that we're not really seeing distress amongst owners."
Mr Oster also believed Australia's unemployment rate would climb higher and faster than the Reserve Bank was anticipating.
The RBA has forecast the jobless rate to hit 4.7 per cent by June 2028.
Mr Oster believed it could be approaching 5 per cent a lot sooner than that, and this could see further deterioration in the property market.
"My worst-case scenario would be that unemployment goes a lot higher than we all think," he said.
"Because at present, what's happening is, sure, people aren't confident, but they've still got a job [and] they can cut back their spending, and they can try and get a second job.
"If you suddenly had a problem in the unemployment market, that would escalate everything.
"And so, you don't need to get unemployment back up to 10 per cent or 11 per cent."
He said nowadays a jobless rate of 5 to 6 per cent would "well and truly be a problem".
That is particularly given Australian households are carrying some of the largest debt burdens in the world, with the nation's household debt to income ratio one of the highest in the world.

BANGKOK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's economic growth increased in July on a monthly basis, supported by the global technology and artificial intelligence upswing, easing conflict in the Middle East, and government stimulus measures, the Bank of Thailand said on Monday.
According to the central bank, merchandise exports excluding gold advanced 2.3 percent in July from a month earlier, mainly driven by electronics shipments that also contributed to improved manufacturing production.
However, exports remained heavily reliant on imported inputs, while private investment dipped 0.3 percent month-on-month as machinery and equipment spending cooled after an earlier acceleration, the central bank said in a statement.

Private consumption rose 1.2 percent compared to the preceding month on stronger spending in services, particularly dining, supported by government measures and domestic tourism during a special long holiday, Pranee told a news conference.
She noted that headline inflation dropped from the prior month as energy costs fell on lower imported oil prices and reduced contributions to the state Oil Fuel Fund, though core inflation edged up slightly owing to cost pass-through in processed food and food ingredients.
Looking ahead, the central bank expects the Thai economy to continue recovering, yet the rebound remains uneven, with key drivers including exports and private investment.
Meanwhile, government measures, reduced inflation, and rising labor income are lifting household consumption as agricultural prices and tourism strengthen, the official added. ■

Exclusive: Musk opposes allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russia, despite recent media reports, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:22:02 UTC
23:22:02 KST

Exclusive: Musk opposes allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russia, despite recent media reports, sources say
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk remains opposed to allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes deep inside Russia, despite recent media reports suggesting otherwise, three sources familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
Kyiv has long sought U.S. approval to use the technology to strengthen its campaign against Russia, including to target ballistic missile launchers. President Volodymyr Zelensky raised the issue during a closed-door meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump on July 28, but Ukraine has yet to receive approval.
The Financial Times reported on Aug. 30 that Musk was open to Ukraine using Starlink-equipped drones to strike targets in Russia, but said the decision would ultimately be a political one requiring approval from the White House.
One of the sources said Musk does not believe allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for operations inside Russia would help bring the war to an end.
"Musk wants a deal in this war, not escalation," the source said.
Musk allegedly held talks with former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov that were "extremely unsuccessful," after which the SpaceX CEO became convinced that he did not want to grant Ukraine permission to use Starlink for such operations, the source added.
Ukraine's relationship with Musk has traditionally been entwined with the figure of Fedorov, who had worked with SpaceX to supply Starlink to the Ukrainian military in the first phases of the full-scale war.
Fedorov, who was controversially dismissed from his post in mid-July, initiated talks with Musk over restricting Starlink access for Russian forces operating in Ukrainian territory. After leaving office, Fedorov said on Aug. 7 he was still in talks with Musk, but did not elaborate on the nature of the discussions or what had been achieved.
Fedorov said that restricting access to the terminals is crucial, warning that Starlink access could give Russia "the ability to control operations from Moscow, fly over roads, change flight paths beyond the reach of our radars and acoustic sensors, take out all the F-16s and Patriots, and strike all military targets."
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22 that an alleged miscommunication between Ukraine's Defense Ministry, Musk, and U.S. President Donald Trump failed to secure Starlink access over Russia and also damaged Kyiv's painstakingly recovered relationship with the White House.
Zelensky said he had previously been told by the Defense Ministry that Musk had approved the use of Starlink over Russia and that he only needed to secure the blessing of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Then, after convincing the U.S. president and agreeing on a funding package with EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa, Zelensky learned that Musk had given no such approval.
"He (Trump) said that I kind of tricked him because Musk denied Ukraine the use of Starlink on the territory of Russia," Zelensky said.
"I went back to our defense ministry, and they said that maybe that's how it was indeed."
Despite the setback, Zelensky said that his team, together with members of the Trump administration, has been continuing talks with Musk in the hope of a breakthrough.
"So far, (Elon Musk) has said that this constitutes an escalation," Zelensky said. "However, he may change his mind once he sees further arguments."
"And we have already begun to receive different, more encouraging feedback. We are awaiting relevant meetings and so on. If no one makes a big fuss about this, I think we might see results," Zelensky added.
After the conversation with Fedorov, Musk's representatives said the decision on whether Ukraine should be allowed to use Starlink-equipped drones for strikes inside Russia should be addressed by the Trump administration. However, the administration indicated that SpaceX should decide whether to allow such use, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
Musk's decision in February 2026 to cut off use of the service for Russian forces was crucial to Ukraine's battlefield successes this year.
According to Zelensky, providing Starlink to Ukraine could reduce "precisely those capabilities that Russia is relying on to drag out the war."
On top of allowing flawless high-speed communications between combat positions and command posts, Starlink internet, when mounted on drones, allows for an almost unjammable connection not constrained by the limits of traditional radio antennas.
In 2026, Ukrainian forces have increasingly used Starlink-enabled drones to strike targets in Russian-occupied territory, particularly within the "middle-strike" range of 50-200 kilometers (30-125 miles) from the front line, where Ukrainian attacks have disrupted Russian logistics routes.
The terminals do not, however, work over Russian territory, where Ukraine's ongoing deep strike campaign against Russian military targets, oil infrastructure, and logistics facilities aims to enact strategic offensive pressure on Moscow.
Using Starlink-equipped drones over Russia has also been touted as a potentially effective counter against Russian ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine, by quickly striking the launchers of Russian Iskander and North Korean ballistic missiles when they move out to launch locations.
Ballistic missiles are among the most dangerous threats to Ukraine, as the U.S.-made Patriot is currently the only air defense system in the country's arsenal capable of intercepting them, and Ukrainian forces face a critical shortage of Patriot missiles. Russia launched nearly 70 ballistic missiles at Ukraine in the first 10 days of August, with only one intercepted, according to Ukraine's Air Force.

He said the disinformation spread through networks of accounts “linked to both Russia and Israel, as well as to the far-right international, which always uses the topic of migration to attack not only Spain but also Europe.”
“The reality we’re facing doesn’t mean that a state actor is necessarily behind this. Unfortunately, we don’t have a complete picture of what happened, we’re continuing our investigation, but the government has to rely on verified facts,” the Spanish prime minister said.
Spain’s Supreme Court ruled in early July that migrants detained while trying to swim to Ceuta or Melilla, Spanish exclaves in North Africa, could not be summarily returned. Thousands of migrants entered Ceuta illegally over the following two weeks, and several dozen people died attempting the crossing. Italy threatened to suspend the Schengen Agreement over the crisis, and Spain responded by introducing border controls for travelers arriving from Italy by air and sea.

”The affected vehicles were sold nationwide between May 22, 2026 and June 23, 2026 through Ford franchised dealers and were also exported to Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho and Eswatini.”

It also announced the recall of 507 Toyota Land Cruiser 300 vehicles and 124 Lexus LX600 models because manufacturing debris in the engine could cause the main bearings to fail, potentially resulting in an engine stall while driving.
The commission urged owners of affected vehicles to visit authorised dealerships for inspections and repairs, which would be carried out at no cost.

How China buried Tibet flood images after Nepal disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:19:00 UTC
23:19:00 KST

How China buried Tibet flood images after Nepal disaster
August 31, 2026
When a catastrophic flash flood swept through the rugged China-Nepal border on August 26, the physical devastation was immediate.
In Nepal, a black torrent of mud and rock tore through communities, leaving hundreds dead and thousands more missing along the borderlands.
But across the frontier in Tibet, an autonomous region of China, the physical disaster was almost instantly mirrored by a digital one: the rapid, high-tech erasure of the catastrophe's visual evidence.
As survivors tried to upload raw footage of the deluge, China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action, executing a sophisticated, precision operation to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truths.
The contrasting realities — a tragic humanitarian crisis in Nepal and a tightly sanitized, triumphant rescue narrative in China — reveal the evolving mechanics of Beijing's modern censorship machine.
Rather than imposing a blunt, blanket blackout, authorities deployed advanced image-recognition technology and "saturated information" tactics to drown out domestic scrutiny while deflecting diplomatic friction abroad.
The fall of the 'National Gate'
In the immediate aftermath of the flood-triggered mudslide, local residents captured dramatic footage of the torrent engulfing Gyirong Port, a critical overland trade hub between China and Nepal.
The most striking video showed a black wall of water and debris crashing into and destroying the border crossing's massive "National Gate."
In an article titled "An Unrecorded Mudslide Rushes into Gyirong Port" on WeChat, a universal app that combines messaging with payment options and social media functions, local blogger "Matou Qingnian" described the chaotic scene.
"The most terrifying moment happened at the Gyirong Port," the author wrote, describing video footage of crowds, including children, fleeing in panic before a pitch-black torrent swallowed the camera's view.
Within hours, both the article and the raw video footage vanished from Chinese social media.
According to China Digital Times (CDT), an independent watchdog that tracks Chinese internet censorship, the video of the collapsing "National Gate" was systematically blocked from being shared on WeChat, even in private messages.
"The footage itself contained no graphic violence, no protests, and no political slogans," explained Mira, a CDT editor who specializes in tracking sensitive keywords and media. "The target of the censorship was the symbol itself: the National Gate."
Digital analysts note that this censorship highlights a significant upgrade in China's internet policing tools. Instead of merely filtering text-based keywords, platforms now rely heavily on video fingerprinting, image hashing, and machine-learning models to recognize specific visual scenes.
Once a visual sequence is blacklisted, it is intercepted before it can ever be posted.
Satiety as a shield: the art of 'saturated' censorship
The suppression of the Gyirong Port disaster reflects a broader shift in Beijing's strategy: from mass deletion to "precision surgery" and narrative flooding.
A search for "Tibet mudslide" on Xiaohongshu — China's popular lifestyle and search platform — reveals the mechanics of this "saturated information environment."
Rather than showing an empty search page, the platform's algorithm feeds users a carefully curated stream of state-media reports from China's state broadcaster CCTV and news agency Xinhua.
The visual landscape is dominated by high-resolution, sterile graphics: "before-and-after" comparisons, maps of high-altitude glacial collapses — the official scientific cause of the disaster — and state-approved aerial drone footage.
The raw, chaotic cellphone videos recorded by eyewitnesses at the border are entirely absent.
By filling the digital space with a high volume of "safe" and visually appealing official content, the state satisfies the public's immediate curiosity while preemptively suffocating independent reporting or organic discussions, ananysts note.
On Weibo, China's microblogging giant, the narrative arc was similarly managed. While "Tibet mudslide" briefly trended on August 26, the domestic casualty figures were quickly frozen the next morning at three dead and 558 missing.
Almost immediately, the platform's trending topics were redirected toward the government's swift response.
Two heavily publicized, lengthy official reports dominated the news cycle: Chinese President Xi Jinping convening a Central Politburo meeting to coordinate rescue and relief efforts, and Premier Li Qiang arriving in Gyirong to personally direct operations on the ground.
These headlines effectively turned a major human tragedy into a highly orchestrated exhibition of state competence.
The dangerous 'half-year' question
Beneath the veneer of efficient state rescue efforts lies a deeper, systemic vulnerability that Beijing was desperate to hide: a history of structural negligence.
On August 27, a hashtag briefly slipped through the censors and trended on Weibo: "Gyirong Port Reopened Only Half a Year Ago." It amassed over 347,000 views in less than an hour before it was abruptly deleted. The hashtag pointed to a damning timeline of infrastructure failures.
In July 2025, Gyirong Port was completely shut down after being devastated by another severe flash flood. It took nearly six months to rebuild and reopen the port on January 1, 2026. Eight months later, the port has been destroyed again.
As the deleted "Matou Qingnian" article noted, Gyirong Port has now suffered mudslides during the flood seasons of 2024, 2025, and now 2026. In 2025, several Chinese personnel went missing or were killed.
By erasing the "half-year" trend, censors blocked an inevitable and dangerous train of public inquiry.
If the state-of-the-art border facility was destroyed twice in 14 months, it raises critical questions about site selection, shoddy infrastructure construction, and the complete failure of glacial lake monitoring and early-warning systems in Tibet.
These questions are especially sensitive in Tibet, a region under intense security and political control since the 1950s. Foreign journalists are strictly barred from entering the region outside of highly choreographed government-led tours.
According to human rights groups, local Tibetans who attempt to speak with foreign journalists or share independent accounts online face immediate detention or arrest.
High-altitude friction
The informational firewall does not stop at China's borders; it has also created a diplomatic rift with neighboring Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the disaster's human toll.
Parshuram Kaphle, a prominent Nepalese foreign policy journalist, publicly accused Beijing on X (formerly Twitter) of failing to share critical trans-boundary data.
"Nepal has been addressing the legitimate security concerns of our neighbors," Kaphle wrote in a post that has since been deleted. "However, it must be said with sadness that our northern neighbor has significantly undermined us. By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life."
He further wrote, "We have continually faced crises originating from their territory, while we continue to address all their concerns, necessary or unnecessary. Why must Nepal alone pay the price of one-sided love?"
The Chinese government has rejected any accountability. On August 27, the Chinese Embassy in Nepal issued a statement on Facebook, dismissing accusations of failing to issue warnings or causing the disaster through upstream dam failures as "fake news."
"Accusation helps nothing," the embassy statement read. "Cooperation saves lives."
But for families searching for more than 3,000 missing loved ones along the muddy banks of the Himalayan border, cooperation remains as obscured as the truth behind the digital firewall.
This article was originally published in Chinese.
Edited by: Keith Walker

Finland Cuts Russian War Criminal’s Sentence, Rules Facial Carving Did Not Cause Enough Suffering

Finland Cuts Russian War Criminal’s Sentence, Rules Facial Carving Did Not Cause Enough Suffering
A Finnish appeals court has reduced the life sentence of Russian militant Voislav Torden, also known as Yan Petrovsky, to 12 years and six months after finding him guilty of three war crimes committed against Ukrainian soldiers in 2014.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Helsinki Court of Appeal partially overturned an earlier ruling that had sentenced Torden to life imprisonment for four war crimes, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported on August 31.
One of the charges dismissed on appeal concerned a Rusich symbol carved into the cheek of a Ukrainian soldier with a sharp object. The court found that the wound was superficial, did not bleed, and did not cause sufficiently severe physical or psychological suffering to qualify as a war crime under the charge considered.
Torden served as deputy commander of the Russian paramilitary group Rusich. Much of the case focused on a September 5, 2014 ambush against Ukrainian troops from the Aidar Battalion in the Luhansk region.
Rusich fighters took part in the attack alongside the Batman Battalion and other Russian-backed formations, using a Ukrainian flag during the ambush. Twenty-two Ukrainian soldiers were killed and four were wounded.
According to Yle, the appeals court found that Torden fired a light machine gun at Ukrainian troops and was guilty of a war crime. However, judges said there was insufficient evidence to prove that he or two other Rusich members personally shot wounded Ukrainian soldiers.
The court also ruled that Torden did not bear command responsibility for the shootings, although it found him partially responsible for the deaths and injuries because of his role in the attack.
Other convictions were upheld. The court found that Torden photographed a Rusich commander posing beside the severely burned body of a dead Ukrainian soldier and later distributed the image on social media.
He was also convicted over online statements presenting it as Rusich policy not to take prisoners and to show no mercy.
In setting the 12.5-year sentence, the court considered Torden’s role as Rusich deputy commander, his participation in the deadly ambush, and the use of material from the attack for propaganda. He was also ordered to compensate wounded Ukrainian soldiers and relatives of those killed.
The Helsinki District Court had sentenced Torden to life imprisonment in March 2025. He appealed the verdict, seeking dismissal of the charges or a reduced sentence.
Torden was detained in Finland in 2023. Ukraine later requested his extradition, but Finland’s Supreme Court rejected the request, citing concerns over prison conditions in Ukraine. Rusich has fought alongside Russian forces in Ukraine and has been sanctioned internationally. Torden is also under European Union and US sanctions.
In a separate case, Ukrainian paratrooper Andrii from the 79th Air Assault Brigade told UNITED24 Media that a Russian surgeon burned the words “Glory to Russia” into his stomach with a medical cautery tool while he was held in Russian captivity. Andrii spent more than 14 months in captivity before returning to Ukraine in a May 2025 prisoner exchange.

60 years of Notting Hill Carnival: 10 essential songs chosen by its veterans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:17:03 UTC

60 years of Notting Hill Carnival: 10 essential songs chosen by its veterans
For London's Notting Hill Carnival’s 60th anniversary, Euronews Culture spoke to 10 people who have helped shape, celebrate and document its culture - asking each of them to choose the one track that, for them, captures the spirit of the biggest festival of its kind in Europe.
This weekend, Notting Hill Carnival returns to the streets of west London for its 60th anniversary - six decades since a small community celebration grew into one of the world's biggest street festivals.
Each year the two-day event, culminating on the bank holiday Monday, is a joyous and physical reminder of the enduring influence of Afro-Caribbean culture on London. Its roots lie in the Windrush generation and the sound system culture brought over from Jamaica, against a backdrop of the racial tensions and violence that gripped Notting Hill in the late 1950s.
Following the 1958 race riots and the 1959 murder of Antiguan carpenter Kelso Cochrane by a gang of white men, local social worker Rhaune Laslett organised a children's street party in 1966 in the hopes of bringing the divided community together. And then when Trinidadian steelpan player Russell Henderson and his band took to Portobello Road, the foundations of Carnival were laid.
By the 1970s, sound systems had become central to the festival, with organiser Leslie Palmer introducing more Caribbean masquerade and live music. As he put it himself: "The sound systems were the voice of the youth." Since then the soundtrack of carnival has continually evolved - from calypso, reggae, dub and soca to jungle, drum & bass, hip-hop, grime and UK garage.
So for carnival's big 6-0, we rounded up ten people who've lived and breathed Carnival - from Channel One legend Mikey Dread to Seduction City's Lady Banton, to costume designers and photographers - and tasked them with picking one track that for them epitomises Notting Hill Carnival.
Mikey Dread (Channel One)
Notting Hill Carnival wouldn't be the same without Mikey Dread. He co-founded the illustrious Channel One Sound System and has been behind the decks since 1983. A serious legend. Don't miss him this weekend - he'll be playing out his collection of conscious reggae and exclusive dubplates for all to enjoy on the corner of Westbourne Park Road.
Mikey's track selection - 'Guess Who's Coming To Dinner' - Black Uhuru (1979)
Wayne Crichlow
Crichlow is a London-based documentary photographer who has spent more than 15 years immersed in Notting Hill Carnival. He's recently released Carnival of Resistance, a photobook made with Wayne Campbell, documenting the festival’s sound systems, Mas, dancers, community and spirit of resistance.
Wayne's track selection - 'Warrior Charge' - Aswad (1980)
Linett Kamala
Linett broke into London's sound-system culture as a teenager, becoming one of the first women ever to DJ at Notting Hill Carnival. She's now a Notting Hill Carnival Board Director and has spent decades promoting music, art and making sure the next generation of women get their rightful turn behind the decks.
Linett's track selection - 'Rum & RedBull' - Beenie Man, Future Fambo, Seanizzle
Oxman (Greensleeves HiFi)
The primary host and selector of Greensleeves Hi-Fi, the sound system project carrying the name of one of reggae's most iconic labels. This Carnival weekend he'll be on deck duties with Becca D and YNG CPTN at The Hoxton in Shepherd's Bush.
Oxman's track selection - 'Police and Thieves' - Junior Murvin (1976)
Lady Banton (Seduction City Sound)
A Carnival veteran. Lady Banton is the force behind Seduction City Sound, a Carnival institution she founded over 30 years ago. Seduction City became the first all-female-led sound system at Notting Hill Carnival. Three decades on, she's still behind the decks, and this Sunday she'll be doing what she does best on Telford Road.
Lady Banton's track selection - 'Three Little Birds' - Bob Marley & The Wailers (1977)
Ras Sherby (Channel One)
One of Channel One’s legendary resident MCs. Mikey Dread's trusted right-hand man with more than 20 years experience at Carnival.
Ras' track selection - 'Live In Love' - Ras Sherby (2024)
YNG CPTN
A London-based DJ known for blending reggae, dancehall, Afrobeats, jungle, garage and house. A regular on London’s Carnival and sound system circuit. This Carnival Sunday, he’ll be busy shelling out at both the Notting Hill Arts Club and The Hoxton.
YNG CPTN's track selection - 'Soul Rebel' - Gappy Ranks ft. Nereus Joseph
Helen Davenport
For 27 years, Carnival costumier Helen has been helping make Carnival look as wild, colourful and larger-than-life as it does. She’s also passionate about passing the craft on, running workshops for people of all ages, cultures and abilities.
Helen's track selection - 'Savannah Grass' - Kes (2019)
Jamie Rodigan
West London-born DJ Jamie Rodigan grew up immersed in reggae, thanks in part to his father, legendary broadcaster Sir David “Ram Jam” Rodigan. His sets draw on everything from reggae and dancehall to jungle, garage and house. He'll be bringing the sound to the Notting Hill Arts Club afterparty on Sunday along with YNG CPTN.
Jamie's track selection - 'Promised Land' - Dennis Brown
Roachee
A certified barrer. East London MC and former member of pioneering crew Roll Deep, joining the collective in 2004. A product of the youth-club and pirate-radio scene that birthed grime.
Roachee's track selection - 'Who Am I' - Beenie Man

The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a suspected drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane earlier this month and to outline its response to the incident in coordination with its European and Nato partners.
The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told the public broadcaster ARD in an interview on Sunday evening: “We are in the process of concluding the investigations; we have reached a broad agreement within the federal government on how we will respond, and we will make this clear in the coming days. It won’t take much longer.”
The government has so far declined to say officially who it thinks was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. There has been widespread speculation that it was coordinated by Moscow.
A drone containing explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. The drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate, according to a report last week referencing the investigation.
About 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted.
Days later, a third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen.
This explosive also failed to detonate but according to media reports, the investigators’ report stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”
Moscow has denied involvement.
Merz indicated that the information the government was due to release was being closely communicated with Berlin’s partners, and any response would also be carried out in cooperation with them.
“It will be a response from Germany, but our partners in the European Union and Nato will not be taken by surprise,” he said.
It has been speculated in Berlin that meetings this week of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, could be used to make the announcement.
Last week Merz stopped short of naming a suspect but said: “They will pay for this.” He underscored the necessity for a decisive response due to the lengths he said those behind the Leipzig plot and other acts of sabotage had been prepared to go.
“Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said.
The daily Die Welt and the news website Politico have reported, citing sources, that the government will blame Russia for the attack and that its retaliatory measures are likely to include a new, extensive package of sanctions coordinated with Brussels to hinder it financially, as well as more forceful measures against Russia’s shadow fleet, the Russian ships illegally transporting oil.

The political dimensions of the government’s response are potentially considerable owing to the timing. The naming dispute comes amid an intensifying US-Canada trade war that has seen Washington impose 50% tariffs on key Canadian goods.
Google previously updated its Maps service to show Lake America to users in the US while retaining Lake Ontario for users in Canada. Users outside the two countries see both names as Lake Ontario (Lake America).
In January 2025, shortly after returning to the White House for his second term, Trump also ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal use.
Google Maps subsequently adopted Gulf of America for US users while continuing to show Gulf of Mexico to users in Mexico and displaying both names internationally.

Swedish firm tests unique unmanned hydrofoil craft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:13:14 UTC
23:13:14 KST

- Aston Harald Composite completed the first test flight of its unmanned GhostFoiler hydrofoil vessel in Stockholm last week.
- The demonstrator, built on hydrofoil technology developed at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, will next join NATO's REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal.
A Swedish composites manufacturer just flew a boat that doesn’t touch the water.
Aston Harald Composite completed the first test flight of an unmanned hydrofoil vessel called GhostFoiler in the waters of Stockholm last week, weaving among ferries and recreational boats in the city’s archipelago. The company said the craft performed well for a first attempt, after resolving grounding and shielding issues that came up during setup.
“The first flight is always special,” the company said. “The test went according to plan, after sorting out the usual grounding and shielding issues, and we were soon flying among ferries and recreational boats in the Stockholm archipelago. It flew well!”
Hydrofoils are not new. Boats mounted on underwater wings have existed for more than a century, using the same lift principle that keeps an airplane in the sky, but applied to water instead of air. What makes GhostFoiler different is that nobody is standing on it. The vessel has to sense the water’s surface, its own height above it, and constantly adjust to stay stable, all without a human balancing on deck the way a foilboard rider would. That’s a substantially harder control problem than keeping a hull floating on the water in the conventional way, and it’s the reason foiling drones have lagged behind ordinary drone boats.
The technology GhostFoiler runs on traces back nearly two decades to a student project at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. In 2008, naval architecture professor Jakob Kuttenkeuler led a group of 15 students in building an early electric hydrofoil board called Evolo, widely credited as one of the first electric hydrofoils ever built and an ancestor of the eFoil boards now sold commercially around the world. Kuttenkeuler has continued that research at KTH’s Maritime Robotics group, developing Evolo into an experimental hydrofoiling testbed for autonomous control systems, sensor fusion and navigation. That academic work was spun out commercially under the name EvoloFoil, which built the hydrofoil rig and flight-control system now flying on GhostFoiler.
Aston Harald Composite, a small Swedish composites manufacturer, built the physical vessel itself. The company designed the hull and manufactured its composite structures, including a carbon-fiber catamaran hull, the lightweight, high-strength material more commonly associated with racing sailboats and aircraft than with typical drone boats. Propulsion comes from two 10-kilowatt electric outrunner motors built by another Swedish company, Zparq AB, which Aston Harald described as extraordinarily quiet, a useful trait for a vessel that may eventually be used for reconnaissance or surveillance work.
The demonstrator is now headed to Portugal, where it will operate under the GhostFoiler name as part of Team Sweden at NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise. REPMUS, short for Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping using Maritime Uncrewed Systems, is an annual NATO exercise where allied nations bring uncrewed underwater, surface and aerial systems to test them together in realistic maritime scenarios, making it one of the main venues where early-stage technology like GhostFoiler gets evaluated alongside systems from established defense contractors.

The transporters are seeking a solution to the 90/180-day rule, under which citizens of non-EU countries can stay in the Schengen area for a maximum of 90 days in any 180-day period.

In Podgorica, Transporters Association President Dordije Ljesnjak said the protest was intended to draw attention to the issue ahead of discussions among Schengen countries.

In Skopje, transporters organized by the Makam-Trans association protested outside the EU delegation.
Makam-Trans Secretary General Biljana Muratovska said transporters had been waiting for a solution for seven months and called for the issue to be included on the agenda of the Brussels meeting.
North Macedonia’s Transport Minister Aleksandar Nikolloski said the government was working on bilateral agreements with Schengen countries to address the issue.
He said agreements had already been reached with Switzerland, Croatia and Romania, while talks were planned with Austria, Slovenia and Germany.
Transporters from the four countries have warned that further protests could be held at EU border crossings on Sept. 14 if no solution is reached at the Brussels meeting.
The issue has been under discussion since Western Balkan transporters protested in January over enforcement of Schengen stay rules.
The European Commission subsequently said it would address concerns raised by professional drivers.

Starting school in Estonia: Top tips for supporting your first grader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:12:00 UTC
23:12:00 KST

Starting school in Estonia: Top tips for supporting your first grader
For thousands of kids in Estonia, starting first grade on September 1 also means starting school. One psychologist offers tips to help families navigate this new chapter.
Children in Estonia generally start school at around seven years old, but Viktoriia Tkachuk, a psychologist at the Tartu Rajaleidja Center, explained in a video guide for "Let's Learn Together" that school readiness involves more than just a child knowing their letters and numbers.
Other factors include a child's emotional, social, cognitive, language and physical development, including their ability to focus, follow instructions, communicate and handle everyday tasks independently.
What matters most, Tkachuk said, is a child's overall, well-rounded development. A child who is curious, active, interested in learning, able to community and responsive to rules and requests is generally ready to start school.
"Other skills will develop along the way," she added.
Tkachuk said children should gradually learn to manage everyday tasks themselves, as independence can build confidence and reduce anxiety. Parents can help by involving kids in simple routines such as getting their school things ready in the morning.
The psychologist also advised encouraging a genuine interest in learning rather than drilling children on skills they'll need in school, including writing letters and numbers.
"The most important thing is to spark the child's interest," she said, warning that forced practice can ultimately backfire, leaving them tired and frustrated.
Starting school in a new language
Children starting school in a different language than those spoken at home face an entire extra layer of challenges, which Tkachuk said can leave even capable children feeling anxious, helpless or simply like an outsider.
Practicing communication skills at home can help, however, including learning basic Estonian phrases and roleplaying teacher-and-student situations in Estonian. Families can also make their own "My First 50 Estonian Words" dictionaries, and even watching cartoons and listening to music in Estonian can help.
At the same time, parents should also continue speaking their home language. Tkachuk said parents often worry this could cause their child to mix up languages or struggle to learn another one, but a strong first language can actually help children learn a second one.
"Your native language isn't an obstacle; it's a support," she emphasized.
As new first graders adjust to attending school, parents can help by talking about school positively, maintaining a predictable daily routine and making time each night to discuss how the day went.
"Children are very sensitive to their parents' emotions, and when parents are calm and confident, kids feel that support," Tkachuk said, suggesting encouraging messages like "Your teacher will help you if you have trouble understanding something."
A lot to handle
If a child says they don't want to go to school, she recommends responding with curiosity rather than jumping straight to arguing. Kids starting school have to navigate new relationships, social skills and a much bigger workload, all while adults can sometimes forget just how young they still really are.
Above all, the psychologist stressed, parents should avoid comparing them with others, as all children are different.
"Talk with your kid about their day," she said. "Ask what surprised them today, and who they played with at recess. Hold space for all their emotions."
If something has put your child off of school, ask what happened or what exactly they don't like.
"Let them be sad, angry or tired, and support them without criticism," Tkachuk said, stressing the importance of maintaining home as a safe environment for your child to be themselves. "Remind them that mistakes are normal and that we're all learning."
When it comes to homework, parents should support their child without taking over. They can explain instructions and check work together, but should let their child solve problems themselves, and praise effort rather than just results.
"Kids can quickly lose motivation when they feel there's no point in trying because their parent can just do it better anyway," Tkachuk explained.
A child refusing to do their homework should also be taken as a sign — and an opportunity to talk to them.
"Tell them, 'I can see this is hard for you,'" she suggested. "'Let's figure out together what to do. Do as much as you can; it doesn't have to be perfect.'"
Helping kids make friends
Social skills develop through practice, Tkachuk said, and simply playing with other children provides valuable opportunities to learn how to communicate, resolve conflicts and cooperate.
"It can also help to talk through social situations together," she said. "If your child has a conflict with someone, talk about what happened without judging. Ask what they think about why the other kid acted the way they did, or how things could have gone differently."
Families should also talk to their kids about how various classmates may speak different languages at home and may need extra time to feel comfortable.
"They may avoid talking to other children even if they really want to because they are afraid of making linguistic mistakes," the psychologist explained.
"But sometimes," she added, "just one friend is all it takes for a child who speaks a different language to feel more comfortable in a new environment."
Ask for help too
While adjusting to starting school can take several months, if your child continues to struggle, Tkachuk said it's worth seeking extra help.
"You can reach out to a psychologist, as well as contact a Rajaleidja center for educational advice and support," she said, adding that families can also talk to their child's teachers or school specialists.
"School is a big step toward independence, but the journey should be shared by the child, their parents and their teachers," Tkachuk said. "You are not alone in this process."
"Let's Learn Together" is a new online resource offering families practical guidance on navigating education in Estonia, from how the kindergarten and school system works to information on what additional help and resources are available.
Available in English, Estonian, Russian and Ukrainian, the site features articles, personal stories, podcasts and videos in which parents, young people and experts share their experiences with adapting to multilingual and multicultural life and education in Estonia.
All "Let's Learn Together" video guides include subtitle options on YouTube.

Russia doesn’t need a military economy, it’s a ‘complete breakdown of the system,’ says former Finance Minister Mikhail Zadornov
Russia’s economy “doesn’t need” to become a military one, and doing so is “impossible,” Mikhail Zadornov — Russia’s finance minister from 1997 to 1999 and later head of Otkritie Bank — told the Russian business news outlet RBC.
A military economy in Russia, he said, “is pure fantasy.”
A military economy would mean a complete breakdown of the system currently in place: it requires its own institutions and different rules of the game, which would have to be enshrined in dozens and hundreds of pieces of legislation. It requires trained personnel who follow these rules at every level, and it requires enforcement mechanisms, since no military economy can exist without them. That is why it is impossible to declare the introduction of a military economy overnight on January 1 or March 1: it takes years to build.
Dismantling the current system, Zadornov said, would trigger an economic downturn — something he called “extremely unwise” in wartime.
The former minister said Russia’s market economy, “despite all its particularities,” has weathered previous crises and “adapted to fairly serious external and internal shocks.” As evidence, he pointed to federal budget spending and inflation data from the years of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
Let me give one figure as an example: federal budget spending this year rose 75% in nominal terms compared to 2022, while cumulative inflation from 2022 to 2026 came to 30%. This shows that our economy is not only capable of growing, but also of financing military spending that has increased roughly 3.5 times over that period. In other words, it is meeting all its objectives.
Debate over shifting Russia’s economy “onto a war footing” has resurfaced over the past month. Andrei Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma’s defense committee — the lower house of Russia’s parliament — said that amid intensifying Ukrainian strikes on Russia, the country needs to move to a military economy and begin “normal military operations.” Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said shifting the economy onto a war footing would kill the country, calling the very discussions of such a shift “worthless” and “unnecessary.”
At the same time, VEB.RF, the Russian state development corporation, fired its chief economist, Andrey Klepach, over his “personal harsh assessments” of Russia’s economic and political development. In one speech, Klepach said Russia is headed toward economic decline and a social crisis.
