Australia risks missing out on AI economic boom due to 'slow' uptake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:36:44 UTC
21:36:44 KST

Australia risks missing out on AI economic boom due to 'slow' business uptake, Treasury says
In short:
Treasury says Australia risks missing out on the economic benefits of AI unless businesses go beyond basic use of the technology and make bigger changes to how they operate.
Fewer than one in 10 businesses report significant AI adoption, while officials say the feared jobs shock has not yet materialised.
What's next?
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says he is confident Australia can capture the economic upsides and avoid the downsides of AI.
Australia will miss the economic benefits of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom unless businesses actually use the technology to make bigger changes, Treasury has warned.
New advice provided to Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Australia's current AI uptake was widespread but shallow, with less than 10 per cent of businesses reporting "significant" adoption.
The Treasury note said much-feared job losses have not yet materialised, but officials are watching young and entry-level workers overseas for early signs.
Officials described AI as the first "credible" accelerant of global economic growth in almost two decades, but found Australia was at risk of failing to capture the benefits of the technology.
Mr Chalmers said AI was shaping up to be the "biggest economic transformation in our lifetime" and he was confident Australia could "maximise the economic upside and minimise the risks".
"Advances in AI are coming thick and fast, with frontier labs reaching new milestones in a matter of weeks, not years,"
"We can't just sit around and hope the benefits of AI fall into our lap. We have to reach out and take them."
Less than one in 10 businesses report 'significant' AI adoption
Treasury said the "rate and breadth" of AI take up in Australian companies "remains slow".
"Around two-thirds of Australian businesses report some AI adoption, [but] less than 10 per cent report significant adoption," the department's note said.
Finance, insurance, information, telecommunication and professional services sectors have had the "highest" rates of AI adoption, but Treasury said access alone would not deliver economic gains.
"Realising productivity gains requires investment in organisational capital, including changes to processes, business models, management practices and workforce skills," the note said.
Additionally, there are large parts of Australia's economy, like health, education, construction and tourism, which are considered much harder to transform with AI.
Treasury said the mass AI jobs wipe-out many feared has not materialised in Australia so far, with most studies finding "limited impacts" on the labour market to date.
Officials are specifically watching young and new workers overseas for the earliest signs of AI displacing people form their jobs.
Enterprize Tasmania chief executive Brian Collins, who leads a group that supports start-ups in the state, said small businesses found it hard to know where to start with introducing AI.
"It's a confidence gap more than it is a skills gap … often times it's that people may think that AI is for big companies or that it's going to cost a lot of money and it's not for a five-person business,"
"Most small businesses don't have a dedicated tech person, so if you want to adopt AI then it's competing with all the other day-to-day operations the owner of a business is needing to balance.
"There's also hundreds and hundreds of AI products … so there's no clear starting point and that creates paralysis rather than creating action."
Judo Bank economic advisor Warren Hogan said government could do more to support businesses to make the AI transition.
The bank specialises in small businesses.
"We risk getting the worst of AI that is the displacement without the best, which is the broader productivity lift and the full employment and the much better economic outcomes that the next five to 10 years offers," he said.
"I think we are on the cusp of the biggest lift in living standards we have seen in a generation and we cannot miss that opportunity."
AI has potential to boost Australia's productivity
The advent of AI has given Treasury "confidence" that its long-run economic growth assumption of 1.2 per cent remains "achievable" for Australia.
Recent weak productivity had sparked questions about the feasibility of the country returning to that 30-year historic average rate of improvement.
To tackle Australia's broader productivity issues, Treasury said AI alone was not a "substitute for structural reform".
The Treasury note considered 1.5 to 2 per cent productivity growth a plausible upside, and between 0.5 and 0.8 per cent a realistic downside.
Even the optimistic scenario does not envisage an overnight AI boom in Australia, while the downside could be the result of the country simply failing to make enough use of the technology.
Data centre investment boom already here
Treasury said the AI investment boom was already boosting economic growth before the promised productivity gains from the technology completely arrive.
Globally, private AI investment totalled almost half a trillion Australian dollars in 2025, which was an increase of about 128 per cent over the year.
Australia's own data centre construction boom is expected to be worth about $150 billion by 2030.
There were about 162 operational data centres in the country as of March, with a further 130 proposed.
Treasury said about two-thirds of the expenditure on data centres goes toward imports meaning the money ultimately flows out of Australia.
A construction boom would still benefit Australian workers and companies, though Treasury said there would be increased competition for resources like labour, concrete, copper and electrical equipment.
Officials likened it to the mining boom with the exception that it was less obvious what Australia would ultimately sell the world in return.
Geopolitics was identified as a major risk for Australia, which remains heavily reliant on overseas technology.
Australia joins AI meetings in US
The federal government is alive to those concerns, with Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles on Monday travelling to San Francisco ahead of meetings with tech giants Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google and Amazon, as well as computer chip manufacturer NVIDIA.
"We're working closely with the US to support Australia's national interests and national security, in areas such as defence and emerging technologies, like artificial intelligence," Mr Marles said.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton is also attending, and has flagged discussions on Australia's expectations for companies to invest in ways that "help build local innovation and capability".
Mr Charlton will then go to North Carolina for a ministerial-level G20 meeting focused on innovation, AI skills and workforce.

“Oct. 1 would mark a new day in Iraq’s statehood,” Al-Zaidi said during a meeting with US Central Command Commander Gen. Brad Cooper, adding that Iraq would be free of any foreign military presence.
The two sides affirmed their agreement to end the coalition’s military mission, while Iraqi-US relations would shift toward economic and security cooperation based on mutual respect for sovereignty and shared interests.
The US-led international coalition was established in 2014 to fight Daesh/ISIS after the terrorist group seized large areas of Iraq and neighboring Syria.
Iraq declared military victory over ISIS in December 2017 after retaking territory held by the terrorist group, while coalition forces remained in the country in an advisory and training role at Baghdad’s request.

Italian shopping baskets containing
food staples have risen in price by almost a third over the last
five years, Il Sole 24 Ore business paper reported Monday.
                                    
                                       
				The 29.5% gain is a rate far higher than the inflation rate
recorded in the same period (21%), with peaks in the prices of
vegetables (+39% for those most commonly used in cooking),
coffee (+51%), and extra virgin olive oil (+47%).
                                    
                                       
				This is according to a survey by Sole24ore, which found that
tomatoes, one of the most commonly consumed products, cost 45%
more, potatoes 44%, and eggplants 41%.
                                    
                                       
				The Sole24ore basket is limited to 31 products, indicative of
the weekly spending of a couple with one child.
                                    
                                       
				Between 2021 and 2026, the price of this shopping basket went
from 100 to 129.5 euros, an increase in line with food inflation
calculated by national stats agency Istat in the same period
(30%) but higher than general inflation (21%).
                                    
                                       
				For fruit, the increase recorded by Istat is 28.6% while for
Sole24ore it is 14% because it only includes apples and bananas,
the most purchased fruits, while the prices of strawberries
(+48%), lemons (+37%) and oranges (+31%) are especially
increasing.
                                    
                                       
				Il Sole24ore further reports that inflation is also affecting
breakfast, with milk prices rising by 21% and yogurt, snacks,
and biscuits by 27%.
                                    
                                       
				The prices of some essential daily items, such as eggs (+43%),
rice (+44%), bread (+28%), and tomato puree (+26%), are also
rising above the general inflation average, as are the average
prices of pasta (+24%) and canned tuna (+25%).
                                    
                                       
				According to the survey by the Confindustria daily, the
percentage of families reporting they have reduced the quantity
or quality of products purchased has also increased, rising to
31% in 2024 compared to 24.3% in 2021.
                                    
                                       
				The price increase for beef over five years is 31%, for chicken
33.7%, and for cooked ham just 21.5%, essentially in line with
general inflation over the period.
                                    
                                       
				The smallest increase among the 31 products analyzed by Il
Sole24ore was for table wine, which rose by just 1.8%, well
below the general inflation average.
                                    
                                       
				According to Il Sole 24 Ore's survey, not only shopping cart
prices have increased during this period, but also those of
other frequent expenses, such as a coffee at the bar (from an
average of €1.07 to €1.30, +21%), a sandwich at the bar (+21%),
and haircuts (+14% for women's haircuts, +11% for men's
haircuts).

Freed Hongkonger sent back to jail as storm delays deportation from Philippines
Lawyer says Tang Lung-wai’s return to maximum-security prison constitutes ‘illegal detention’ after severe weather halts deportation
A Hong Kong man has been returned to a Philippine prison in what his legal team condemned as “illegal detention”, after severe weather halted his deportation following his release.
Tang Lung-wai’s Philippine lawyer, Blessie Rose Carpena, told the South China Morning Post that prison authorities escorted Tang to the Bureau of Immigration last Friday.
However, because government offices were suspended due to a passing typhoon, he was returned to the maximum-security New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa.
“[The Bureau of Immigration’s] delay of his release can constitute illegal detention,” Carpena said, describing Tang as “frustrated and devastated.”
Tang was arrested in the Philippines in July 2000 for possessing methamphetamine, also known as ice, and sentenced to 40 years in prison in 2011. He has maintained his innocence and fought the conviction for more than two decades.
In late July, a Manila court ruled that Tang’s sentence was fully served after factoring in good conduct time allowances, ordering his immediate release and deportation.

FACTBOX: What to know about Eastern Economic Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:30:01 UTC
21:30:01 KST

TASS FACTBOX. Vladivostok will host the 11th Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) from September 1 to 4. Its main theme for 2026 is "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." The TASS Factbox editorial team has compiled background information on the forum.
Key Information
The Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) is one of Russia's largest international conferences. It has been held annually since 2015 on Russky Island (Vladivostok, Primorsky Region) at the Far Eastern Federal University, in accordance with a decree by Russian President Vladimir Putin dated May 19, 2015. The forum was canceled only once, in 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The event aims to accelerate the economic development of the Russian Far East, provide expert assessments of its potential, and expand international cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region, including with ASEAN. It also serves to promote and showcase the investment attractiveness of the region, its Advanced Development Territories (ADTs), and the Free Port of Vladivostok. A large number of agreements are traditionally signed at the EEF. Since 2018, at least 3 trillion rubles ($35 bln) worth of deals have been done each year, with a record set in 2025: 358 agreements worth a combined 6.058 trillion rubles ($71 bln).
Organization and Partners
Preparations for the EEF are overseen by an organizing committee chaired by Yury Trutnev, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister and Presidential Plenipotentiary Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District. The forum's operator in 2015 was the non-profit Eastern Economic Forum Foundation; since 2016, the Roscongress Foundation has served in the role.
The EEF's title partners for 2026 are the A7 Russian international payment system and VEB.RF. The forum's general sponsors and partners for 2026 include VTB, Gazprom, RusHydro, and the Elga coal company, with Aeroflot serving as the official carrier. TASS is the general media partner of the EEF.
Guests: Top Officials
Russian President Vladimir Putin has attended the EEF every year since its inception in 2015. High-ranking foreign officials have participated in the forum since 2016, with a total of 13 heads of state and government from nine foreign countries attending over the years. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe did not miss a single EEF between 2016 and 2019. Representatives of the Republic of Korea attended the event twice: Presidents Park Geun-hye and Moon Jae-in in 2016 and 2017, respectively. In 2019 and 2024, the forum received Malaysian Prime Ministers Mahathir Mohamad and Anwar Ibrahim. Mongolian President Khaltmaagiin Battulga participated in 2017, 2018, and 2019, while the country's Prime Ministers, Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene and Gombojavyn Zandanshatar, attended in 2022 and 2025, respectively. The forum was also attended once by Chinese President Xi Jinping (2018), Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (2019), Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (2022), Myanmar Prime Minister Min Aung Hlaing (2022), and Lao Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone (2025).
EEF 2026
The program of the 11th EEF includes over 70 business events, featuring panel sessions, roundtables, and business dialogues. The program is divided into five main thematic blocks:
· Living and Working in the Far East;
· Mechanisms for Attracting Private Investment;
· The Far East: A Pole of International Interaction (including business dialogues featuring Russia-China, Russia-India, Russia-ASEAN, and others);
· Technologies of the Present and Future;
· Logistics and Infrastructure for Economic Growth.
Business events will also take place as part of the traditional "Far East Street" cultural project. In addition, the EEF will feature the Creative Industries Forum, the "Day of the Future" youth forum, the International Falcon Day Forum (September 1), the Small and Medium Entrepreneurship Forum, the APEC International Conference on Cooperation in Higher Education, and the conference titled "Crossroads of Civilizations: The Role of Transport Integration in the History of the Asia-Pacific Region." According to the Roscongress Foundation press service, representatives from 80 countries have confirmed their participation in the 2026 forum.
Sports and Cultural Programs
The Eastern Economic Forum is traditionally accompanied by a rich cultural and sports program.The 2026 lineup includes the Roscongress Chess Cup, the EEF Open Water Swimming Cup, international table tennis and mass-wrestling tournaments, and the 5th International Vladivostok Regatta. Football joined the sports program for the first time on August 28, 2026, with a gala match featuring legends of the Spartak Moscow football club.
As part of the cultural program, the Primorsky Stage of the Mariinsky Theatre will host a concert by pianist Denis Matsuev, accompanied by the Russian National Youth Symphony Orchestra.
The "Far Eastern Seasons" Arts Festival will showcase the culture of the indigenous peoples of the Far East, with its gala concert also taking place on the Primorsky Stage of the Mariinsky Theatre. Meanwhile, the Primorsky State Art Gallery will host the grand opening of the exhibition "Russian Impressionism: The Element of Color."
On September 2, a free concert titled "The Soul of Russia: A Language Understood by All" will be held at the Square of the Fighters for Soviet Power in Vladivostok, featuring popular performers from Russia and China.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan hold first Mecca Defense Agreement meeting as more countries eye joining pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:29:24 UTC
21:29:24 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan hold first Mecca Defense Agreement meeting as more countries eye joining pact
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan hold first Mecca Defense Agreement meeting as more countries eye joining pact
Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said over the weekend in the UK that six to seven Muslim-majority countries have expressed interest in joining the pact
Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan gathered in Istanbul on Monday for the inaugural meeting of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed August 7. Ahead of the meeting, Pakistan said several countries have already shown interest in joining the defense pact.
Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said over the weekend in the UK that six to seven Muslim-majority countries have expressed interest in joining the pact, without naming them, adding that officials are working on a framework to make accession easier. Bangladesh has been the latest country to signal openness to joining. At the same time, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said earlier this month the pact could expand to include other regional states, like Egypt.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all, similar to NATO's Article 5 collective defense clause.
Following the meeting, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described the Mecca Defense Agreement as complementary to NATO rather than a rival framework. "The Mecca Alliance is a historic step based on the principle of defense and complementing NATO," Fidan said. "We have taken practical steps to build a practical security structure in the region, and we are working on a roadmap for other countries to join the alliance."
Fidan also directed sharp criticism at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of prolonging regional conflict. "This criminal, Netanyahu, who takes pleasure in shedding Palestinian blood and Muslim blood, must now be stopped," Fidan said, adding that Netanyahu's approach was causing "immense harm to Israel, to Palestine, and to the entire region."
The Turkish Foreign Minister also said Netanyahu's statements made clear he opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state and does not intend to relinquish "ongoing occupations in countries across the region," calling it evidence Netanyahu wants a "genocidal and occupying approach" to continue. "This is no longer a threat only to us; it is a major threat to the entire region and to the international community," Fidan said, calling on "the international system" to confront what he described as the threat posed by Netanyahu.
Suggested articles
The agreement brings together three Sunni Muslim US allies concerned by the ongoing Iran war and the broader regional conflict, which has included Iranian missile fire on Gulf oil exporters. Six months into the war, negotiations remain at an impasse, and the Trump administration has escalated financial pressure on Tehran through what it has called an "economic D-Day."
Turkey, which fields NATO's second-largest military, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia is open to further expansion and is not intended to replace existing alliances. President Trump praised the agreement, calling it a bold first step that allows nations to defend themselves.

Germany: Sven Schulze takes on the far-right AfD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:28:00 UTC
21:28:00 KST

Germany: Sven Schulze takes on the far-right AfD
August 31, 2026
"It's far from decided." State Premier Sven Schulze likes to repeat his big campaign message over and over again ahead of the impending election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. His audience, however, rarely responds with enthusiasm.
The German public and international media alike are watching this election closely. Never before has the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed right-wing extremist" — had a better chance to take over a state government. The party is polling at over 40% compared to Schulze's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at around 23%.
Schulze is hoping the AfD will stay below 50% and so be unable to secure a majority in the state parliament — and, with no other party willing to join it in a coalition, the AfD would be unable to form a government. That would leave it up to Schulze to form a coalition, perhaps with as many as three partners, and remain in office. "We are fighting for every single voter right now," he told DW on August 7.
Young, family man, engineer, cyclist
Schulze was just 11-years-old at the time of German reunification. Now, at 47, the qualified industrial engineer and father of three is the youngest of Germany's 16 state premiers.
He only took over leadership of the state at the end of January, when his predecessor, Reiner Haseloff — then aged 71 — retired after nearly 15 years in office. The early handover to Schulze was supposed to improve the younger man's prospects in the state election. After all, a sitting premier is said to enjoy an "incumbency bonus."
Schulze is now touring the state of two million inhabitants. On some days, he has been seen out and about on his bicycle, complete with cycling jersey and helmet, handing out ice cream on hot summer days, and engaging in small group discussions. Aware that his party leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is not exactly popular in Germany right now, one of his recurring messages has been that he is not there "to sell the Berlin government's ideas to Saxony-Anhalt." Instead, he says, his task is "to bring issues from Saxony-Anhalt to Berlin." Not everyone in Merz's government is necessarily pleased about this message.
Celebrities welcome, the chancellor not so much
This became particularly evident when Schulze appeared at campaign events in the state's larger cities alongside Dieter Hallervorden — an actor and comedian who is a household name in Germany, and who was born in Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt nearly 91 years ago.
Hallervorden, not previously known as a CDU supporter, has now joined Schulze on stage during the election campaign four times. The venues were packed, and the events easily ranked among the best-attended of Schulze's campaign. The comedian showed no compunctions about criticizing the federal government's defense and arms export policies. During one of his musical performances, an image of protesters bearing a banner with the slogan "Stop the genocide in Gaza" was briefly visible in the background.
Schulze calmly rejected sharp criticism of this from his party's headquarters in Berlin. He maintained that he did not share, and even rejected some of Hallervorden's views, but had shared the stage with him to demonstrate his commitment to freedom of speech. The AfD, Schulze noted, seeks to abolish freedom of speech, while he does not.
A threat to German culture
Dessau is known around the world as being one of the homes of the Bauhaus movement, which propelled art and architecture into the modern era starting in 1919. The Nazis sought to stifle the movement when they took power in 1933.
Now, 90 years later, some members of the AfD have again been directly echoing the Nazis' language about the famous movement: In a speech to the state parliament last year, AfD representative Hans Thomas Tillschneider described Bauhaus as a "wrong track of modernism" — a direct quote from the 1928 book "Art and Rac"e by architecture critic Paul Schultze-Naumburg, who influenced Nazi thought.
Schulze has accused the AfD of wanting to return to Germany's past eras of oppression, and sought to tie the far-right party to East Germany's communist dictatorship. "When the AfD sings the GDR anthem at the end of its party events, it shows exactly what it wants: a return to the days of the GDR," Schulze told DW. "And I do not want us to wall ourselves in again, as happened here before. That is not what the people want."
Running a local campaign
At campaign events, Schulze attempts to shift the focus away from federal or global political issues and toward the situation within the state of Saxony-Anhalt. He often cites local businesses that rely on foreign employees and on exports to worldwide markets. Regarding healthcare and care for the elderly, he warns against simply adopting, without debate, the recommendations of a commission appointed by the federal government. That again directly contravened Merz's message, who said that those recommendations, which some say contain several cuts to public services, should and would be followed to the letter.
Much Schulze remains undeterred, and has vowed to keep discussing the issues that matter to the people of Saxony-Anhalt. "I trust the people here," he said. He says he is counting on the people of Saxony-Anhalt to stand up against having their state "turned upside down." Sometimes, he says the election boils down to "Sven Schulze or the AfD."
This article has been translated from German.

Israel and Greece sign US$3.5 billion defence deal, largest ever between the 2

Israel and Greece sign US$3.5 billion defence deal, largest ever between the 2
Buyers favouring Israel's battle-tested weapons have helped push its defence exports to record highs
Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece, the largest between the two Mediterranean countries, as Israeli defence exports soar.
Israel’s Defence Ministry said on Monday the nearly €3 billion (US$3.5 billion) defence export deal, coined Achilles Shield, was one of the country’s largest and included a multilayered air defence system for Greece using Israeli technology.
“Israel and Greece share common strategic interests and face shared regional challenges. At a time when actors with hegemonic ambitions are seeking to expand their influence and undermine stability in the region,” said Defence Minister Israel Katz.
The agreement comes as Israeli weapons exports have reached record highs with more than US$19 billion last year, a 30 per cent increase from 2024, according to official data, despite widespread criticism of Israel’s conduct in its wars in Gaza, with Hezbollah and with Iran.
Experts say governments look to Israel because its weapons are battle-tested and they are able to see in real time that the munitions and systems work.
Israel and Greece have deepened defence ties in the last decade. Monday’s signing, however, marks the most significant deal between the two as Greece focuses on modernising its armed forces to keep pace with its neighbour and fellow Nato member Turkey amid long-standing disputes over sea boundaries in the eastern Mediterranean.

Rehabilitation and support for a child in the first years of life: what services can be received free of charge
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:26:23 EEST
21:26:23 KST

Rehabilitation and support for a child in the first years of life: what services can be received free of charge
Kyiv • UNN
Prematurely born and ill infants can receive rehabilitation free of charge under the Medical Guarantees Programme. Services are available until the age of three with a referral.
For children born prematurely, as well as children with congenital conditions, the state has provided the opportunity to receive free rehabilitation tailored to individual needs, UNN writes.
Rehabilitation for young patients is paid for by the state under the Medical Guarantees Programme. Rehabilitation care may be provided on an outpatient or inpatient basis and/or at the child’s place of residence. Services can be received regardless of the child’s place of registration or residence, the National Health Service of Ukraine explains.
According to the NHSU, in 2026, under the package "Medical rehabilitation of infants born prematurely and/or ill during the first three years of life," 13.39 thousand patients across Ukraine received medical care.
What the infant rehabilitation package provides for
Care begins with an initial examination and consultations with specialists from a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team. According to the NHSU, a comprehensive functional assessment is carried out using international standardised scales, tests and questionnaires; the child’s development is assessed and, where necessary, screening is conducted to identify signs of autism spectrum disorders.
Based on the assessment results, an individual rehabilitation plan is developed, defining goals for the child and the family. The team subsequently regularly assesses progress and, in accordance with changes in the child’s functional status, adjusts the plan and determines the further rehabilitation pathway.
The package includes the necessary laboratory and instrumental examinations, in accordance with medical needs and sectoral standards. The child may also receive consultations with doctors of other specialties, depending on their condition and diagnosis; pain assessment and timely pain relief when indicated; as well as assessment of nutritional status and its correction in case of disorders.
Rehabilitation also includes support for parents
Services are provided by specialists from a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team. Depending on the child’s needs, the care team may include doctors of physical and rehabilitation medicine, paediatricians, paediatric neurologists, physical therapists, occupational therapists, psychologists, speech and language therapists, nurses and other specialists.
An important part of the care is working with the family. Parents are provided with information about the specifics of caring for the child, the child’s development, preventing possible complications and following the rehabilitation team’s recommendations. Psychological support for parents is also provided.
If necessary, specialists select and adjust assistive rehabilitation devices and teach the family how to use them in the child’s natural environment. If the child requires specialised medical care at another facility, the team arranges the appropriate referral.
How to receive care
The basis for receiving services under this package is a referral from a primary care doctor selected under a declaration, a referral from the attending physician, or a transfer from another healthcare facility.
Services under the package are free of charge for the patient, provided they are received at a facility that has the relevant contract with the NHSU.
For example, as UNN reported, such services are provided at the Kyiv Perinatal Centre. Since 2020, specialised early-intervention spaces have operated at this facility, where infants receive qualified care from the first days of life. Follow-up monitoring and medical rehabilitation for infants are also provided there. As the Kyiv Perinatal Centre told UNN, during the past year alone, 279 infants successfully completed individual rehabilitation programmes.

Regional geopolitical shifts felt as Mecca Alliance, Israel-Greek pacts develop - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:25:54 UTC
21:25:54 KST

The first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee, established under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, began in Istanbul on Monday. It comes as Israel and Greece also signed a multi-billion-dollar defense deal.
The two events happening on the same day are a coincidence, because both have been in the works for some time.
However, it is symbolic of how the Middle East is being reshaped.
The October 7 attack was meant to change the region. Iran and Hamas plotted to carry out a massive war against Israel. Hamas launched the opening shot of the multi-front war.
The attack came after several years of relative peace in the region. After the defeat of ISIS, the region had been working toward stability and integration. The Abraham Accords were part of this process, bringing together Israel, the UAE, and Bahrain.
Hopes of Saudi Arabia joining Abraham Accords dashed as national alliances shift
This was expected to be part of a larger process that would include India, the US, and other countries. Greece-Israel-Cyprus relations were also growing stronger, along with other developments in the Eastern Mediterranean.
However, high hopes that Saudi Arabia might join the Abraham Accords have now shifted. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Syria, and other countries are growing closer together.
Where relations between Ankara and Cairo were once more negative, things have now shifted. Israel, meanwhile, has not shown flexibility on the Palestinian issue, and Israel has taken a hostile attitude toward the new government in Syria.
The result is that Jerusalem now views the emerging Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan alliance as a potential threat.
Other processes the underway. Israel’s work with US Central Command has increased. US-Israel strikes on Iran have brought the US and Israel closer together. Iran’s attacks on the Gulf, particularly threats to US bases, have led the US to move a large number of refueling aircraft to Israel.
This has led to speculation that the US may move bases away from the Gulf. Israel could benefit by becoming a base for US forces.
This would knit together the Israel-CENTCOM relationship even more than in the past.
It is only in the last half-decade that Israel has officially become part of CENTCOM's area of operations. This is owed to an anomaly where Israel was seen as part of Europe, because many countries in the region didn’t have peace with Israel in the past.
Now, with peace with Egypt, Jordan, the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco, there are more reasons for Israel to be linked to regional security.
What happened in Turkey on Monday, August 31
Reports say that Ankara “is hosting the inaugural meeting of the committee, which was established to provide strategic direction for activities under the agreement and brings together the foreign ministers, defense ministers and chiefs of general staff of Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia,” according to Turkey’s Anadolu.
“The meeting began with the participation of Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, National Defense Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu; Pakistani Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar, Federal Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff Gen. Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili,” the report said.
The goal is to work on “interoperability among the three countries’ armed forces, deepening defense industry cooperation, including joint production and research and development, and strengthening joint efforts to combat terrorism.”
The report notes that “the agreement stipulates that an attack against any one of the signatory states will be considered an attack against all parties. It also seeks to foster a new culture of regional cooperation and remains open to the participation of actors that respect international law and share a vision of peaceful cooperation.”
Meanwhile, in Israel, Israel’s Minister of Defense, Israel Katz, said, “My visit to Greece a few months ago, as the guest of Greek Defense Minister Dendias, was another expression of the depth of the strategic relationship between Israel and Greece and of our shared determination to keep strengthening it.”
His statement came as Israel and Greece signed the new defense deal.
Katz discussed his earlier meetings in Greece: “In that meeting, we agreed to deepen defense cooperation between our two countries. Israel and Greece share common strategic interests, and face shared regional challenges. At a time when actors with hegemonic ambitions are seeking to expand their influence and undermine stability in the region, Israel and Greece will continue to deepen their defense and strategic cooperation, and will act with determination to preserve stability and safeguard their security and shared interests.”
Israeli air defense systems key to Greek defenses
Greece’s Minister of National Defense Nikos Dendias also put out a statement on the Shield of Achilles defense concept that Greece is developing.
The Israeli air defense systems are key to this.
“The 'Achilles Shield’ is an important link in the reform of the Armed Forces and an imperative response to the geopolitical and technological challenges of our time. It is part of the ‘Agenda 2030’ reform, with which our Homeland is moving into a new reality. In a new concept of Defense and Deterrence,” Denias said.
He added that the Achilles Shield “marks the transition from a sum of weapons systems to a holistic deterrence system. Ships, aircraft, land assets, autonomous systems, new satellites, and more generally, every platform equipped with sensors, are integrated into a single network-centric architecture.”
This will enable 4th and 5th generation aircraft to play a “broader deterrent role,” he said. Satellites and communications will be key to this.
“Greece has acquired a fleet of microsatellites and is preparing for its first large geostationary satellite,” he said. Greece’s defense industry will also be strengthened. “The goal is clear: for Greece not to remain a passive buyer and user of defense systems. To actively participate in their design, production and development, strengthening domestic know-how,” he said.
In Tel Aviv, the head of the International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT) at the Israel Ministry of Defense (IMOD), Brig.-Gen. (res.) Yair Kulas added that “The 'Achilles Shield' deal is another milestone in the defense relationship between Israel and Greece. It reflects the deep trust our partners in Greece place in Israeli technology, the defense industry, and the government-to-government cooperation model led by the Israeli Ministry of Defense through SIBAT.”
Taken together, the story of the defense deal with Greece and the meeting in Istanbul are examples of how the region is changing.
While some may see these two events as symbolic of rivalry, they don’t have to be. The Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan alliance is built in the wake of the chaos of the Iran war. Iran has been attacking countries across the region, as it did with attacks on Jordan and the UAE overnight.
Countries need to work together toward stability. This is a lesson a decade after the war on ISIS and also after the fall of the Assad regime. The region needs stability and integration. The Israel-Greece deal bolsters key countries in the Eastern Mediterranean.
As such, it also adds to stability. This is part of the broader trend reshaping the region in the wake of decades of war and chaos that began with the Gulf War in 1991.
These are signposts of the new world order that has emerged decades after the collapse of the Soviet Union, as the world once again becomes more multipolar and regional or middle powers step up their cooperation.

Hezbollah shifts to guerrilla warfare, drone strikes as terror group  prepares for prolonged war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:24:57 UTC
21:24:57 KST

Hezbollah has continued to invest in its recovery and adapt its strategy for what it anticipates could be a prolonged, low-intensity war with Israel, according to the latest assessment by the Alma Research and Education Center, published on Sunday.
Based on incidents recorded over the past several months, the center assessed that Hezbollah could increasingly turn toward guerrilla warfare, including small-scale infiltrations into the security zone and potentially Israeli territory, as well as drone and explosive attacks.
The group’s ability to carry out its previous plans to seize the Galilee has been significantly diminished by the destruction of its infrastructure and the continued presence of the IDF in southern Lebanon, the center assessed. However, Hezbollah is still likely to attempt to operate within the security zone.
Given the limited scope of such operations, Hezbollah infiltration attempts would likely be thwarted, according to the center. However, the attempts themselves could indicate that the group is seeking to identify vulnerabilities that could later be exploited.
The center noted that, given Hezbollah’s extensive underground infrastructure and the area’s dense terrain, operatives could still be hiding within the security zone. Some may be cut off from their command networks, but their continued presence could still pose a threat to IDF personnel through planted explosives or other attacks.
Hezbollah continues to operate above and underground
The IDF has encountered several individual Hezbollah operatives in the area over the past several months, which the center said supports the possibility of a continued Hezbollah presence.
Hezbollah’s underground and above-ground infrastructure, often embedded in civilian areas, is also frequently booby-trapped, making the task of locating and destroying these networks particularly dangerous.
A shortage of skilled operators is preventing Hezbollah from fully utilizing its arsenal of first-person-view (FPV) drones, low-cost unmanned aerial vehicles with a range of up to 60 kilometers that have been used in recent months to target Iron Dome batteries and other Israeli assets and personnel. The shortage of trained operators, however, has not prevented Hezbollah from making FPV and other drones core components of its strategy, according to the center. Hezbollah has also increased the pace at which it is training operatives to use the technology.
Estimated 15,000 rockets, 40,000 active operatives
Though Hezbollah appears to be moving away from the use of precision-guided missiles, cruise missiles and shore-to-sea missiles due to their assessed poor cost-benefit ratio, the center estimated that the group could still possess as many as 15,000 rockets. Alma further estimated that Hezbollah has fewer than 40,000 regular operatives remaining, while retaining tens of thousands of reservists.
At the same time, efforts to reduce Iranian influence in Lebanon have not succeeded in completely removing the IRGC’s presence, according to Alma. The center claimed that members of the IRGC’s Quds Force Lebanon Corps continue to operate in Beirut and the Beqaa Valley.
Iran has also continued to smuggle resources to Hezbollah, though it has been forced to become more creative in its attempts since the fall of the Assad regime, the center continued. Last month, Iran allegedly attempted to send weapons to Hezbollah in a fuel truck through the al-Tanf crossing.
The center claimed that its research had identified smuggling attempts on a near-weekly basis, though it remains unclear how many of these attempts are successful. Syria, it reported, continues to serve as a logistical area for the transfer of weapons to Lebanon.

Israel intensifies military incursions into southern Syria

On Sunday evening, Israeli forces targeted the area around Tal al-Ahmar in Quneitra province with three artillery shells.
The strikes came hours after Israeli forces entered the village of Al-Samdaniya al-Gharbiya in the governorate's central countryside with four military vehicles.
The incursion coincided with the establishment of a temporary checkpoint in the village of Al-Ajraf, where Israeli forces searched passers-by. It followed earlier bulldozing operations near a checkpoint in Tal al-Hawa, a strategic geographical area and hill located directly south of Jubata al-Khashab in the northern countryside of Quneitra.
Israeli forces also entered the area with two tanks, according to the Sijil Center, a Syria-based monitoring and human rights organisation specialising in documenting and reporting Israeli military operations and alleged violations inside Syrian territory.
Fadi Al-Asma'i, the editor-in-chief of the Golan Media Foundation, told The New Arab that Israeli forces have stepped up their incursions and military movements across southern Syria, including in Quneitra province, western Daraa province and the town of Beit Jinn in the Damascus countryside.
He said that, amid reported negotiations over a security agreement between Israel and the Syrian government mediated by the United States, Israel is putting pressure on local communities in Syria.
According to Al-Asma'i, this is intended to send a message to Damascus that Israel will not relinquish Jabal al-Sheikh, also known as Mount Hermon, the Golan Heights which were occupied in 1967, and other areas seized after the Assad regime's downfall in December 2024.
"I believe that if Israel leaves the buffer zone once an agreement is reached, it will try to stay in the hills, including the eastern hill of Ahmar," al-Asma'i said.
Israel claims to be pursuing agents of the Lebanese Hezbollah group in the area, but al-Asma'i said that reports of a Hezbollah presence are "baseless and false". He added that Hezbollah members had left the area and could not have remained there following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.
Al-Asma'i said the Israeli claims were intended to secure further security gains for Israel, while serving the political interests of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's forthcoming elections.
He said Netanyahu was seeking to reassure his supporters that he would prevent another October 7-style attack in the occupied Golan, similar to the events in Gaza, presenting Israel's occupation as a deterrent against such a scenario.
Israel is seeking to keep the buffer zone around the occupied Golan in a state of tension, according to journalist Samer Al-Miqdad, who told The New Arab that Israel has used "incorrect and unrealistic pretexts" to justify its actions.
Al-Miqdad said Israeli forces have also carried out near-daily abductions of farmers in the area, sometimes releasing them on the same day.
This comes as Syrian rights monitors report that Israeli military forces have carried out at least 1,004 incursions into southern Syria since rebels led by current Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa overthrew the regime of former dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
The Israeli army has expanded the scope of its operations in the last year, conducting search and abduction campaigns, reinforcing its troops and bulldozing agricultural land.
Nearly 460 Israeli incursions into Syria were recorded last year, while 530 incidents have been recorded since the beginning of this year.
Despite ongoing Israeli attacks, there has been a reported meeting between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani and Israeli Mossad chief Roman Gofman in Jordan, raising further questions about the possibility of reviving Syria-Israel negotiations after months of deadlock and escalating tensions on the ground.
The meeting was mediated by the United States and hosted by Jordan, with security and military officials from both sides taking part, according to Syrian government sources.

Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a briefing that there remained a "high probability" that Russia’s adversaries abroad would stage extremist and protest actions to discredit the State Duma elections.
Voting in State Duma elections in unfriendly countries could be accompanied by various provocations and attempts to discredit the electoral process, Russian Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova said.
Extremist organizations and foreign agents are preparing to conduct fake voter polls abroad, near Russian embassies, on September 20 in order to claim in Western media that State Duma elections were rigged even before they end, Vasily Piskaryov, chairman of the State Duma commission investigating foreign interference in Russia’s internal affairs, said.
State Duma elections
Elections to the ninth State Duma will take place in Russia in the fall of 2026.
Voting will take place from September 18 to 20.
Residents of Donbass and Novorossiya will take part in State Duma elections for the first time.
Elections to legislative assemblies will be held in 39 regions, while senior regional officials will be elected in seven regions by direct vote and in three others by regional parliaments.
About 23,000 seats will be filled in total.

Ministers consider closing social mobility watchdog as part of planned shake-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:23:02 UTC
21:23:02 KST

Ministers are considering a shake-up of the government’s social mobility watchdog that could range from giving it more teeth to abolishing it outright.
The move comes amid concerns that the Social Mobility Commission (SMC) – originally conceived under Gordon Brown’s government in 2010 – has become ineffective.
Bridget Phillipson, the equalities minister, and others are said to feel strongly that work to improve social mobility – and thus the life chances of poorer children and families – should be a core function of government rather than being outsourced to arm’s lengths bodies such as the SMC.
It is understood to be within the scope of a Cabinet Office review of such bodies and was considered for closure last year on the basis that central government could carry out its limited functions more effectively.
The commission has no powers to determine government policy, hold public bodies to account or make recommendations to ministers. Instead, its sole statutory responsibility is to produce an annual state of the nation report on social mobility in the UK, which evaluates opportunities and inequalities.
However, while the SMC was conceived as the Child Poverty Commission by the previous Labour government in 2010, those in the Burnham government believe its focus on child poverty was diluted under the coalition government and subsequent Tory administrations. “It has essentially become a thinktank inside government,” said a source.
It was renamed the Child Poverty and Social Mobility Commission in 2012, before becoming the SMC in 2016, when Iain Duncan Smith scrapped then legally binding child poverty targets.
  Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister now leading a review into the million young people who are Neet (not in education, employment or training), was appointed chair but resigned in 2017, saying government was “unable to devote the necessary energy and focus to the social mobility agenda”.
A year later, a report from the education select committee made a series of recommendations to give the SMC “real teeth”, all of which were rejected by the then children’s minister, Nadhim Zahawi.
A Whitehall source said: “Reducing inequality and supporting working-class communities is at the heart of this government’s agenda. Tracking progress will always be important, but ultimately this is work that should be a core function of government.
 “We’re looking at all the options to make sure we’re really set-up to deliver the change people want to see in their lives as quickly and effectively as possible.”
Any changes would be expected to be announced over the course of this parliamentary term, but new legislation would be needed to disband an organisation set out in statute.
The body is chaired by Alun Francis, who is also the chief executive of Blackpool and The Fylde college, alongside two deputy chairs and four commissioners. They are supported by a secretariat of about 20 civil servants working in the Cabinet Office.
The SMC’s most recent state of the nation report said former industrial communities across Britain face “entrenched disadvantages” stretching back decades and highlighted “extreme regional differences”, citing poorer childhood conditions, fewer job opportunities, less innovation and lack of growth.
The report said Yorkshire, the north-east, the Midlands, Wales and Scotland were still living with the impacts of deindustrialisation, describing “half a century of economic disadvantage and decline”.
Burnham, who has previously rejected what he characterised as Westminster’s fixed view of social mobility, has prioritised local devolution, technical education and housing policy at the heart of his vision of social mobility.
Phillipson, the former eduction secretary and now Labour party chair whose equalities brief includes sponsorship of the SMC, has also consistently spoken about social mobility, drawing on her own experience as a child of a working-class family in England’s north-east.

Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:22:53 UTC
21:22:53 KST

Senior Reform UK figures like to boast that the summer time – and parliament’s longest recess – is when the party makes hay.
Supposedly, it is when Nigel Farage and co can muscle in on the news cycle with provocative statements and new policies, painting “establishment” opponents as workshy layabouts.
Last year’s summer break came with an added opportunity, which the rightwing populist party eagerly grasped, in the form of protests against hotels housing asylum seekers. As Labour and the Tories tempered their language, Farage eagerly weighed in, warning of the prospect of “civil disobedience on a vast scale”.
Yet as August comes to an end, and with Reform preparing for its annual conference in Birmingham later this week, the party might look back on summer 2026 as a damp squib, or worse.
While almost weekly Reform press conferences have taken place and new policies have been rolled out – Robert Jenrick has been particularly busy with promises to slash the benefits bill and scrap supposed “red tape” for businesses – there has been no repeat of last summer’s unrest in England, aside from disturbances in the Norfolk market town of Thetford.
There have also been missteps of Reform’s own making, not least the hint of internal divisions related to the noisy pronouncements of its home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf. Farage was eventually forced to reprimand him for calling Ben Wallace, a former Conservative defence secretary and veteran, a “traitor”.
Divisions also surfaced around the suspension of Tim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives.
However, perhaps the biggest error was Farage’s decision to spark a byelection in Clacton in an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over questions about an undeclared £5m payment by the Reform megadonor Christopher Harborne. Farage himself scaled back press events amid scrutiny after the payment was first revealed by the Guardian.
Though he cruised to victory over his closest challenger – Count Binface – the need to get the vote out meant Farage was pinned down in a corner of Essex for six weeks, rather than being free to roam the UK at will and entice media coverage in a way his lieutenants fail to.
The prospect of a “people versus the establishment” battle which Farage so clearly craved did not materialise when other main parties ignored the contest, while a parliamentary standards investigation into the payment has once again started after it was only paused during the byelection.
Opponents have taken note.
“You could say that Reform are quite good at tactics but bad at strategy, and with Clacton he made a strategic mistake because it bound him to one part of the country for six weeks,” said Giles Dilnot, the editor of ConservativeHome and a former political adviser who covered Farage for years for the BBC.
“He made that decision in anger and you never make good strategic decisions when you are angry. Then he had to take a break because of the understandable toll the byelection and all that went before it this year would have taken.”
Dilnot suggested two other issues that will have caused worries in Reform ranks. First, despite Reform consistently attacking the Tories, signs of a knockout blow do not seem to have materialised. Second, the centralised way in which Farage has always run his political projects may now be taking a toll.
“Over the 15 years it’s always the case he is both the biggest asset and biggest weakness of any party he has led. Everything is centralised, he falls out with people and voters can also be very polarised,” said Dilnot.
Recent polls have indicated that the surge in support for Reform has stalled, with the party failing to break out beyond core supporters and signs that Farage himself might even be a drag on its further growth.
A poll released last week by More in Common put the party at 23% – four percentage points behind Labour and Reform’s worst performance in 18 months. Labour also now leads Reform for the first time since the general election in Ipsos polling – 28% to 25%.
Nearly two-thirds of the public (65%) do not believe Farage is ready to be prime minister, according to Ipsos, while nearly three-quarters backed continuing the standards investigation even before the Clacton result.
Aside from struggling to shake off questions about the £5m, there was yet another reminder last week of another drag – namely Reform having to look over its shoulder at the siren call to its voters from Rupert Lowe’s hard-right Restore Britain party.
The latter was a factor in a much-watched byelection last Thursday on Dover district council, where Reform had swept the board during Kent local elections last year, but where Farage’s party was narrowly pipped by the Greens after Restore polled 10%.
Nonsense, say Reform sources, pointing to new policies and attention-grabbing moves by councils such as Kent, which announced plans to “protect” communities from immigrants.
“We’re coming out of this summer with a plethora of policies, our councils are getting on with it and at conference there will be more headlines, a proper fringe discussing ideas and a business engagement programme which is a major step up from last year,” said one.
Reform says it will use the conference at the Birmingham NEC to set out the first 100 days of what a government led by it would do. One of the biggest questions will be whether any dissent emerges.

Who are the world’s most polite tourists? These nationalities have the best travel manners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:22:13 UTC
21:22:13 KST

A new survey reveals which nationalities are the best behaved, biggest tippers, biggest spenders, most adventurous and most passionate about food.
Good manners can go a long way when you’re travelling, and according to a new survey, some tourists have them down to a fine art.
Japanese travellers have been named the world’s politest tourists, with Norway and Switzerland following behind, while other nationalities picked up the top spots for everything from generous tipping to adventurous holiday habits and a love of local food.
A new survey from safaribookings.com, an online marketplace for African safaris, asked 192 of its tour operators the following five questions: Which nationality is the politest? Which nationality tips the best? Which nationality spends the most money while travelling? Which nationality is the most active and adventurous? Which nationality is the biggest foodie?
The results make for very interesting reading – here’s what they revealed.
The most polite tourists
Japan came out on top in the ranking of the most polite tourists worldwide, with 21.1% of mentions from tour operators.
Tourists from Norway and Switzerland followed behind, with 10.6% and 10.4% respectively, and Canadian and American travellers were next.
In last place in the list were Italian tourists, with just 1.3% of the survey respondents rating them the politest nationality in the world.
Nevertheless, European travellers were praised by those who were surveyed, with one tour operator from Imara Tours Zanzibar saying: “Many of our European guests are very interested in wildlife behaviour and often ask detailed questions about animals and conservation. Their curiosity makes game drives very engaging.”
The best tippers and biggest spenders
The US is known for its divisive tipping culture, so it’s little surprise that Americans were identified as the best tippers among all tourists. In fact, they had 29.5% of all mentions from tour operators, which was far ahead of all other nationalities.
Tourists from Germany, Canada, and Switzerland were also found to be decent tippers, scooping 13.1%, 10% and 8.6% in the ranking, respectively.
When it comes to the biggest spenders, Americans also topped the list. They got 24% in the ranking and were, again, followed by travellers from Germany and Canada who got 12.8% apiece.
The most adventurous tourists and biggest foodies
With regards to the most adventurous tourists, the top three places in the ranking are taken up by travellers from European nations.
Germans were the most adventure-seeking travellers, with 21.1% in the ranking, followed by the French with 17.8% and the Dutch, who got 11%.
At the other end of the scale, the British and Indians both got just 4.5%, while the Spanish only achieved 4.3%, suggesting that those nations are a little more likely to want to put their feet up while on holiday.
The top five of tourists who travel to eat were mostly made up of Asian nations, with India, Japan and China in first, second and fourth place respectively.
France was in third place, with 12.4%, and the Netherlands was in fifth, with 7.7%, just 0.1% above Italy in sixth.

EU expected to lobby allies to give Patriot interceptors to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:20:38 UTC
21:20:38 KST

Ukraine is running out of Patriot interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and other airborne threats. The EU executive is expected to put pressure on Mediterranean nations, like Greece and Spain, to give theirs up at a defence meeting on Tuesday.
European countries that still hold significant stocks of interceptor missiles are expected to face pressure from the European Commission to transfer them to Ukraine, as Kyiv’s need for air-defence systems grows increasingly urgent, EU officials told Euronews.
Spain and Greece, in particular, are expected to come under pressure at a defence meeting on Tuesday in County Wicklow, Ireland, to provide some of their stocks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late August that deliveries of Patriot interceptors had declined even as Russian missile attacks on Ukraine intensified. He said Kyiv needs an estimated 300 interceptors to fend off what is already shaping up to be a bitter winter battling another year of Russia's full-scale invasion.
The war with Iran has forced the US to draw heavily on its own Patriot reserves, shrinking the pool of interceptors available to replenish allies — including Ukraine — at precisely the moment Kyiv needs more.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier this year Madrid pledged to donate five Patriot missiles to Ukraine amid the shortage. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Athens has “resisted” pressure to transfer any of its six Patriot batteries to the war-torn nation in the past. He argued they are critical for defending the country’s own airspace.
One EU diplomat speaking to Euronews on condition of anonymity, due to the sensitivity of the matter, said the issue of Madrid and Athens keeping a tight grip on their Patriot interceptors is not new. But the issue is gaining pace with Zelenskyy voicing louder requests for interceptors, with the air defence system proving to be the “debate of the summer”, they said.
The European External Action Service (EEAS), the EU's diplomatic arm, is currently speaking with Japan and South Korea to convince them to share some of their stocks with Ukraine.
However, diplomats are wary that potential tensions with China are due to limit how much the two Asian countries are willing to share. Greece may also be reluctant to draw down its stockpile amid rising tensions with Turkey in recent months.
Three EU diplomats agreed that Ukraine’s shortage of Patriot interceptors is a “big issue” with broader questions about how to fill the gap. “What this will look like, I am not sure,” one EU diplomat said, adding that Tuesday's meeting is informal and therefore not expected to produce any formal conclusions.
The effectiveness of Europe’s own defences, particularly in the wake of a series of hybrid threats, is also expected to be a key focus of the talks.
Moldova, an EU candidate country, was recently rocked by a series of drone incursions. Five unmanned aerial vehicles entered the country’s airspace on 27 August, with the president Maia Sandu offering a defiant statement in response.
The meeting comes after media reports also reveal the director of the CIA, John Ratcliffe, embarked on a secret trip to Moscow.
In the wake of the visit, which reportedly centred on warning the Kremlin against any form of aggression towards Baltic nations, various leaders from the region have insisted their threat assessments of a Russian attack on Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania remains the same.
The former president of Estonia, Toomas Hendrik Ilves, went so far as to tell Euronews he is sceptical that Ratcliffe was dispatched to warn Russia against escalation. He argued that Washington remains more concerned about Iran.
Meanwhile, one European Commission official revealed to Euronews that Kyiv is mulling whether to use the next funding envelope of the €90 billion support loan to purchase anti-ballistic systems, which could either be Patriots or the Franco-Italian version, the SAMP/T NG system.
To find other ways of plugging Ukraine’s anti-ballistic gap, the EU executive recently rubber-stamped a €6.1 billion defence procurement to supply the country with air and missile defence systems, missiles, ammunition and radars.

EU subjects ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox to stricter oversight under Digital Services Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:19:12 UTC
21:19:12 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
The European Commission on Monday designated ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox as very large digital services under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA), subjecting them to additional obligations and oversight.
ChatGPT was designated as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE), while Reddit and Roblox were designated as Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs), the Commission said.
The three services reported at least 45 million average monthly users each in the EU, meeting the threshold for the designations.
The services will have four months, until the end of December 2026, to comply with the additional DSA obligations.
These include assessing and mitigating systemic risks linked to the dissemination of illegal content, effects on minors, users’ physical and mental well-being, fundamental rights, electoral processes and public security.
The Commission said the designations give it investigative powers to assess the services’ functionalities and, where applicable, related systems.
The Commission will supervise compliance with the DSA in cooperation with Ireland’s Coimisiun na Mean in the case of ChatGPT and Reddit, and the Netherlands’ Authority for Consumers and Markets in the case of Roblox.
“These new designations mean that ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the European Union, in line with their large impact on our citizens and society,” Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s executive vice president for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said.
“We continue to watch the digital landscape closely and will not hesitate to designate any platform that meets the threshold for enhanced supervision under the Digital Services Act,” she added.
The Commission said ChatGPT qualifies as an online search engine under the DSA because it can respond to users’ prompts and queries, including by searching the web.
Reddit is a discussion-based platform where users create, share and interact with content in topic-based communities, while Roblox allows users to create, publish and play games developed by other users.
The Commission said Reddit and Roblox qualify as online platforms because they enable users to disseminate third-party content to the public.
The three services are already subject to the DSA’s general obligations for online platforms and search engines.
With the latest designations, the Commission has designated 28 very large online platforms and search engines under the DSA.
DSA supervision and enforcement are shared between the European Commission and national Digital Services Coordinators responsible for enforcement in EU member states.

Beyond profit: Why Dutch firms want impact-driven leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:17:35 UTC
21:17:35 KST

Partner content
Beyond profit: Why Dutch firms want impact-driven leaders
The Netherlands is fast becoming a testing ground for business that treats social and environmental impact as a measure of success. Its universities are adapting too: Nyenrode Business University runs an English-language Impact MBA, taught in Amsterdam and Breukelen, that builds sustainability into leadership training rather than setting it apart as a separate subject.
On April 8, 2026, the Netherlands’ National Coordinator for Sustainable Development Goals, Anna Pot, was handed a copy of the recently hashed out Impact Agenda 2030 at the Social Enterprise Government Congress in Nijmegen.
Described by the collaborative coalition of social entrepreneurs, foundations, municipal leaders, knowledge institutions and civil society initiatives that participated in its making as a “national framework for a future-proof and resilient economy”, the Impact Agenda aims to move the Dutch economy towards a system that has social and environmental metrics embedded in its core – not merely as an afterthought after profits are tallied.
“Impact is not a niche, it is a necessity,” is the message the Dutch Impact Ecosystem says it’s sending to national leaders. “And it has real economic value – for impact-driven organisations and traditional businesses alike.”
The agenda – which focusses on such themes as impact governance, procurement and finance, social and digital innovation and education and is in line with the European Commission’s Social Economy Action Plan – is just the latest national accomplishment that cements the Netherlands’ standing as a world leader in the move to sustainability and societal impact in its business sectors.
A recent report looking at how firms balance profit with impact found that of the 77 large companies the private-public consortium surveyed doing business in the Netherlands, the majority believe the initial regulatory hassles of the EU’s CSRD [Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive] are overshadowed by its long-term benefits, all while helping their businesses.
The report found that “Dutch companies are leading the way in integrating impact governance into their strategies.”
Learning laboratory
The country’s strong collaborations between businesses, government and knowledge institutions create an environment of innovation and entrepreneurship that has led professionals worldwide to increasingly choose the Netherlands to learn how businesses can create both commercial success and positive societal change.
In the Netherlands’ dynamic Dutch business ecosystem, leaders have the opportunity to put theory into practice.
New leaders
Driven by European sustainability regulations, evolving investor expectations, rapid technological developments such as AI and growing stakeholder expectations, companies today are looking for leaders who can navigate complexity rather than optimize a single bottom line.
And the country’s universities and knowledge institutions are keeping pace. Nyenrode Business University, with locations in Amsterdam and Breukelen, offers an English-language MBA program focused on creating the future leaders of this brave new business world.
Its Impact MBA was designed as a response to changing employer needs rather than as a traditional MBA program. Instead of teaching sustainability as a standalone subject, the curriculum integrates leadership, digital transformation and sustainability throughout the learning experience.
“Sustainability transitions involve long-term developments with significant short-term implications for organizations,” says Prof. Dr. Nicolas Chevrollier, Professor of Sustainability Transitions and designer of the Impact MBA. “This requires new competences, new collaborations and sometimes entirely new business models.”
Chevrollier emphasises that organizations cannot solve today’s challenges independently. Businesses increasingly operate within ecosystems involving governments, knowledge institutions, investors and civil society, meaning effective leadership depends on building partnerships rather than optimising organisations in isolation.
“Many organisations suffer from tunnel vision,” he says. “To truly innovate, leaders need to broaden their perspective.”
The Impact MBA gives tomorrow’s leaders a chance to do just that: innovation and a systems-thinking approach are embedded in its curriculum, creating business trailblazers who can balance financial and societal objectives while thinking across entire systems instead of just individual organizations.
Are you looking to develop the new capabilities needed for the profound transformations taking place in today’s business world? Then check out Nyenrode ‘s Impact MBA, available both part-time and full-time, or join one of their on-campus and online events to discover more.

Nearly all Wang Fuk Court owners accept buy-out, leaving 17 holdouts as offer ends
17 of 1,984 Wang Fuk Court owners fail to accept offer as deadline ends, facing compulsory acquisition at lower compensation levels
More than 99 per cent of homeowners at Hong Kong’s fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court have accepted a government buy-out of their flats, leaving just 17 households facing potential compulsory acquisition after the scheme closed on Monday.
By the cut‑off time at 5pm on Monday, 1,967 or 99.1 per cent of the estate’s 1,984 flat owners had returned acceptance letters. The remaining 17 may face compulsory acquisition at lower compensation levels in the future.
Among those who accepted, 1,559, or 78.6 per cent, have signed formal sale and purchase agreements with the government.
“The government will continue to follow up on the procedures for acquiring the remaining titles at full speed to take forward the title acquisition exercise” it said on Monday.
The HK$6.8 billion (US$867.24 million) scheme was announced in February after a fire tore through seven blocks of the Tai Po estate last November, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 residents in Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze in more than seven decades.
In June, the government extended the buy-back offer to Wang Chi House, the only block spared by the fire, adding another HK$1 billion to the scheme’s cost. Officials have ruled out on‑site redevelopment.
Under the scheme, the government is acquiring flats at HK$8,000 or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the owner has paid the land premium.

Coalition budget talks still deadlocked with hours to go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:11:17 UTC
21:11:17 KST

Coalition budget talks still deadlocked with hours to go
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Plans to cut more than €6 billion from social security and to change the way savings and investments are taxed are in the balance, as the three coalition parties struggle to agree next year’s budget among themselves with only hours to go before it is due for review.
D66, the VVD and the CDA negotiated through the whole of Sunday and into the early hours of Monday without reaching a deal, and are still talking on Monday afternoon. The meeting at which the full cabinet has to sign off the budget, first scheduled for 11am, has been put back twice and is now set for 6pm.
Until last week, the main question was whether the minority coalition could win enough opposition votes to pass the budget. Prime minister Rob Jetten ended those talks on Friday, saying the plans would go to parliament without a majority.
That has left the coalition parties to settle the budget between themselves, and they remain divided. Jetten acknowledged on Friday that the three parties still disagree fundamentally on some key points.
What they are arguing over
 Broadcaster NOS reported that two issues are holding up a deal: the box 3 tax and the planned social security cuts.
Box 3 is the tax on income from savings and investments, which the government has been trying to reform for years. The coalition’s spending plans also include cutting more than €6 billion from social security – the benefits paid to people who are unemployed, older or too ill to work.
The largest opposition party, the left-wing PRO, has made scrapping that cut a condition of its support and wants wealthy households taxed more instead. Led by Jesse Klaver, PRO already won a concession from the government this year, when it dropped a plan to raise the retirement age more quickly.
D66 and the CDA want to avoid tilting the budget too far to the right, so as to keep PRO within reach. The VVD is wary of concessions to the left that could sour its relations with the far-right JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.
The coalition could pass the budget through the lower house with JA21 and SGP support, but that combination would leave it well short in the senate, where PRO’s backing offers the more realistic route to a majority.
The draft is due at the Council of State, which reviews the plans before they are presented on Prinsjesdag on September 15.
