====================================================================================================

Why Food Keeps Making Everybody Sick This Summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

This summer, every meal feels like a risk.
Just as the US is recovering from a major cyclospora outbreak stemming from tainted iceberg lettuce, salmonella has turned up in jalapeños, eggs, and even dog food. The jalapeño-related outbreak is now responsible for at least 431 illnesses and 57 hospitalizations in more than two dozen states. Meanwhile, a dual-pathogen outbreak of E. coli and salmonella linked to alfalfa sprouts has affected 55 people across 15 states.
But is it just your overactive imagination that these outbreaks are worse than normal?
To answer that, WIRED tallied up publicly available numbers from the Food and Drug Administration’s investigations of foodborne illnesses. The agency has identified more than 12,800 illnesses tied to foodborne outbreaks in 2026, already far surpassing the number it has identified in any year since 2020. For comparison, there were 895 cases related to foodborne outbreaks last year.
Experts say the summer of sickness is the result of chronic underfunding in food safety systems, gaps in federal food policy, and recent cuts to the country’s public health infrastructure by President Donald Trump’s administration.
“What is happening this summer just demonstrates to me the vulnerabilities in the system—and what happens when you stress the system,” says Barbara Kowalcyk, director of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition.
To understand how this summer became so swamped with foodborne illnesses, one needs to understand the scale of the cyclospora outbreak, which “was absolutely unprecedented,” says Jennifer McEntire, a food microbiologist and founder of the consulting firm Food Safety Strategy.
The FDA’s numbers, drawn from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s case count, establish this cyclospora outbreak as the largest the agency has investigated in the US since the 1990s. Yet even this figure undercounts how many people actually got sick, according to the CDC’s own calculations.
The FDA’s figures only count illnesses directly linked to a specific outbreak under investigation. So far, about 67 percent of the CDC’s 17,180 laboratory-confirmed cases in the US have been linked to Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce; the rest are linked to other outbreaks or one-off infections, which require a full-blown FDA investigation. On top of that, the CDC is aware of at least 11,844 additional cases that have either not been confirmed by a lab test or require further analysis for other reasons.
Previously, cyclospora infections were rare compared to other common foodborne bugs like salmonella and E. coli. The previously obscure pathogen typically causes a few hundred to a few thousand illnesses a year in the US. Because it is—or at least was—relatively uncommon, cyclospora isn’t included in standard panels that test for several types of gastrointestinal disease. That can mask the true size of an outbreak, on top of the many people who may have gotten diarrhea from the parasite but decided not to go to the doctor.
Cyclospora is also particularly tricky to get rid of, with its tendency to lodge itself into the crevices and folds of leafy greens, herbs, and berries. These foods are typically eaten raw, and food sanitizers aren’t effective at removing the parasite because it forms a tough, protective outer shell.
But the quirks of a parasite cannot fully explain the scale of the outbreak. Last October, WIRED reported that the CDC had reduced its staff through layoffs and buyouts by about 3,000 employees—roughly a quarter of the workforce—since Trump’s second term began. That includes people who worked in a lab that responded to cyclospora outbreaks. According to the team’s former leader, molecular parasitologist Joel Barratt, the lab’s staff was cut from 11 people to just three.
Fewer staff to handle outbreaks is compounded by the nation’s health agencies lacking leadership at the highest levels. The CDC was without a dedicated director for nearly a year, until the Senate voted in early August to confirm Erica Schwartz to the role. The FDA, meanwhile, has not had a permanent commissioner since Marty Makary resigned in May.
In 2025, the Trump administration cut roughly $12 billion in grants for state health departments, which are the first to respond to outbreaks of foodborne illness. In Michigan, the loss of these funds meant 23 fewer infectious disease workers and 123 fewer county health staff, Reuters reported in late July. Health department employees told Reuters they’ve had to pull staff from other areas—and still didn’t have the resources to investigate the thousands of cyclospora cases in the state that’s been at the center of the outbreak.
Putting new food safety policies in place could help prevent large outbreaks, but a traceability rule issued by the FDA in 2022 has yet to be implemented. The rule requires businesses that manufacture, process, pack, or hold leafy greens and other high-risk foods to maintain more detailed recordkeeping. In November, Congress voted to delay implementation of the rule until July 20, 2028. A coalition of food safety and consumer health groups sent a letter to Congress earlier this month urging members to reconsider the delay, saying the rule “would facilitate faster and more effective investigations.”
Even with the new rule, though, outbreaks like the one tied to Taylor Farms lettuce imported from Mexico would be hard to track due to a loophole. De Ann Davis, senior vice president of science at the Western Growers Association, which represents farmers in Arizona, California, Colorado, and New Mexico, says the rule does not apply to importers, brokers, or trading companies that coordinate the movement of food but do not physically possess or handle it.
“In other words, the food can come in without anybody checking that it actually has the necessary traceability information,” she says. “The importer is the one who has to make sure that the food is compliant with those regulations, but they're not subject to the regulations.”
That makes tracing foodborne illness outbreaks tied to foreign products difficult, especially if the original supplier isn’t keeping detailed records. “We are relying on those foreign countries to be informed about the regulations of the US, but they are not subject to the regulations of the US,” Davis says.
There are also lapses in food safety inspections that predate the Trump administration. A January 2025 report from the US Government Accountability Office found that the FDA conducted an average of 917 foreign inspections per year from 2018 to 2023, far fewer than the 8,353 domestic inspections it conducted over the same period. But CBS News reported that inspections have fallen even further since last year’s budget cuts. Taylor Farms’ Mexico facility linked to the cyclospora outbreak has not been inspected since 2019, according to CBS.
In a statement to WIRED, the FDA says that it asked for expanded state and local information sharing, as well as foreign food facility fee collection authority, in its 2027 budget proposal. The agency says that its “robust response” identifying the source of the cyclospora outbreak “demonstrates exactly how the agency's risk-based oversight system is designed to work,” adding that under the Trump administration, the FDA has “increased the number of unannounced foreign inspections and is actively expanding staffing at foreign posts.”
“Suggesting that the FDA's ability to protect the food supply can be measured by a single inspection statistic ignores the agency's comprehensive oversight system,” the statement continues.
Beyond cyclospora, McEntire says the other outbreaks of foodborne illness are still concerning even if they’re smaller in size than the cyclospora crisis. “Multiple visible outbreaks with different organisms associated with very different types of products is kind of unusual, not unprecedented, but certainly unusual,” she says.
Contaminated jalapeños have caused the biggest salmonella outbreak in the US since 2024, when an outbreak of the bacteria in cucumbers caused 551 illnesses that summer. (That’s far below the worst outbreak, though, when an estimated 224,000 people fell ill in 1994 after eating Schwan’s ice cream.)
It’s also rare to find two different disease-causing pathogens in the same product at the same time, which is the case with alfalfa sprouts contaminated with E. coli and salmonella. The outbreak has caused 55 illnesses, with two people getting infected with both pathogens. Everything Sprouts is recalling certain lots of alfalfa sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands at retailers and grocery stores. The sprouts were grown in a hydroponic facility in Minnesota.
Kowalcyk warns that the summer of sickness isn’t over yet, though the calendar is about to turn to fall. Many pathogens thrive in hot, humid environments. Plenty of warm weather is still ahead, and what’s shaping up to be the strongest El Niño on record could jack up temperatures in some locations even further. That means anyone looking for peace of mind at the drive-thru or in the produce aisle after Labor Day may not find it.
“A lot of our foodborne illness cases peak in August, September, even early October,” Kowalcyk says. “So we're just in the beginning.”

Sánchez takes rare swipe at Spain’s king over Ceuta crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:57:51 UTC
19:57:51 KST

Sánchez takes rare swipe at Spain’s king over Ceuta crisis
The prime minister pointedly contrasted his government’s hands-on handling of the surge of migrants in the North African city with the monarch’s absence.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addresses journalists after meeting King Felipe VI of Spain at the Almudaina Palace in Palma de Mallorca on July 29, 2026. | Jaime Reina/AFP via Getty Images
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez appeared to criticize King Felipe VI on Monday over his lack of involvement in the ongoing migration crisis in Ceuta, chiding the monarch for his failure to visit the city.
It is highly unusual for members of the Spanish government to publicly challenge the Crown’s actions. Yet Sánchez’s statement hinted at his frustration with the head of state’s absence from the Ceuta response, which he contrasted with his own emergency visit to the city, and his government’s on-the-ground handling of the still unresolved crisis.
Advertisement
“A lot of people think I’ve been governing for a long time, but I’ve only been in power for eight years,” said Sánchez, who has visited Ceuta four times since becoming prime minister. “The king has reigned for 20 years. How many times has he gone to Ceuta and Melilla? Not once.”
Sánchez’s statement was technically incorrect: Felipe VI has only been on the throne since 2014. The prime minister appeared to be referring to former King Juan Carlos I’s five-hour visit to Ceuta in 2007 — the last time a Spanish head of state visited the city.
The only other Spanish heads of state known to have visited were King Alfonso XIII, who traveled there in 1927, and President of the Second Republic Niceto Alcalá-Zamora, who visited Ceuta in 1933.
While declining to “share the content of the conversations I have with the head of state,” Sánchez emphasized he had recommended the king travel to the city. He said a royal visit would happen but declined to say when, noting it depended on “there being the conditions for it to happen.”
In the past, Spain’s kings have played an important role in the country’s interactions with Morocco. Juan Carlos I had a deep personal friendship with the late King Hassan II of Morocco, and was frequently called upon to handle back-channel negotiations when Madrid and Rabat clashed.
But Felipe VI is not known to have a similarly close relationship with Morocco’s current monarch, Mohammed VI. According to the Sánchez government, Spain’s king was asked to call his counterpart in Rabat in the immediate aftermath of the crisis but declined to do so.
Advertisement
Thousands remain
Both the Spanish government and EU officials previously stated that nearly all of the unauthorized migrants who had crossed into Ceuta had returned to Morocco within just a few days, but Sánchez on Monday said that around 5,000 remain in the Spanish semi-exclave.
Sánchez expressed solidarity with Ceuta’s residents and said he was confident normality would soon be restored. He compared the current situation to previous mass entries of migrants into the Canary Islands in 2020 and 2021, which he said the government had been able to handle.
The prime minister said that in the coming weeks, the approximately 1,200 unaccompanied minors who entered the city would be relocated to shelters on the Iberian Peninsula. Nearly all the other migrants are subject to deportation, he said, because “the majority of people who entered Ceuta did so for economic reasons” and therefore do not qualify for asylum.
The prime minister carefully avoided blaming Morocco for the crisis, instead attributing the surge to human-smuggling mafias, as well as to online campaigns orchestrated by Russia, Israel and “an international far-right group that always uses migration not only to attack Spain but also Europe, and divide it.”
“Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs,” Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said on X in response to Sánchez’s interview.
Advertisement
“What would Morocco gain from these kinds of tactics?” asked Sánchez. “I have no information from Spanish security forces or our intelligence services that would cast any doubt on Moroccan authorities.”
“This crisis can only be resolved with cooperation,” he insisted. “Showing a lack of confidence in Morocco will only aggravate this situation.”
Governmental turbulence
Sánchez denied the suggestion that his government had ignored intelligence warnings and downplayed the growing rifts within his government regarding who knew what and when.
Last week, Defense Minister Margarita Robles told lawmakers in the Spanish parliament that the National Intelligence Center — which handles foreign and domestic intelligence as well as counterintelligence — had alerted national authorities that a surge could take place. The statement contradicted those made by Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, who has systematically insisted the government had no way of knowing such a crisis could take place.
In his statements on Monday, Sánchez attempted to strike a compromise, saying that while intelligence services had detected an increase in illegal entries into Ceuta in the days preceding the crisis, none of the alerts they issued predicted its magnitude.
He also rejected the criticism he received for going on vacation in the immediate aftermath of the crisis, saying: “Even politicians have the right to rest, but I can assure you that the prime minister does not disconnect.”
Advertisement
Sánchez has previously stated he will not only stand for reelection but that he intends to remain in power for years to come. On Monday, however, he struck a less confident tone, saying he would be willing to run for reelection if his Socialist Party selects him as its candidate next year.
The prime minister added that his “intention is to complete the term” that concludes next year, but he declined to rule out calling snap elections ahead of the nationwide local and regional votes scheduled for next May.
While conceding that “change is always good,” Sánchez warned of the possibility of the far-right Vox party coming to power. “We are talking about a regression that has been seen in other parts of the world and that I, of course, am going to fight tooth and nail to prevent from happening in our country.”
This article was updated with comments from Gideon Sa’ar.

Two Malmö teenagers find their voice in Bulgarian folk music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:57:21 UTC
19:57:21 KST

Author
Gergana Mancheva
News
Two Malmö teenagers find their voice in Bulgarian folk music
Monday 31 August 2026 13:03
Monday, 31 August 2026, 13:03
PHOTO EABA
Font size
Elena and Ekaterina are both 18, were born and raised in Malmö, Sweden, and learned Bulgarian at home from their Bulgarian parents. They have only recently begun singing together, but Bulgarian folklore – and folk songs in particular – has long been part of their lives.
The two met through a Bulgarian youth and children’s cultural group in Malmö and have now formed a duet. Their performance of the traditional song Katerino, mome earned them first prize for a group in the 15–18 age category of the Lyubka Rondova singing competition, organised by Bulgaria’s Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad (EABA). The award brought Ekaterina Pishieva and Elena Serafimova to the attention of Radio Bulgaria’s international audience.
Beyond singing, the two were behind the project An Easter Tale in Malmö, using a kamishibai-style picture story to introduce the local community to Bulgarian customs and traditions.
PHOTO EABA
In early August, Elena and Ekaterina took part in the International Festival of Authentic Folklore in the village of Dorkovo. There they performed as dancers with BG Folk Rhythms, a Bulgarian folklore group bringing together participants from Denmark and Sweden. They later joined the traditional educational summer camp organised by EABA in Brodilovo, a village in the Strandzha region near Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast.
“We get together all the time and celebrate with the other Bulgarians in our community in Sweden. We are always together for national holidays and anniversaries. We have a large dance group from Sweden and Denmark – around 50 people, sometimes even more. We also have a children’s group for children from towns around Malmö. We are far away, but we are still close to Bulgaria. We have our dance group, we sing folk songs, and that keeps the connection alive,” Ekaterina Pishieva says.
PHOTO Bulgarian Orthodox Church and Cultural Community “Holy Mother of God” in Malmö
There is no Bulgarian school in Malmö, she tells us, but the Bulgarian community is active. People come together for national holidays and cultural events, while folk dancing and music are an important part of community life.
For Ekaterina, Bulgarian music has a strong personal meaning:
“I love Bulgarian music more than any other. The music hits me in the heart. I feel it as part of myself, as something that comes from my roots – I don’t know exactly how to explain the feeling. I really feel it inside me as something of my own, as home.”
She plans to continue dancing with Mladost na Megdana, a group of young Bulgarian folk dancers living abroad.
“We are young people from abroad who dance Bulgarian folk dances, aged between 15 and 25, and we are preparing for a performance at the National Palace of Culture in Sofia this autumn.”
PHOTO Bulgarian Youth and Children’s Cultural Group in Malmö
Elena Serafimova shares much of that experience. Like Ekaterina, she was born in Sweden and has always attended a Swedish school, while Bulgarian language and culture have remained part of her life at home.
Katerino, mome was the first song the two learned together – and they taught themselves, using recordings online and listening to established Bulgarian folk singers.
“My parents are from Sofia. There are no musicians in my family, so I’m happy that I can be a little different and have the opportunity to perform,” Elena says. “I really like Bulgarian folklore, and I’m very pleased and happy that Ekaterina and I managed to learn Katerino, mome entirely on our own. Of course, there will be other songs like it that we will perform.”
Unlike the earlier suggestion that the girls rarely visit Bulgaria, Elena says she comes back often – and would eventually like to make the move permanent.
PHOTO Bulgarian Orthodox Church and Cultural Community “Holy Mother of God” in Malmö
“Yes, I come back to Bulgaria very often, but the long-term goal is to return permanently, to my family and my roots, because it really is very different to be here, to feel all that energy, to be at home.”
Bulgarian music in Sweden is not confined to folklore. Elena says DARA’s Eurovision-winning song Bangaranga has become popular among Bulgarians there.
“I also really like the Bulgarian song with which DARA won Eurovision. Bangaranga is very popular among Bulgarians in Sweden. She toured there and gave several concerts, and she really managed to bring the Bulgarian community together.”
For Elena and Ekaterina, Katerino, mome is only the beginning. Having taught themselves their first song and taken it to a prize-winning performance, the two are already planning to add more Bulgarian folk songs to their repertoire.
Editor: E. Karkalanova
This publication was created by: Elizabeth Radkova

Russia Attacks Ukraine With Nearly 1,500 Drones in Four Days, Including 800 Jet-Powered UAVs
Russia has launched nearly 1,500 drones of various types against Ukraine over the past four days, including around 800 jet-powered UAVs, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his evening address on August 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy, Russia’s current aerial attack tactics are aimed at exhausting Ukraine and its population through sustained waves of drone strikes.
“Our warriors shoot down a significant share of them. There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in these four days alone—around 800 of them jet-powered. The most difficult task is intercepting the jet-powered ones. Now, it is mainly our combat aircraft that protect against them,” the president stated.
Ukraine currently relies primarily on combat aircraft to counter such drones, according to Zelenskyy. At the same time, the country is working to expand the use of specialized interceptor drones as a less resource-intensive means of combating Russian UAVs.
Four Ukrainian companies have already developed interceptor systems designed for the task, Zelenskyy said, adding that one of the designs is currently demonstrating the strongest results.
The president called on Ukraine’s Defense Ministry and the military to expand the country’s capabilities as quickly as possible to intercept all types of Russian drones.
Zelenskyy also set a target for Ukraine’s air defenses to achieve an interception rate of more than 90% against Russian drones this fall, as Moscow continues to intensify its use of unmanned systems in attacks across the country.
The scale of the threat was evident during another large-scale Russian aerial assault on August 29, when Moscow combined ballistic and anti-ship missiles with waves of attack drones, including jet-powered UAVs.
During the overnight attack, Russian forces launched an Oniks anti-ship missile, an Iskander-M ballistic missile, and 267 attack drones across Ukraine.

Russia’s 80-Missile Nuclear Battlecruiser Set to Return After Nearly 30 Years in Repair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:53:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s 80-Missile Nuclear Battlecruiser Set to Return After Nearly 30 Years in Repair
Russia’s nuclear-powered missile cruiser Admiral Nakhimov is nearing the end of trials after spending almost three decades undergoing repairs and modernization, potentially bringing an 80-cell missile platform back into active service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on August 30, the Project 1144 Orlan-class cruiser is completing factory and sea trials. Russian reports cited by the outlet indicate that state trials are expected to take place before the end of 2026, ahead of the ship’s planned return to the Russian Navy.
Admiral Nakhimov entered Soviet Navy service in 1988. The vessel was transferred to a repair facility in July 1997, although its overhaul was formally recorded as beginning in August 1999. If the cruiser returns to operational service as planned, it will have spent close to 30 years inactive, under repair, or undergoing modernization.
The prolonged program has also come at significant cost. Defense Express reported that current Russian estimates put the modernization bill at more than 200 billion rubles, equivalent to approximately $2.3 billion at current exchange rates. Previous estimates cited by the outlet suggested the total cost could have reached as much as $5 billion.
A major element of the modernization is the cruiser’s expanded missile armament. Admiral Nakhimov is equipped with 80 vertical launch cells designed to accommodate Kalibr cruise missiles, Oniks anti-ship missiles, and Zircon hypersonic missiles.
According to Defense Express, this configuration would make Admiral Nakhimov the most heavily armed surface combatant in the Russian Navy in terms of its offensive missile capacity.
The ship also retains nuclear propulsion, giving it long endurance without the need for conventional refueling. Admiral Nakhimov is one of Russia’s Project 1144 Orlan nuclear-powered cruisers, known in NATO terminology as the Kirov class.
Defense Express noted that the concentration of substantial weapons and resources aboard a single vessel has raised questions among military observers about the operational value and vulnerability of such large warships in modern warfare.
The modernization comes as the role of large surface warships is being reassessed amid the growing use of relatively inexpensive unmanned systems at sea. Ukraine has repeatedly demonstrated the ability of naval drones and long-range weapons to strike Russian naval assets, particularly in and around temporarily occupied Crimea.

Putin Uses Orcas “Tearing Bears Apart” to Explain Russia’s War Against Ukraine to Children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category

Putin Uses Orcas “Tearing Bears Apart” to Explain Russia’s War Against Ukraine to Children
Russian leader Vladimir Putin drew a parallel between Russia’s war against Ukraine and the behavior of animals in the wild, telling educators that children should learn about predators and food chains to understand “what kind of world we live in” and why Russia is waging its war.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Putin made the remarks during a meeting with students and teachers at Moscow State Pedagogical University on August 29.
The exchange began after Putin spoke with Dmitry Balanchukov, a Chinese-language teacher from Russia’s Belgorod region who had traveled to the North Pole. Putin asked whether he had seen polar bears before turning the conversation to orcas.
“There are orcas living nearby. They eat these bears like small fish. Yes, they simply attack in a pack—boom! —and tear them apart. It’s all very interesting. That’s the food chain,” Putin said.
He then connected the example directly to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“Children should also be told about this so that they understand what kind of world we live in and why we are conducting the special military operation ,” Putin said.
During the same discussion, Putin also referred to Jack London and described practices among some northern Indigenous communities in which, according to his account, elderly people who could no longer travel with the group were left behind for wolves.
“Yes, it all looks rather harsh, but that is their life,” Putin said.
Putin’s claim that orcas prey on polar bears is not supported by documented observations of the animals’ diets. While both species occupy parts of the Arctic ecosystem and their ranges can overlap, there are no confirmed cases of orcas hunting and eating polar bears.
Russia continues its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022. Moscow officially describes the invasion as a “special military operation,” while Russian authorities have increasingly incorporated narratives supporting the war into schools and other educational institutions.
Putin’s comments also follow remarks by Russian State Duma Deputy Speaker Pyotr Tolstoy, who called for strikes on Ukrainian cities aimed at demoralizing civilians. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said the comments amounted to public calls for war crimes and argued they warranted scrutiny by the International Criminal Court.

Mother tells how daughter slipped away in north Cyprus ferry disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:53:23 UTC
19:53:23 KST

Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as a ferry capsized off northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing at least eight people.
Her daughter Miray and 6-year-old son Mehmet Asaf were among nearly 20 people still missing on Monday as search teams looked for survivors in waters more than 500 meters (1,640 feet) deep.
"She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Ayten Bicer sobbed.
A suitcase fell on top of her, forcing the girl from her grasp. The mother caught hold of the daughter's foot, but her shoes, coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel, slipped through her hands.
The double-hulled ferry with 267 aboard took in water and flipped over on Sunday just off the port city of Kyrenia, leaving survivors clinging to the overturned hull. They were rescued by passing vessels and the coastguard authorities.
Separate accounts said the wide-bodied vessel jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface with part of its bow bursting open on impact. Severe storms hit Cyprus on Saturday, and the seas were still rough on Sunday, when the disaster occurred.
Debris remained scattered across the water on Monday, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry.
Families wait for updates
Outside the port in Kyrenia, some of those waiting sat and silently wept, while others scrolled on their mobile phones for updates.
It was unclear if people remained trapped on the vessel, now lying on the seabed.
Footage posted on social media suggested that at the time the ship flipped, there were still people trapped in one compartment of the vessel.
Ayten Bicer's husband, Hayri, said everything happened suddenly.
"We couldn't intervene. We lost our children. We made a lot of effort, but we couldn't save our children. Two of my children are gone. One of my sons is alive. Two of my children are gone. Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go," he said.
Divers from Turkey were assisting the search, officials said. They gave differing estimates of the missing, with some saying 19, and others 18.
The ferry ran into trouble shortly after leaving Kyrenia for the Turkish port of Tasucu, in Mersin province, one of several daily sea shuttle links with Turkey.
Authorities have detained the captain and crew of the vessel for questioning.
Ayten Bicer sat on a deck chair outside the port in Kyrenia on Monday, waiting for updates. Her eyes were swollen shut from crying.
"It was slipping like oil; there was diesel, and our feet were slippery. It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand. Mehmet Asaf held on to his father here," Ayten Bicer said, showing the collar of her T-shirt. "Saying, 'Baba'(Dad)."

Cornered by Stalemate, Putin Prepares to Escalate the War in Ukraine
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s refusal to back down in Ukraine is rooted in the survival instincts of Russia’s “gangster politics,” The Economist reported on August 30.
The report noted that the cornered leader is now planning to escalate the war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His predatory worldview was recently on display during an August 29 meeting with university students in Moscow, where Putin bizarrely claimed that orcas eat polar bears to illustrate “the food chain” and justify the war.
While factually inaccurate, The Economist noted that the remark provided a window into the mindset of a leader facing a strategic dead-end. With the Russian army stalemated and suffering tens of thousands of casualties each month, and Ukrainian drone strikes inflicting visible damage on Russian infrastructure, Putin is seeking a new way to escalate his way out of the crisis.
Western intelligence agencies are increasingly anxious about his next moves. The Economist highlighted several recent indicators of this growing alarm: CIA Director John Ratcliffe unexpectedly flew to Moscow on August 25, Finland requested Swedish military assistance to monitor its border for incursions, Romania destroyed a Russian naval drone targeting a drilling platform, and authorities in Germany and Slovakia foiled suspected sabotage plots linked to Moscow.
Putin himself has ended his long silence regarding Ukraine’s successful drone campaign against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, including warehouses belonging to the e-commerce giant Wildberries. In an August 22 address, he accused Ukraine of opening a “Pandora’s box” and promised severe retaliation.
Earlier that same day, he dismissed any notion of peace negotiations, vowing to his political party that the military operation would move “only forward.”
Sources close to the Kremlin told The Economist that after weeks of deliberation over the summer, Putin appears to have formally chosen the path of escalation. Waning public tolerance for the war is becoming an increasing concern; independent polling from the Levada Centre shows 57% of Russians now describe the situation as “tense,” citing the rising death toll, mobilization fears, and a lack of a future.
The mood among the Russian elite is even more pessimistic. Insiders cited by The Economist reveal a growing consensus that the nearly five-year war is a failure because of the sheer amount of time wasted, regardless of the outcome. However, the criminal logic guiding Putin’s regime dictates that he can never show weakness.
A failure to achieve even his minimum goal of capturing the entire Donbas region could put his life in physical danger. “They will hang me,” he reportedly confessed to cronies earlier in the war, The Economist wrote.
While the exact shape of the impending escalation remains unclear, The Economist suggests Russia will likely intensify hybrid warfare and sabotage operations targeting European supply routes to Ukraine. On the battlefield, Russian sources indicate Putin is prepared to throw an additional 300,000 to 400,000 men into the fight.
Rather than announcing a highly unpopular new mobilization wave, the Kremlin is expected to rely on localized coercion by regional governments to fill the ranks. Ultimately, these escalatory measures are designed to project strength and ensure regime survival, even as they guarantee further instability and suffering.
Russia’s manpower crisis is further underscored by Western intelligence estimates indicating Moscow is losing roughly 6,000 more troops each month than it can recruit. Despite enlisting about 1,000 personnel daily, the Kremlin remains unable to cover battlefield casualties, driving Russian forces to intensify long-range missile strikes against Ukraine’s civilians instead.

The Barghouti ‘myth’: Why Palestinians still want a leader they barely know - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:53:14 UTC
19:53:14 KST

Despite spending 24 years behind bars, imprisoned senior Fatah figure Marwan Barghouti continues to command significant support among Palestinians, largely because of the “myth” surrounding him and what he has come to symbolize, Dr. Michael Milshtein, head of the Palestinian Studies Forum at Tel Aviv University’s Moshe Dayan Center for Middle Eastern and African Studies, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
Serving five life sentences for murder and membership in a terrorist organization, Barghouti has been absent from Palestinian society for nearly a quarter of a century. He has not witnessed firsthand how the Palestinian economy has been changed by technological advances, the COVID-19 pandemic, or the events that have reshaped Palestinian society since October 7.
However, despite his long absence from public life, polls conducted by the Ramallah-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research have consistently shown Barghouti to be the leading choice among Palestinians for the next president.
In its latest poll, published earlier this month, the PCPSR found that Barghouti would receive 54% of the vote, putting him well ahead of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya, while current PA President Mahmoud Abbas would receive just 14%. In a poll conducted 10 months earlier, Barghouti was also the most popular choice for president, receiving 49% of the vote.
Asked how it was possible that a man with limited communication with the Palestinian people could enjoy such popularity, Milshtein shared that Qassam Barghouti, the son of the imprisoned Fatah leader, once explained to him that it was Barghouti’s absence that allowed his popularity to grow.
People don't know Marwan the person; they admire Barghouti, the myth
“He told me, ‘Listen, people do not really know Marwan the person, but they admire Barghouti, the myth. He represents, for most Palestinians, mainly the young ones, all the symbols, dreams and aspirations they support. He is quite clean. He is not corrupt like other senior figures in the PA. He represents the prisoners. He represents the resistance, the Mukawama (resistance). He represents a lot of things that most Palestinians are affiliated with,” he recounted.
Milshtein suggested another reason for Barghouti’s popularity is the poor perception of the alternatives. The Palestinian Authority has failed in its promises to weed out corruption, Abbas continues to hold onto the presidency despite his term expiring in 2009, and the Palestinian economy continues to struggle. State employees have been paid a fraction of their wages for a year, PA schools run part-time, and hospitals have struggled to operate at normal, full capacity in the West Bank.
“Their basic image is related to corruption and other negative phenomena. So, I even assess that if tomorrow there were elections in the Palestinian arena for the presidency, not the coming elections to the parliament, I’m almost 100% sure that he would be the president,” Milshtein continued, explaining that Qassem had once told him that it would hardly matter to Palestinians if their president were governing the West Bank from inside an Israeli prison cell.
Governing from inside a prison cell would be a 'headache' for the PA, Israel
Such a possibility would be a “headache” for both the Palestinian Authority and Israel if it ever materialized, he continued. Beyond “the fact that he doesn’t really know what the Palestinian street looks like and what the basic changes have been regarding the economy, society, culture and, of course, politics,” Israel would not be inclined to release a prisoner serving multiple life sentences who would be likely to incite another intifada.
Interestingly, Barghouti’s support extends beyond Fatah. During the hostage-ceasefire negotiations in 2024 and 2025, reports indicated that Hamas pushed for his release as part of a potential deal. While Palestinian prisoners from multiple factions were released as part of the agreements, few were singled out and discussed as prominently as Barghouti.
After nearly a quarter of a century in detention, Barghouti has had extensive interactions with Hamas operatives and leadership, Milshtein said, offering this as part of his explanation for Barghouti’s cross-factional popularity. In 2006, he co-authored the National Conciliation Document of the Prisoners alongside officials from Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the PFLP. These interactions helped build a degree of support for Barghouti within Hamas’s camp, Milshtein explained.
A second, more calculated reason, Milshtein said, was that Barghouti could help Hamas project an image of national unity among Palestinians.
“Hamas’s basic assumption was that if Marwan Barghouti were released because of Hamas, because of a military operation that Hamas promoted, maybe he would feel that he owes them,” he offered. “These conditions could make the idea of reconciliation, and maybe Hamas’s involvement in the Palestinian regime, easier.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin is preparing to escalate his war against Ukraine by sending up to 400,000 additional Russians to the battlefield, sources close to the Kremlin told The Economist.

Israel Election 2026: The parties, blocs and battles that will shape Israel's future - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:52:59 UTC
19:52:59 KST

As the October 27 election nears, Israel’s already fast-paced political scene appears to be speeding up even more, with an ever-revolving mix of old and new faces making an appearance, some who have shuffled around and others making a comeback.
This election will be the first to take place since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, with the political landscape and the issues at the forefront of voters’ minds having shifted significantly since the previous vote in 2022.
Some of the central issues include the IDF’s severe manpower crisis after three years of war, contentious haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription legislation, and calls for a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures surrounding the attack.
Meanwhile, traditional election issues, such as the establishment of a Palestinian state, have moved further to the background as Israel’s security outlook has changed.
Another major issue is the fate of long-serving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has led Israel for a total of 19 years.
Prof. Ofer Kenig, a political expert and research fellow with the Israel Democracy Institute’s Political Reform Program, told The Jerusalem Report that the upcoming election will “mark the direction in which Israel’s democracy is heading.”
Kenig, who is also a lecturer at Ashkelon Academic College, said that the outgoing coalition differed from previous Netanyahu-led governments in that it was “full Right,” a change that was felt by Israeli society due to stark policy changes over the past four years.
“Most Israelis do want some kind of broad government – without the extremists. Without the haredim and without the Arabs, for that matter,” Kenig noted.
Among the major issues will be the haredi draft laws and a state commission of inquiry, along with key domestic policies such as the rise in the cost of living.
Additionally, he said it will be interesting to see what happens with the political alliances between the parties hovering on the electoral threshold, what is becoming known as “the third bloc,” a new batch of parties offering an alternative to the current right-wing parties.
Kenig said it was important to also keep watch on the Arab parties, noting that the formation of a new Joint List could weaken Netanyahu’s bloc, but, it could also complicate the formation of a government for the opposition bloc.
He said that Netanyahu’s recent calls to form a “broad national government,” suggest that the Prime Minister is facing a “less than optimal situation” as his own party, Likud, continues to slip in the polls.
“If [Netanyahu] were in a much better position in the polls, I’m quite convinced we wouldn’t hear that this was the Likud’s main election slogan,” Kenig noted, adding that there appears to be a shift in Netanyahu’s strategy away from attempting to win to “just trying not to lose.”
Netanyahu may be aware that he “doesn’t have the cards in his hands to win,” and could instead be focusing on not losing, Kenig said.
The question might no longer be whether Likud can remain the largest party, but whether Netanyahu can assemble a coalition with himself at the helm.
In that case, Kenig theorized, Netanyahu could seek an election result in which the opposition bloc falls short of a majority, allowing him to remain in power as head of a transitional government until another election.”
So, even as Israelis cast their vote at the ballot box, the real fight might come afterwards with coalition haggling deciding the outcome of this fateful election.
Following is a breakdown of parties running in the election with a realistic chance of making it into the next Knesset. The factions are generally divided into two camps: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition, with a new so-called ‘third-bloc’ offering an alternative to the ruling right-wing coalition.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud
Likud, the ruling party, is led by Netanyahu. The party held 32 seats in the 25th Knesset, but recently has been polling far less, at approximately 22 seats.
The party is one of the few to hold primaries to elect its Knesset slate; however, its new list also includes eight slots hand-picked by the prime minister himself, leading to controversy and internal tensions within Likud.
Likud introduced the controversial political commission of inquiry bill to probe the October 7 attack, as Netanyahu has consistently spoken out against judicial appointments leading the investigation.
Initially, at the beginning of the government’s term, the party pushed for a contentious judicial reform amid an ongoing rift with the judiciary, which led to mass protests across the country.
Likud also introduced, and passed, the communications reform bill, which controversially overhauls regulation of Israel’s media and broadcasting sector.
In addition, throughout his latest term in power, Netanyahu has been under criminal trial both in Israel and abroad. At home, he is being tried in three separate cases, and abroad, an arrest warrant for alleged war crimes was issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit
Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, held six seats in the recent Knesset and is now polling at approximately eight seats.
In the previous election, the party ran on a joint ticket with the Religious Zionist Party, allowing them to cross the electoral threshold. One condition of Otzma Yehudit’s coalition agreements with Netanyahu was a law mandating the death penalty for terrorists. The controversial legislation, which is largely aimed at Palestinians convicted of terror offenses, was passed in March 2026.
As National Security Minister, Ben-Gvir also led reforms in Israel’s prison service, significantly worsening conditions for Palestinian inmates, arguing that both the death penalty and harsher prison conditions create deterrence.
Internationally, Ben-Gvir’s statements and actions, including repeated trips to the Temple Mount with calls to break the status quo, have led multiple European countries to declare him persona non grata.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party
The Religious Zionist Party (RZP), led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, held seven seats in the 25th Knesset. It is currently polling at approximately four seats.
Smotrich’s platform has been focused on Jewish identity, settlement expansion, and Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank.
During the previous term, RZP ran the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, with Minister Ofir Sofer introducing tax exemptions for new immigrants and increased recognition of foreign diplomas.
MK Simcha Rothman was the driving force behind efforts to significantly weaken the attorney-general’s power to influence and have oversight over the government.
Additionally, Smotrich has pushed to expand Israeli settlements in the West Bank, with over 100 initiated during his tenure, sparking tension for Israel diplomacy and leading him to also be declared persona non grata by several European countries.
The haredi faction: Arye Deri’s Shas and Yitzhak Goldknopf’s United Torah Judaism
There are two haredi parties in the Knesset: The Sephardi Shas Party, led by MK Arye Deri, and the Ashkenazi United Torah Judaism Party, led by MK Yitzhak Goldknopf.
Shas held 11 seats in the previous Knesset and is currently polling at around seven, while UTJ held seven and is polling at nine.
Netanyahu has relied on the haredi parties as key coalition partners, even though they have faced increasing criticism over their stance regarding ultra-Orthodox enlistment amid the IDF’s severe manpower shortage. Despite this, the leaders have continued to push for legislation that critics argue will not increase haredi representation in the army.
Two other contentious pieces of legislation sponsored by the haredi parties, which were passed by the Knesset were a bill to enshrine Torah study as a fundamental value in the country’s Basic Law, along with a bill to temporarily freeze arrests of haredi draft evaders.
The Opposition
A central unifying issue in the opposition bloc’s campaign is the promise to establish of a state commission of inquiry to investigate the government’s failures surrounding the October 7 attack.
Opposition parties argue that Netanyahu bears responsibility for those failures and can no longer remain in office.
The parties in the bloc have all pushed to form a framework to enforce haredi conscription to the IDF, though some party leaders have expressed a more hardline stance on the matter.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar
Yashar, led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, has recently emerged as the largest party in the opposition bloc, with polling putting him at around 26 seats and steadily pulling ahead of even Likud.
Eisenkot was previously a member of the Blue and White Party, led by MK Benny Gantz. After resigning from the Knesset in 2025, he stated that he would not serve as second-in-command and has repeatedly rejected offers to unite with other parties.
Unlike the other parties in the opposition bloc, Eisenkot’s approach to drafting haredim has been more lenient, and he has also indicated that he would be willing to sit in a government with Shas.
He has also pledged to conduct a state commission of inquiry into government failures on October 7, claiming the government used the attack to evade responsibility.
The party has presented itself as centrist, and Eisenkot himself appears more reserved, unlike the loud personas politicians tend to project.
As a bereaved father who lost his son and two of his nephews during the Israel-Hamas War, he appears to speak to Israelis on the ground who have suffered from the devastation of the last three years.
Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad
B’Yachad, led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, was formed from an alliance between Bennett and current opposition leader, Yair Lapid. Lapid, also a former prime minister, accepted the second slot on the party list. The party has recently been polling at approximately 14 seats.
Bennett became prime minister in June 2021, entering a rotation government with Lapid. His government was the first in Israel’s history to include an Arab party, Ra’am, in the coalition – a highly controversial move.
He has since taken a firm stance against including any Arab faction in a future coalition. Additionally, Bennett has also said he would not form a coalition with the haredi parties, calling to cut all state funding for anyone evading military service and reverse contentious haredi-backed legislation passed by the outgoing government.
Bennett said that during his time away from the political scene, he consulted experts to prepare a comprehensive plan for the country’s future, which includes the establishment of a written constitution, raising competition in the market to lower the cost of living, improving transportation, cutting down the crime rates, and investing in AI to advance the country’s technology and defense.
Yair Golan’s The Democrats
The Democrats Party, led by Yair Golan, held four seats under its previous name, Labor, in the 25th Knesset. It is currently polling at about 10 seats.
Golan is a reserve major-general and served as the IDF’s deputy chief of staff under Eisenkot.
Though Golan has previously expressed support for a two-state solution with the Palestinians, and other party members have called for a Palestinian state, after October 7, Golan has argued that the approach should be more nuanced.
The party has committed to a list incorporating gender parity through a zipper system alternating between women and men, while also guaranteeing representation for Meretz, which merged with Labor in 2024 to help form the Democrats, the rural sector, and minority communities, including an Arab candidate in a realistic slot.
It held internal primaries to determine its slate.
It is notably one of the only parties in the opposition bloc that actively calls to form a coalition with the Arab parties, leading to tension.
Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu
Yisrael Beytenu, led by Avigdor Liberman, held six seats in the 25th Knesset and is currently polling at about 10 seats.
Liberman has been a fixture in Israelis politics for more than three decades, serving in key government positions such as defense minister, foreign minister, and finance minister.
Yisrael Beytenu is traditionally hawkish on security, calling for a more decisive stance to fully eliminate Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Iranian regime.
In addition, the party advocates for expanding Israeli settlements in the West Bank, while also strongly advocating for the separation of religion and state.
Liberman is fierce critic of Netanyahu’s current government and has been open about his aim of becoming prime minister. He has taken a hardline on haredi conscription, calling for legislation to ensure there will be no exemptions, and for those who do dodge service to be prevented from receiving any financial aid from the state.
Benny Gantz’s Blue and White
Blue and White, led by former IDF chief of staff Benny Gantz, held eight seats in the 25th Knesset – out of the 12 belonging to the National Unity alliance – and is currently polling below the electoral threshold ahead of the upcoming election.
Blue and White has been distanced from the opposition bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu in the upcoming elections, as Gantz has said he would not object to teaming up with Netanyahu, calling for a “broad Zionist government” to bring together parties on both sides of the aisle.
While underscoring the importance of a broad Zionist government, Gantz has drawn a red line to sitting in a coalition with the haredi or Arab parties.
Despite the many MKs leaving his party, such as Eisenkot and Chili Tropper, Gantz has repeatedly asserted that he has no intention of resigning.
Numerous reports say he is considering joining a political alliance, and he has said that would ensure he does what is necessary to regain support and pass the electoral threshold.
The Arab faction: Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am, Yousef Jabareen’s Hadash-Ta’al, and Sami Abu Shehadeh’s Balad
Four Arab parties are running: the religious Ra’am Party, led by Mansour Abbas; the secular Hadash-Ta’al, led by Yousef Jabareen; and the hardliner Balad Party, led by Sami Abu Shehadeh.
Hadash-Ta’al is a reduced Joint List that agreed to run together in the 2022 election, and Balad, which has fails to pass the electoral threshold in polls, recently signed an agreement to join the two, while still leaving the door open for Ra’am to join.
Despite polls showing that the Arab parties would earn more seats together, Abbas has held off on joining the Arab alliance out of hope that his Ra’am Party could be invited to the next coalition.
The parties all call to address the spike in Arab crime and advance equality for Arab citizens, and have stated that their main objective would be to remove Netanyahu and far-right figures such as Ben-Gvir from government. The parties also advocate for a Palestinian state.
The third bloc
Zionist Home-The Reservists, Unity Party, and People of Israel
Amid tensions over the haredi draft issue, three new right-wing parties have emerged, voicing dissatisfaction with the existing right-wing parties in Netanyahu’s coalition: Knesset member Chili Tropper and former minister Yoaz Hendel’s Zionist Home-The Reservists, former ambassador and minister Gilad Erdan and Knesset member Yuli Edelstein’s Unity Party, and Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter’s People of Israel.
According to recent polls, these parties are hovering near the electoral threshold, and all have been informally termed the “Third Bloc” by pundits. All three state that they aim to provide a “political home” for right-wing voters who feel no existing party reflects their beliefs.
Tropper and Hendel have stated that a primary condition for them to join a coalition would be the passage of a draft law requiring haredim to serve in the IDF, as well as universal conscription.
Similarly, Erdan and Edelstein, both former members of Likud, have vowed to uphold right-wing principles and fight for universal IDF conscription.
Winter’s faction, which includes Arab-Israeli activist Yoseph Haddad and former Jerusalem deputy mayor Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, as well as reservists and bereaved relatives, aims to bring together people who were not part of the political or security failures surrounding October 7, but who fought during the war, paid personal costs and are now prepared to enter politics.
According to polls, Winter’s roster could win five seats, largely at the expense of Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, which would then fall beneath the electoral threshold.
With at least two of the parties potentially securing four seats each, these new factions may find themselves in the role of kingmaker in the upcoming election. ■

US maintains plan for expansion in Indian Ocean despite setback in Iran — Kobyakov

MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Despite the setback in Iran, the US administration is maintaining its plans for expansion in the Indian Ocean region, Russian Presidential Adviser and Executive Secretary of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) Organizing Committee Anton Kobyakov said in an interview with TASS ahead of the Eastern Economic Forum.
According to Kobyakov, Russia's opponents are developing a concept to create a unified region around the Indian Ocean, linked by some sort of free trade zone, in order to advance bloc-based military and political interests.
"Since June this year, the US Indo-Pacific Command, which had existed since 2018, has returned to its customary Pacific format; the Indian Ocean has once again been handed over to the Cold War-era relic known as the Central Command (CENTCOM)," he said. "But this does not mean that plans for continental expansion have been shelved. The setback in Iran simply convinced the Pentagon that the country is self-sufficient as a forward line of the Eurasian security system; hence the idea of separating the theaters of military operations targeting Iran and China once again," Kobyakov added.
According to him, Southeast Asia is a key region from the standpoint of military and political stability because transit routes for energy supplies to rapidly developing Asian countries, primarily China, run through the region. ASEAN is also increasingly asserting itself in this region not only as an economic force but also as a geopolitical one. "The importance of the association in global affairs is rapidly growing as the Eurasian security system is being built, which [Russian President] Vladimir Putin first announced in June 2024," he said.
As an example, the presidential adviser cited the second Russian-Indonesian naval exercise in recent years, which recently concluded in the Sea of Japan. Kobyakov also noted that military and military-technical cooperation with Myanmar is expanding, while military contacts with Vietnam and Laos remain in place, as do contacts with India outside ASEAN.

For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
A source in the Iraqi Prime Minister's office, who preferred to remain anonymous, told The Media Line, "The decision will be made in the coming period, and it is hoped that the procedures will begin during 2027."
Iraq’s central bank released an official statement that said: "There is no decision yet to print a new Iraqi currency, and any future move to restructure currency denominations or remove zeros will be preceded by several legal and regulatory stages."
The US dollar is currently trading at 1,320 Iraqi dinars according to the official exchange rate, while it is trading at 1,530 Iraqi dinars per dollar on the parallel black market. The Iraqi currency is considered overvalued, with Iraqis receiving salaries in the hundreds of thousands or millions of dinars, while housing units are purchased for hundreds of millions or even billions of Iraqi dinars.
Iraq’s currency consists of several denominations, the smallest being 250 dinars, and increasing to 1,000, 5,000, 10,000, 25,000, and 50,000 dinars.
Change a part of campaign against corruption
According to observers and politicians, the move, if approved, would be part of the government’s broader campaign against corruption, which has already targeted several politicians. These campaigns led to the discovery of trillions of dinars hidden on the farms or in the homes of some politicians.
The currency in their possession will become worthless without being exchanged for the new currency, which will lead to the discovery of even more of these funds or the confiscation from those holding them.

What's next for Syria's economy as US removes nation from state terror list? - analysis

The United States announced on Aug. 24 that it was rescinding Syria’s designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, ending a status that had been in place since 1979 and removing an additional layer of legal restrictions that had shaped the country’s relationship with the international financial and commercial system for decades.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
This move opened a new chapter for the Syrian economy, but it does not mean money and investment will flow into the country overnight.
The decision is part of a broader US effort to ease restrictions on Syria following the fall of the former government. The United States also delisted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, the group led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa before he took office, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization in the same announcement. Washington ended its comprehensive Syria sanctions program in 2025, and the Caesar Act was repealed in December of the same year.
The significance of the latest decision, therefore, lies not in lifting all remaining sanctions on Syria at once, but in removing a legal and political designation that affected foreign assistance, certain export controls, financial transactions, and the US position on financing for Syria through international financial institutions.
For Syrians and investors, however, the more important question is no longer whether the designation has been lifted, but whether its removal will translate into banks willing to deal with Syria, easier financial transfers, foreign investment, and financing for reconstruction.
Syria removed from US terror list after nearly 50 years
Syria was placed on the US list of State Sponsors of Terrorism on Dec. 29, 1979, and was among the countries originally designated when the list was established.
Over the following decades, Washington linked Syria’s continued presence on the list to the Syrian government’s support for groups the United States designated as terrorist organizations, the presence of leaders and members of Palestinian organizations in Damascus, and, later, Syria’s relations with and support for Hezbollah and Iran.
The designation carried a range of legal restrictions, including bans on US arms exports and sales, controls on certain dual-use goods, restrictions on US foreign assistance, and financial constraints, as well as US opposition to certain forms of financing for Syria through international financial institutions.
The US sanctions architecture targeting Damascus gradually expanded far beyond the State Sponsor of Terrorism designation.
In 2004, additional restrictions took effect under the Syria Accountability and Lebanese Sovereignty Restoration Act, targeting exports and dealings with Damascus over Syrian policies in Lebanon and its support for groups designated by Washington as terrorist organizations.
After protests against Bashar Assad’s government erupted in 2011, Washington imposed successive rounds of sanctions targeting Syrian officials and entities over the repression of protesters and human rights abuses.
Pressure intensified again when the Caesar Syria Civilian Protection Act took effect in 2020. The law authorized sanctions against Syrian and foreign parties providing material support to the Assad government and, alongside earlier measures, contributed to Syria’s increasing isolation from the international financial and investment system.
Syria’s removal from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list in 2026 therefore closes the oldest layer of a US restrictions framework dating back to 1979, while forming part of a broader process of dismantling restrictions accumulated over decades.
Saudi-Syrian businessman Nabil al-Mazloum told The Media Line that the decision changes how investors view the Syrian market, even if it does not make investing in the country risk-free.
“For us as businesspeople, removing Syria from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list does not mean the market became safe overnight, but it fundamentally changes the way we look at it,” al-Mazloum said.
He said the obstacle in recent years had not simply been a lack of investment opportunities, but also difficulties with transferring money, dealing with banks, obtaining financing, and ensuring that a transaction would not become a legal risk due to sanctions.
“When a barrier of this magnitude is removed, an investor can move from asking, ‘Can I even enter Syria in the first place?’ to asking a completely different question: ‘Where should I invest, with whom, and what return can I achieve?’” he said.
Syria requires substantial capital to rebuild post-war
Syria needs substantial amounts of capital to rebuild sectors severely damaged during years of war, from electricity, energy, transportation, and infrastructure to industry, housing, services, and banking.
Al-Mazloum said the scale of the country’s needs creates significant investment opportunities but stressed that US political decisions alone will not be enough to attract capital.
“Capital does not move on emotion or political decisions alone. Investors want to see banks capable of processing transfers, stable laws, enforceable contracts, guarantees protecting property rights, and the ability to repatriate profits,” he said.
Investors who enter the Syrian market early may encounter greater opportunities, al-Mazloum added, but will also assume greater risks than those who wait until the market's rules become clearer.
The banking sector may prove to be one of the clearest indicators of whether the shift in US policy moves from the political sphere into the real economy. Even when certain transactions were legally permitted during earlier periods, years of sanctions and restrictions led many international financial institutions to avoid dealings with Syria due to legal risks and compliance costs.
Anas Bitar, a businessman working in real estate development and money transfers in Damascus, told The Media Line that removing the designation carries economic and banking significance that goes beyond its political implications.
He said Syria’s presence on the list had increased the perceived risks associated with virtually any financial dealings involving the country, prompting banks and international institutions to stay away from the Syrian market.
Bitar said removing the designation could gradually ease that caution, open the way for the restoration of banking relationships, facilitate transfers and trade financing, and signal to foreign investors that dealing with Syria no longer carries the same level of legal and political risk.
The effects, however, will not be immediate, he said. “International banks move very cautiously and need time to reassess risks, update their compliance policies, and verify which entities and individuals remain subject to sanctions.”
One of the most important potential developments would be the restoration of correspondent banking relationships between Syrian banks and foreign financial institutions. Such relationships are essential for international transfers, trade financing, and the normal processing of cross-border payments.
“The real indicator of whether this step succeeds will be seeing foreign banks restore correspondent relationships with Syrian banks, dollar and euro transfers taking place normally, and international companies able to finance their investments and repatriate their profits,” Bitar said. “Only then can we say that removing the designation has moved from a political decision to a tangible economic impact.”
Despite the significance of the decision, Syria’s removal from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list does not mean that all US sanctions connected to the country have ended.
The United States continues to retain authorities allowing targeted sanctions against Assad and his associates, human rights abusers, those involved in the Captagon trade, and certain actors linked to destabilizing activities, terrorism, or proliferation.
Syrian legal expert Fadi al-Hawari told The Media Line that distinguishing between removing the designation of the state itself and lifting all sanctions is essential to understanding the decision’s actual consequences.
“From a legal perspective, removing Syria from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list does not mean that all US sanctions and restrictions related to Syria automatically disappear, because the designation represents a specific legal framework, while other measures and sanctions are based on different laws and executive orders and may target specific individuals or entities,” al-Hawari said.
In his view, Syria’s removal from the list eliminates “an important legal layer of restrictions that surrounded its foreign relations for decades” and provides governments, institutions, and companies with a clearer legal basis for reassessing their dealings with the country.
Reducing legal risks could open the door to greater participation by foreign companies in Syria’s reconstruction, but it does not resolve domestic problems that could continue to deter investors from entering the market.
Foreign banks and companies will also need to continue screening the parties with which they do business to avoid transactions involving individuals or entities that remain under US sanctions.
Al-Hawari said this will continue to influence decisions by international institutions because companies and banks consider not only whether a transaction is currently permitted but also the risk of future sanctions or legal exposure.
The decision also carries a political benefit beyond its economic implications. Syria’s removal from a list it had been on since 1979 eliminates one of the most prominent symbols of the country’s decades-long isolation and opens the way for rebuilding its relations with the United States and international institutions on a different footing.
Al-Hawari said the durability of the opening will depend on the Syrian state’s conduct and international commitments, as well as the ability of Damascus and Washington to build a political and legal framework that gives investors and international institutions confidence that the new course “is not temporary and subject to rapid reversal.”
For Syria, then, the greatest value of the decision may not be an immediate influx of capital, but rather the removal of one of the barriers that for years kept the country outside the normal calculations of banks, companies, and investors.
The real test will come later: when a foreign company attempts to transfer millions of dollars into a project in Syria, when a Syrian bank seeks to restore a correspondent banking relationship in New York or Europe, or when an international investor decides whether the opportunity presented by a market requiring extensive reconstruction is worth the risk.
Only then will it become clear whether Syria’s removal from the State Sponsors of Terrorism list merely closed a legal and political chapter - or whether it helped open a new economic one.

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on the Party's self-governance is set to be published on Tuesday.
The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 17th issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee.
The article calls on Party organizations at all levels, as well as Party members and officials, to strengthen their sense of responsibility and mission in the Party's self-governance.

Party organizations and leading officials, especially chief officials, bear the primary responsibility for exercising full and rigorous self-governance of the party in their respective localities or departments, according to the article.
Leading officials at all levels should strictly fulfill their responsibilities and foster upright conduct, it adds. ■

Economic Watch: China's August PMI signals improved sentiment, steady new momentum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:50:40 CST
19:50:40 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) edged up in August from a month earlier, signaling improved business sentiment amid policy support and weakening extreme weather effects, while new momentum drivers continued to gain steam, official data showed Monday.
The PMI for China's manufacturing sector stood at 49.8 in August, up 0.6 percentage points from July, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 reflects contraction.
In August, the manufacturing sector's overall business climate saw notable improvement, said Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the National Bureau of Statistics, citing that among the 21 industries surveyed, 16 reported a higher PMI compared with the previous month.
This sector saw expansion in both manufacturing output and market demand in August. The production sub-index and new orders index climbed to 50.4 and 50.6, up 0.5 percentage points and 2.1 percentage points from July.
Driven by the pick-up in both production and orders, enterprises' willingness to purchase strengthened, with the procurement volume index reaching 50.5, up 1.1 percentage points from the previous month, said Huo.
The development momentum of new growth drivers continued to improve in August, she said.
The PMI for the equipment manufacturing industry and the high-tech manufacturing industry stood at 51.4 and 52.9, respectively, both remaining in the expansion zone.
Affected by recent upward movements in crude oil and non-ferrous metal prices, the purchasing price index for major raw materials and the factory price index for manufacturing stood at 56.6 and 50.4, respectively, up 3.4 percentage points and 2.6 percentage points from the previous month.
The PMI for large manufacturing enterprises came in at 50.6, up 1.1 percentage points from the previous month and returning to the expansion zone.
Wen Tao, an analyst at the China Logistics Information Center, attributed the rebound in domestic manufacturing market demand to multiple factors, including diminishing extreme weather conditions compared with July, further implementation of domestic demand policies, such as the "six major infrastructure networks" initiative, and steady summer consumption.
Wen expected the manufacturing sector to stabilize and pick up further in September, with pro-growth policies set to intensify and extreme weather conditions continuing to ease, while certain segments including automobiles, computers, consumer electronics and textiles are poised to enter their traditional peak season.
The PMI for non-manufacturing sector came in at 49 in August, unchanged from the level in July.
He Hui, vice president of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing (CFLP), noted that while the non-manufacturing business activity index remained below 50 percent in August due to seasonal factors such as high temperatures and heavy rainfall, positive structural changes began to emerge.
The driving effect of summer consumption continued to be visible, with business activity indexes for railway transport, air transport, accommodation, scenic spot services, and cultural, sports and entertainment-related industries all staying in expansion territory, said He.
Online shopping-related activities remained vibrant, lifting the business activity index for the postal industry to above 60 percent, a new high for the year, while service consumption potential is expected to continue releasing in the fourth quarter, he said.
Zhang Liqun, a special analyst at the China Logistics Information Center, said the rise in the August PMI indicates that factors supporting economic stabilization have increased, calling for accelerated implementation of existing policies and timely introduction of incremental ones to further strengthen market confidence.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, existing policies will be implemented at a faster pace, incremental policies will be moderately rolled out, and market-driven growth drivers will accelerate their release, creating favorable conditions for China's economy to maintain steady and sound development, said He. ■
