Iran attacks Jordan, UAE after US bombs Larak Island: What’s the latest?
The retaliatory attacks came after the US targeted and hit two Iranian launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran says it has attacked US bases in Jordan and US military assets in the United Arab Emirates in retaliation for strikes on Larak Island in the first active exchange between the two sides since late July.
The Iranian response came after the United States claimed to have hit two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. A US official told Al Jazeera Arabic following the attack that the launchers were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines towards the waterway.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3What’s behind the US move to hit Egyptian bank with Iran sanctions?
- list 2 of 3Top officials from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to meet in Istanbul
- list 3 of 3US plans to sanction another bank to keep economic pressure on Iran
In his first comments since the attack, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran was “not looking for war”, but would “never sit still in the face of any aggression” either.
Iran “will give a decisive response to the aggressors” if attacked, Pezeshkian was quoted as saying by the Iranian news agency Fars. “Instability and unrest in the region are not in the interest of any country and will challenge everyone.”
Here’s what we know so far and what could happen to the diplomatic efforts to end the six-month-old war that has disrupted global oil supply and jolted the global economy.
What happened?
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said the US attacks on Sunday night had killed and wounded several Iranian soldiers and civilians.
Iran’s Fars news agency also reported IRGC spokesperson Sardar Mohebi accusing the US of making “a strategic and fatal mistake” for which it will face consequences “in both the economic and military arenas”.
But on Monday morning, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a post on X that the IRGC’s statement that the attack on Larak Island was an “act of aggression” was false, and said forces took “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz”.
“In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce,” it added on X.
US President Donald Trump on Monday claimed that Kharg Island is being “blown to smithereens” in a post on his Truth Social platform. Iran has yet to comment on Trump’s claims.
Last week, the US president said all mines had been detonated or removed from the waterway, and Iran was told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.
What has been the response?
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the US strike on Larak Island in a statement as a “direct violation of national sovereignty and territorial integrity”.
It added the attack caused civilian and military casualties.
Shortly after the US strikes, the IRGC said a combined missile and drone operation targeted the King Hussein and Al Azraq US military bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
The strikes “destroyed the technical and repair infrastructure, as well as the enemy fighter deployment sites”, causing significant damage, the IRGC said in a statement.
Tehran dubbed the strikes on Jordan as “a legitimate exercise of self-defence” under the UN Charter.
“Iranian armed forces launched retaliatory missile strikes against US military positions in Jordan, targeting bases identified as the launching ground for a Sunday night attack on Larak Island,” the statement said.
“Aggression and crimes will not solve the enemy’s desperation in attempting to weaken the Islamic Republic’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and every attack will be met with even more devastating responses.”
At the same time, a US official told Al Jazeera Arabic that they were able to intercept Iran’s attacks against Jordan, adding that “the missile attack on US forces in Jordan proves that Iran is no longer the power it once was”.
They added that Tehran had launched medium-range ballistic missiles towards Jordan.
And in a statement released on Monday, Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles fired by Iran. “Air defence systems intercepted eight missiles that breached the Kingdom’s airspace at dawn today,” read the statement, quoting the army’s spokesperson.
Early on Monday morning, Iran’s Fars and Mehr news agencies cited a statement from the IRGC that said its air defences had intercepted “a long-range American MQ9 drone” over the Strait of Hormuz, which then fell into the Gulf.
Harlan Ullman, a retired US senior naval officer, told Al Jazeera that the attacks on Jordan were a “political statement”.
“They are signalling to Jordan that it is a target,” he said.
“It is a politically significant target,” he said, adding that the Iranian attack was carried out “with malice aforethought, not necessarily to impose damage on the Americans, but to tell the Jordanians: Are you sure you want to support the Americans?”
Iran’s army also said in a statement carried by Iranian news agencies that dozens of drones were launched at US military assets at the Al Menhad airbase in the UAE.
It said the attack targeted locations where US forces and helicopters were stationed at the base, adding that it was revenge for members of the IRGC and civilians who had been killed during the attack on Larak Island.
On Monday morning, the UAE’s Ministry of Defence said its air force responded to a drone over its territorial waters, approaching from Iran. The ministry, however, rejected Iranian claims that its airbase was targeted.
UAE’s ministry of foreign affairs “strongly condemned the Iranian aggression” in a post on X.
Still, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said it would respond decisively to any further military aggression and said the US and parties supporting its actions were fully responsible for any escalation.
What does this mean?
Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Manuel Rapalo explained that the tit-for-tat exchanges are the scenario that US diplomats who have been working with other countries to bring a diplomatic off-ramp did not want.
“The Trump administration has been signalling over the course of the last week that talks have deteriorated, that diplomacy has lost momentum, and we have seen that shift in strategy away from kinetic action and towards economic pressure,” Rapalo said.
“This is something that the treasury secretary spoke about specifically on Sunday, saying that there would be more sanctions coming up in the next few days,” he said, referring to economic sanctions targeting entities accused of doing business with Iran.
Last week, the US announced the latest sanctions on Iran in what officials called an “economic D-Day” and officially named “Operation Economic Outcast”, as Washington intensifies pressure on Tehran six months into the war.
Tehran, which has been under US sanctions for decades, says the new economic pressure will fail and shows that the US’s military approach has not worked.

Russia details roles for its two-seat Su-57D fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:18:50 UTC
18:18:50 KST

- Rostec says the two-seat Su-57D will train pilots in specialized flight regimes and serve as an airborne control platform for uncrewed aircraft.
- Some analysts believe the program was built partly to support export contracts, with India cited as a country interested in a two-seat variant.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec disclosed new details this week on the two-seat Su-57D fighter, a designation in which the “D” likely stands for “Demonstrator,” saying the aircraft is intended for two main roles: training pilots on flight regimes that cannot be replicated on ground simulators, and serving as an airborne control platform for uncrewed aircraft.
The two-seat prototype, which first flew in May, is currently undergoing flight testing. Rostec described the aircraft’s second role as central to what it called sixth-generation technology, since the rear cockpit allows the fighter to function as an airborne command post for drone operations.
“This is important for controlling highly intelligent systems such as the Okhotnik, as well as swarm and group systems, when the attention of the main pilot and crew is focused on carrying out the primary combat mission,” said Mikhail Strelets, director of the Sukhoi Design Bureau, part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation, speaking on the program “Military Acceptance.”
Rostec said the two-seat variant will also serve as a testbed for combat artificial intelligence systems currently under development by specialists at United Aircraft Corporation.
The aircraft flying today was not built from scratch. Aviation researcher Andreas Rupprecht identified the prototype by its bort number, 055 Blue, matching the fifth Su-57 flight-test prototype, T-50-5, which suffered a severe engine fire on the runway at Zhukovsky in 2014, reportedly witnessed by an Indian delegation. The airframe was rebuilt as T-50-5R and has now been reconfigured with a second cockpit rather than replaced with new-build hardware.
Some Western defense analysts and outlets, including The Defence Blog, have described the two-seat program’s public framing as only part of the picture. Analysts have suggested the aircraft was built in connection with a series of potential export contracts, intended to demonstrate the program’s readiness to prospective foreign buyers rather than to meet a purely domestic training requirement. India has been named as a country with particular interest in a two-seat configuration, drawing on its operational experience flying the two-seat Su-30MKI.
Russia and India signed a contract in 2010 for preliminary design work on the Fifth Generation Fighter Aircraft, a joint program based on the T-50 prototype that specifically required a two-seat variant. India withdrew from that program in 2018 following disputes over cost, workshare and the aircraft’s stealth performance. Russia has continued pitching a two-seat Su-57 to India in 2026, presenting the offer at the Wings India exhibition in Hyderabad, including proposed technology transfer and integration of Indian-origin weapons such as BrahMos and Astra missiles, according to Indian defense reporting. India has not indicated whether it will accept.
The two-seat prototype’s tail carries a logo depicting both the Su-57 silhouette and the S-70 Okhotnik stealth drone, a visual pairing that matches Rostec’s stated goal of using the aircraft to coordinate crewed and uncrewed formations.
Rostec has not disclosed a production timeline, a finalized designation for the aircraft, referred to variously as Su-57D or Su-57UB in Russian reporting, or a target date for integrating the combat AI systems it says the program will help develop.

What to watch at SCO summit as Eurasian bloc marks 25th anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:16:18 UTC
18:16:18 KST

Some of Eurasia's most powerful leaders are meeting for a two-day event in the Kyrgyzstan capital Bishkek, bringing together a mix of bilateral ties, longstanding rivalries and regional conflicts.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin will be among those attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Heads of State summit, which marks the group's 25th anniversary.
The gathering comes amid a tentative thaw in China-India relations following years of border tensions, as India and Pakistan navigate the aftermath of their brief conflict last year.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will also attend as Tehran faces ongoing confrontation with Washington and growing US economic pressure, while conflicts and instability stretching from the Middle East and Ukraine to Afghanistan are expected to feature in discussions.
The meeting comes as SCO members seek to capitalise on shifting global economic and geopolitical dynamics by strengthening trade, transport links and economic cooperation across Eurasia.
SCO as united front against West
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues, but Putin and Xi have also used the summit to promote their vision of a multipolar world and to present a united front against the West.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states”.
However, at last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation”, referring to US-Chinese tensions.
The meeting comes after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that he would encourage G20 members to re-examine terms of trade with China, denouncing Beijing’s $1.2 trillion global trade surplus as unsustainable.
Diplomacy to watch in Bishkek
One of the most closely watched encounters will be between Xi and Modi as Asia's two most populous countries seek to build on a tentative thaw after years of tensions over their disputed Himalayan border.
Senior Chinese and Indian officials held another round of boundary talks in Beijing on August 25, agreeing to continue efforts toward a settlement and maintain stability along the frontier.
Relations deteriorated sharply after deadly border clashes in 2020, making the leaders' interactions in Bishkek an opportunity to gauge how far the recent improvement in ties has progressed.
The interaction between Xi and Putin will also offer a window into the increasingly close relationship between China and Russia and how the two powers coordinate within the SCO.
The gathering will also put the leaders of India and Pakistan in the same room just more than a year after the two nuclear-armed neighbours fought a brief conflict.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is slated to attend, bringing him together with Modi as tensions persist between the two countries, primarily over Kashmir.
Another leader to watch will be Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is scheduled to meet Putin on the sidelines of the summit, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
His visit comes as the US threatens increased secondary sanctions against countries and entities that continue doing business with Tehran.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will address the summit session to be held in an expanded format and hold bilateral meetings with participating leaders on Tuesday.
What’s on the official agenda?
According to the SCO Secretariat, leaders are expected to discuss major regional and international security challenges, including wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, the situation in Afghanistan and India's relations with China and Pakistan.
The Eurasian organisation has taken a more visible collective position in 2026 on Iran and the broader Middle East, including Israel’s war on Gaza, calling for restraint, dialogue and political and diplomatic solutions.
At a July meeting, SCO foreign ministers expressed particular concern over developments in the Middle East and around Iran, reiterating that international conflicts should be settled through political and diplomatic means in accordance with international law and the UN Charter.
Afghanistan remains a longstanding regional priority, particularly because of concerns over terrorism, drug trafficking and cross-border security.
Ukraine is also expected to feature in discussions, though there has been no indication that the war will be a separate focus of the summit.
Counterterrorism remains a core area of cooperation through the SCO's Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure, based in Tashkent. The summit is expected to approve its plans for the coming year, including possible joint exercises.
Economic connectivity will be another major focus, with transport infrastructure and a proposed SCO Development Bank among the projects under discussion.
One major transport project involving SCO members is the 7,200-kilometre International North-South Transport Corridor, which links St. Petersburg with Mumbai through Iran and ports on the Gulf. The future of this corridor amid the ongoing US-Israeli war on Iran is also likely to be discussed among the leaders in Bishkek.
The organisation also agreed in 2025 to establish a network of Silk Road Stations to support international freight traffic across Eurasia.
Members are meanwhile continuing talks on establishing an SCO Development Bank. A fourth round of consultations was held in Shenzhen in June, though its structure and operating arrangements remain under negotiation.
What is the SCO?
The SCO traces its roots to the "Shanghai Five," established in 1996 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to reduce military tensions and address border disputes following the breakup of the Soviet Union.
Uzbekistan joined when the SCO was formally established in 2001, and the grouping remained largely centred on China, Russia and Central Asia for much of its early history.
Its international profile grew significantly with its expansion in 2017, when India and Pakistan became full members, followed by Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.
For Iran, membership marked a major diplomatic opening after years of geopolitical isolation, while Belarus's accession reflected its broader pivot toward non-Western partners.
Today, the Eurasian organisation has 10 members: Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus.
Turkmenistan is the only Central Asian country outside the SCO, reflecting its longstanding policy of permanent neutrality. Afghanistan and Mongolia have observer status, while dialogue partners include Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Saudi Arabia.
Together, SCO members have a population of around 3.4 billion, span a vast stretch of Eurasia and account for around 25 percent of global GDP.
Unlike NATO, the SCO is not a military alliance, nor is it an economic union like the EU. Instead, its consensus-based structure provides a forum for security cooperation, economic ties and diplomacy among countries that do not necessarily share the same interests.
Latest SCO Summit aims
The summit is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the SCO's 25th anniversary, alongside documents on the organisation's development and regional and international issues.
It will also mark the end of Kyrgyzstan's chairmanship and the handover to Pakistan, which is set to lead the organisation for the next year and host the 2027 leaders' summit.
The SCO lacks the binding commitments of a military alliance or economic union, but its scale has made it an increasingly significant forum for dialogue across Eurasia.
The summit underscores how an organisation founded to resolve border disputes has grown into a major multilateral grouping.
Its next challenge will be turning that scale into influence while maintaining consensus among an increasingly diverse membership.

KAI President Semenova: our management model, legal form provide autonomy all other universities want
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:15:26 EEST
18:15:26 KST

President of National University Kyiv Aviation Institute (KAI) Kseniia Semenova states that KAI’s management model and organizational-legal form provide the autonomy that all other higher education institutions desire, but they are unwilling to take on the responsibility.
"The supervisory board specifically represents the interests of the state and also monitors that these interests are taken into account during the management of the university. The supervisory board was formed according to the principle defined in the resolution: seven people covering various areas. It brings together very diverse competencies that are super useful for the university and provide broad experience. The supervisory board operates as a management body, meaning it is not an advisory body—it is not about ‘sharing contacts of acquaintances’ or ‘taking photos at a ceremonial event’—it is about management, document analysis, strategy development, financial plan analysis, and making strategic decisions," Semenova said in an exclusive interview with the Interfax-Ukraine agency.
She noted that in contentious matters, the final word rests with the supervisory board, though she retains the opportunity to convey her vision.
"The appointment of top management goes through the supervisory board, which makes it possible to unseal the university system. Because in the old system, there is zero possibility for an outsider with different expertise to come in and develop a direction using experience other than what exists inside the institution. This is a super important story. But at the same time, internal matters regarding content, where it is indeed necessary to have this internal expertise and experience of how things were built at the university for many years, remain with the Academic Council," the president said.
Answering a question regarding criticism that such a format of supervisory boards could become a tool of influence for the Ministry of Education and Science over universities and centralize this hierarchy, Semenova stressed that KAI is one of the most state-independent universities.
"Right now, the Ministry of Education and Science sets KPIs for rectors of all other 119 universities and monitors their execution. Can the Ministry of Education objectively monitor the work of such a large number of higher education institutions? Hardly, yet this currently happens centrally. Furthermore, all universities lack financial autonomy—all financial decisions go through the Ministry of Education… Our management model and organizational-legal form provide the autonomy that everyone else wants, but they do not want to take on responsibility alongside it," she emphasized.
Clarifying whether she believes students or university staff should have representation on the supervisory board, Semenova stated no, because other mechanisms exist for that.
"The Academic Council is fully composed of representatives of the staff and students. Plus, the university has the Conference of the Labor Collective as the highest collegiate body, which approves the charter, working conditions, labor discipline, and so on. The main issues related to working conditions at the university are still approved by a body consisting of staff representatives. The philosophy of the supervisory board is for it to be an independent body representing the interests of the state, not the staff. It should not turn into either student self-government or an employee trade union. It must clearly defend the state’s interests in this organization because sometimes the interests of the state do not coincide with the interests of individual employees," the president noted.
She also believes the academic community (staff and students) should not be involved in the election process for the university head.
"The head of a university is an executive director who has key performance indicators and clear tasks set by the supervisory board. Is the head of a student self-government body competent regarding the qualities a company CEO should possess? No. A supervisory board is professional activity; it is not simply seven highly moral people whom we all trust deeply and who will definitely protect student interests. These are professional specialists who know how to work as supervisory board members," she stated.
Semenova noted that as soon as an element of elections and staff representatives is included, it immediately transforms from a professional activity into a political realm.
"For that, there are elections to the Academic Council, which is also a governing body with significant powers; for that, there is the Conference of the Labor Collective; for that, there is student self-government. These are the tools that allow them to exert influence and participate in university management. Including them on the supervisory board is an uncharacteristic function for students, who are the primary clients of the university," she stated.
As reported, in September 2024, the Cabinet of Ministers launched an experimental project in three universities to strengthen the role of supervisory boards. Specifically, participants in the experiment included National Aviation University (NAU), which was reorganized into the state non-profit enterprise National University Kyiv Aviation Institute (KAI), as well as Zaporizhia National University and Vasyl Stefanyk Precarpathian National University.
In April 2024, Kyiv City Council member Kseniia Semenova was appointed acting rector of the then National Aviation University. In August 2025, following elections by the supervisory board, Semenova was elected president of the reformed State Enterprise Kyiv Aviation Institute.
KAI President Semenova states that the university aims to be similar to Finland’s Aalto University, Technical University of Munich, or Delft University of Technology, but over the next 2-4 years will compete for students with universities in the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Poland.

Nepal rescue teams seek hundreds of workers trapped in hydropower tunnels by deadly floods

Nepal rescue teams seek hundreds of workers trapped in hydropower tunnels by deadly floods
Supported by experts from China and India, Nepal's rescue teams on Monday endeavoured to reach hundreds of workers believed to be trapped in hydropower tunnels blocked by the devastating flood of mud, water and debris that swept through the Himalayan region last week.
Issued on: Modified:
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Nepal's rescue teams, helped by Chinese and Indian experts, stepped up efforts on Monday to reach hundreds of workers believed to be stuck inside blocked hydropower project tunnels in the aftermath of last week's Himalayan flood that carved a trail of destruction in the country's valley towns and villages, as well as across the border in China.
The unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris along the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday – blamed on a glacier collapse – killed more than 900 people while nearly 5,000 are still missing.
Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves in the plains of the Himalayan country after having been swept down the mountains by the torrent and decomposing amid the humid conditions.
Nepali officials said that the focus was on reaching the 933 workers believed to be trapped at 11 hydropower projects, including many in tunnels, in the two hard-hit districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot.
Read moreRescuers grapple with a mountain of challenges after the Nepal-Tibet floods
Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night as workers watched.
Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.
The Nepali army said search-and-rescue teams were using controlled blasts, excavators and search lights to clear water and mud to reach trapped people. Teams recovered three bodies after entering two tunnels, while other sections remained buried in mud and were still being searched, it said.
“A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters. “Our main focus is on opening the tunnels.”
'Unprecedented disaster'
On Monday, Nepali authorities said 903 people had died, with 4,247 missing, including the 933 at hydropower plants. On the Chinese side, authorities said 16 people were killed in Gyirong County and 546 were missing.
The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and it remained challenging to compile a complete assessment of the damage.
“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday, adding that nearly 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers.
On a visit to Kyrgyzstan, Chinese President Xi Jinping said Beijing is making every effort to search for missing people following the disaster, Xinhua reported on Monday.
Beijing has said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries remain unaccounted for in Tibet, near a key border crossing with Nepal.
China’s state-run CCTV reported that Beijing has mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($33 million) to support relief efforts. It has been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.
Climate change takes a toll
Although Nepal has said that it does not need foreign help in general rescue and search, it has leaned on giant neighbours India and China for their expertise in tunnel rescue.
Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border as a result of the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal's rivers.
China’s state television CCTV said that another lake formed by a landslide upstream had largely drained as water flowed out naturally.
Authorities are now monitoring an impact crater carved out near the site of the glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, which by Saturday evening had expanded to 174,000 square metres, state media said.
The crater has an estimated reservoir of 2.5 million cubic metres, which if breached, could lead to a chain reaction to lakes further downstream, authorities warned.
CCTV said there is risk of further landslides along the river that could create additional lakes, as investigators identified eight high-risk locations for geological disasters.
The flood was "caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming", the state broadcaster reported, saying it was a "new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters" on the Tibetan plateau.
Two Nepali officials told Reuters that China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels following a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that a lack of data sharing could hamper future disaster preparedness.
On Monday, the Chinese foreign ministry said that Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to "strongly support" Nepal's disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries' common interests.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Exhibitions, cinema and literature at the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Berlin

News
Exhibitions, cinema and literature at the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Berlin
Monday 31 August 2026 11:01
Monday, 31 August 2026, 11:01
PHOTO Facebook /Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Germany
Font size
The Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Berlin has announced its programme for September. It features two exhibitions, a literary premiere, a film premiere, and two-day Bulgarian language courses for children.
The latter is being organised to mark the International Day of Languages. The Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Berlin has organized language courses on September 24 and 25 at several libraries across Berlin.
According to information from the Institute, language learning will be enhanced through a practical activity: a short course on writing the Cyrillic letters, which will introduce students to the graphic features of the alphabet.
At the end of the workshop, all participants, under the guidance of Militsa Todorova, will present what they have learned in a joint exhibition by writing their names in Cyrillic. The mini-courses will take place at Schiller-Bibliothek (Müllerstr. 149) and Fahrbibliothek (Götzstr. 8/10/12).
Here is more information about other Bulgarian events in in the German capital, organised by the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Berlin:
PHOTO Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Berlin
The exhibition “Traces in Space”, curated by Hanna Schwarz and Petar Mitev, remains open to visitors until September 8. The exhibition features more than 30 stage design projects and works created for theatrical productions that transcend the boundaries of the stage and take on an independent life as works of visual art. The projects on display reflect both universal human themes embedded in classical drama and pressing issues facing contemporary society.
PHOTO Evgenia Krasteva-Blagoeva, personal archive
Fans of Bulgarian literature will have the opportunity to attend the presentation of Evgenia Krasteva-Blagoeva’s novel “Rivers of Time”. The novel traces the invisible threads of the past that bring together the fates of two families who lived through the Balkan Wars, the Second Balkan War and the First World War, as well as the horrors of the Kutsiyan and Belene labour camps.
The book paints a moral portrait of a generation that lived through the wars for national unification and fell victim to communist terror, yet managed to preserve its values and pass them on to its children.
The book presentation will take place on September 8, with the participation of Boris Despodov, Goran Blagoev and Desislava Bobenkova.
PHOTO Facebook / /Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Germany
The exhibition “GRENZENLOS” (BOUNDLESS) explores the concepts of freedom and materiality, raising an important question: what happens when we move beyond imposed boundaries—physical, spiritual, social and creative?
Through their works, 12 established Bulgarian artists engage in a visual and philosophical dialogue beyond fixed boundaries—where limitations disappear and infinite horizons open up. Transparent and translucent materials become a medium that refracts light, captures memory and reveals what is hidden.
The exhibition, curated by Prof. Orlin Dvoryanov, will open on September 11.
A still from Valeska Grisebach’s film “The Dreamed Adventure”
PHOTO Miramar Film
The film “The Dreamed Adventure”, directed by German filmmaker Valeska Grisebach, will premiere on September 24 at Kino International, located at Karl-Marx-Allee 33.
The story follows Veska, an archaeologist who has returned to her hometown of Svilengrad to take part in archaeological excavations. Unexpectedly, in the Bulgarian border region with Greece and Türkiye, she encounters Said, an old acquaintance from the Rhodope Mountains who has been drawn to the town by shady business dealings.
Gradually, stories from the time of the great changes of the 1990s emerge—stories of freedom and shattered dreams, violence and easy money. Supported by her friends in Svilengrad, Veska begins to write her own story.
The film was shot in the Svilengrad area in the summer of 2024, with all the roles played by Bulgarian non-professional actors. It is Valeska Grisebach’s second film set in Bulgaria.

Israeli police clash with ultra-Orthodox Jew protesters over military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:12:41 UTC
18:12:41 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Lina Altawell
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
Israeli police and ultra-Orthodox Jewish protesters clashed in Tel Aviv on Monday during a demonstration against military service.
In a statement, the police said demonstrators blocked roads near the Tel Hashomer recruitment office as officers moved to disperse the anti-draft protest.
Officers repeatedly warned demonstrators through loudspeakers before accusing them of “disturbing public order,” blocking roads and clashing with police, it said.
Video footage showed police officers forcibly removing protesters from a street near the recruitment office in Tel Hashomer.
The Jerusalem Post reported that dozens of ultra-Orthodox protesters tried Monday morning to block roads leading to the recruitment office.
The protest aimed to prevent the recruitment of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the army. The demonstrators slept on the ground outside the site to be present when recruitment procedures began at dawn, the newspaper said.
Ultra-Orthodox Jews, also known as Haredim, have continued protests against army service after Israel’s Supreme Court ruled on June 25, 2024, that they must be drafted and that financial aid should be withheld from religious institutions whose students refuse military service.
Senior rabbis, whose followers view their rulings as religious edicts, have urged ultra-Orthodox Jews to refuse enlistment and even “tear up” draft orders.
Haredim make up about 13% of Israel’s population of 10 million and reject military service, saying they dedicate their lives to studying the Torah.
They also argue that integration into secular society threatens their religious identity and the continuity of their community.
For decades, members of the community avoided conscription at the age of 18 by obtaining repeated deferments on the grounds of religious study until reaching the current exemption age of 26.

Five people complained to the Ministry of Health about the private Odrex clinic
Kyiv • UNN
Five citizens filed complaints with the Ministry of Health about the activities of the private Odrex clinic over the past four years. In response to these complaints, the regulator conducted unscheduled inspections of legal entities associated with the brand, and one of them had its license to practice medicine fully revoked.
Over the past four years, five citizens have contacted the Ministry of Health with complaints regarding the activities of the private Odrex clinic. At the same time, the activities of legal entities associated with the brand became the subject of unscheduled inspections by the Ministry of Health over issues concerning the quality of medical care. And after the latest appeal — a complaint from the widow of deceased patient Ihor Melai — the Ministry instructed the Odesa Regional Military Administration to conduct a clinical-expert assessment of his treatment at the "Medical House "Odrex," reports UNN.
The UNN editorial team contacted the Ministry of Health with a request after the widow of deceased Odrex patient Ihor Melai filed a complaint regarding the circumstances of her husband's treatment.
In response to the editorial team's inquiry, the Ministry of Health reported that the appeals to the Ministry concerning Odrex's activities were not isolated.
"According to the EDMS data, during the specified period, 5 citizens contacted the Ministry of Health regarding the activities of the Odrex clinic," the Ministry's response states.
Claims regarding the quality of treatment at Odrex, which in recent years have been publicly voiced by relatives of deceased patients and former patients, are not limited to the media space — appeals concerning the clinic's activities were also submitted directly to the relevant state authority.
Odrex, criminal cases and patient deaths
The name of the Odrex clinic often appears in high-profile stories connected with patient deaths and their families' claims regarding the quality of treatment.
In particular, a court hearing in a criminal case concerning the clinic's doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska is ongoing in Odesa in the case involving the death of businessman Adnan Kivan. The medical professionals are accused of improper performance of their professional duties.
According to the investigation, after surgery at the Odrex clinic, businessman Adnan Kivan may not have been prescribed the necessary antibacterial therapy, and the postoperative complications may not have been properly addressed. A forensic medical examination indicates that this could have led to the development of sepsis and the patient's death. The accused do not admit guilt.
The court has now moved on to examining the evidence: medical documentation, expert conclusions, clinical protocols and other case materials. The next hearing is scheduled for September 3, 2026.

Former Rusich commander's sentence for war crimes against Ukraine reduced in Finland
The Helsinki Court of Appeal has reduced the sentence of former Rusich Group commander Voislav Torden (Yan Petrovsky) from life imprisonment to 12 years and six months after finding him guilty of three war crimes against Ukraine instead of four.
Source: European Pravda, citing Finnish public broadcaster Yle
Details: The Helsinki Court of Appeal announced its ruling on the appeal against the original sentence handed down to Yan Petrovsky, a former commander of the Rusich Group who used the alias Voislav Torden, for war crimes committed against Ukraine in 2014.
Petrovsky was found guilty of three war crimes and sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison.
In the original ruling in March 2025, the Helsinki District Court sentenced him to life imprisonment after finding him guilty of four war crimes. He subsequently appealed, seeking either the dismissal of the charges or a reduced sentence.
The Court of Appeal ruled that the evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that Petrovsky had personally shot wounded Ukrainian soldiers or that he could be considered primarily responsible for doing so. Meanwhile, the court found that he bore at least partial responsibility as a participant in the events.
The Court of Appeal also ruled that carving the symbol of the Rusich Group into the cheek of a Ukrainian soldier did not constitute a war crime. The court concluded that the available evidence indicated that the injury was superficial and did not meet the threshold for causing severe physical or mental suffering, which would have constituted a war crime.
Petrovsky was detained while attempting to enter Finland in 2023. A court refused to extradite him to Ukraine, citing poor conditions in Ukrainian prisons.

Woman futsal star Gholami hangs up the boots
TEHRAN - Iran women’s futsal star Nasimeh Gholami has officially announced her retirement from the national team after almost 20 years of service.
Gholami was one of the standout players of Iran’s golden generation, winning the AFC Women’s Futsal Asian Cup twice and representing Iran at the FIFA Futsal Women’s World Cup.
She also helped the national side finish third at the Asian Indoor Games.
“Deciding to say goodbye to the national team was not easy at all,” Gholami said. “For some people, retirement may simply mean saying a sentence, but for me it means the end of a part of my life — a part that I lived for with all my heart for almost 20 years.
“I didn’t just collect memories with the national team; I found my sporting identity there. I grew up, suffered defeats, got back on my feet, celebrated championships and went through many difficult days. Naturally, saying goodbye to such a journey is extremely difficult.
“But I felt the time had come to make this decision. I wanted to leave the national team while I still loved this shirt with all my heart, rather than being forced to leave or reaching a point where I no longer had the ability or motivation to continue.”

Lithuania to require vocational training for foreigners in Lithuanian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:09:00 UTC
18:09:00 KST

Vocational training for foreigners in Lithuania will no longer be offered solely in foreign languages starting in September, with courses required to be taught in Lithuanian or bilingually, the Education, Science and Sports Ministry said Monday.
Under the new rules, bilingual instruction will be provided until a student reaches the level of Lithuanian proficiency required for their chosen profession, the ministry said.
“Immigration processes and changes in the labour market are driving a growing need among newcomers to acquire professional qualifications in Lithuania,” Deputy Education Minister Rolandas Zuoza said in a statement. “We have seen cases where vocational training providers, adapting to the needs of foreign students, organise training in a foreign language.”
“By creating better opportunities for foreigners to learn in Lithuanian, we are promoting their smoother integration into the labour market and our society,” Zuoza said.
Education Minister Raminta Popovienė has approved regulations governing bilingual vocational training, setting out how such programs are to be organised, the ministry said.
The changes follow amendments to Lithuania’s Vocational Education and Training Law adopted by the parliament in March requiring vocational training in the country to be conducted in Lithuanian.
The Lithuanian-only or bilingual requirement will apply not only to foreigners seeking their first professional qualification, but also to those enrolled in continuing vocational training programs to improve an existing qualification or obtain an additional one.
The policy is part of broader efforts to strengthen Lithuanian-language use among foreign workers and support their integration.
Starting in January 2026, stricter Lithuanian-language requirements have applied to foreigners working in the service sector and selling goods. They must be able to serve customers in Lithuanian at no lower than a basic proficiency level.

Türkiye’s trade with Turkic states rises 6.6% to $10.1B in first seven months of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:08:58 UTC
18:08:58 KST

Türkiye’s trade with fellow members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) has risen 6.6 percent year-on-year to $10.1 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to the Turkish Trade Ministry.
The ministry said on Monday that trade between Türkiye and other OTS members had expanded nearly twentyfold since 2002, rising from $871 million to $16.9 billion by the end of 2025.
Kazakhstan was Türkiye’s largest trading partner among OTS members last year, with bilateral trade totalling $7.8 billion.
It was followed by Azerbaijan with $4.3 billion, Uzbekistan with $3.1 billion and Kyrgyzstan with $1.6 billion.
Trade with observer countries also grows
Türkiye’s trade with OTS observer countries — Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus — increased 6.8 percent in 2025 to $10 billion.
In January-July 2026, trade with the observer countries rose 5.1 percent from the same period a year earlier to $6.1 billion.
Annualised trade with OTS members and observer countries consequently reached $27.8 billion as of July, according to the ministry.
The OTS was established in 2009 and adopted its current name at the Istanbul Summit in 2021. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, while Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus have observer status.
Global production shifts to the east
The ministry said the eastward shift in the centre of global production and trade over the past quarter-century had increased the strategic importance of the Turkic region within international trade and logistics networks.
It added that opportunities offered by the Trans-Caspian East-West-Middle Corridor, commonly known as the Middle Corridor, held significant potential for deeper economic integration across the Turkic world.
The ministry said Türkiye would continue efforts to strengthen economic and commercial integration within the OTS and make effective use of the Middle Corridor’s strategic advantages.
It said these efforts would help further reinforce the Turkic world’s position in global trade.

Achilles Shield: Israel, Greece sign over NIS 10b. air defense deal against Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:08:42 UTC
18:08:42 KST

Israel and Greece formalized one of the largest defense export agreements in Israel’s history on Monday, signing a €3 billion government‑to‑government deal that will see Israel design and deliver a complete, multi‑layered national air defense architecture for the Hellenic Republic’s Achilles Shield project.
Signed in Tel Aviv by Defense Ministry Director-General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram and his Greek counterpart, Maj.-Gen. Ioannis Bouras, the agreement marks a significant expansion of bilateral defense cooperation and places Israeli missile defense systems as the backbone of Greece’s long‑term air defense modernization program.
Senior officials from Israel’s Defense Ministry’s International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT), the Defense Research and Development Directorate (MAFAT), and the Israeli Missile Defense Organization attended the signing, alongside the CEOs of Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI).
MAFAT head Brig.-Gen. (res.) Dr. Daniel Gold called the deal “a badge of honor for Israeli technological power” and said that Jerusalem will continue to develop additional technological breakthroughs to strengthen its standing in the world.
“The ability to field a multi-layered, comprehensive, and modern defense architecture - grounded in proven operational experience and at the forefront of global technology - is what contributed to Greece's choice of Israel as a key strategic partner,” he said.
Deal will include deploying SPYDER batteries to Greek islands
The project will integrate several Israeli‑made systems into a unified national network. At its core are David’s Sling, BARAK MX, and SPYDER missile defense systems developed by the Israeli defense companies and already deployed operationally within Israel’s own air defense array.
The package also includes MMR radars produced by IAI subsidiary ELTA for air surveillance coverage and a new national command‑and‑control system developed by Rafael to integrate all layers into a single operational picture.
Greek companies are expected to receive about €700 million of the deal’s total value as subcontractors for Rafael and IAI.
The agreement represents the first time Israel will supply a complete, end‑to‑end air‑defense array to another country. According to a statement released by the Defense Ministry, the architecture is based entirely on Israeli systems and incorporates operational lessons drawn from Israel’s recent wars wherein these systems played central roles in intercepting thousands of hostile aerial targets, including drones and ballistic missiles launched by Iran, Hezbollah, and the Houthis in Yemen.
In addition to the main package, the two sides concluded a €26 million supplementary deal for Rafael’s Drone Dome counter‑UAV system, intended to protect Greek strategic sites and reinforce existing defenses against unmanned aerial threats.
"The choice of Rafael systems, including David's Sling, SPYDER, and our command-and-control systems, as part of the national infrastructure reflects growing trust in Rafael's air defense capabilities and the unique operational experience accumulated in Israel,” Rafael CEO Yoav Tourgeman said.
The agreement also includes provisions for expanded industrial cooperation. Israel will transfer knowledge and technology to Greek defense industry partners as part of the government‑to‑government framework, deepening a relationship that has grown steadily over the past decade.
For Greece, the Achilles Shield constitutes one of the most ambitious air defense modernization efforts in its history. For Israel, it reflects a broader strategic effort led by Defense Minister Israel Katz and Baram to increase defense exports as a means of strengthening the IDF’s force buildup and expanding Israel’s international defense footprint.
Since the outbreak of war, Israel’s defense industries have been operating under an emergency production framework, supplying both the IDF and partner nations abroad. Despite vocal criticism, Europe has increasingly turned to Israeli air defense technology over the past decade, especially after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the growing demand for rapid, combat‑proven systems. Several Israeli systems, including the Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Spyder, have been selected by European governments.
"The Achilles Shield deal is another milestone in the defense relationship between Israel and Greece. It reflects the deep trust our partners in Greece place in Israeli technology, the defense industry, and the government-to-government cooperation model led by the Defense Ministry through SIBAT. We will continue working to expand strategic cooperation with Greece and with additional countries, while strengthening Israel's defense industry and its standing in the world," SIBAT head Brig.-Gen. (res.) Yair Kulas, said.
Influence of Turkey in pushing Israel, Greece defense industries closer
The wider geopolitical context cannot be ignored. Both Greece and Israel face assertive neighbors and volatile regional dynamics.
IAI CEO Guy Barlev said that the two countries “share common challenges and interests, and cooperation between them is an important pillar in strengthening defense capabilities and safeguarding the security of their citizens.”
Greece’s sweeping military modernization program is unfolding against the backdrop of Turkey’s own ambitious drive to expand and indigenize its defense capabilities, creating a dynamic that could reshape the balance of power in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Turkey has made its defense autonomy a national priority, aiming to meet nearly all of its military needs domestically by 2030.
Turkey has launched the $6.5 billion Steel Dome program, a multi-layered air defense network designed to rival Israel’s Iron Dome or Greece’s Achilles Shield and provide protection against aircraft, drones, and ballistic threats.
Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan claimed that the Steel Dome “will instill confidence in friends and fear in enemies.”

Why is the EU looking for new member states? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot

2026-08-31

18:08:35 KST

Iceland has voted against reopening EU membership talks, with 52.8 percent rejecting the government's proposal. This comes as the EU wants to expand and strengthen unity. But why does the EU want to enlarge? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
On 29 August, 52.8 percent of Icelanders voted “No” in a referendum on resuming membership talks to join the European Union. The EU had already opened accession negotiations in 2010, but Reykjavik dropped them in 2013 following a change of government.
For the EU, Iceland’s membership was about whether the EU could still attract a wealthy, stable democracy that chooses to join for reasons beyond seeking financial and economic stability.
With Russia’s war destabilising Europe, weakening ties with Washington, and the conflict in the Middle East, the EU views enlargement as vital to its own future. A larger bloc boosts influence in trade, defence, and diplomacy.
When countries join the bloc, they give up part of national sovereignty to the EU but gain a seat in European institutions and benefit from common policies, including foreign, security, and trade. They must contribute to the EU budget but can access funds and support.
To join the EU, candidate countries need to adopt the EU’s principles and implement the EU acquis communautaire, a set of laws that form the core of EU legislation.
They must implement reforms across 35 policy areas to establish stable institutions that ensure democracy and the rule of law and a functioning market economy.
Currently, seven countries have opened accession negotiations. Montenegro is the frontrunner, followed by Albania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Moldova and Ukraine, which applied for membership in 2022. Negotiations with Türkiye stalled in 2018.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to intervene against Cockroach Janata Party's protest march on September 5, saying that maintenance of law and order was primarily the responsibility of the government and police.A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana said that there is no reason to presume that the proposed demonstration would insult in any untoward incident."We will at least, as of now, presume everybody will behave in a peaceful manner. Right now there is no compelling circumstance to assume that any untoward thing will happen," the CJI observed.The bench issued notice to the Centre and Delhi Police and posted the next hearing for September 10, along with other matters concerning the student protests.This comes after a plea was filed by retired Delhi Police officer Rajendra Singh, seeking directions to ensure that large-scale demonstrations and protest marches in sensitive areas of the national capital are held only after obtaining requisite police permissions.The counsel, appearing for Singh, urged the apex court to hear the matter on September 3, citing the proposed march and the upcoming BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12-13.
The counsel referred to the violence during the July 20 Sansad March announced by the CJP and cautioned that another incident could occur, even if not directly attributable to the organisers.The CJI, however, said the court could not proceed on the assumption that something untoward would happen and reiterated that the police authorities were competent to deal with any law-and-order situation.
"Before us, there is no identified group. You please impress upon the Union or NCT Delhi. It's for them to maintain law and order. They should act as per law," the CJI said."They are expected to maintain law and order, and the enforcing agency has the responsibility to maintain law and order... We are expecting them to act within that framework. From both sides, we are expecting that they will respect, they will conduct themselves, and they will follow the law of the land...," he added.The CJP has announced the September 5 march in Delhi, alleging that the Centre failed to honour its commitment to withdraw cases against students who participated in the July protests over the alleged examination paper leak

UN committee says countries must consider reparations for slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:07:58 UTC
18:07:58 KST

A UN committee said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination, which it says persists today.
Guidance published on Monday by the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination stated that the obligations arise from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a "paradigm shift" away from debates over historical responsibility, which governments have often used to resist reparations claims.
"States Parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for people of African descent, covering all aspects of remedies," said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination called the largest forced displacement in history.
Calls for reparations gain momentum
Calls for reparations - ranging from official apologies to financial compensation - have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The European Union and Britain abstained from a UN resolution on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade at the time - the so-called intertemporality principle.
But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.
"Irrespective of the legal characterization of the original historical acts, States Parties remain bound by their present obligations under the Convention to address structural inequalities," the UN document states.
Financial compensation alone is not sufficient, it adds, urging "transformative" measures including opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
Pela Boker-Wilson, a committee expert from Liberia who helped draft the document, said she expects states to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.
"We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action," she told Reuters. "We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimized or forgotten."

However, digitalization in China's special education sector remains at an early stage, with shortages of resources and insufficient application still posing challenges, the official said.
China has stepped up efforts to promote the high-quality development of special education over the past decade. By 2025, the country had 2,464 special education schools, 927,000 special education students and 85,100 full-time special education teachers, representing increases of 33 percent, 145 percent and 95 percent, respectively, from 2012, official data showed.
The enrollment rate of school-age children with disabilities in compulsory education had reached 97 percent in 2025, with the plan aiming to keep it above 97 percent through 2030.
The plan also calls for further improvements to support mechanisms for special education, enhanced digital and intelligent capabilities, and the establishment of a high-quality, integrated and inclusive special education system by 2030. ■

Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has exposed new details about Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missile, including its design, warhead, guidance systems, and the companies producing it – along with foreign equipment used in its manufacturing.
The Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) said the Zircon was originally developed as an anti-ship weapon for Russia’s nuclear-powered submarines and Project 22350 frigates equipped with 3S14 launch systems.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But Russia’s Black Sea Fleet has struggled to operate safely during the war, forcing Moscow to adapt the missile for launch from Bastion-M coastal missile systems, according to HUR.
Despite being one of Russia’s most expensive strike weapons, the Zircon carries a relatively small warhead of about 120 kilograms (264 pounds), HUR said. That is lighter than the roughly 150-kilogram (331 pounds) warhead carried by Russia’s smaller Banderol cruise missile.
What’s inside the Zircon?
The missile uses a two-stage propulsion system. A solid-fuel booster first accelerates it to the altitude and speed needed to activate its main solid-fuel engine.
Guidance and stabilization systems initially steer the missile toward its target. During the cruise phase, the Zircon uses an inertial navigation system before switching to an active radar seeker during the final stage of flight.
The missile also carries Russia’s Baget-83 digital onboard computing system, according to HUR.
Kyiv Endures Unprecedented 5-Day Drone Blitz as Russia Alters Tactics
Its rear section features electro-hydraulic control systems and folding aerodynamic fins. The entire tail section is reportedly made from titanium.
Russia has claimed the Zircon can reach Mach 9, but HUR said the highest recorded speed is around Mach 6.8 and that the missile cannot sustain that speed throughout its flight.
The disclosure comes as Russia continues expanding its use of ballistic weapons against Ukraine.
HUR also pointed to Russia’s reported use of an upgraded ballistic missile dubbed the Iskander-1000, which reportedly has a larger engine and launch system allowing it to strike targets at greater distances.
At the same time, Ukraine is facing growing pressure on its air-defense stockpiles. Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat has warned of shortages of missiles for Patriot and other air-defense systems, including those deployed on ground and aircraft platforms.

Armen Putra, head of the Sinabung Volcano Observation Post, said a thick, dark ash column rose about 3,500 meters above the summit and drifted east and southeast.

China Focus: Modern tech helps prevent geological risks in China's Three Gorges region
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
17:07:12 CST
18:07:12 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 20, 2026 shows a drone collecting image data of a collapsed area in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Zhang Yang)
WUHAN, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Integrated modern technology is helping geologists "tame" the treacherous rock formations of the mountainous Three Gorges Reservoir region, bolstering efforts to prevent and mitigate geological disasters.
Thanks to years of efforts in field investigation and technological exploration, the Wuhan Center of China Geological Survey has established interrelated means to fend off geological disasters in this region, according to Li Ming, a senior engineer at the center.
These technological means include a multi-dimensional rock monitoring system, an integrated information platform for geological hazard prevention and control, as well as a series of ecological restoration techniques for dangerous rock masses.
The Three Gorges project is a vast multi-functional water-control system on the Yangtze River, China's longest waterway.
The Three Gorges Reservoir region is characterized by steep mountains, precipitous slopes, and complex rock formations, making it one of the areas in China most prone to geological disasters. So far, more than 3,000 potential hazard sites have been identified.
To cope with the potential hazards, the center has established an information platform for geological hazard prevention and control, integrating multi-source data including geological base maps, disaster registries and monitoring and early-warning information, Li said.
He noted that one deep rock crevice in Zigui County, central China's Hubei Province, extends more than 110 meters deep. Over 50 crevices cut through the mountain massif, forming an unstable rock body with a total volume exceeding 3 million cubic meters.
The engineer further explained that the upper section of the dangerous rocks consists of hard rock, while its lower section comprises relatively soft coal-bearing strata. The unstable rock body sits right next to the main navigation channel of the Yangtze River.
"Should it collapse and plunge into the river, the surge wave generated instantaneously would pose a severe threat to the safety of passing vessels," Li said, adding this dangerous rock mass is currently stable thanks to multiple engineering measures.
Various devices installed on the cliff face are providing round-the-clock precise monitoring of subtle deformations in the rock mass, summarizing data once every hour and uploading it in real time for monitoring and early warning, Li said.
To address the challenge of dangerous rock masses in the reservoir area, the center has developed a specialized technology by fixing such rock masses with lightweight anchor cable and explored an ecological restoration technique for rock crevices using microorganisms combined with fiber filling, according to Dai Zhenwei, who takes charge of the center's geological disaster monitoring and early warning.
The technological explorations are similar to putting a "safety belt" on the unstable rocks. They provide a new approach to solving the challenge of poor durability of traditional protective structures in water-rich environments, Dai said.
In the meantime, drones and diverse satellite monitoring devices have been put into service to conduct the round-the-clock monitoring works to assess the stability conditions affected by the fluctuations in reservoir water levels, according to Huang Jue, a senior engineer at the Wuhan center.
Huang explained that traditional manual inspections normally take a long period of time and costs are high. The drones can fly close to steep cliffs, dangerous rocks and other areas that are difficult for people to reach.
"Moreover, drones can take off immediately when traffic is disrupted after disasters occur and provide first-hand information for rescue decision-making in a timely manner," he added. ■
This photo taken on Aug. 20, 2026 shows a monitoring device in operation at an unstable rock body on a mountain in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Zhang Yang)
This photo taken on Aug. 20, 2026 shows an unstable rock body in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Zhang Yang)

Israel, Greece sign €3 billion deal to build multilayered defense based on Israeli architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:05:04 UTC
18:05:04 KST

Israel and Greece signed a €3 billion ($3.48 billion) defense agreement on Monday under which Israel will build a multilayered air-defense system for Greece, Israel’s Defense Ministry said.
The ministry said a separate supplementary agreement worth €26 million will see Israel supply Greece with Drone Dome systems designed to detect and counter unmanned aerial threats.
The signing moves forward one of the largest defense projects ever undertaken between the two countries and formally launches the implementation phase of Greece’s planned “Achilles’ Shield” air and missile defense network.
The project is expected to take about 35 months to complete.
The agreement was signed between procurement officials from the Greek Defense Ministry and SIBAT, the International Defense Cooperation Directorate at Israel’s Defense Ministry.
Greece aims to build a multilayered network capable of confronting a wide spectrum of threats, ranging from small drones and unmanned aircraft to cruise and ballistic missiles.
Under the plan, Athens is expected to integrate systems it already operates with advanced Israeli platforms including Spyder, Barak MX and David’s Sling, alongside Patriot batteries and other capabilities.
The central concept is to create a single network in which radars, sensors, command-and-control systems and interceptors can communicate with one another, allowing operators to select the most appropriate response for each incoming threat.
An advanced command-and-control system incorporating artificial intelligence capabilities is expected to sit at the heart of the network.
The system will collect information from multiple radars and sensors, identify threats and help determine which defensive layer should respond.
That has become increasingly important as military planners grapple with skies crowded by relatively inexpensive drones and other unmanned aircraft. Using a costly interceptor against every low-cost drone is neither economically nor operationally efficient.
The network is therefore intended to match each threat with the most suitable defensive response, reserving more expensive and sophisticated interceptors for targets that require them.
The agreement also contains a significant industrial component for Greece.
Around 12 Greek companies are expected to participate in the project, with their involvement valued at more than €700 million. Greek industry is expected to account for roughly 25% of the overall project.
For Athens, the goal is to ensure that the investment goes beyond the simple purchase of foreign weapons systems and also contributes to technology transfer, local expertise and the development of Greece’s domestic defense industry.
One of the key issues during negotiations was Greek access to the source code behind software operating the network.
Such access could give Greece greater independence in maintaining, modifying and upgrading the system in the future, an increasingly important issue in major advanced-weapons deals.
Monday’s signing marks another step in rapidly deepening defense ties between Israel and Greece.
For Greece, the project is designed to provide a modern, integrated defense architecture against a rapidly changing threat environment dominated increasingly by missiles and drones.
For Israel, the agreement represents another major export deal for its defense industry and further strengthens strategic cooperation with one of its closest partners in the eastern Mediterranean.

Taiwan Begins Deploying Harpoon CDS Coastal Systems Recently Received From U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:02:32 UTC
18:02:32 KST

Taiwan has begun deploying the Harpoon Coastal Defense System (CDS) anti-ship missile systems purchased from the U.S.
This was reported by the Taipei Times.
The first launchers, command vehicles, and radar systems have already arrived on the island. The military has begun preparing the equipment for operation.
The systems are currently being delivered to units of the Littoral Combat Command, which is responsible for conducting combat operations in the coastal zone.
Under the terms of the agreement, Taiwan has ordered 100 Harpoon Coastal Defense System (HCDS) coastal missile systems from the United States.
The program calls for the delivery of 400 RGM-84L-4 Harpoon Block II anti-ship missiles, 100 transport and launch vehicles, and 25 radar vehicles.
In addition, the U.S. package includes four training missiles, storage containers, spare parts, maintenance equipment, training equipment, and other components.
The total cost of the program for Taiwan exceeds $2.85 billion. The Taiwanese military plans to complete the delivery of all equipment by the end of 2028.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that in October 2025, Taiwan received its first Harpoon coastal defense systems for coastal defense.
These missile systems are intended to strengthen Taiwan’s anti-ship defense and complement domestic systems as part of efforts to deter China.
At the same time, the island is ramping up production of its own anti-ship missiles from the Hsiung Feng II and Hsiung Feng III families, forming a multi-layered coastal defense system.
The Taiwanese military is also expanding infrastructure to accommodate coastal missile units. They are constructing new positions and bases in various regions of the island, including Tainan, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung. Part of the new infrastructure is scheduled for completion by 2027.
The Harpoon has long been part of the Taiwanese Armed Forces’ arsenal. The procurement of the coastal variant of this missile also contributes to the standardization of weaponry across the Army, Air Force, and Navy.
At the same time, Taiwan is implementing a large-scale program to strengthen its defense capabilities, for which it plans to allocate 40 billion U.S. dollars. The program aims not only to enhance anti-ship defenses but also to provide additional protection for the island against air threats.
In 2026, Taiwan’s defense spending rose to 3.3% of gross domestic product. By 2030, the country plans to increase this figure to 5% of GDP, which Taiwan’s authorities describe as the largest sustained investment in the military sector in the country’s modern history.

European gas prices hit highest since January 2023 on Middle East supply fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:02:07 UTC
18:02:07 KST

Ebru Sengul Cevrioglu
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
European natural gas prices rose to their highest level since January 2023 on Monday as renewed tension in the Middle East raised concerns over further disruptions to liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the Persian Gulf.
 
The front-month Dutch TTF gas contract was trading at €69.90 per megawatt-hour (MWh) at 11.34 a.m. local time (0834 GMT), up 4.4% from Friday's close of €66.97.
 
EU gas storage facilities were 64.7% full, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE), leaving inventories below historical levels for this time of year and raising concerns over efforts to refill storage ahead of the winter heating season.
 
While milder weather forecasts for early September are expected to curb near-term demand, low storage levels and uncertainty over LNG supplies from the Gulf are putting upward pressure on prices.
 
Geopolitical tensions also added to supply concerns after the US military struck two targets on Lark Island overnight, while Iranian media reported missile launches against targets in the region following the strikes.
 
Competition with Asia could intensify
 
Disruptions linked to the conflict have raised concerns over LNG exports from major Gulf producers, particularly Qatar, tightening the global LNG market.
 
A prolonged disruption to Gulf LNG exports could force European buyers to compete more aggressively with Asian buyers for available cargoes, potentially putting further upward pressure on European gas prices.
 
Analysts say the combination of geopolitical risks, low European storage levels and tighter global LNG supply could keep the market volatile in the period ahead.

China will stop Russia from going nuclear, Finland’s Stubb says

Alexander Stubb on his arrival for a dinner hosted on the occasion of the Summit of the Coalition of the Willing to Support Ukraine at the Elysee Presidential Palace in Paris on July 13, 2026. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
China has privately assured Finland that it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in an interview.
Speaking exclusively with Paul Ronzheimer of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Stubb was emphatic when asked whether Russia could resort to nuclear weapons, arguing that Beijing provides a powerful brake on Moscow escalating its war in Ukraine.
“I had the foreign minister of China visiting me this summer, and I raised the issue,” Stubb said. “And he said, we will never allow it to happen. And I think that’s a pretty good deterrence.”
Advertisement
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met Stubb in Helsinki on July 5, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and European security among the issues discussed. China remains one of Moscow’s most important economic and diplomatic partners.
Stubb also argued that Moscow benefits from keeping Europeans fixated on the prospect of nuclear escalation or a direct attack on NATO.
“Russia wants us Europeans to sit here and discuss: Will Russia escalate? Will Russia use nuclear weapons? Will Russia attack NATO and Europe?” the Finnish leader said.
His prescription was characteristically restrained: “Stay calm, stay cool, stay collected, stay vigilant. Don’t dramatize, prepare for the worst in order to avoid it.”
That measured tone is familiar from Stubb. In May, after a drone entered Finnish airspace near Helsinki and fighter jets were deployed, he insisted Finland was “not facing any direct military threat.”
In the interview, he similarly played down fears of an imminent Russian assault on NATO, describing Moscow’s attempts to probe the alliance as “more like teasing” than preparation for war. Russia’s troops remain tied down in Ukraine, he said, while NATO’s deterrence makes a direct attack highly unlikely.
Advertisement
But Stubb also argued that Europe is approaching the point when it should reopen direct political dialogue with Moscow — a notable call from the president of a country that shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia and joined NATO after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“I’m sure we are approaching the day when it would be useful for Europeans to be in more direct contact with Russia,” he said, “especially because we need to avoid misunderstanding.”
Europe is “not there yet,” Stubb stressed, with the immediate priority remaining support for Ukraine.
“You can’t sort of press mute. You have to open the discussion,” he added.
