Baseball in Israel made history when more than 100 children from 11 cities across the country took part in the first-ever Under-12 National Tournament on July 9 and 10, with games being played simultaneously on four fields.
The American pastime has established a firm presence in the Israeli sports landscape and continues to grow, offering programs throughout the country for players of every age and level, from 5-year-olds all the way to the highest levels of international competition, including the World Baseball Classic.
At Israel’s first-ever U12 National Championship game, played at the Sportek Field in Tel Aviv’s Hayarkon Park on a hot and humid Friday, Efrat defeated Modiin in the final. While Efrat was elated with its championship victory, the achievement represented much more than a win for the players, coaches, and parents. It was also a significant victory for the steady growth and expansion of Israel’s baseball community.
The final was the culmination of two days of baseball featuring nine teams from throughout the country, including Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, Ra’anana, Misgav, Efrat, Modiin, Beit Shemesh and Bat Hefer. Teams and clubs from Misgav and Efrat, which have existed for years, met for the first time in the tournament.
The tournament also featured teams from the up-and-coming community of Karmey Gat, as well as a young startup team from Beersheba, founded by one baseball-loving father, Jonathan Leiman. A die-hard Baltimore Orioles fan, Leiman was so determined to have his children fall in love with baseball that he took responsibility for starting a team himself.
Boys and girls from all over Israel playing baseball
Boys and a few girls from all over Israel spent the two days playing baseball, eating pizza, bantering playfully, and watching games together from the stands. At the championship game - held early enough on Friday so that Shabbat observers could get home with plenty of time before the start of Shabbat - children and adults watched together as Efrat cruised to victory.
The parents, many of them immigrants from the United States, enjoyed communicating in English with others who had similarly moved to Israel and found baseball to be a useful tool for providing what many described as a “soft landing” for their children.
The number of teams and players gathered in Tel Aviv on that sunny Friday was a testament to just how far baseball has come in Israel. It was not always this way.
For many Jews around the world, Israeli baseball has typically been associated with the storybook run of Team Israel at the World Baseball Classic and its appearances on the Olympic stage. Many baseball-loving Jews have taken pride in seeing some of their favorite Major League Baseball players - including Danny Valencia, Ike Davis, Kevin Youkilis, and Brad Ausmus - wearing yarmulkes, standing on the base paths for Hatikvah, and competing for or managing Team Israel.
But as the successful U12 championship demonstrated, baseball in Israel is about much more than its national team. It is also about the dedicated parents, coaches, players, and organizers who are building the sport from the ground up.
Each club is run by a dedicated Regional Director, who serves as the engine of growth for baseball in each city. In Jerusalem, Callie Mitchell, a Christian mother of four and daughter of longtime Major League Baseball catcher, coach, and manager Jerry Narron, serves as the Jerusalem Regional Director for the Israel Association of Baseball (IAB) and directs the Jerusalem Lions Baseball nonprofit.
Mitchell has helped introduce baseball to children ages 5 to 18, as well as to adults, and is involved in many of the day-to-day nuts-and-bolts issues unique to running a baseball program in Israel - from setting up WhatsApp groups and ordering buses to making soccer fields work as baseball practice fields and securing baseballs, gloves, and catcher’s equipment through Amazon and US-based baseball connections.
The first Hebrew-language baseball program in the country
Mitchell enjoys watching what her colleagues are accomplishing with their teams and programs throughout Israel. She praises Judah in Bat Hefer, who “brings a baseball aesthetic to the field. He makes dugouts, backstops, a round portable pitcher’s mound, and beautiful shelving for his shed. It’s really inspiring, and I love what he’s doing for the children in his program.”
In Misgav, Yaniv Rosenfeld is introducing baseball to native Israeli sabras. He goes into schools and teaches baseball during sports and English classes. Rosenfeld has built the only real Hebrew-language baseball program in the country so far, expanding the sport in northern Israel even during these past years of war, sirens and conflict.
Jeff Oshrin, manager of the Efrat team, shares Mitchell’s enthusiasm for watching baseball grow in Hebrew.
“In Gezer, they play baseball in Hebrew!” he said, noting that in Misgav and Gezer, more and more Israelis are playing the sport. “There are Israelis teaching Israelis how to play baseball!”
Oshrin has enjoyed watching baseball grow and thrive in his community of Efrat and takes great pride in what the community has accomplished.
“We are immensely proud of what we have brought to Efrat. Baseball is our rock - and it has helped ease the aliyah stresses for many who have moved to Efrat. There are currently programs for all ages and batting cages, bleachers, and a lit field. We play for the love of the game. We have built something very special.”
The primary goal for 2026 and beyond, according to Israel Association of Baseball President Ari Varon, is for baseball in Israel to provide “a complete pathway from first grade through adulthood.”
Baseball is both a team sport and an individual sport, allowing players to pursue personal excellence while also emphasizing cooperation and collaboration with their teammates.
Varon and the IAB executive board, with the organization celebrating its 40th anniversary this year, are focusing on several goals and strategies to continue expanding baseball in Israel. They include an emphasis on increasing participation and strengthening local clubs.
“Excellence remains essential, but excellence cannot be built sustainably without a broad and growing base,” the IAB notes. “For this stage of baseball in Israel, quantity must come before quality.”
The organization stresses that “a larger player base is the foundation from which stronger clubs, better competition, deeper coaching systems, and higher-level national teams can emerge.”
The IAB recognizes that baseball is competing with two hugely popular sports in Israel - soccer and basketball. But the organization believes baseball can offer an important alternative for children who give up on those sports because they are too time-consuming or competitive, yet still desire the opportunity to compete.
The IAB is therefore looking for ways to get more children - especially those in first through sixth grades - playing baseball in more communities across Israel.
Varon and the IAB acknowledge that, unlike soccer and basketball, many Israelis still do not know much about baseball.
“We need school exposure, community events, introductory sessions, visible local activity, social media, tournaments, family events, and repeated opportunities to try the game,” Varon said.
He elaborated on the organization’s long-term vision.
“The long-term objective is the development of a complete baseball ecosystem in which a child can discover the game in first grade, continue through elementary and middle school, compete at higher levels in high school, play in adult and Premier League competition, and eventually return as a parent, coach, volunteer, or club leader with children of his or her own.”
During the past year, baseball has expanded into Kiryat Gat and Beersheba, with further development underway in Even Yehuda. The IAB is also working to create baseball opportunities for people living in communities near the Gaza border and to expand the sport in northern Israel.
Varon notes that “baseball can offer children routine, teamwork, physical activity, personal goals, mentorship, and a safe place to belong.” He says that growing baseball in the Gaza border communities and in the North is “part of both a sports-development strategy and a broader commitment to resilience, excellence, and community.”
The IAB sums up its growth plan with three Ps: Players, people and places.
The leagues will recruit and retain players who will progress through the various age groups. People will include more coaches, umpires, volunteers and commissioners. And places will include additional fields and facilities, including indoor training centers.
Varon concludes with a vision that extends far beyond youth baseball.
“The long-term vision is not a youth program with an endpoint. It is a baseball life cycle. A healthy sports culture should allow a player to enter elementary school, continue through teenage competition, participate in adult baseball, and remain connected to the sport even after regular competitive play ends.
“The Premier League and other adult frameworks are therefore an important part of the development model, even though the largest numerical emphasis remains on younger ages. When former players become coaches, parents, officials, donors, board members, and club founders, the sport begins to reproduce itself.
“That is the point at which baseball becomes more than a collection of programs. It becomes a sustainable community and a permanent part of Israeli sport.”
If all goes according to plan, these homegrown young 12-year-olds may one day grow up to represent Team Israel at the highest levels of international competition - perhaps even at the World Baseball Classic and the Olympics.

Expansion of electricity generation capacity continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:49:18 UTC

Expansion of electricity generation capacity continues
TEHRAN- An official has stated that in the renewable energy sector, production capacity has increased from 1,250 megawatts to approximately 7,000 megawatts, and in the thermal power plant sector, about 3,000 megawatts have been added to the country's generation capacity.
According to the Mehr News Agency from Iran's Power Generation and Distribution Company (known as Tavanir), Abolfazl Asadi, Deputy for Planning and Economic Affairs at Tavanir Company, in a radio interview referring to the one-year performance of the country's electricity industry, said: "To ensure reliable and stable electricity for the people, the most important challenge ahead is the imbalance between production and consumption, for which there are two fundamental solutions: first, increasing production capacity, and second, optimizing consumption. In recent years, to encourage investors to build renewable power plants, the Green Board was created, and for thermal power plants, the Free Board was established on the Energy Exchange. These boards have made it possible for private sector investors to offer their generated electricity on the Energy Exchange, with buyers also coming from the private sector. This new model is based on the obligations of the Seventh Development Plan, which envisions the expansion of Energy Exchange transactions for the Ministry of Energy, and we have taken steps to realize it."
* Historic leap in renewables and introduction of energy savings board to electricity market
Stating that significant investment has been made in the electricity generation sector during the 14th government, he added: "In the renewable energy sector, production capacity has increased from 1,250 megawatts to about 5,600 to 7,000 megawatts, and in the thermal power plant sector, about 3,000 megawatts have been added to the country's generation capacity. Additionally, for the first time, the Energy Savings Board was unveiled on the Energy Exchange, which has provided a suitable financial model for investors. Under this model, any industry that invests in energy savings can offer and sell its saved electricity on the market. This initiative has increased the number of energy savings contracts from 2 contracts per year to 59 contracts in the lighting sector and especially in cooling, including the replacement of water cooler motors with low-consumption (BLDC) motors and the replacement of low-efficiency coolers with high-efficiency ones."
The Deputy for Planning and Economic Affairs at Tavanir Company, emphasizing that the Seventh Development Plan also stresses the expansion of Energy Exchange transactions, stated: "Large industries are obligated to supply part of their electricity needs through the construction of dedicated power plants by the end of the plan. Fortunately, industries have moved in this direction, and so far about 100 to 200 megawatts of this capacity has been realized. This approach both helps boost supply and production and, through consumption optimization, gradually reduces the imbalance. By strengthening these boards, we are changing past practices and will increase the pace of progress."
* Removing transmission bottlenecks with 140 mega-projects and developing small-scale power plants
Referring to investments made in the electricity transmission and distribution network, he added: "Fortunately, the goals we summarized in the form of 140 mega-projects in September last year have been realized in the transmission and distribution sectors, and we currently have no limitations in transmission capacity. Additionally, small-scale power plants (2 to 5 megawatts) are being built by the private sector at consumption sites, which, in addition to supporting the network, can also offer their electricity on the Free Board."
The Deputy for Planning and Economic Affairs at Tavanir Company concluded by expressing gratitude for the cooperation of the people, saying: "All these achievements have been made under the special circumstances of war and unprecedented heat. The people, through their savings and cooperation, played an effective role in passing the peak consumption period, which deserves appreciation and thanks. We hope that with the continuation of this cooperation and the development of Energy Exchange boards, we can provide more reliable electricity for the people."

‘Europe’s climate and security challenges are inseparable,’ Hoekstra tells Euronews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:47:16 UTC
15:47:16 KST

In an exclusive Euronews interview, Hoekstra argues climate resilience, energy security, and geopolitical independence are now inseparable. EU gas storage remains below target as the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked.
Europe must spend more upfront to protect itself from increasingly severe climate disasters, European Union Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews, arguing that paying for fires, floods and other damage after they strike will ultimately cost far more.
"All evidence shows that making the upfront investments is way cheaper than just being hit by fire, being hit by floods and then paying for the damage. That's just way more costly," Hoekstra told Europe Today, Euronews' flagship morning show.
Describing the summer as “dramatic”, the Dutch Commissioner said the EU was better prepared than last year, with more firefighters, planes and helicopters deployed, but that the scale of destruction had barely improved.
An area twice the size of Luxembourg was lost to fires, while estimates of the economic damage range from €50 billion to €70 billion or more. Spain and France lost thousands of hectares to the blazes, while at least 14 first responders died fighting the fires.
The Commissioner rejected the idea that the EU can attach a single figure to climate resilience. Instead, he called for a more fundamental overhaul of how infrastructure is built, with bridges, for example, rebuilt to withstand the next flood rather than simply replacing what was lost.
Pressed by Euronews for a specific figure, Hoekstra did not commit to one but suggested the bulk of the funding would still come from national budgets.
"The reality is that we need to become much more granular and do a couple of things at the same time. That means we need the same assessment of the type of impact we're going to see for the whole Union," Hoekstra said.
"We need to be crystal clear about who is responsible for what. What is for the local governments, what is for regional governments, what is for national governments and what is for Europe."
But EU governments are under pressure to reduce spending, with tension mounting as talks resume to decide on the EU’s proposed long-term budget for 2027–2034, with Germany, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden seeking to cut it.
Hoekstra acknowledged the fiscal tight situation but maintained that upfront investment is cheaper than repeatedly paying for climate damage. He also pushed back against attempts to frame climate action and economic competitiveness as competing priorities.
"There is no easy way out and there's no alternative to continuing with our climate ambition," the Commissioner added, after a summer of devastating fires and heatwaves that caused an excess death of at least 30,000 people, according to the European Mortality Monitoring Platform, which tracks data across 23 countries.
Hoekstra's preferred formula combines climate action, competitiveness and European independence. This means continuing the green transition while reducing Europe's dependence on China for clean technologies, Hoekstra noted. He pointed to Finland, Denmark and Sweden as examples where climate policy and competitiveness can reinforce each other.
"It is imperative that we marry-bridge climate action with competitiveness and with independence," stressed Hoekstra.
For the Dutch Commissioner, the direction of the bloc's climate policy is directly linked to Europe's energy vulnerability, particularly amid uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for 20% of the world's oil and gas transit and affects global energy prices.
He also stressed that, in the long term, a successful climate transition will boost the EU's economic sovereignty.
"In the medium term, by far our best bet is to move to a completely different energy system and that is where the money should be going," Hoekstra said.
The EU cannot rely indefinitely on imported fossil fuels, he warned, citing the around 80% dependence on gas imports and 95% on oil imports as a signal the EU has “a very bad hand”. His proposed escape route includes more nuclear, solar and wind, combined with electrification and more European energy production.
On the immediate gas situation, which is currently at its lowest level (around 62%) since 2011, the Commissioner said EU countries must continue filling storage and prepare for the possibility of low storage combined with a severe winter, which he calls a scenario “no one can afford”.
"Our gas comes primarily from the US and from Norway. That makes it slightly easier, but of course it is a global market, so there is a fight for this gas potentially coming to us as well," Hoekstra said.

Vilnius council approves 83-year lease extension for American school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Vilnius City Council has approved extending the lease of two municipal buildings used by the American International School of Vilnius until 2109, extending the current agreement by 74 years.
The decision, approved last week, covers a school building and a sports hall on Subačiaus Street. The existing lease was due to expire in 2035.
Vilnius Mayor Valdas Benkunskas said the long-term agreement was important for ensuring the school’s continued operation and strengthening ties between Vilnius, Lithuania and the United States.
“The main thing is that the American side sees Vilnius and Lithuania as its partner and sees the continuity of relations even 100 years into the future,” Benkunskas said. He added that the agreement sends a clear signal that diplomats’ children, Lithuanians and other foreigners attending the school have a future in Vilnius.
The American International School says it has invested about 3.5 million euros in the municipal property and has committed to investing at least another 1 million euros by the end of 2027.
The school currently pays 0.29 euros per square meter per month, for a total monthly rent of 1,101.50 euros. The lease provides for the rent to be indexed every five years.
Council member Aleksandras Nemunaitis questioned the economic benefit to the city, arguing that municipal property should not be leased to a private institution below market rates.
“Indexing is a very good thing, but we should not be indexing from 29 cents,” Nemunaitis said.
He also said the school was a commercial private institution and noted that, according to his figures, about 70% of its students last year were Lithuanian citizens.
Council member Almantas Stankūnas similarly questioned why about 3,800 square meters of municipal buildings in central Vilnius should be leased for a symbolic price for more than 80 years.
He also noted that annual tuition at the school can exceed 20,000 euros, arguing that the municipal support primarily benefits children from affluent families.
Council member Gintautas Babravičius defended the arrangement, describing the school as a symbol of Lithuanian-US relations and saying its broader diplomatic significance outweighed the financial considerations.
The Lithuanian parliament in April ratified a government agreement with the United States allowing the school to lease state or municipal real estate for up to 99 years for purposes related to its establishment, operation, organisation or education.
The agreement also allows the school to build, renovate and maintain leased property at its own expense.

Rebuilding damaged industries to protect production, ensure financing supply chain stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:44:46 UTC
15:44:46 KST

Rebuilding damaged industries to protect production, ensure financing supply chain stability
TEHRAN- The US-Zionist imposed war, in addition to causing direct damage to some production units, also affected parts of the country's industrial supply chains. However, planning for the swift return of damaged units to the production cycle and preventing the halt of related industries has now become one of the central axes of industrial policymaking. In this path, securing financial resources, prioritizing strategic industries, and utilizing domestic capacities form the basis of support measures.
In a report that comes below, IRNA has investigated the issue:
The new strategy of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade in this regard is not limited merely to rebuilding the buildings and equipment of damaged units, but is pursued with the aim of preserving production capacity and strengthening the resilience of supply chains. Alongside reconstruction, the modernization of industries is also on the agenda so that directly damaged industries, units affected by supply chain disruptions, and small and vulnerable enterprises, depending on the type of damage, are covered by support packages and reconstruction programs.
To achieve this goal, financial resources are needed, and it has been decided that the use of capital market capacities and modern financial instruments, alongside reconstruction funds, should also be considered. Saeed Shojaei, Deputy Minister for Planning at the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, has announced the issuance of a permit for 100,000 billion tomans in facilities for the reconstruction of industries, stating that this permit has been issued by the cabinet and that, for its implementation, approval from the Supreme Supervisory Council on Banks is also required.
According to him, measures such as obtaining approval for certain budgetary items, including the issuance of 25,000 billion tomans in bonds, are also necessary from higher authorities, including the heads of the three branches of government or the Supreme National Security Council, and must be taken into consideration.
Alongside securing financial resources for damaged units, another important issue concerning the regeneration of industries has also been taken into account. Under this plan, industries are divided into three categories: "directly damaged," "damaged within the supply chain," and "small and vulnerable industries," with special operational packages developed for each category.
In this plan, a specialized platform has been designed for registering the type of affliction of each company. Through this system, the demands of industries are connected to a network of expert consultants and management specialists in the country, so that the reconstruction process can begin swiftly based on scientific methods and lived experiences from the era of the Sacred Defense (Iran-Iraq war).
In this regard, Tahmoures Lahouti Ashkouri, Deputy Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade and CEO of the Small Industries and Industrial Parks Organization of Iran, in an exclusive interview with IRNA, while explaining his organization's new strategies in dealing with the consequences of the war, stated that "protecting production capacities" and "reviving damaged industrial units" are the two main pillars on the agenda of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade.
He emphasized that maintaining the stability of the production flow and precise monitoring of the supply chain of essential goods goes beyond a routine task; it is a defensive priority for the organization to prevent the disruption of upstream and downstream production links, from agriculture and processing industries to the final consumer market.
Referring to the damage inflicted on industrial infrastructure across 17 provinces of the country, Lahouti Ashkouri said: "One-third of all damaged units were concentrated in industrial towns and zones—units that played a vital role in supplying industrial requirements and strategic goods."
The CEO of the Small Industries Organization identified "financing" as the main bottleneck in industrial reconstruction and announced that a special support package has been drafted with the active participation of the Ministries of Economy, Labor, and the Central Bank, and is in the final stages of approval. After final approval by the Supreme National Security Council and the heads of the three branches of government, this plan will be communicated as the operational framework for reconstruction.
He added that special arrangements have been made for the allocation of land in industrial towns with the lowest down payments and long grace periods. Furthermore, for more than 1,500 industrial units, financial processes have been facilitated with the aim of settling debts arising from usage rights, in order to minimize the financial risks faced by enterprises.
Lahouti Ashkouri emphasized that resource allocation will prioritize medical equipment, pharmaceutical and food industries, as well as "leading industries," as these sectors act as the driving engine for downstream chains and ensure the stability of the entire country's industrial ecosystem.
According to the explanations provided by officials of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade and the Small Industries Organization, the national strategy for rebuilding damaged industries represents a shift from mere physical reconstruction toward the resilient regeneration of the country's industrial ecosystem.

GERB leader Borissov urges right-wing parties to unite for presidential vote

Candidates from individual right-wing parties stand no chance in the upcoming presidential election unless the democratic right unites, GERB leader Boyko Borissov told reporters. He said the party was still considering different options for taking part in the vote.
“There are about ten days left for common sense to prevail, so that the entire right can stand against the left,” Borissov said. Otherwise, he added, Iliana Iotova might as well be congratulated now.
According to the GERB leader, this presidential election is different from previous ones. He said the incumbent president would be nominated by an initiative committee and backed by the governing Progressive Bulgaria party. Former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, the likely candidate of We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, would also be nominated by an initiative committee and would then seek broader support.
GERB MP Delyan Dobrev, one of the party’s prominent figures, said GERB should field its own candidate.
“If Gyurov is supposed to be the candidate who unites the right, no one from GERB will vote for him.”
Dobrev said three figures could take responsibility for GERB’s presidential bid: Burgas Mayor Dimitar Nikolov, GERB Deputy Chair Tomislav Donchev and former prime minister Rosen Zhelyazkov.

Foreign students beneficial to Dutch economy, CPB says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:39:25 UTC
15:39:25 KST

Foreign students beneficial to Dutch economy, CPB says
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
International students in the Netherlands more than pay for themselves over their lifetimes, and capping their number would do little to ease the housing shortage, according to new research by the government’s economic policy analysis bureau CPB.
The money the government spends on them – student grants, healthcare, social security – is on average more than recouped, the CPB said, mainly because a growing share stay after graduating and pay tax.
More international students do add to housing pressure in the short term, the bureau found. But over time the effect is limited, because the market adjusts – and how far it does depends on housing policy, not student numbers.
A university graduate from outside the European Economic Area contributes about €243,000 over their lifetime, the CPB calculates, and one from an EEA country €82,500. For graduates of universities of applied sciences, the figures are €117,000 and €13,300.
Staying on
 Around 17% of students in the Netherlands last year came from abroad, most from the EEA – the EU plus Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. Like Dutch students, they pay only the statutory tuition fee, €2,694 this year, and can apply for student finance under certain conditions.
Students from outside the EEA have no right to student finance and pay the full cost of their courses, so cost the government little.
They are also staying on in greater numbers. Five years after leaving higher education, about one in five EEA graduates and two in five from outside the bloc are still in the Netherlands – roughly a quarter more than a decade ago.
“The longer they work here, the more tax they pay,” CPB researcher Paul Verstraten told broadcaster NOS. Graduates are also finding work faster, he said, partly because of the tight labour market.
Changing course
 The study was commissioned by the education ministry itself, now run by D66’s Rianne Letschert, whose approach is more accommodating than the previous Schoof cabinet. Graduates who stay make relatively little use of social security and are mostly highly educated, Verstraten noted, so cutting numbers is not obviously the answer.
In 2024 the Schoof cabinet wanted to reduce enrolment to save nearly €300 million and ease pressure on housing and public services. Five universities warned the cuts would hit the economy hard.
Letschert’s ministry has since left universities and colleges to manage the intake themselves, steering recruitment towards shortage sectors such as engineering and healthcare. International student numbers fell for the first time in two decades this year.

TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Japan on Monday kicked off a new round of discharge of nuclear-contaminated wastewater from the crippled Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant into the sea, marking the 23rd such release since the controversial operation began in 2023.
The discharge started at 11:29 a.m. local time. According to the plant's operator, Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (TEPCO), about 7,800 tonnes of wastewater containing approximately 1.2 trillion becquerels of radioactive tritium will be released into the ocean.
The latest discharge, also the fifth round in fiscal 2026, is scheduled to continue through Sept. 18.
In August 2023, Japan unilaterally launched the discharge of nuclear-contaminated water from the Fukushima Daiichi plant into the ocean despite concerns and opposition from the international community. Aug. 24 this year marked three years since the controversial operation began, with a cumulative total of approximately 173,000 tonnes of wastewater released to date.
According to data from TEPCO, as of Aug. 13, storage tanks at the Fukushima Daiichi plant still held about 1.235 million tonnes of nuclear-contaminated water. ■

Across China: China builds pest radar network to protect grain crops
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:38:58 CST
15:38:58 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- A network of insect-tracking radars is being expanded across China to help farmers battle migratory pests that threaten the country's food supply.
In east China's Zhejiang Province, a key migration corridor where northern and southern rice-growing regions meet, a radar station operates at the edge of a paddy field. When a small pest flies past, the system can capture its size, weight and other identifying data.
One target is the rice plant hopper, a migratory insect weighing just 1 milligram and measuring a few millimeters long. It pierces rice stalks and sucks out sap.
During a demonstration test, technicians flew a drone carrying only one rice plant hopper about 300 meters from the radar. Moments later, a monitoring screen displayed the pest's body length, width and weight. Such milligram-level measurements can now be achieved with precision, said Liu Dazhong, an associate researcher at Zhejiang-based Xianghu Laboratory, which monitors major migratory pests. "It has placed us at the forefront globally," Liu noted.
This tiny pest can pose a substantial threat. Of the 11 pests on China's list of first-class agricultural pests, eight can ride seasonal winds and travel more than 100 km overnight across regions. From 2021 to 2024, these eight pests infested an average of 83 million hectares of grain fields annually, accounting for 40 percent of all pest-related damage to the country's rice, wheat and corn, according to the National Agro-Tech Extension and Service Center.
Wu Kongming, an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said a single adult migratory pest can produce over 1,000 offspring. "The offspring of one adult pest can reduce yields by one-third or even more," he noted.
Outer winds from recent typhoons have accelerated pest migration into the region this month, while high field humidity has created favorable conditions for rapid plant hopper breeding. The pressure on pest and disease control has, as a result, increased greatly in this area recently. Scientists warn that once pest numbers get too high, rice plants will turn yellow and fall over. In severe cases, it may lead to total crop failure.
Rice grower Sheng Yunxiong, based in central China's Hubei Province, said he had rarely seen so many plant hoppers in previous years, but their numbers surged suddenly this August. "I followed the guidance from agricultural technicians and applied pesticide in time. The infestation is now under control," he said. He added that many farmers used to mistakenly believe that rice near maturity did not need pest protection.
Chinese research teams have developed multiple types of insect radars that now provide real-time data on where pests originate, their numbers and their trajectory. The system moves the warning window from "detection after arrival" to "alert before landing," giving farmers 24 to 48 hours of advance notice, a critical period for coordinated control efforts.
Across the country, 65 insect radars are now connected to a national monitoring platform. By 2030, the network is expected to exceed 150 radars, covering all primary migration corridors and eliminating blind spots in core farming areas.
It will form a three-tier defense: radar-based high-altitude monitoring, aerial interception of adult insects and precise ground trapping.
Moreover, migratory pests are a global problem. For example, the fall armyworm, a pest native to the tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas, has devastated maize and other staple crops across Africa since its arrival in 2016. In January 2019, the fall armyworm migrated from Myanmar into southwest China's Yunnan Province, and quickly spread to 18 provincial-level regions. Such threats make international cooperation essential.
China has, notably, shared its tech expertise in cross-border migratory pest control with other Asian countries including Laos, Vietnam and Kazakhstan, via the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization's South-South cooperation programs. ■

15:38:44 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Chinese laborers and students who were killed in a massacre in Japan after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake were remembered at memorial events in Tokyo on Sunday, with participants calling on the Japanese government to squarely confront the country's history as a perpetrator.
This year marks the 103rd anniversary of the atrocity. On Sunday morning, a group of people gathered at Sakasai Bridge in Tokyo's Koto Ward to commemorate Wang Xitian, a leader of Chinese workers in Japan who was killed by Japanese soldiers during the massacre.
Wang was born in 1896 in Changchun City of northeast China's Jilin Province. In 1922, he founded and served as the chairman of the "mutual aid association of Chinese workers in Japan," dedicating himself to assistance work for Chinese laborers and confronting the Japanese government on their behalf.
Following the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, Wang was killed by the Japanese military while working to help Chinese laborers and investigate the truth behind the massacre. He was only 27 at the time of his death.
Naoyuki Maniwa, a member of the Koto City Assembly, said, "Each of us bears responsibility for our own country's history. As a politician, it is absolutely unacceptable to show no reflection on the mistakes our country has made and the harm it has inflicted in the past."
In the afternoon, another memorial ceremony for the Chinese victims of the massacre was held at the Higashi-ojima Culture Center.
Speaking at the event, Zhou Chunhua and Zhou Songquan, descendants of Chinese victims, said efforts must continue to uncover the truth of this chapter of history and pursue fairness and justice. They also called on the Japanese government to confront historical crimes and responsibility.
Japanese political figures including Mizuho Fukushima, leader of Japan's Social Democratic Party, and Yoshifu Arita, a member of the House of Representatives, sent written messages to the event. They said Japan should face its history squarely, eliminate discrimination and xenophobia, and prevent tragedies from happening again.
On Sept. 1, 1923, a 7.9-magnitude earthquake struck Japan's Kanto area, resulting in over 140,000 casualties. In the ensuing chaos, Japanese militarist mobs fanned xenophobic sentiment and fabricated pretexts to incite violence against Chinese and Korean laborers. Over 750 Chinese laborers and students, as well as more than 6,000 Korean laborers living in Japan, were brutally killed.
In 1924, Japanese authorities formulated a compensation plan for the victims of the massacre, but it remains unfulfilled to date. ■

'They wrote little letters': How kids in Portugal are making money off their neighbours' plastic waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:37:36 UTC
15:37:36 KST

The first ever bottle deposit return scheme in southern Europe is helping the environment - and funding kids' bucket list trips.
Sisters Ariela and Alice had already been using Portugal's bottle return scheme to earn money but since June they have upped the ante: now, instead of just returning their own bottles, they are asking their neighbours' for their empty plastic bottles and making money off those too.
Since April this year, when the Volta scheme launched, plastic bottles in Portugal have a €0.10 deposit included in the cost. If you return the empty bottle to a supermarket with a Volta machine, you're given a receipt which can be exchanged for discounts or cash.
Ariela and Alice have big plans for their cash: Alice, who is ten, wants to do a three-week exchange in South Korea. Her sister Ariela, 13, wants to do the same in the United States
"They wrote little letters and I printed them with their project and the time when they were going to collect the bag," explains their mother, Karina Lauro, who moved to Portugal from Rio de Janeiro in 2024. "They leave the bag at people's doors and every day, at nine o'clock in the evening, they go back to pick up that bag with the bottles."
The empty bottles are then exchanged for money. With a clear goal: by June next year they aim to collect 120,000 bottles so they can make €6,000 each.
It was the girls who came up with the idea of using Volta to raise funds and to involve the neighbours, after their mother warned them that just using the bottles from home would not make them much money. "It was very little, wasn't it? Because it was just the bottles from our house," says Karina Lauro. "Basically, if it were only us, there would be no way."
Some people go through rubbish bins to find bottles to return
Under the Volta scheme, plastic bottles of up to three litres now carry a deposit charge of ten cents. This money can then be reclaimed if the bottles are returned. The bottles are returned via machines in supermarkets, which issue a receipt that can be converted into discounts or cash. Kiosks are also starting to appear in other busy locations or to process large quantities of bottles.
This system, run by SDR Portugal, is the country's way of responding to the Single-Use Plastics Directive (DSUP), which requires 90 per cent of deposit bottles to be collected by 2029. The directive allows European Union countries to set up deposit systems in order to reach this target.
In Portugal, the system was rolled out in April. As consumers were getting used to it, reports began to appear of bins being rummaged through, leaving rubbish scattered on the ground. In Lisbon, several residents and parish councils complained about the rubbish pile-ups. At the end of July, the PSP arrested a man for rummaging through bins, whom it described as a "rubbish miner".
This scenario was not entirely new. In an interview with Euronews last year, the president of the Portuguese Environment Agency (APA), José Pimenta Machado, spoke about possible associated environmental risks. The report also noted that in Germany, which has had a deposit return system since 2003, it is common for homeless people to rummage through rubbish in search of bottles.
But not everyone who looks for bottles is homeless. Some are doing it as a way of earning a bit of extra money and, for some young people, it has become a real summer challenge.
That is the case for two young men who work at a beach concession in Loulé. In an interview with Rádio Renascença, they insist that they do not go "digging around in the rubbish", but simply put into Volta the bottles they already have to pick up at work.
Karina Lauro is aware of the phenomenon of people searching through bins for bottles, including "people who are indeed saving them to have an income". But in this case her daughters do not go through rubbish either.
"No, they're always given to us. We don't pick anything out of the rubbish," the mother explains. "Besides, we don't go out on the streets looking for them; we go straight to people's homes."
This is also an environmental project, supporting recycling, already with another of Alice's dreams in mind: studying at Harvard.
"The aim behind this is for them really to reach that recycling figure, so that it also counts as an environmental project for Alice," the mother explains, recalling the entry criteria for North American universities.
Plastic bottles are funding food for rescued cats
António Casa Branca is the owner of Gatil Original, a sanctuary in Vendas Novas that takes in older, sick and vulnerable cats. Around a month and a half ago he had an idea: to set up partnerships with local businesses.
Partner businesses hand over their empty bottles to the cattery, which takes them back and keeps the money. The funds are then used to buy food for the animals.
"In Vendas Novas there are lots of 'bifana' [a classic Portuguese sandwich] shops and we try to set up a partnership whereby every week we go and collect the bags they set aside from that recyclable rubbish, those plastic bottles and cans," he explains. "We then go to the machine, exchange them for vouchers and go to the supermarket to swap them for pâté."
On the first attempt, donations from one bifana restaurant filled a van.
"One of the bifana owners filled my van with bags of litre-and-a-half bottles and tiny ones. I filled the van and it came to around €50," António says.
The cattery already has five partnerships, which also involve a pastry shop, and there is even an accountancy office keen to help by donating the bottles used by its staff. António Casa Branca's plan is to go around the partner businesses every day after work. "For me it's gold. I don't mind going out to ask, to beg," he says.
"If we can get €50 a week from each restaurant, from three or four restaurants, that is already enough to cover the animals' food."
It's working: António Casa Branca manages to buy all the food for the roughly 40 cats he has at the cattery. Other costs, such as the vet's bill and medicines, are still unaccounted for.
Volta machines give the option to send the money to charity. Volta's website gives the examples of the Portuguese Firefighters' League, Caritas, the League for the Protection of the Environment and the Portuguese League for Animal Rights. The organisations available depend on the machine.
But some organisations are going further in this fundraising drive. They are asking donors to bring them refund vouchers or even the bottles themselves, taking on the task of depositing them at collection points.
"We can't let this fall apart"
For the past two weeks there has been a bin at Ota Parish Council's office for residents to leave their empty plastic bottles. In the centre of the parish a 1,000-litre container has also been left for bottles to be deposited - it filled up with bottles in just a few days.
"As we have a lot of people using it, we're thinking of putting out two more containers, one at each end of the parish," explains Nelson Mota.
Nelson grew up in Ota and remains closely connected to the area. He is part of Guarda à Casa, a civic movement that wants to restore the building where the forest rangers of the Serra da Ota used to live.
"We decided that we can do something; we can't let this fall apart," he says. "If the competent authorities can't reach us, because this year, with the deluges we've had, it's normal that the councils can't support certain projects."
Then the idea emerged of using the Volta system to raise money.
"Volta is an easy way to raise some money. It's not substantial amounts, but the kind of sums you need to start organising some events."
As well as the containers, the group also has the support of the Recreational and Sports Association, which is donating the bottles from its bar. Members of the civic group are also collecting bottles from friends and at work and then, themselves, reclaim the money at a Volta machine.
"I myself made a deposit yesterday; it came to €11.60. In other words, it was 116 bottles," explains Nelson Mota. "I handed in 116 bottles, which didn't take up space in the car, and it gave me €10 with no difficulty. I think it's worth it, isn't it?" he tells Euronews.
The success of the initiative does not surprise Nelson Mota: "Of course we're getting a good reception. People in Ota, whenever there are initiatives of this kind, always try to help. That's just how people are there."
"I never imagined it would get this big"
Ariela and Alice's project is being given a big boost by social media. Their "Sonho na garrafa" pages explain the collection process and keep a running tally of how many bottles they have managed to gather so far.
"I wanted to create that social-media presence and show this project so that it would reach people and be recorded for her future," says Karina Lauro, referring to her daughter's university dream. "But I never imagined it would get this big, because people started to embrace it."
The Instagram account has more than 12,000 followers and the TikTok has more than 250,000 likes. In this way more people have started to send encouraging messages and also to want to contribute, including people living abroad.
"Once the internet started to see them, people began wanting to donate bottles as well, to donate the money from exchanging bottles," says the mother, adding that she only accepts donations if they come from bottle deposits.
"There is a person in Ireland who sends money every week. In Ireland it's 25 cents per bottle, so she exchanges them there and sends it to the children."
Another big boost came from restaurants, which also wanted to get involved in the project. It is the mother herself who now collects the bottles from the restaurants, once a week.
By mid-August they had collected more than 5,300 bottles and €537.
"But now more messages have started to come in from other restaurants, wanting to help as well. So, with the restaurants coming on board, that number will probably double."

Car inspection rules relaxed on 1 September: What changes for you?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:37:31 UTC
15:37:31 KST

From 1 September, the deadlines and conditions for vehicle inspections are being relaxed in Flanders. Passenger cars over four years old will now only need to be inspected every two years. The insurance certificate will no longer be checked during the inspection, a separate inspection of the tow bar will no longer be required, and the deadline for having major faults repaired will be extended to two months.
At present a passenger vehicle requires its first MOT or car inspection when the car reaches the age of four, calculated from the date of first registration. After that, the car must be inspected every year. From 1 September, this will only be required every two years.
In addition, the insurance certificate will no longer be checked during the MOT or car inspection. This check is already carried out at the federal level using ANPR cameras. A separate inspection of the tow bar is also no longer required.
If major faults are identified, the driver will be given two months to rectify them. Previously, this period was 15 days. Furthermore, the three-month temporary roadworthiness certificate issued for administrative shortcomings is being abolished. You will now receive a roadworthiness certificate with the standard period of validity, but the missing or incorrect documents must still be rectified.
The inspection date is also changing for other vehicle categories. Vans and light goods vehicles will gradually transition from annual to biennial inspections. In the first phase, this will apply to vehicles that are no more than four years old. Taxis and buses will now only need to be inspected every other year.
Not everybody happy
The federation representing the sector GOCA Vlaanderen and trade unions, amongst others, have previously criticised the reforms, which, according to the trade union front, “seriously undermine road safety, the objectivity of inspections and employment in the sector”.
Nothing changes in Wallonia and Brussels. A roadworthiness certificate therefore remains valid for just one year there. However, you do not have to have your car inspected in the region where the vehicle is registered or where you live. A roadworthiness certificate is therefore valid throughout the country.
Motoring organisation Touring fears ‘inspection tourism’, whereby motorists from Brussels and Wallonia have their cars inspected in Flanders. Touring is therefore calling for the same rules to apply throughout Belgium.
Further relaxations in the pipeline
From next year, further relaxations will be introduced. The second-hand vehicle inspection required when selling a car or motorbike will be abolished from 1 January, but only for cars sold within Belgium.
Motoring organisation Touring considers this a regrettable situation, as it means buyers have less certainty about the condition and faults of a second-hand car. Touring recommends having second-hand cars inspected by an independent expert or mechanic before purchase.
Furthermore, the Car-Pass, which records a car’s mileage history, remains compulsory. The seller of a car must still attend the inspection to have the mileage recorded and will receive a Car-Pass based on an inspection that may be up to two years old.
By the end of 2027, MOTs or car inspections can be carried out by official inspection centres but also by an authorised garage.

Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:36:37 UTC
15:36:37 KST

Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 11 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods, the country’s disaster management authority has said.
The death toll from the unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 903, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. Nearly 5,000 are missing on the two sides of the border.
Rescue efforts are complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.
The swollen Trishula River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.
Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains of the Himalayan region.
Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.
About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.
The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.
Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”
His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.
The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”
Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.
“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”
The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”
The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts have linked to the climate crisis.
Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.
“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.
Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.
“There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said , a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”
Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.
China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.
Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.
Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.
The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.
In the holy town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.
Two Nepali officials said China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.
China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.

US Trains Polish Special Forces to Operate in High-Drone-Activity Zones, Drawing on Ukraine War Experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:34:52 UTC
15:34:52 KST

In Germany, Polish special forces are taking part in military exercises designed to teach them how to operate in areas where they could easily be detected by drones.
The Associated Press reports that the U.S. military developed the training program based on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.
The special forces are practicing how to move through a 3,000-square-kilometer area controlled by a simulated enemy and how to carry out simulated strikes on key targets using drones.
According to the exercise scenario, the Polish troops must secretly move through the positions of U.S. soldiers playing the role of the enemy.
The U.S. troops also monitor reports from local residents to the police, which could help them detect and locate the Polish team.
The special forces must then travel about 100 kilometers across Germany to reach another training area in Grafenwöhr, where they are tasked with destroying a simulated target.
During the mission, the troops must avoid detection not only by military personnel but also by civilians. To do so, they move through villages and farms, where surveillance cameras are also in operation.
The U.S. military plans to conduct these exercises several times a year and expects special forces from more NATO countries to take part.
Meanwhile, the U.S. approach to developing counter-drone capabilities remains unclear.
Shortly before these exercises, the U.S. Army shut down a specialized unit in Europe that focused on studying warfare involving drones.
Despite this, the United States has been systematically studying the use of drones in Russia’s war against Ukraine for several years.
This work is carried out both by specialized units and by combat formations, which receive new drones and counter-drone systems to test during military exercises.
One of the key initiatives is the Transforming in Contact (TiC) program, under which the U.S. Army delivers new technologies directly to combat units for testing during deployments and training.
The 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division tested new drones, electronic warfare systems, command-and-control systems, and mobile platforms while deployed in Europe.
The brigade fielded more than 150 unmanned systems of various types, designed for a range of different missions.
Another initiative is the JIATF 401, a U.S. military interagency task force responsible for countering unmanned aircraft systems. Its main mission is to rapidly integrate advanced counter-drone technologies into military units.
JIATF 401 personnel are also studying the experience of Ukraine and European countries, where the widespread use of drones has become a routine part of modern warfare.

A cold shower from the north as Iceland rejects EU membership talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:32:27 UTC
15:32:27 KST

Good morning, readers. We’re back. Europe Today is live on your screens from 8.00 CEST every weekday — and back in your inboxes from 8.30. I’m Mared Gwyn, with you today and for the rest of the week.
We’re kicking off with an exclusive interview with the EU’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, who told my colleague Maria Tadeo that Europe must invest more to protect itself from climate disasters, despite capitals’ tight budgets. More in our top story below.
But first – Brussels awakens from its summer slumber this morning to a cold shower from the north: Iceland has voted 52.8% to 47.2% against restarting EU membership talks, freezing the possibility of joining the bloc for the foreseeable future.
A chilly setback: It’s a major knock for Brussels, where officials have been pushing to reinvigorate the EU’s enlargement agenda in recent months. The ‘No’ from Icelanders raises major questions over the EU’s ability to attract wealthier, northern countries to its ranks, with all current candidates lagging severely behind Reykjavik on economic indicators.
The response from the EU institutions has been notably muted – with a Commission spokesperson issuing a few brief words “taking note” of the result. European Council President António Costa exchanged messages with Iceland’s Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir on Sunday, saying the EU “fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic population” and vowing to continue strengthening the bilateral relationship.
Meanwhile, hard-right leaders including Marine Le Pen took the opportunity to hail the outcome as a win for national sovereignty.
Despite the temptation to frame the vote as a geopolitical reckoning – amid US threats against Greenland, Trump’s tariffs and China’s assertiveness – concerns over Iceland’s lucrative fishing industry ultimately proved decisive.
The fish factor: Fish accounts for a massive 40% of Iceland’s export value, and Icelandic fishers land more fish annually than any other EU nation. Fish – as it did in the 2016 Brexit referendum – became a highly politicised symbol of Iceland’s sovereignty, with many industries warning against losing control over the country’s prized 760,000 square kilometre exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
Taking ‘control’: Iceland’s powerful fishing industry had been spooked at the prospect of joining the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), a set of rules for managing the EU fleet and conserving fish stocks, despite officials in Brussels saying they were open to “creative solutions” in talks on Iceland’s access to the bloc’s agriculture and fisheries programmes.
Speaking to Europe Today earlier, Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, secretary general of the Icelandic Farmers Association, also said the desire to avoid joining the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) had been a crucial factor in the vote. “Icelanders voted to keep decisions about Iceland in Iceland,” she said, stressing that the island had not “rejected Europe”, but rather “full EU membership”.
‘Very disappointed’: Pro-EU voices have meanwhile been left deflated by the narrow defeat. Former Reykjavik mayor Dagur B. Eggertsson told Europe Today that he was “disappointed” after what he described as a “very harsh campaign”, which he said had “echoes of Brexit and the Brexit playbook”.
My colleague Jorge Liboreiro has these four takeaways from the referendum result, and Vincenzo Genovese has more on the implications for Brussels.
NATO security under spotlight: How secure is the central military operational headquarters at the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), and who wants to spy on it? These questions are at the heart of a court case playing out in Mons, Belgium today. My colleague Angela Skujins writes in to report on the unravelling espionage tale from the usually quiet country town now sitting at the centre of a security scandal.
In July, the Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office arrested a Canadian national of Chinese origin for allegedly carrying out spy activities for a third country while interning at NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe. She was ordered to remain in detention before the trial kicked off — something her legal team has appealed.
So, who is she? And was she spying for China?
Investigative media Follow The Money reports that the individual is a woman in her thirties called Claire Biwei Zhang, and may have been abetted by accomplices while the Belgian authorities mounted their legal case. While a lot of this case is confidential, we do know that pre-trial detention underscores the veracity of the charges and what potentially is at stake, with media reports filling in the blanks. Angela will have more details from the Mons courthouse during the day.
Also today: Hungary could meet all EU criteria to unlock €10 billion in post-Covid EU recovery funds as soon as today, my colleague Sándor Zsiros reports. To unlock the cash, frozen under the previous government of Viktor Orbán, Budapest needs to deliver on 27 so-called milestones, including judicial and anti-corruption reforms, by the end of today.
Both Hungarian and EU officials have previously told Sándor that work is progressing well, and that it was “realistic” for Budapest to meet its targets on time. The government led by Prime Minister Péter Mayar has said it wants to “bring home every cent due to Hungary.”
‘Europe’s climate and security challenges are inseparable,’ Commissioner Hoekstra tells Euronews
Europe must invest more to protect itself from increasingly severe climate disasters, EU Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra has exclusively told Euronews, warning that paying for the damage after fires and floods strike will cost the bloc far more.
“All evidence shows that making the upfront investments is way cheaper than just being hit by fire, being hit by floods and then paying for the damage. That’s just way more costly,” Hoekstra told our EU Editor Maria Tadeo in an interview for Europe Today, Euronews' flagship morning show.
Describing the summer as “dramatic”, the Dutch commissioner said the EU was better prepared than last year, with more firefighters, planes and helicopters deployed, but the scale of destruction had barely improved.
An area twice the size of Luxembourg was lost to fires, while estimates of the economic damage range from €50 billion to €70 billion or more. Spain and France lost thousands of hectares to blazes, while at least 14 first responders died fighting the fires.
Pressed by Euronews for a specific figure, Hoekstra did not commit to one but suggested the bulk of the funding would still come from national budgets.
“We need to be crystal clear about who is responsible for what. What is for the local governments, what is for regional governments, what is for national governments and what is for Europe,” he said.
Hoekstra also underlined the importance of the climate transition for the EU’s economic sovereignty, amid continued uncertainty around the transit of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz,
“In the medium term, by far our best bet is to move to a completely different energy system and that is where the money should be going,” Hoekstra said.
Watch the full interview.

South Korea hands jail term to Unification Church leader

South Korea hands jail term to Unification Church leader
August 31, 2026
Han Hak Ja, leader of the powerful and secretive Unification Church in South Korea, was handed a two-year prison sentence on Monday by a Seoul court on bribery charges.
Han is the widow of influential church founder Sun Myung Moon.
She was accused of giving South Korea's former First Lady Kim Keon Hee several expensive gifts in exchange for securing political favors. Kim has also been convicted of graft charges.
The 83-year-old has denied that she passed items, such as a designer handbag, to Kim via an intermediary. Han's lawyers have already announced that they will launch an appeal.
Kim's husband, former President Yoon Suk Yeol, is also currently jailed following an ill-fated bid to declare martial law in South Korea. Before his removal from office in 2025, his tenure had been noted for democratic backsliding and repression of the media.
Kim herself received a 20-month prison term in January for receiving gifts from the Unification Church, which sought political favors. An appeals court in April increased the sentence to four years in prison, after convicting her of additional charges.
What is the Unification Church?
Formally titled the "Family Federation for World Peace and Unification", the church began in the 1950s under the leadership of Han and her late husband, who at times claimed to be the second coming of Jesus.
The church has become known for its mass weddings, secrecy, and accusations of cult-like behavior and influence peddling.
Its reach has extended outside of Korea, most notably in Japan — where former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe was assassinated in 2022 by a man who was motivated by Abe's deep family ties to the church.

Men view dieting as feminine — but supportive spouses could be the solution, according to new study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:30:46 UTC
15:30:46 KST

Men find weight loss difficult due to a lack of support and the view that diet programmes are “feminine spaces”, according to new research.
Men struggle to lose weight due to viewing dieting as feminine, according to a new study, which highlights how gender perceptions can affect healthcare goals.
The study, published in the peer-reviewed journal PLOS One, also found that elements of competitiveness and social interaction were more likely to lead to successful weight loss strategies among men.
Led by a research team at Anglia Ruskin University in England, the researchers conducted a small focus group of men aged 30 and over, most of whom were white, married and educated.
When asked about their previous experiences with weight loss, the majority responded negatively to the restrictive and supposed quick-fix nature of dieting.
“I think diets are often a short-term crash programme and it’s very difficult to sustain those,” said one participant. “I think diet is a very negative word because as soon as you mention the word diet everybody automatically thinks restriction, restriction, restriction,” said another.
The participants also discussed viewing diet culture as a more feminine space, citing the aesthetics-focused imagery and discourse attached to it.
“When you look at articles if you go online and they used to have slimming stuff on TV [sic] would always have women so there was always an ad there that women need to look slim,” one man told the researchers.
However, the study also found that when men were supported by their female partners, their perceptions of dieting became less of an issue — and they felt more motivated to bypass any early weight loss hurdles.
“For some of the men on the study, the only reason they had lost weight in the past is because their spouses were almost overseeing the nature of the [dieting] programme,” Justin Roberts, a professor of Nutritional Physiology at Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge and co-author of the study, told Euronews Health.
“Then we had some men that talked about a mentor, someone they could either look up to with experience or expertise, or someone who's gone through the programme that could show them the way.”
Obesity continues to be one of the biggest global health issues of our time, with the World Health Organization (WHO) reporting that 43% of adults aged 18 and over were overweight and 16% were living with obesity in 2022.
The prevalence of obesity also appears to be higher in males, with 70% more men overweight compared to 62% of women in 2024, according to the National Health Service (NHS).
While this latest research contains bias in its selection of participants, as the study authors note, it also points to larger issues around how we structure and talk about weight loss programmes — and how those can lead to continued cycles of failure.
Ultimately, Roberts believes men are more likely to succeed if better support initiatives, including regular check-ins and personalised coping strategies, are implemented.
“If you can get in and quickly assess those points earlier on so they don't have these kinds of pitfalls, then you're more likely going to get sustained benefits,” he said.

Wildfires in Algeria Highlight the Scale of the Global Fire Landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Severe late-August wildfires across northern Algeria have brought residential areas, agricultural lands, and critical transport corridors directly into the path of rapidly spreading flames. The destruction across Jijel, Béjaïa, and Tizi Ouzou claimed at least 12 lives and forced the emergency closure of major national highways. The latest outbreak follows a summer of repeated fires across the country, with authorities recorded nearly 2,000 fires nationwide in July, while fires in the northeastern province of Annaba at the end of the month forced more than 100 people to leave their homes and damaged nearly 150 houses. The current fires have again brought residential areas, roads and other infrastructure into the path of rapidly spreading flames. Forest fires occur regularly in northern Algeria during the summer, with increasingly frequent drought and periods of intense heat contributing to more severe fire conditions.
The situation in Algeria forms part of a wider 2026 wildfire season affecting communities across multiple continents. As of August 1, 112.3 million hectares had burned globally, according to data from the Global Wildfire Information System compiled by Our World in Data. Africa accounted for 55.1 percent of the total burned area, with the Democratic Republic of Congo recording the largest national total at 13.6 million hectares, followed by Australia at 11.8 million hectares and Angola at 7.5 million hectares. The figures include agricultural and prescribed burning, meaning they do not directly represent the extent of uncontrolled wildfires.
According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), 634,473 hectares had burned across the European Union by August 27 in fires larger than 30 hectares. Although the figure remains below the 984,559 hectares recorded during the same period in 2025, it is more than twice the 2006-2025 average of 313,246 hectares. EFFIS forecasts very extreme conditions in isolated areas across central Europe and the Balkans, as well as Portugal, eastern Spain and the Atlas Mountains of North Africa, with extreme danger extending through parts of southeastern Europe and toward Ukraine. The forecast for August 31 to September 6 also indicates above-average temperatures across the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa, while below-average rainfall is expected in parts of the Iberian Peninsula, France, Italy and the Balkans.
Related Article
The Impact of Wildfires on Building Codes: Reflections on the Recent Los Angeles Fires
Spain has experienced one of the most severe fire seasons in Europe this year, with approximately 226,391 hectares burned by August 1. France has also faced major fires, while simultaneous fires in the two countries have led to mass evacuations. In the United Kingdom, fires have affected areas including the Cairngorms, while elsewhere in Europe, communities have faced smoke, evacuations and damage to homes and infrastructure. The impacts extend beyond Europe and North Africa. Canada had recorded approximately 2 million hectares burned by August 1, with fires across several provinces forcing communities to evacuate and sending smoke into parts of Canada and the United States. The United States had recorded approximately 2.4 million hectares burned, with major fires reported in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. Australia recorded approximately 11.8 million hectares burned during the same period.
The scale and geographic spread of this year's fires are unfolding alongside increasingly hot and dry conditions associated with climate change. The combination of higher temperatures, drought and dry vegetation can create conditions that allow fires to spread more rapidly and become harder to contain. At the same time, the immediate impacts remain highly local: homes are evacuated, roads are closed, landscapes are burned and communities face the difficult process of returning and rebuilding. For the built environment, the consequences of the current fire season are particularly visible where fires reach settlements. Homes can be damaged or destroyed alongside roads and other infrastructure, while evacuations can rapidly turn ordinary streets and highways into critical emergency routes. In Algeria, the closure of three national highways demonstrates how wildfire can disrupt regional connectivity in addition to threatening individual properties.
Across different regions, extreme weather and seismic events have caused significant loss of life and damage to communities in recent weeks. On August 26, a glacier collapse triggered flash floods along the Nepal–Tibet border, destroying villages and leaving at least 350 people dead and more than 1,300 missing, with the most affected areas including Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. Earlier this month, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia, causing damage across several cities and killing at least 111 people. The event followed four significant earthquakes in Japan, the United States, and Venezuela within a 36-hour period in June, highlighting the range of environmental risks currently affecting communities and the built environment.
