Emails sent to Estonia's state institutions from Russian servers will be quarantined
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:20:00 UTC
14:20:00 KST

Emails sent to Estonia's state institutions from Russian servers will be quarantined
Emails sent from Russian servers – addresses ending in .ru – will no longer reach state institutions immediately from September, and will be sent to quarantine for additional checks to prevent cyberattacks.
Many Estonian residents, particularly among the Russian-speaking population, still have their email accounts on Russian servers. This means they use email addresses ending in .ru.
From the end of August, these emails will no longer reach many state institutions as quickly as before.
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) said the decision is an additional measure to protect Estonian state institutions from cyberattacks.
"Since 2022, cyberattacks against Estonia have increased exponentially. It is absolutely clear that a very large number of these cyberattacks are linked to Russia. Unfortunately, we see that we have to strengthen our defenses, and we are doing so in many different areas and places," Pakosta explained.
"Thanks to determined work, these cyberattacks have not succeeded against Estonia, but unfortunately massive cyberattacks against the public sector have succeeded in Latvia and Lithuania, as we have been able to read in the news. We have to improve our cybersecurity, and this is simply one small measure in all the extensive work we are doing to improve cybersecurity," she continued.
However, not every institution will participate in the new measure, and neither are local governments.
While others have gone further. For example, Estonia's courts have already said they will ask parties to proceedings to stop using email addresses ending in .ru in communication.
"It depends on what security rules the particular institution has established. In fact, all state institutions have very strict rules and they have to comply with cybersecurity requirements. A very large proportion of these state institutions have already moved behind a unified, strong cyber shield, and this transition is continuing all the time," Pakosta said.
The new arrangement will not create additional bureaucracy for government agencies.
"There will actually be no additional bureaucracy; the rerouting is automatic. In other words, the government agency does not have to do any work for this. It is rerouted centrally, and this arrangement applies to all those state institutions that are already operating within the state's secure cyberspace," the minister said.

Global coral reef coverage risks irreversible decline, new report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:19:05 UTC
14:19:05 KST

Global coral reef coverage risks irreversible decline, new report warns
Coral reefs make up just 1 percent of ocean coverage, but host a quarter of all life in the sea.
Coral reefs are experiencing bleaching events so frequently that they no longer have time to recover before the next one strikes, scientists have warned.
Global coral cover is now well below normal levels and at risk of irreversible decline, the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) said in a report released on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3World ‘very likely’ to exceed 1.5C climate goal in next decade: UN
- list 2 of 3World’s oceans experience hottest June ever, scientists say more heat ahead
- list 3 of 3Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
“If we give them enough time, they have the capacity to recover,” lead author Manuel Gonzalez Rivero said. “But we haven’t seen that amount of time being allowed. In fact, the frequency of those bleaching events has pretty much doubled.”
Bleaching occurs when corals expel the colourful algae living in their tissues. Without this algae, they become vulnerable to starvation and disease. Bleached coral are not dead, but they need time in cooler water to recover.
“We had 40 years of coral cover around the world that had remained relatively unchanged until 2010,” said Gonzalez Rivero, a scientist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science. “Since 2010, there has been a very steep change.”
The latest bleaching in 2023 was the most extensive on record, impacting 77 percent of the world’s coral reef areas.
Rivero warned that another such event is “very likely” this year given elevated temperatures globally.
Coral reefs are critical barometers for global ocean health, supporting more than 25 percent of all marine life despite covering less than 1 percent of the ocean floor.
The GCRMN’s warning came as organisers of the annual Pacific Islands Forum announced that at least five leaders of the 18-nation group will skip the group’s summit.
The forum has been touted for decades as a symbol of regional unity, and is used to discuss pressing matters facing Pacific states, including climate change and ocean health.

Body of 46-year-old man recovered after Grand Canyon flash flood, park service says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:17:58 UTC
14:17:58 KST

Popular tourist spots, including the Bright Angel Campground, the North Kaibab Trail and Phantom Ranch, home to a historic canteen and dormitories, remained closed on Sunday.
One person died and around 15 people are missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood at the Grand Canyon forced evacuations, swept large boulders into the Colorado River and knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents, the National Park Service said on Sunday.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered late on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said without providing additional details. Coroner’s officials were at the scene.
Weekend flooding in Arizona’s Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, happened on Saturday afternoon.
More than 60 people were evacuated from the depths of the canyon. The park service said it had yet to account for 15 people and asked anyone with details about hikers or campers in the canyon to get in touch.
The Arizona Department of Public Safety was helping with additional evacuations on Sunday.
Because the main water line was out of service, starting on Monday tourists won't be able to stay overnight at lodges and hotels within Grand Canyon National Park. Year-round residents are being asked to conserve water.
“These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park said in a statement.
Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and extending an existing river rapid or creating a new one.
The flood was a major blow to an enduring effort to modernise the pipeline that serves 6 million visitors a year and roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.
“Heaven help us if the whole thing down there at the bottom has to be reconstructed,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Centre for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University.
“Where are they going to get the money? It's a nightmare for the park service. And thank God nobody was hurt or killed.”
Halting overnight stays at the park because of a lack of water is rare, although the pipeline frequently has failed over the years.
A $208 million (€179 million) rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.
Popular tourist spots, including the Bright Angel Campground, the North Kaibab Trail and Phantom Ranch, home to a historic canteen and dormitories, remained closed on Sunday.
Between 1-2.5 cm of rain fell within about 20 minutes on a rocky slope where there’s a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Darren McCollum in Flagstaff. The deluge was preceded by two smaller systems that drenched the area hours earlier.
“So when the main storm moved in, torrential rain fell on everything that was already soaked, and that caused all the problems that we're seeing," McCollum said.
The weather service said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping around 1,828 meters.
More rain and thunderstorms were possible for the area into Monday.

Ukraine’s Renaissance Legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:16:00 UTC
14:16:00 KST

When I walk down Andriivskyi Descent in Kyiv toward the Podil district, I pause for a moment to admire the prominent exquisite mural, titled “Renaissance,” by French artist Seth Globepainter and Ukrainian artist Aleksey Kislow.
Its message is unmistakably about Ukraine’s renaissance as a nation. In the palm of a young woman’s hand, the future in the guise of a small child. Apparently, the painters were strongly inspired by the architecture featured in the early Renaissance frescoes of Masaccio and Pierro della Francesca. Her body is beautifully intertwined with the image of a town: a Romanesque arch extends into her robe, while her left hand protectively embraces the houses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Also striking is the surreal motif of the two Cossack heads, from which buildings rise (might these be architects?).
“Don’t mess with this lady,” was one of the thoughts that crossed my mind.
Sadly, she does not have the means to protect the Kyivans from the harsh reality of ballistic missiles. Even so, her intense, focused gaze reminded me of the story of a former Latin teacher who joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine in 2022 and reportedly became one of the best snipers – call sign Panoushka – taking out Russian invaders (who had killed her beloved) from up to 1.6 kilometers away.
As for the Renaissance: its essence was articulated in 1486 in the “Oratio de Hominis Dignitate” (Oration on the Dignity of Man), the humanist manifesto by the Italian scholar and philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494). In it, a brilliant young man, barely 23 years old, argued that God, having created the heavenly globes and the earthly world teeming with all manner of animal life, still longed for a creature that could give meaning to His creation, be moved with love at its beauty, and be smitten with awe at its grandeur.
UK Ukrainian Church Leader on Faith, Diaspora & 35 Years of Independence
In His heavenly studio, however, there was no archetype left to fashion humankind. Therefore, the Divine Artist decided to grant Adam – ”unlike all other creatures who were defined and restricted within laws” – the privilege “to be the free and proud shaper of your own being, fashion yourself in the form you may prefer”, adding “it will be in your power to descend to the lower, brutish forms of life; you will be able, through your own decision, to rise again to the superior orders whose life is divine.”
In short, according to Pico, the dignity of man lay in his self-determination. There are parallels with Ukrainians, who in their “Revolution of Dignity” Maidan uprising, certainly acted in his spirit. Incidentally, Pico was born on Feb. 24 – a date forever marked in the memory of Ukrainians, albeit also one on which they decided en masse to fight for the right to shape their own future.
But isn’t it also remarkable that the flag and coat of arms of Pico’s family and birthplace Mirandola feature the same two colors as the Ukrainian flag? Set against a sky-blue background is an inverted V-shape – a gold-colored chevron – which, in heraldry, resembles the rafters of a house and has traditionally symbolized protection, builders or loyal service. Needless to say that such concepts have taken on an unprecedentedly profound significance for Ukrainians.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Take Lacity Ukraine, an Odesa-based charity foundation and media agency, that is helping to defend Ukraine’s independence and appears to be indebted to the Mirandola flag design, as it turned the golden roof rafter into an L for their own logo.
Perhaps it is time that Pico was honored with a statue on the Maidan. And if that were to happen, let the mayor of Mirandola unveil the statue.

Ukraine and Israel Draw Closer as Israeli Elections Loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:13:00 UTC
14:13:00 KST

Relations between Ukraine and Israel appear to be entering a period of cautious rapprochement, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reaching out directly to President Volodymyr Zelensky as Israel approaches national elections.
In a letter marking Ukraine’s Independence Day on Aug. 24, Netanyahu congratulated Zelensky and the Ukrainian people, praised Ukraine’s resilience, and described Iran as a common threat facing both countries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky made the letter public two days later, saying Ukraine and Israel share deep ties between their societies, economies, and cultures.
“It is therefore good to hear of Israel’s desire to strengthen these existing ties,” Zelensky wrote. He added that Kyiv was counting on productive cooperation to increase security.
Netanyahu also added a handwritten note referring to his brief meeting with Zelensky in Washington in late July.
The Washington meeting
The two leaders spoke and shook hands at the funeral of the late US Sen. Lindsey Graham on July 28, during Zelensky’s visit to Washington. It was their first face-to-face contact since September 2023 and their first reported conversation since January 2025.
Attempts to arrange a formal bilateral meeting in Washington did not produce one, but the brief exchange was described as cordial.
The same day, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar spoke with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and invited him to visit Israel. Sa’ar identified Iran as a threat facing both countries and said he wanted to deepen cooperation with Ukraine.
Can Ukraine Set a New Standard in International Law?
The contacts marked a noticeable change after several years of complicated relations between Kyiv and Jerusalem.
Stolen grain strained relations
Israel has provided Ukraine with humanitarian aid, advanced early-warning technology, generators, and components for Patriot systems since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. It has nevertheless resisted Kyiv’s requests for major Israeli weapons systems and maintained channels with Moscow.
Relations then deteriorated sharply in April over grain shipments to Haifa that Kyiv said originated in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
Ukraine first called on Israel to investigate after the Russian vessel Abinsk arrived in Haifa carrying wheat allegedly taken from occupied Ukraine. Kyiv later asked Israeli authorities to arrest the shipment, but the vessel left and the cargo was never detained.
The dispute escalated when a second vessel, the Panormitis, approached Haifa with another cargo allegedly linked to occupied Ukrainian territory. Kyiv summoned then Israeli Ambassador Michael Brodsky and prepared an official protest note.
Sa’ar dismissed Kyiv’s public criticism as “Twitter diplomacy,” arguing that Israel had not received a formal request to seize the vessel or detain the cargo. The Israeli foreign ministry later said Ukraine’s legal-assistance request contained factual gaps and lacked supporting evidence.
The Israeli importer ultimately rejected the Panormitis cargo, but the public dispute exposed broader tensions over Israeli military assistance, Ukraine’s voting record at the UN, and the way the two governments communicated.
Iran creates common ground
The US-Israeli war against Iran has created significantly more common ground between Kyiv and Jerusalem.
Iranian-made Shahed drones have been used extensively by Russia against Ukraine, giving Kyiv years of experience in intercepting the weapons that are also central to Israel’s security concerns.
In March, Kyiv Post reported that Jerusalem had approached Ukraine about possible cooperation against Iranian drones. A source in Zelensky’s office said Ukraine was open to working with Israel and could share operational experience and domestically produced drones. Kyiv, in return, expected greater Israeli military support.
Ukraine has since expanded its role in the Middle East by offering its drone-interception experience to regional partners while developing relations with Israel and the Gulf states.
Israel has remained sensitive to Ukraine’s contacts with regional governments that have difficult relations with Jerusalem. These tensions were among the issues in a July Kyiv Post analysis of what the Iran war means for Ukraine.
Elections
The current improvement in relations is unlikely to produce an immediate major change in Israeli policy toward Ukraine, despite support for closer cooperation in some Israeli political and security circles.
Israel will hold national elections on Oct. 27. The president will then consult the parties elected to the Knesset and assign a member of parliament to form a government.
Under Israeli law, that person initially receives 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. The process could therefore continue into December, and longer if the first nominee fails.
A Kyiv Post source in Jerusalem said they do not expect major decisions concerning Ukraine before the election and the formation of the next Israeli government.
According to the source, the largest window for significantly expanding Israeli assistance to Ukraine opened roughly two years ago. No comparable shift should be expected during the current election period.
For now, the rapprochement is therefore more likely to produce renewed political dialogue and work on specific areas of common interest than an immediate change in military assistance.
The election will determine whether Netanyahu remains in office or a new coalition takes power. Kyiv is already positioning itself to work with the government that emerges.

Heavy school backpacks can strain children's bodies. Here’s how to lighten the load
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:08:58 UTC
14:08:58 KST

As back-to-school shopping gets underway, experts warn that overloaded backpacks can strain children's bodies.
Backpacks can be fashionable and functional, but they can also be too heavy — weighed down by books, digital devices, musical instruments, sports equipment and more.
It's good to be prepared, but children who walk to school or participate in extracurricular activities may be lugging more than their bodies can handle.
As families begin back-to-school shopping, here's how to know if your child's backpack is too heavy, and how to lighten the load.
How heavy is too heavy?
The modern school backpack has evolved, but it hasn’t necessarily got lighter. Whether students have textbooks, digital devices or both, they often are accompanied by notebooks, water bottles, lunch containers or workout clothes. Individually, those items may not seem heavy, but together they can add unnecessary strain to children's bodies.
According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, signs a backpack may be too heavy include a child leaning forward to support its weight or having difficulty walking. Straps should not dig into the shoulders.
Back injuries are uncommon but possible, particularly if a child falls while carrying a heavy backpack, said Sadika Kendi, a physician who chairs the academy’s injury-prevention efforts.
“It’s worse if, for example, they trip and fall and they have a huge, heavy backpack on their back. Then that’s just more weight that could increase the severity of an injury,” she told the Associated Press.
Although 10% to 15% of a child’s body weight is often cited as a backpack guideline, there isn’t enough evidence to establish a one-size-fits-all approach, Kendi said. Children vary in size, strength, physical development and daily routines, so caregivers should consider each child’s individual needs and, in general, keep backpacks as light as possible.
Choosing the right backpack
Health authorities recommend backpacks with two wide, padded, adjustable straps.
The straps should be tight enough to hold the bag close to the body and should be adjusted so that the bottom sits just above the child’s waist. A backpack with a waist belt can also help support some of the weight.
Backpacks with wheels can be helpful, especially for children with injuries, but experts say they may be problematic in schools with stairs or crowded walkways, where they can pose a tripping hazard.
Carry only the essentials
After families receive back-to-school checklists for classroom materials, they should take an audit of what a child really must carry every day.
According to Samantha Ness, a history teacher in Phoenix, in the United States, parents should focus on making sure children have basic supplies rather than getting caught up in trendy, decorative or expensive items.
Her pupils have access to classroom textbooks but are still expected to carry a laptop and charger each day. As technology becomes more central to schoolwork, some students have stopped bringing paper altogether, she said. They rely instead on their devices, which can also become distractions.
As students get older, Ness said, backpacks can become more like personal storage than school supplies, carrying items such as makeup, nail polish and hair dryers.

Can Ukraine Set a New Standard in International Law?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:05:00 UTC
14:05:00 KST

Russia is waging war not only against Ukrainian culture but against Ukrainian identity. Ukraine is seeking to make international law recognize the full extent of that campaign.
When Russian forces enter a Ukrainian city, they do not look only for military personnel and officials whose names appear on their lists. They also search for teachers, priests of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, museum workers, local historians and librarians. Russia is waging war on memory, and those who carry that memory are more dangerous to it than weapons.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
International law is not powerless in the face of attacks on culture: conventions and statutes already prohibit many such acts. Yet this legal framework primarily recognizes what can be counted, while the deepest dimension of the crime does not fit neatly into any existing category.
We have become accustomed to discussing the destruction of culture through the language of losses: how many sites have been damaged or destroyed and what exactly has been lost. This is a necessary and legitimate conversation, but it overlooks an important point: culture is a much broader and deeper concept. It holds communities together, transmits values, shapes consciousness and identity, and creates practices and an entire way of life around them.
A church is not only its walls but also its community. A school is not only a building but also a language. A local history museum is not merely a collection of objects but a city’s answer to the questions of who we are and where we come from.
Ukraine’s Renaissance Legacy
Russia understands this perfectly well, and the consequences of its actions are becoming increasingly evident not only on the battlefield but also under occupation.
Raphael Lemkin, who coined the term genocide, warned from the outset that a group could be destroyed without every member being killed. It was enough to take away what made its members a group: their culture and collective consciousness.
Today, we call this cultural genocide. Yet the final text of the 1948 Genocide Convention did not include cultural genocide as a separate punishable act. Attacks on culture can be prosecuted as war crimes or crimes against humanity and may serve as evidence of genocidal intent, but cultural destruction alone is not among the acts listed in Article II of the Convention.
Law Moves Only When the Damage Is Obvious
One could object that international courts have repeatedly developed the interpretation of existing legal norms.
In the Krstić case, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia treated the destruction of religious and cultural property as evidence of an intent to destroy a group. In cases concerning the shelling of Dubrovnik, the tribunal prosecuted attacks on the historic city as violations of the laws or customs of war. In the Akayesu case, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda recognized that rape and sexual violence could constitute genocide when committed with the specific intent to destroy a protected group.
These rulings are rightly regarded as groundbreaking. But the consequences of the crimes were so extensive and immediately visible that they could not be denied: destroyed mosques were there for all to see, the shelling of a medieval city was broadcast to the world, and the scale of violence in Rwanda left no room for doubt. The judges did not so much get ahead of their time as recognize what had become impossible to ignore.
It seems that the law is capable of evolving only when the damage has become too obvious to overlook.
Damage to culture, however, is not always immediately visible. A child taught someone else’s history does not look like a victim in a photograph. A community deprived of its place of worship quietly disperses. A language retreats from one generation to the next. The most devastating consequences emerge later, among descendants who no longer know what was taken from them.
The law, however, demands harm that can be presented here and now. What unfolds over decades is, at best, treated as “context” and, at worst, as nothing at all.
Twelve Years That Change Everything
This is where Ukraine may occupy a distinctive position. Russia’s war against Ukrainian culture has been underway since at least 2014. Crimea and the occupied parts of the Donbas have lived under forced Russification for more than 12 years.
This means something terrible but legally invaluable: the delayed consequences that the law has rarely had the opportunity to observe have already begun to emerge, and they can now be documented in real time.
Children who entered school in occupied Crimea in 2014 are adults today. Researchers can trace how their language, historical memory and values have changed under an education system designed to replace Ukrainian identity with a Russian imperial one.
The consequences also extend to territories occupied during the full-scale invasion. Oleksandr Mustiatse, a 19-year-old from the village of Krynky in Kherson Oblast, was listed as missing on Ukraine’s Children of War platform after Russia occupied his home in 2022. He was later identified as serving in the Russian army. According to the Back to Ukraine initiative, he explained his decision by saying that “Russia was always in his heart.” His case is one example of where the systematic indoctrination and militarization of Ukrainian children under occupation can lead. — Ed.
For the first time, judges could be presented not only with the perpetrator’s policies and decrees but also with evidence of the consequences those measures produced — from school materials designed to reshape historical memory to measurable changes in language, affiliation and identity.
The damage that was not obvious in the first years has become visible.
The duration and nature of Russia’s occupation allow Ukraine to advance new legal arguments about how attacks on culture should be understood and classified. This evidence would not remove the requirement to prove specific genocidal intent, nor would it expand the Genocide Convention by itself. It could, however, help demonstrate that coordinated attacks on language, education, religion, memory and cultural institutions form part of a campaign intended to destroy a group.
Ukraine also faces an enforcement problem absent from the Krstić and Akayesu prosecutions. Those were cases against individuals before ad hoc international tribunals. Efforts to hold Russia accountable must contend with the fact that the accused state is a permanent member of the UN Security Council. That political reality does not change the legal definition of genocide, but it profoundly affects the prospects for enforcement.
A New Ukrainian Standard?
For years, professional communities and civil society organizations — including the Raphael Lemkin Society, the Dofa Fund, the Ukrainian Heritage Monitoring Lab and dozens of other initiatives — have documented Russian crimes against Ukrainian culture: destroyed museums and churches, looted collections, rewritten history and the persecution of cultural figures.
From thousands of separate episodes, one thing has emerged above all: a pattern. The same process is repeated in occupied city after occupied city. Once that pattern is visible, the next step is to find the language in which it can be legally defined.
That step has already been taken. Draft Law No. 15331 proposes adding a cultural dimension to the genocide provision of Ukraine’s Criminal Code. It would cover the destruction, damage or appropriation of cultural heritage, as well as the systematic denial of access to language, education, religious practices, traditions, historical memory and cultural institutions, when intended to eliminate a group’s cultural identity as a condition or means of its physical or social destruction.
In essence, Ukraine is seeking to bring back into the legal sphere what was removed from the Genocide Convention in 1948 — and to define the obvious as obvious.
The initiative is part of a broader shift. Ukraine has begun treating cultural heritage as a national-security concern, created a specialized Cultural Property Protection unit within the Armed Forces and established specialized prosecutorial units to investigate crimes against cultural heritage.
These are the opening arguments Ukraine is bringing to a broader debate: an attempt to move cultural genocide from the margins of academic papers into the realm of evidence, prosecution and judgments.
This is where a possible Ukrainian standard lies — not in punishing the destruction of heritage sites more severely, but in teaching the law to recognize the second dimension of the crime: the harm done to social bonds, values and identity, demonstrated through long-term consequences.
This will require new methodologies. But more than 12 years of occupation, as bitter as that experience is, have already created an evidentiary record that no country had before Ukraine.
The law has always been reluctant to classify crimes against culture. It has waited for consequences that are immediately visible and treated the wider issue as too complicated to address. Ukraine may be able to teach it a different approach — one shaped by awareness, painful experience and the terrible consequences of failing to act.
The empty space left in 1948 could then be filled not with declarations, but with judgments.

Expelling individual Russian diplomats or closing the Russian House in Berlin is no longer an adequate response to the Leipzig drone incident, one source said. Tougher steps were needed, the source said — harsher sanctions or even more extensive arms deliveries to Ukraine.
Berlin has also begun preparing for a sharp response from Moscow, according to Politico.
Sources who spoke to Politico described Germany’s upcoming move as a ”Zeitenwende 2.0” — a second turning point, echoing the Zeitenwende, the term former Chancellor Olaf Scholz used after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when he announced an abrupt overhaul of Berlin’s relations with Moscow.
On August 25, Merz said those behind the attempted sabotage in Leipzig would be held accountable, though he leveled no specific accusations. He promised to say more about the investigation’s findings soon. The government had been working with intelligence agencies on “intensive” efforts to identify those responsible, he said.
A drone of unknown origin was found at Leipzig airport overnight into August 5, German media said. It later emerged that multiple drones had been involved in the attempted sabotage. The first drone, discovered beside a Ukrainian Antonov transport plane loaded with ammunition, had explosives and a detonator attached. A second drone apparently collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing and go around because the airport had closed. A third drone did not turn up until 10 days after the incident. Investigators found about 50 grams (1.8 ounces) of explosives nearby.

Lower pollution, longer range: How a new type of car tyre is reversing a hidden downside of EVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:02:48 UTC
14:02:48 KST

Electric cars are cleaner to drive - but their tyres pose a pollution problem. Better materials could help fix the problem.
Electric cars are widely seen as the cleaner choice on the road. But according to Gunnlaugur Erlendsson, founder and CEO of technology company ENSO, there is a significant environmental cost hiding in plain sight: the tyres.
"Tyres are one of these really complicated products we don't really see very often, even though they're absolutely everywhere," Erlendsson tells Euronews Earth. "The whole global economy runs on tyres."
That ubiquity comes at a cost. Raw material extraction, energy-intensive manufacturing and the wear generated every time a vehicle stops, starts or turns all add up.
"Tyres are both a source of major air pollution, which is also a microplastic. So it's one of the biggest sources of air pollution in cities. It's also one of the biggest source of microplastic pollution in our oceans," Erlendsson says.
Disposal adds another layer to the problem. "We actually burn almost two billion tyres every year because so few of them are actually recycled back into tyres again," he explains.
ENSO was founded to address these impacts while supporting the shift to electric vehicles. "Our mission really is about enhancing electric vehicles while we're addressing the problems that tyres cause," Erlendsson says.
Why electric vehicles wear tyres faster
Electric vehicles might be cleaner to run, but according to Erlendsson, they place greater demands on tyres. "Electric vehicles are fairly unique because they're really heavy. They have really high torque. So they tend to wear out tyres faster than traditional cars ever did," he says.
Driving behaviour makes the issue worse. "They're really fun to drive. People drive them more aggressively, which again wears tyres faster," Erlendsson notes, adding that EVs are often used in cities, where frequent stopping, starting and turning generates more tyre pollution.
There is also a less obvious factor: efficiency. Erlendsson explains that electric vehicles convert around 90 per cent of energy into motion, compared with roughly 30 per cent for petrol cars.
"That efficiency gain with electric vehicles is positive, but it makes them incredibly sensitive to tyres," he says. "If you don't put a good tyre on an electric car, you lose a lot of range and you buy a lot more electricity."
To tackle this, ENSO changed the raw materials, formula and construction used in its tyres, while also drawing on data collected from vehicle fleets. "When we deploy onto fleets, it means that we get data. We take that data, that insight, that knowledge, that know-how, and we put it back into the product again," Erlendsson says.
Designed to handle the high torque and heavy battery weight of EVs, ENSO's advanced polymer compounds and tread chemistry reduce tyre particulate pollution by up to 35 per cent compared to conventional tyres. They also improve overall energy efficiency and vehicle driving range by up to 10 per cent, according to the company.
Scaling up with major partners
ENSO has built its growth around partnerships with large-scale taxi and delivery fleets rather than individual consumers. The company already works with Uber, supplying tyres to electric vehicle drivers across the UK, with plans to expand beyond it.
"Ultimately, it's about enabling these high mobility use cases that drive a lot to get better products," Erlendsson says, noting that high-mileage vehicles see the greatest savings in energy, cost and pollution.
Recognition from the Earthshot Prize, where ENSO was a finalist in 2023, helped raise the profile of an issue Erlendsson believes the industry has long avoided.
"Tyre pollution has been this kind of industry topic that hasn't really been addressed by, I would say, the mainstream industry. They don't really want to talk about it," he says. He credits Prince William's involvement with bringing wider attention to the issue, calling it "really substantial in terms of highlighting... how we can actually use technology to enhance better air we breathe, reduce the microplastics in our oceans."
Looking ahead, ENSO plans to keep expanding its fleet partnerships and broaden its range of tyre sizes to match new electric vehicle models entering the market, with the United States identified as its next major growth market.
"We want the rest of the industry to follow us," Erlendsson says. "We just want to be the catalyst that makes the change happen."

‘It was like fighting a dinosaur’: Sydney shark attack survivor recalls left hook that helped save her life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:01:26 UTC
14:01:26 KST

An Australian woman who lost an arm after a shark attack at a Sydney beach has described delivering a “left hook” punch to the four-metre great white as its open mouth came within centimetres of her face.
Leah Stewart, 34, a teacher and mother of a one-year-old, was attacked by the shark while on a morning swim at Coogee beach in Sydney’s eastern suburbs on 13 June.
She remained in a critical condition for more than two weeks while receiving treatment for life-threatening injuries that required the amputation of her arm.
In her first media interview since the attack, Stewart recalled the moment she spotted the great white shark.
“I’ve never screamed that loud and that crazy in my life … I’m just thinking, ‘surely the lifeguards will hear us screaming, a jetski is going to come out any second and scare it away’,” she told Nine’s 60 Minutes.
“But a minute went by and it was still there and no one had come to save me.”
Stewart said the shark got as close as “about 30cm from my face”, remembering “its black little beady eyes”.
“Its face was horrific. I’ll never forget its face,” she said.
“It sort of started opening its mouth and I’m like, ‘it’s going to get my face … I’ve got to try and punch it. I’ve got to try and push it away or else it’s going to bite my head off’.”
Being right-handed, Stewart said the split-second decision to deliver “a left hook” came after asking herself: “Which limb am I willing to lose?”
Stewart said the following moments happened “in slow motion”, describing it as “like fighting a dinosaur”.
“In my head I was like, ‘you ugly fucker, you are not taking me away from my daughter’, and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again,” she said. “It was so big. It was like punching a brick wall.”
The shark delivered damaging bites to her left arm and thigh before help reached her. Lying on the beach and drifting in and out of consciousness, Stewart recalled thinking “I can’t die right now” as she thought of her one-year-old daughter, August.
“I could feel my life slipping away,” Stewart said. “It just felt like everything was leaving my body and I was going somewhere and just as I was about to reach the end of the tunnel, I just got a vision of August.
“I thought, ‘she’s not going to have a mum. She’s going to grow up without a mum.’
“I couldn’t handle that. I didn’t want her to not have a mum.”
Stewart spent several weeks in intensive care receiving treatment for life-changing injuries that she says she is “still coming to terms” with.
“I get really frustrated. You know, August will put up her hands and she’ll want me to pick her up. I’m just desperate to, I just really want to pick her up and I just can’t,” she said.
“I do have a disability, but I don’t want that to hold me back. I’m going to find ways to be able to conquer this and to be the best version of myself … I’ve been given a second chance.”
She said she had “come out of the other side with a knowledge and a power that I didn’t have before”.
“I wasn’t just a girl that got mauled on the beach … I’m the woman that punched the shark in the face,” she said.

Russian strikes destroy 12 million books ahead of Ukraine's first week back at school
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
06:01:12 BST
14:01:12 KST

Russian strikes destroy 12 million books ahead of Ukraine's first week back at school
- Published
Viktoria Haidai surveys the mangled remains of the printing press, which should have been busy churning out textbooks ready for the new school year.
The plant, on the edge of Kyiv, was hit during the night by a Russian missile, just as production was ramping up to deliver 1.3 million books – 10% of Ukraine's schoolbooks.
In the ashes there is a charred page from an English language textbook: "My name is William, I'm from the UK. My grandmother lives in Nottingham. It's a beautiful city."
Russia has hit printing presses and publishing houses across Ukraine in a series of recent attacks, destroying 12 million books and damaging other icons of Ukrainian history and culture. Local media report, external that Russia has destroyed one third of all the books printed in Ukraine this year.
Nothing is salvageable at this Kyiv printing press. Even the pages that survived the flames have succumbed to water damage, from firefighting or exposure to the elements from the collapsed roof.
"I believe it is deliberate on the part of the Russian Federation," says Haidai, commercial director of the Konvi publishing firm. "Over the past two months, some of the largest publishing houses have lost their logistics warehouses, where very large quantities of books were stored.
"The Russians are also destroying printing houses in an attempt to erase Ukraine as a nation. But frankly they will not succeed."
More than 35 publishing facilities have been hit over recent weeks.
But it's not just fresh pages coming under attack. Kyiv's Pochaina second-hand book market was also struck, wiping out hundreds of individual stalls and countless treasured tomes.
Before firefighters had finished extinguishing the blaze, I found Liliya Velyka, a 28-year-old book blogger, raking through the smouldering ruins, seeing if anything could be saved. She clutched a soaking copy of a sci-fi novel.
"Books are saving us and losing this is like losing our hearts," she says.
Museums, art galleries, film studios, libraries, and opera houses have also been damaged. At Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, the capital's large medieval monastery and cultural heritage site, the golden domes of the Dormition Cathedral were hit.
Religious artefacts were moved to safety but a large section of the roof was set ablaze after a drone attack. Repairs are predicted to cost $11.2 million (£8.2m) and will take two years.
The site is also home to Ukraine's museum of books and printing. Unesco listed the complex in 1990, and added it to its register of world heritage sites in danger in September 2023.
At recent celebrations marking 975 years since the monastery's founding, Unesco's Director-General Khaled El-Enany said he was "deeply saddened" to see "the significant damage".
"Unesco firmly condemns all attacks against cultural property protected under international law," he told gathered dignitaries, including President Volodymyr Zelensky.
El-Enany toured the cathedral with Ukraine's minister of culture, Tetyana Berezhna, who told me the cultural and military impacts of Russia's war should not be separated.
"This is an existential war, so Russia wants to destroy us as a nation, to erase us as a nation, like Ukrainians do not exist and have never existed. That's why Russia targets our cultural heritage, the symbols of our presence here for a long time.
"They understand that it's very important for us because we protect our identity, we protect our culture, and Russia wants to ruin everything that it cannot appropriate."
Berezhna says Russia has attacked over 1,900 pieces of Ukrainian heritage and more than 2,000 cultural institutions. Digitisation is part of the strategy to protect art and literature and ensure children can still learn, despite the attacks on physical books.
There are warnings Ukraine's entire publishing sector is under threat and needs international support to remain viable.
At the bombed Kyiv printing press Viktoria Haidai told me protecting the industry was vital to preserving Ukrainian literature. "The word is everything. It is our development, our culture, and our historical heritage that is passed down from generation to generation."
In a 2021 essay, titled On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that Ukrainians and Russians were one people, and questioned the legitimacy of an independent Ukrainian state and culture.
In a statement to the BBC, the Russian embassy to the UK blamed Ukraine's own government for damage to its cultural heritage, saying monuments had been dismantled and streets renamed. It also claimed cultural sites had been used to conceal military facilities.
The Kremlin has repeatedly denied deliberately hitting civilian targets throughout the five years of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, despite repeated and widespread missile and drone attacks on residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk, Volodymyr Lozhko and Anastasiia Levchenko

The ministry pointed out that China uses military exercises to intimidate Taiwan.
Through its cyber warfare forces, China integrates resources and continues to invest in technology and personnel to strengthen capabilities for cyberattacks and malware deployment, the ministry said, per Liberty Times. China regards cyberspace as a key domain of modern warfare, adopting a model of peacetime infiltration and wartime disruption, it said.
The ministry added that the PLA integrates firepower resources across branches to establish a joint strike system. Depending on mission requirements, it has targets set on key military facilities and critical infrastructure in Taiwan.
China focuses on saturation and surprise attacks to disrupt Taiwan's command and communications, air defense, and logistics.

====================================================================================================

The hidden bill: How Europe's scorching summers are reshaping national budgets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Another summer of record heat, drought and wildfires is leaving European governments with a bill that will land months later in the form of emergency relief, farm compensation, infrastructure repairs, unpaid taxes and food inflation.
The true price of the European heatwave and drought, as well as the consequent wildfires, only surfaces in public accounts months later.
Once the fires are out and the rivers refill, finance ministries are left compensating farmers, rebuilding roads and rail, propping up health services and absorbing revenue a slowed economy never generated.
That burden is outpacing the reserves governments hold against it and this year's stress is severe.
Half of the EU and the UK was under drought in late July, 9% at the most extreme "alert" stage, according to the Copernicus European Drought Observatory, while the rivers Loire, Po, Rhine and Danube touched record lows in August.
Wildfires had burnt more than 505,000 hectares by early August, according to the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, outpacing the same point in 2025, the worst year on record.
Extreme weather caused €822 billion in direct losses across the EU between 1980 and 2024, a quarter in the final four years, as per the European Environment Agency (EEA).
Asked by Euronews whether that concentration marked a genuine break with the past, the agency was unequivocal. "This is a step change," it said, explaining that it smooths volatile annual figures using a 30-year moving average to isolate the trend.
"The trend for the European economic loss data shows an increase of 3.4% per year and we have seen it accelerating in the data. First estimates of 2025 show that the trend will further accelerate."
Only about a fifth of those losses were insured, and for droughts, heatwaves and wildfires coverage collapses to 10% or 11%.
The reason, the EEA told Euronews, is that these hazards "mostly relate to indirect losses, such as reduced agricultural yields, loss of life, ecosystem degradation, lost working hours... and these are often difficult to assess".
"The insurance protection gap is increasing, meaning that the rise in total losses is not supported by more insurance," the EEA added.
That leaves governments as the insurer of last resort. However, only four EU member states, Austria, France, Hungary and Italy, maintain dedicated disaster funds as the rest rely on ad-hoc reallocations that disburse slowly.
To make matters worse, European money offers little cushion. The Brussels-based economic think tank Bruegel puts EU disaster funding for 2028-2034 at roughly €5 billion, equal to 10% to 15% of the damage from the 2021 western European floods alone.
Governments miscalculate the bill
France has produced the boldest number. Opening a drought crisis meeting on 12 August, Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut estimated this summer's heatwaves would cost €10 billion to €15 billion in direct and indirect costs, between 0.3% and 0.5% of GDP against a growth forecast of just 0.7%.
The figure, however, was immediately contested.
The national statistics institute INSEE, to which it was initially attributed, denied having produced any such projection. The ministry then clarified the extrapolation was its own, drawn from INSEE data for previous years, and Barbut conceded the numbers needed treating with caution.
In Spain, roughly 172,400 hectares had burnt by late July, about half of last year's total. Applying the per-hectare costs used by the Navarre forest agency and industry association Asemfo puts firefighting alone at €1.7 billion to €3.3 billion, before restoration, which forestry engineers say typically costs more than putting the fires out.
Brussels approved €120.55 million in emergency aid for Spain last month, covering only damage from the previous summer.
Portugal illustrates the deeper problem of the lack of appropriate calculations for the real costs of the wildfires.
Its civil protection authority has acknowledged publicly it "is not possible to determine, rigorously, the total cost of a specific occurrence" because financial and operational data sit in separate systems.
An independent commission investigating the August 2025 fires received an aggregate figure of about €18.8 million that could not be broken down by fire. The national audit court flagged the same gap in 2021.
Capturing indirect costs properly, the EEA told Euronews, would mean combining event records with "labour, health, transport, energy, agricultural and macroeconomic data provided by the sector organisations."
Revenue that never arrives
Spending is only half the equation.
Bruegel's review of the evidence finds economies still smaller years later, with GDP 1.5% lower two years after a heatwave and 3% lower four years after a drought. The 2022 drought alone cut EU per-capita GDP growth by 1.35%, a €203 billion loss.
For this summer, Triodos Bank puts the cost of extreme heat to EU economies at around €180 billion, roughly 1% of output.
Yet the immediate hit can look surprisingly mild.
Oxford Economics calculates record-low Rhine levels could shave 0.2% off German third-quarter growth but sees no wider collapse.
"This is more about offsets elsewhere in the economy," Tomas Dvorak, senior economist at Oxford Economics, told Euronews, pointing to defence manufacturing, transport equipment, retail and consumer services.
Summer factory shutdowns also lower capacity utilisation. "The Rhine is a major transport and logistical artery, but it ultimately only affects a small portion of the economy," Dvorak explained.
Food is where the damage surfaces, slowly.
The European Commission has cut its EU olive oil production forecast by 5%, driven by an 18% fall in Greece, while Spain expects its cereal harvest to fall from 24 million tonnes to little over 18.5 million. Oxford Economics expects heat and drought to add up to 1% to eurozone food inflation next year.
"This is simply how pricing works for food," Dvorak explained to Euronews. "It follows a sort of cascade from commodities to agriculture, processing and finally retail. Each step tends to take a month or two to filter," he added.
Forecasters have stopped treating these summers as anomalies. Oxford Economics has already built the costs into its baseline, with medium-term food inflation projected to average around 2.5%.
The danger is also that these pressures compound.
Bruegel describes a "climate sovereign doom loop" in which disaster losses depress growth and tax receipts, widening deficits and raising borrowing costs, leaving less room for the prevention spending that would limit the next disaster.
The ECB calculates a one-in-25-year drought would put nearly 15% of eurozone output at risk.
Yet, EU adaptation spending runs at about €29 billion a year against estimated needs of €35 billion to €500 billion, even though the UN estimates every euro spent returns up to ten in avoided losses.

Squash salad and chocolate mousse: Dean Parker’s recipes for early autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

As the days start to shorten and the temperature drops (finally!), the produce becomes richer, sweeter and more comforting, and the onset of autumn is a time of year that naturally brings people together around the table, which is something I’ve always loved about food. At the restaurant, we try to let the ingredients do the talking, and we work closely with growers and producers to make the most of whatever’s in season. Today’s recipes celebrate some of my favourite seasonal flavours: the salad is simple but deeply satisfying, balancing sweet roast squash with bitter greens and a punchy black olive tapenade. For dessert, meanwhile, chocolate mousse with poached fruit is my idea of autumn in a bowl, not least because quince has a beautiful, floral character that develops as it cooks, and pairs perfectly with dark chocolate and the nutty richness of browned butter. The creme fraiche adds freshness and balance, and brings everything together. Both dishes are rooted in the philosophy that guides my cooking: celebrate the season, respect great ingredients and create food that encourages people to slow down and enjoy each other’s company.
Roast squash and cavolo nero salad with black olive tapenade
This is the sort of dish that works just as well as a light lunch or as part of a larger feast shared with friends. If you like, top the finished salad with some crumbled feta, shaved pecorino or a spoonful of thick yoghurt.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 40 min
Serves 4-6
For the salad
1 medium butternut squash, halved, deseeded, peeled and cut into wedges
2 tbsp olive oil, plus a little extra for the cavolo nero
  1 pinch dried chilli flakes
  Sea salt and black pepper
  1 roughly 250g bunch cavolo nero
  Juice of ½ lemon
  2 tbsp toasted pumpkin seeds, or walnuts
For the tapenade
100g black olives, pitted
1 small garlic clove, peeled
1 tsp capers, drained
1 small handful flat-leaf parsley
  2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  1 tsp red-wine vinegar
  Black pepper
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Put the squash in a large roasting tray with the olive oil and chilli flakes, season generously and toss to coat. Spread out the squash into a single layer, then roast for 30-35 minutes, turning once halfway, until golden and tender.
Meanwhile, strip off and discard the thick stalks from the cavolo nero and tear the leaves into large pieces. Blanch these in salted boiling water for two minutes, then drain and refresh briefly under cold running water. Squeeze dry, put in a bowl and toss with the lemon juice and a little olive oil.
Now make the tapenade. Finely chop the olives, garlic, capers and parsley, either by hand or by pulsing in a food processor, then put them in a medium bowl. Stir in the olive oil and vinegar to form a rough paste, then season lightly with black pepper to taste.
Arrange the cavolo nero on a serving plate and top with the warm roast squash. Spoon over the tapenade, finish with a scattering of toasted pumpkin seeds and serve warm or at room temperature.
Chocolate mousse with poached quince and brown butter milk crumb
All the various elements of this dish can be made ahead, ready for assembly on the day. Quince season proper is a few weeks off still, so if you can’t wait, try making this with firm apples or pears instead, until the real thing appears on grocers’ shelves.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 2 hr
Chill 4 hr+
Serves 6
For the mousse
200g 70% cocoa dark chocolate
  3 eggs, separated
40g caster sugar
  300ml double cream
  Creme fraiche, to serve
For the poached quince
55ml clear honey
  375ml apple juice, or kombucha
20ml apple cider vinegar
  1 bay leaf
  3 black peppercorns
  ¼ cinnamon stick
  ¼ lemon
  250g quince
For the brown butter milk crumb
60g butter
  100g milk powder
  50g plain flour
  40g caster sugar
  1 pinch flaky sea salt
To make the mousse, melt the chocolate over a bain-marie, until smooth, then leave to cool slightly. Whisk the egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually work in the sugar until glossy. Lightly whip the cream to soft peaks.
Beat the egg yolks, stir into the melted chocolate, then fold in the whipped cream. Gently fold through the whisked egg whites until everything’s well incorporated, then spoon the mix into a container, and chill for at least four hours.
Now for the quince. Pour the honey in a medium-sized pan on medium heat and leave to cook until it starts to caramelise. Add all the remaining quince ingredients except the quince itself, and bring to a simmer.
Peel and quarter the quince(s), then cut out and discard the core(s). Add the quince to the honey pan, cover, turn down the heat to very low and leave to simmer gently for an hour and a half. Take the pan off the heat, leave to cool, then lift out the quince and cut into 2cm x 2cm dice.
For the milk crumb, heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Melt the butter in a small saucepan, then cook until it turns nut-brown and smells toasty. Mix the milk powder, flour, sugar and salt in a small bowl, pour in the melted brown butter and stir until the mix turns into small crumbs. Spread these out on a greased and lined oven tray, then bake for 12-15 minutes, stirring once halfway, until golden. Remove and leave to cool completely.
To assemble the dish, put a quenelle or spoonful of chocolate mousse on each plate, then dip a spoon in hot water and use the back of it to create a well in the centre of each portion of mousse. Spoon about 10 cubes of quince around one side of each serving of mousse, then generously scatter some brown butter milk crumb on the opposite side. Spoon a generous dollop of creme fraiche on top of the mousse and serve at once.
- 
  Dean Parker is head chef and co-owner of Celentano’s in Glasgow

NHS to offer free high-street cholesterol tests in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

The NHS in England is to offer free finger-prick blood tests for cholesterol on the high street for the first time under plans to reduce heart disease and stroke deaths by a quarter within the next decade.
The seven-minute tests will be available at participating pharmacies as part of a national rollout to spot “ticking timebombs” earlier.
People aged 40 to 84 who are not pregnant and have not had a blood test in the past year will be eligible to walk in and get tested.
Blood will be taken from a person’s fingertip using a lancet – a small, sharp medical tool used to prick the skin – and analysed immediately. A pharmacist prescriber can then provide lifestyle advice and determine whether any treatment, such as statins, may be needed.
Patients will receive a copy of their results by email. They will also be offered a blood pressure check as part of a clinical consultation with a pharmacist prescriber.
Details of the scheme – the first of its kind globally – were announced during the European Society of Cardiology’s annual congress in Munich, the world’s largest heart conference.
David Webb, the chief pharmaceutical officer for England, said pharmacies could be a vital first line of defence against serious illness.
He said: “By making it easier for people to get a quick and convenient cholesterol health check on their local high street, we can spot ticking timebombs earlier, helping people take action, and prevent heart attacks and strokes before they happen.
“This is the latest in a series of initiatives involving pharmacies in delivering care previously only offered in GP surgeries as part of the 10-year health plan to bring care closer to where people live.”
The rollout follows a successful pilot in north London by Barts Health NHS trust in collaboration with UCLPartners and the cholesterol charity Heart UK, in which 2,493 patients had checks.
Nearly one in five patients (19%) were found to be at high risk of a heart attack or stroke within the next decade. These people were offered advice and referred for treatment. At least 88 people started taking statins as result.
In the first phase of the national rollout, about 100 NHS pharmacies across England will begin offering the checks from this autumn.
Dr Sotiris Antoniou, the clinical lead for the scheme at Barts Health, said: “By scaling this approach across England, we can support pharmacists to identify cardiovascular risk earlier and, importantly, act on the results through timely advice and treatment.
“This has the potential to improve outcomes and reduce health inequalities, particularly in communities where the burden of cardiovascular disease is greatest.”
Dr Rani Khatib, NHS England’s national specialty adviser for cardiovascular disease prevention, said everyone should strive to be aware of the most common risk factors for heart disease, including high cholesterol and blood pressure, and “know their numbers”.
“This initiative will help people manage their risk factors earlier and reduce their risk of having heart attacks or strokes,” he said.
Alison McGovern, a health minister, said it was “exactly the type of innovation” she wanted to see across the NHS. “We’re making it easier for people to spot potential problems earlier and take action to protect their health,” she said.
“Early detection can help prevent serious conditions such as heart attacks and strokes, helping people stay healthier for longer while reducing pressure on NHS services.”

‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:15 UTC
14:00:15 KST

For Fatin, one of the teenage girls now living in limbo in a makeshift camp in the Spanish city of Ceuta, the decision to leave her home in Morocco began to form when she had to give up school.
She wanted to continue studying, she says, but at home she was expected to take responsibility for the housework instead. As classes and learning gave way to domestic chores, the future she had imagined for herself began to feel increasingly distant.
Fatin was one of 29 girls who shared their feelings about their past and future with the Guardian. All of them had been part of the mass crossing from Morocco in late July that made headlines around the world.
Nearly a month later, the girls are among hundreds of young Moroccans sleeping in an improvised settlement in El Príncipe, one of Ceuta’s most deprived neighbourhoods – uncertain if they will be allowed to remain in Spain or returned to Morocco.
For the girls who shared their thoughts, writing in Arabic and Darija, Spanish, French and English, the same aspirations surface repeatedly: to finish their education, to work, to earn their money and to have a greater say over the decisions that will shape their adult lives. Many wrote about professions. One wanted to be a nurse. Another a psychologist. Others imagined becoming chefs, footballers or sport trainers.
Some hope that if they succeed in Spain, they will be able to help their parents financially. Others describe conflict at home, interrupted schooling or restrictions they did not want to accept. What connects many of the conversations is less a rejection of Morocco than a desire to have more control over what comes next.
Malak, 17, says problems within her family prevented her from continuing her studies. She had known since childhood what she wanted to do: work in the intelligence services. Reaching Spain, she says, was partly an attempt to recover a future she felt had been closed off to her.
Others describe different pressures. One teenager says she does not want her family or anybody else to decide who she should marry. She wants to choose for herself. Another speaks about the difficulty of imagining financial independence in a place where she saw few opportunities to work.
In Morocco, the gap between men and women’s participation in the labour market remains stark. In the second quarter of 2026, just 18.1% of working-age women were part of the labour force, compared with 66.5% of men, according to Morocco’s High Commission for Planning.
The imbalance begins long before women enter the workplace. Women and girls aged 15 and over in Morocco spend 20.8% of their time on unpaid care and domestic work, compared with 3% for men and boys, according to figures from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
For Wiam, 16, her professional aspirations coexist with a strong sense of responsibility towards the family she left behind. She came from a town on Morocco’s Mediterranean coast, and wrote that she wanted to continue her studies and pursue a football career in Spain. But then she added another reason. “And also, to take a little of the burden off my parents,” she wrote. “God willing, I hope I achieve everything I came for.”
Other ambitions are expressed in only a few words. Soraya is 16. She came from a town near the border with Ceuta. She writes that she wants to become a nurse.
Some girls describe their ambitions in broader terms. One teenager writes that what she wants is “a healthy and stable life”. Another, 16, says she came in search of “a better future and a dignified life” and hopes to work in the restaurant industry. “I want to work with dignity and contribute to society,” she writes.
For now, their immediate needs are more basic than the futures they describe on paper. Safe accommodation, healthcare, privacy, education and clear information about what comes next. Ahmed Enfed-dal, president of the El Príncipe neighbourhood association, says local people have tried to create a protected space for the girls. But the limits of that protection are obvious.
“If they need to go to the toilet or take a shower, we try to make sure they are accompanied and never alone,” he says. By 17 August, prosecutors in Ceuta had recorded 13 formal complaints of sexual assault since the mass crossing began, with three minors among the victims.

New ranking reveals the 10 best wildlife encounters worth travelling for
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

From mountain gorilla trekking in Rwanda to African wild dog safaris in Botswana, here’s what you should be booking for your next wild experience.
There’s a reason that a safari is at the top of many people’s travel bucket lists. Wildlife encounters – the truly wild ones, where you see animals in their natural habitat – can only be described as magical.
While the Big Five dominate the conversation, it’s a wide, wild world out there, with everything from black rhinos in Namibia to the elusive snow leopard in the Himalayas.
To help narrow down the search, travel company Bailey Robinson has created the Wildlife Experience Index which ranked 30 of the world’s most remarkable experiences.
Each experience was evaluated across six factors, including rarity, based on population numbers and how difficult it is to encounter the animal in the wild; remoteness, or how far the experience is away from tourism infrastructure; conservation importance, which was informed by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species; exclusivity, which looked at access restrictions and visitor limitations; accessibility, or how easy it is to reach the encounter; and, finally, encounter potential, by examining the known opportunities for observation.
Each of these factors was scored out of 10 before being combined to produce a score out of 100.
The best wildlife encounters around the globe
The top score overall went to mountain gorilla trekking in Rwanda or Uganda, thanks in part to its 10/10 encounter potential score, with expert trackers ensuring you see what you came for.
In the case of Rwanda, there are just 96 permits issued each day, making the experience as exclusive – and as unobtrusive to the gorillas themselves – as possible, while at Uganda’s Bwindi National Park, treks are limited to just eight visitors per habituated family per day.
Second place went to Antarctica’s emperor penguin expeditions, with the experience scoring 10 out of 10 for both remoteness and exclusivity. Kazakhstan's saiga antelope expeditions were ranked third.
Asia and Africa dominated the list, while eight of the top 10 experiences involved threatened species.
“What particularly stood out to us was the relationship between rarity and remoteness,” Sarah Parker, sales director at Bailey Robinson, said.
“The world's most extraordinary wildlife encounters tend to involve travelling further, going deeper into wilderness and experiencing something that very few travellers will ever have the opportunity to see.
“For us, the real luxury is the opportunity to experience something rare and meaningful, while travelling responsibly and supporting the places and conservation projects that make these encounters possible.”
The top 10 wildlife experiences around the world
- Mountain gorilla trekking in Rwanda or Uganda – 90/100
- Emperor penguin expedition, Antarctica – 88.5/100
- Saiga antelope expedition, Kazakhstan – 87/100
- Snow leopard tracking, Ladakh or the Himalayas – 85.5/100
- Javan rhino tracking, Indonesia – 85/100
- Black rhino tracking, Namibia or Kenya – 84.5/100
- Polar bear expedition, Svalbard – 84/100
- Bornean orangutan encounter, Borneo – 84/100
- Eastern lowland gorilla expedition, Democratic Republic of the Congo – 81.5/100
- African wild dog safari, Botswana or Tanzania – 81/100

Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
The ingredients for rocky, potentially habitable planets may have appeared just 100 million years after the Big Bang, billions of years earlier than scientists once expected.
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- University of Portsmouth
- Summary:
- Rocky planets may have been able to start forming just 100 million years after the Big Bang, thanks to enormous early supernovae that scattered planet-building elements across space. Simulations found enough solid material and water around a young star to suggest that Earth-like worlds could have appeared far earlier than previously believed.
- Share:
The ingredients needed to build rocky planets may have appeared as early as 100 million years after the Big Bang, according to new research from the University of Portsmouth. That would place the beginnings of planet formation remarkably close to the dawn of the Universe, even before the first galaxies had fully emerged.
Scientists have long thought that planets took much longer to become possible, with significant planet formation beginning several billion years into cosmic history. The new findings suggest that the necessary conditions may have developed far sooner.
The First Stars Seeded Space With Planet Ingredients
Some of the earliest stars were extremely massive and ended their lives in violent explosions. These stellar blasts spread large quantities of elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron into the surrounding gas.
Known as 'Pop III supernovae', these explosions acted as the Universe's first major sources of the heavier elements required to make planets and, eventually, life.
Dr. Daniel Whalen, from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, said: "Our new paper, in which my PhD student Chris Jessop ran the first part of the simulation chain, shows that the precursors of terrestrial planets can form around low-mass, long-lived stars in the debris of the first cosmic explosions 100 million years after the Big Bang.
"To put this into perspective, the Universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so this is remarkably early in cosmic history."
Powerful Supernovae Could Create Planet-Forming Disks
One especially energetic kind of Pop III supernova, called a pair-instability supernova, can eject more than 100 times the Sun's mass in heavy elements during a single explosion.
That material can dramatically increase the abundance of heavy elements in nearby clouds of gas. As gravity pulls those enriched clouds together, they can form rotating disks around young stars, similar to the disk of material that eventually produced our own Solar System.
Dr. Whalen added: "In our computer simulations of the early Universe, we found one such disc around a young star about 70 percent as massive as the Sun. Within that disc, enough solid material accumulated to create several Earth-masses' worth of planetary building blocks at roughly the same distance from the star as Earth is from the Sun.
Water Was Already Present
The simulations revealed another striking feature: the disk contained a substantial supply of water.
"Most surprisingly, the disc also contained substantial amounts of water, only a few times less than what was available when our own Solar System formed. This means that any planets forming there could potentially have received water in a similar way to Earth, which is thought to have gained much of its water from material left over during the planet-building process.
"Our findings suggest that the conditions for planet formation may have existed much earlier than previously thought. If that's the case, it raises an intriguing question: could potentially habitable worlds have appeared far earlier in the Universe's history as well?"
The findings suggest that rocky planets, and possibly worlds with some of the ingredients associated with habitability, may have become possible much earlier in cosmic history than scientists previously expected.
The paper is published in The Astrophysical Letters Journal.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Portsmouth. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Eduard I. Vorobyov, Daniel J. Whalen, Muhammad A. Latif, Alexander Skliarevskii, Christopher Jessop, Ryoki Matsukoba, Takashi Hosokawa, Devesh Nandal. Planet Formation at Cosmic Dawn: Planetesimals in H2O-rich Disks around Low-mass Stars. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2026; 1007 (2): L51 DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/ae907c
