04:00:16 UTC
13:00:16 KST

Housebuyers are paying a premium of almost a quarter to own a property located within a UK national park, with the New Forest the most expensive national park to live in, according to Britain’s biggest building society.
Nationwide found that a property located within a national park cost 24% more on average than a similar property elsewhere, while buyers were also stumping up a 6% premium for homes within three miles of a national park.
The lender said that, as well as the attractions of the beautiful countryside, restricted development in national parks meant construction of new housing was limited, which kept house prices relatively high.
The average property in the New Forest was £563,000, followed by the South Downs park at £485,000, and the Peak District at £450,000.
Nationwide also found a 14% premium for properties located in the national landscapes of England and Wales, formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, such as Surrey Hills and the Chilterns.
Surrey Hills is the most expensive national landscape in which to buy property, with average prices of £710,000, the building society said. Designated in 1958 and covering approximately a quarter of the county of Surrey, the area is home to about 40,000 people who mostly live in small villages and rural hamlets, such as Shere, Mickleham and Westhumble.
The premiums paid on properties in these areas appear to be remaining remarkably consistent, with similar research by Nationwide from 2024 showing that homes in national parks attracted a 25% premium, while national landscape properties were 15% more expensive.

====================================================================================================

Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:00:16 UTC
13:00:16 KST

Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised.
“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”
Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake.
For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930.
For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate. “My being involved with advocating for Pluto started on the day of the vote,” says writer, actor and amateur astronomer Laurel Kornfeld. “I was like: wait a minute, this is wrong.” When we meet on Zoom she is wearing a T-shirt that says: “Pluto Resistance, 20 years: 2006-2026.”
The campaign to reinstate Pluto – with its passionate advocates, ongoing debates, occasional protests and petitions – seems to be largely confined to the US. “It is more of an issue in the United States,” says Metzger. “This was the one we discovered.” So, the planet’s demotion was a source of wounded pride? “I’ll admit there was some of that – among the public, not the scientists.”
More recently, the campaign has taken on a populist tinge, with Trump’s Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, telling a congressional committee in April that he was in favour of a rethink. “I am very much in the camp of Make Pluto a Planet Again,” he said.
The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?
Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?
In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.
It was the last point in particular that upset a lot of Pluto advocates, because a body’s ability to clear its neighbourhood depends a lot on the neighbourhood. “One of the biggest flaws with the IAU definition is that you can have the same object in two different orbits,” says Kornfeld. “In one, it’s considered a planet, and in the other, it’s not considered a planet.” If the Earth were towed out to Pluto’s position, the planetary scientist Alan Stern argued, it wouldn’t be able to clear its zone either, and would no longer meet the IAU definition of a planet.
“You could even have small asteroids, that are too small to be round, clearing an orbit if they’re close to a star,” says Metzger. “It just goes to show that orbit clearing isn’t really that meaningful of a category.”
To its detractors, the IAU definition seemed crafted with a specific intent. “A reason was invented to exclude Pluto,” says Kornfeld.
Pluto’s demotion created two opposing scientific teams: the so-called geophysical camp, which believes the physical properties of a celestial body should count toward its planethood; and the dynamicists, who are more concerned with the position a body occupies, its surroundings and its direction of travel. You could characterise the split as planetary scientists v astronomers. Many planetary scientists, including Metzger, simply do not use the IAU definition.
When the New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of Pluto in 2015, the geophysical camp seized what it saw as an advantage. Pluto definitely had the geophysical makings of a planet, they maintained. It had mountains, evidence of recent geological activity, and water ice hills floating on frozen nitrogen. It might even be able to support life. How could that not be a planet?
Those agitating for Pluto’s planetary status do not, by and large, recognise any problems stemming from reinstatement. They welcome a definition broad enough to take in hundreds of new planets, as taxing as that might be for children and their wallcharts. “The more the merrier,” says Paul Byrne, associate professor of earth, environmental and planetary sciences at Washington University in St Louis. “There are 1,025 official Pokémon species, and I’ve never heard a kid say that’s too many.”
Those against Pluto’s reinstatement say the problem isn’t with a larger number of planets, per se – but with a primarily geophysical definition that would encompass, among other bodies, planetary moons, including our moon.
“I have no problem with having a larger number of planets,” says the astronomer Mike Brown, over email. “My argument is simply that we decided long ago that the moon is not a planet and that also precludes Pluto.” Brown is often described as The Man Who Killed Pluto, because he led the team that discovered Eris back in 2005, setting the whole de-planetisation in motion. It’s a title he leans into: he even wrote a book called How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming.
Brown often says that the moon is bigger than Pluto; it’s round and has a complex geophysical history, and would certainly meet the criteria for a planet if you excluded any requirement concerning orbit. What he’s saying is: if Pluto’s a planet, so is the moon.
“I don’t have an issue with calling the moon a planet,” says Byrne. “Because I can be a brother and a husband at the same time, and it doesn’t require that I be one or the other. And so I don’t see why the moon can’t be a satellite and a planet.”
For the outsider, this debate can often seem mired in political, even procedural questions, with Plutonians contending that the IAU vote was incorrectly conducted and therefore void. “You could make the argument that they never officially voted on a planet because they didn’t follow the procedure that was required,” says Metzger.
Brown denies there was anything political about the decision. “The only people who complain about the voting procedure were the ones who didn’t like the outcome.”
So the question remains: why does any of this matter?
“It was almost like a coup,” says Kornfeld. “And as a result, kids are learning less. They’re learning eight planets, and that’s it.”
For Metzger, the planetary definition excluding Pluto is based on an outmoded notion of the solar system. “They were creating a reactionary view towards an orderly cosmos, rather than the more modern scientific view where it’s chaotic,” he says. “The second problem was that I think they misread the room. The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.”
Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. In 1915, the astronomer Percival Lowell published calculations based on peculiarities in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune, predicting the existence of a new, ninth planet, which he called Planet X, with a mass somewhere between Earth’s and Neptune’s. In 1930, the long search for Planet X bore fruit: the new body, discovered at the observatory that bore Lowell’s name, was christened Pluto.
Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, it was small – even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.
Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, may stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?
“People have locked in,” says Metzger. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognise that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”

Spain beyond the beach: the best places to visit this autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:00:13 UTC
13:00:13 KST

Spain is the top choice for September travel, taking 43% of bookings. Beyond its beaches, historic cities, charming villages and inland landscapes define the new season.
Spain's top autumn destinations include the islands among their biggest attractions. Tenerife has become the most-booked destination for September, ahead of Rome and Paris, according to data from eDreams, one of the leading travel booking platforms.
Palma de Mallorca, Madrid and Ibiza round out the top spots, while Gran Canaria also makes it into the most in-demand national destinations.
Interest in travelling within Spain remains particularly high this month: the country accounts for 43% of bookings for September, well ahead of Italy with 11% and France with 6%.
Bookings for September have also risen by 57% compared with last year, according to online travel agency eSky. Milder temperatures, fewer crowds and lower prices explain part of this increase.
But beyond the destinations leading the booking rankings, which places in Spain are worth visiting this autumn?
Far more than sun and sand
Spain is not just a beach destination. When autumn arrives, inland tourism takes centre stage, with cities and villages offering an alternative to coastal resorts.
The city of Salamanca is one option for those who prefer to swap the beach for an urban break. Its old town, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site, invites visitors to explore on foot places such as the Plaza Mayor, the Casa de las Conchas, the Huerto de Calixto y Melibea and the University.
Autumn also brings a calmer atmosphere to the city and makes it easier to combine a visit there with an excursion around the province.
Just a few kilometres from the provincial capital lies Candelario, in the heart of the Sierra de Béjar and part of the Los Pueblos Más Bonitos de España network of Spain's prettiest villages. Its cobbled streets and traditional houses with their characteristic half-doors make Candelario an especially attractive autumn getaway.
The municipality allows visitors to combine a walk through its historic centre with routes in a natural setting that changes colour as the season arrives. And when November brings the first drops in temperature, the popular saying "On All Saints' Day, snow on the heights" makes sense, reminding us that the first snow can appear in the highest areas.
Forests and autumn landscapes
For nature lovers, the Ambroz Valley in Cáceres is another destination worth keeping on the radar if you are thinking of getting away this autumn.
Spain's autumn destinations guide includes this area among its recommendations thanks to its chestnut and oak woods, as well as its rivers and natural scenery, which are particularly beautiful at this time of year.
Choosing these destinations for a break can also be a way to support local economies in areas that have suffered the impact of forest fires. That is the case of the Ambroz Valley, the Sierra de la Culebra in Zamora, Gredos in Ávila, and Las Médulas in León, where tourism can help maintain economic activity and support the recovery of affected areas.
In the north, Asturias offers a highly recommended combination of landscapes, villages and gastronomy. Its forests and valleys are perfect for enjoying hiking routes and rural escapes in autumn, while dishes such as fabada asturiana and cachopo, local cheeses and traditional Asturian cider make up an ideal offering for this time of year.
Autumn through wine and food
The season is also a great time to discover Spain through its products and traditions. La Rioja and Ribera del Duero are two options for combining inland landscapes with experiences linked to the grape harvest and the world of wine.
As autumn progresses, chestnuts and mushrooms take centre stage in many rural areas and become another attraction for planning a mycological getaway.
From the islands to charming cities, via small villages and natural spaces, Spain offers autumn alternatives for almost every type of traveller, beyond the beach destinations that tend to be favourites during the summer months.

DUSHANBE, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- China, as one of the founding members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), has consistently expanded the organization's cooperation agenda and contributed to its development, SCO Deputy Secretary-General Ahmad Saidmurodzoda said in a written interview with Xinhua.
Established in 2001, the SCO has followed its own path of steady development over the past 25 years, Saidmurodzoda said.
From the very beginning, the founding members reaffirmed their commitment to the goals and principles of the UN Charter, he said.
Moreover, in their first declaration, the leaders of the six founding countries also expressed their readiness to develop dialogue, contacts and cooperation in various forms with other states, as well as international and regional organizations, he recalled.
"Today, 25 years later, it can be stated with confidence that the SCO has never strayed from its originally declared goals," Saidmurodzoda stressed, noting that, in terms of territory, population and economic potential, the SCO has become the world's largest trans-regional organization.
Highlighting China's important role as a founding member, Saidmurodzoda said China has consistently contributed to the organization's development.
China has made significant contributions during each of its terms as SCO chair, helping advance cooperation in regional security, trade and economic affairs, as well as cultural and humanitarian fields, while enhancing the SCO's role and influence in regional and global affairs, he said.
Saidmurodzoda attached particular importance to the SCO Tianjin Summit, held from Aug. 31 to Sept. 1, 2025, under China's chairmanship.
"The summit truly turned a new page in the history of the organization," he said.
What distinguished the Tianjin Summit, he noted, was its high efficiency and focus on practical solutions and concrete agreements, with its outcomes marking important milestones in the organization's long-term development.
Specifically, Saidmurodzoda highlighted the adoption of the SCO Development Strategy until 2035 at the summit, describing it as a "roadmap" and a comprehensive action plan for the decade ahead. ■

Column: SCO at 25: a model for new type of int'l relations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:57:09 CST
12:57:09 KST

by Al Mamun Harun Ur Rashid
As the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) enters its 25th year, the international system stands at an important historical crossroads, marked by escalating geopolitical tensions and zero-sum thinking. While Western countries erect exclusive blocs to deter the Global South and preserve their superpower dominance, China actively advances the SCO, not a military alliance, but a platform of partnership and mutual cooperation to build a community with a shared future for humanity.
Established in Shanghai on June 15, 2001, by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, the SCO evolved from the Shanghai Five mechanism. India and Pakistan joined in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, bringing its full membership to 10 countries.
What began as a Central Asian security mechanism now spans Eurasia, covering security, trade, transport, energy, agriculture, science, education, health and culture. It is neither a military alliance nor an economic bloc, but a platform for cooperation among states with mutually diverse interests and foreign policies.
This expansion reflects the magnetic appeal of the "Shanghai Spirit," which rejects exclusive alliances to practice "harmony without uniformity." It provides an institutional space where diverse nations cooperate on an equal footing while fully preserving their strategic autonomy and distinctive development paths.
The China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has also become an important element of economic discussions within the organization. Several SCO members have supported efforts to connect BRI projects with other regional economic initiatives, including the Eurasian Economic Union. It is estimated that the combined economic aggregate of the SCO member states stands at close to 30 trillion U.S. dollars.
Countries across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East have increasingly called for greater representation in global decision-making, particularly in institutions whose structures were established under different geopolitical and economic conditions.
At the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus" Meeting on Sept. 1, 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping emphasized taking actions to uphold international fairness and justice, urging member states to oppose hegemonism and power politics. This stance reinforces the SCO's role as a pillar of global governance reform.
Beyond security, the SCO is developing financial cooperation, including greater use of national currencies and financing mechanisms. The New Development Bank, though a BRICS institution rather than an SCO body, reflects the expanding Global South development finance architecture, with 42.9 billion U.S. dollars approved for 139 projects by the end of 2025.
The SCO's expanding network of partner countries also gives non-members channels for engagement on trade, transport, energy, tourism, education and other issues.
For regional countries such as Bangladesh, the SCO's significance can therefore be viewed through the prism of connectivity and economic development.
Bangladesh does not need to choose between competing geopolitical camps to engage with emerging Eurasian institutions. Its interests could include greater access to Central Asian markets, transport connectivity, energy cooperation, food security, digital development and wider South-South economic links.
The 25-year journey of the SCO proves to the world that a more representative and balanced international order is entirely achievable.
The SCO has already demonstrated that countries with respective interests can maintain a common institutional framework. Its next challenge is to translate that political durability into more measurable gains in trade, connectivity, development, security and people-to-people cooperation.
Editor's note: Al Mamun Harun Ur Rashid is a diplomatic correspondent at The New Nation, a leading English-language mainstream newspaper in Bangladesh. He covers Bangladesh's foreign policy, diplomacy, regional affairs and international relations, with a particular focus on China, the broader Asia-Pacific region and the Global South.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

The VAT inflows jumped 3.2 trillion won in the cited month, driven by a growth in final VAT filings for the first half of 2026 and robust import expansion.
The country's imports surged 26.5 percent from a year earlier to 68.57 billion dollars in July.
Revenue from the securities transaction tax added 1.1 trillion won, while the special tax for rural development, levied on stock transactions, mounted 2 trillion won last month.
The expansion was backed by a spike in trading volumes of listed stocks, which skyrocketed 232.4 percent over the year to 2,087.2 trillion won in June.
The collection of income tax climbed 1.8 trillion won in July from a year earlier, supported by higher payroll payouts alongside a recovery in the housing market that increased the collection of capital gains tax.
Most other tax categories logged a modest increase, with the collections of corporate tax, inheritance and gift tax, and individual consumption tax rising 0.1 trillion won each.
Meanwhile, the transportation, energy and environment tax decreased 0.3 trillion won, reflecting the government's decision to expand fuel tax cuts. ■

The business expectation index for the construction sector remained flat at 51.8.
Monday's data also showed that the PMI for China's manufacturing sector stood at 49.8 in August, up 0.6 percentage points from July. The composite PMI output index rose from 49.3 to 49.5. ■

Seoul district offers foreigners multilingual help to navigate South Korean rental market
The foreign population in Gangbuk has nearly doubled over the past decade to roughly 7,000 residents
To help bridge this informational divide and protect vulnerable foreign renters, Gangbuk, a northern administrative district in Seoul, is expanding a comprehensive municipal programme designed to safeguard foreign residents throughout the housing lease process.
Under the enhanced initiative, foreign tenants visiting local neighbourhood centres to register their move-in address or file for an official “fixed date” status (hwakjeong ilja) will receive automated administrative guidance stamped directly onto their documentation in nine languages. The legal stamp – covering English, Chinese, Vietnamese, Mongolian, Tagalog, Uzbek, Japanese, Taiwanese and Thai – outlines essential protections under the Housing Lease Protection Act.
In the South Korean rental market, obtaining an official fixed date is a critical statutory step that grants tenants legal priority to reclaim key security deposits should a landlord face foreclosure or property auction.
Alongside the multilingual stamps, district offices are distributing QR code stickers linking directly to My Seoul, a dedicated mobile application operated by the Seoul Metropolitan Government. By scanning the code, foreign residents can easily install the application to access multi-language housing guidelines, municipal safety updates and multicultural social services.

Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:55:00 UTC
12:55:00 KST

Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' in US
August 31, 2026
Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" for users in the US.
It comes days after President Donald Trump ordered the lake to be renamed, which included changing the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see 'Lake America,' those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario,' and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names," Google said in a brief statement.
"These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now."
Google's decision to follow through with Trump's order echoes its 2025 move to label the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America." Mexico sued Google in response.
Why did Trump order the name change?
Lake Ontario gets its name from the Indigenous Wendat word "Ontari'io," meaning "big, beautiful lake." The province of Ontario to the north later adopted this name after the lake.
Trump's decision to change this centuries-old name comes amid a trade war between the US and Canada.
The two countries had spent weeks negotiating a deal to resolve the war which was prompted by Trump's tariffs on Canada, but Ottawa pulled out after Prime Minister Mark Carney complained of "last-minute changes" that were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."
Among the sticking points, Carney said, were American objections to French product labeling laws as well as French content requirements for streaming services in Quebec.
Canada puts up signs, takes down websites
On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a new sign on the shore of the lake.
It read, "Lake Ontario: Now and always" — in both English and French.
"President Trump can call it whatever he wants, but I can tell you, the rest of the world will always call it Lake Ontario," Ford said.
However, the new name "Lake America" did sneak into some applications north of the border.
A number of government-run websites in Canada that use Google Maps saw the name change automatically. This included the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, which had actually pulled American alcohol off the shelves as part of the trade war.
"Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps," Ontario's public services minister Stephen Crawford said on Sunday evening.
"Following recent changes by Google, we're actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario."

MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. "The Council’s activities are now largely confined to expert-level contacts and remote meetings of its working bodies," Lavrov concluded.

Unknown

2026-08-31

12:52:42 KST

The US attacks on Iran are the first in around a month as the Trump administration had shifted its war objective to inflict maximum economic pain on Tehran. Washington says the strikes were aimed at preventing Iranian forces from disrupting global shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran said on Monday that it has launched strikes targeting US military positions in Jordan in response to Washington’s first attack on its territory in a month, marking a fresh flare-up in the six-month war.
Tehran's elite IRGC said it struck two US military air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing "heavy damage".
Shortly after Iran’s announcement, the Jordanian army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
The strikes came after the US revealed on Sunday that it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on Larak, a small island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the strategic waterway.
"US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz," the US Central Command wrote in a post on X.
"Last week, CENTCOM completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes," said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for the US Central Command.
"US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway," he said.
The IRGC said the US strikes resulted in "casualties".
Strikes on top of economic pressure
The exchange of fire came just days after the war hit the six-month mark amid little to no visible progress in negotiations between the two sides to end it.
In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump and his administration prioritised "economic warfare" over military strikes on Iran amid intense domestic and international pressure to end the military campaign, which Washington said would be short-lived, but has since extended to months with no end in sight.
Tehran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic sea lane through which around one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the US and Israel launched the war’s opening salvo on 28 February.
Iran went on a near-daily campaign of missile and drone strikes against US facilities and allies in the Gulf region, hitting targets in Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, among others, dragging the wider region into conflict.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by two main mediators Qatar and Pakistan, have tried for months to bring an end to the war.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming, and Washington has since declared "economic warfare" against Tehran.
A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran during a shortfall in domestic production, as the US ramps up the pressure.
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, and the collapse of the interim deal over the summer have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement.
The last US strike on Iran prior to Sunday's came on 29 July in response to "an attempted surprise attack on US forces" in the region, the US military said. Earlier in July, CENTCOM attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights.
Tehran’s closure of the strategic waterway has inflicted significant economic pain worldwide through logistical and supply chain crises, price hikes, and shortages of fertiliser and energy.
Oil prices rose after news of the renewed US strikes on Iran. Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed back above the symbolic $90 per barrel for the first time in a month. During the peak of the fighting, oil prices surpassed $120 per barrel for the first time in decades.

US President Donald Trump late Sunday shared an AI-generated video of the imagined destruction of Iran's Kharg Island, saying that strategic oil hub is “being blown to smithereens.”
“Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Tensions between Tehran and Washington have remained high since the war began with strikes on Iran in late February.

He added that Iran and North Korea have significantly strengthened this Russian advantage through their assistance. In addition, Russia is exploiting Ukraine's shortage of ballistic missile interceptors – a NATO-wide inventory problem that grants Russia leverage and enables sustained ballistic missile salvos.

Egypt rules out using Suez Canal to settle government debt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:44:42 UTC
12:44:42 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Tarek Chouiref
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
Egypt on Sunday ruled out using the Suez Canal or other state assets to settle government debt, saying the strategic waterway is not part of any such plan.
The Cabinet issued the statement after a proposal circulated suggesting that some state assets could be transferred to the Central Bank of Egypt in exchange for reducing part of the government’s domestic debt.
It said the proposal was a “purely personal view” and did not reflect government policy, stressing that the idea was “unacceptable and will not happen.”
The Cabinet was particularly categorical about the Suez Canal, saying there are no plans to swap, mortgage or transfer ownership of the waterway in exchange for debt.
It said the canal is directly tied to Egypt’s national security and sovereignty and plays a central role in both the country’s economy and global trade.
The government also rejected the broader premise of shifting state assets to the Central Bank, arguing that moving assets and liabilities between public institutions would not reduce the country’s overall obligations.
Public debt, it said, must instead be addressed through its structure, servicing costs, domestic liquidity, and the broader impact on fiscal and monetary policy.
Hassan Heikal, an adviser to the prime minister, floated the idea Saturday, suggesting that Egypt could use stakes in state-owned companies or even the Suez Canal to offset domestic debt by transferring the corresponding liabilities to the Central Bank.
He cited a recent debt settlement involving Egypt’s National Media Authority, formerly known as Maspero, as a possible model.
On Thursday, the government announced an agreement to settle 88.3 billion Egyptian pounds ($1.77 billion) owed by the authority to the National Investment Bank, without disclosing the terms of the settlement or the assets involved.

Israeli commander shows no remorse for Gaza strikes that killed 7 aid workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:41:34 UTC

Rania Abushamala
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
The Israeli commander who ordered the 2024 drone strikes that killed seven World Central Kitchen (WCK) aid workers in the Gaza Strip has defended his decision, saying he does not regret authorizing the attack.
“I’m not sorry for what I did,” Col. Nochi Mendel, who was dismissed as chief of staff of the Israeli army’s Nahal Brigade after the attack, told Australia’s public broadcaster ABC News.
The interview was conducted in October 2025 but published on Thursday following an Israeli military decision not to launch a criminal investigation or take further action against those involved.
Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, 43, and six colleagues were killed on April 1, 2024, when Israeli drones struck three clearly marked WCK vehicles traveling in a coordinated humanitarian convoy in central Gaza.
The three vehicles were hit separately over four minutes as survivors attempted to move from one car to another.
Mendel claimed that drone footage showed armed Palestinians mixing with WCK personnel near a warehouse in central Gaza and that an armed man later entered one of the vehicles.
He said personnel operating the drone from Palmachim air base had confirmed the alleged presence of an armed man before he authorized the strike.
Asked whether any armed Palestinians were killed, Mendel said: “Maybe one, or maybe none.”
The Israeli army initially described the attack as a “grave mistake” resulting from the misidentification of the convoy’s occupants. It later said that what soldiers believed was a weapon carried by a person entering one of the vehicles was actually a bag.
An Australian investigation led by former air force chief Mark Binskin found that senior Israeli commanders had refused an earlier request by Mendel and another officer to attack vehicles near the warehouse because of their proximity to the humanitarian convoy.
The inquiry also found that the strikes were approved despite a direction from a divisional commander that no further attacks should take place near humanitarian convoys that night.
Mendel claimed the WCK vehicles had deviated from a route coordinated with the Israeli military. The Australian inquiry, however, found that the decision to attack had already been made before the convoy changed direction, meaning the turn could not have influenced the authorization.
The WCK rejected Mendel’s allegations that the organization had links to Hamas as “false and outrageous,” accusing him of attempting to shift responsibility away from the Israeli army.
The organization renewed its demand for a full and independent investigation into the killing of its personnel.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also demanded that Israel commission an independent investigation, while Frankcom’s family criticized the Israeli military for refusing to provide recordings of communications between the drone operators and commanders.

'They filmed here to say the city was dead': new families breathe life into war-battered Kiryat Shmona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:38:05 UTC
12:38:05 KST

After more than a decade of standing deserted, Hermon Square in Kiryat Shmona came back to life Thursday as a group of families who moved to the city in recent months inaugurated a cafe and cultural center aimed at restoring vibrant commercial activity to the area.
When the host of the opening event asked the city’s new residents to raise their hands, hundreds went up. Jacqueline Elharar, 83, a mother of 18 who immigrated to Kiryat Shmona from Morocco in the late 1950s, was invited onstage as a representative of the city’s longtime residents and received a bouquet from one of the families that had moved to the city only the previous week. “It was very moving to meet them,” she said. “They bring light. There is a feeling that good news is coming here too. That is not something we take for granted.”
The initiative to establish the cafe and local cultural center is being led by Danny Koten, a social entrepreneur and one of the founders of the Kiryat Shmona Garin, a community group whose members have relocated to the city. Koten himself moved from Tel Aviv and is working to help absorb the new families.
“We want to create a place here that feels different, that feels like Kiryat Shmona,” he said. “A place for beer and performances — not somewhere for a one-time event, but a place that will bring foot traffic back and give other entrepreneurs and business owners a lively space where they can open businesses.”
In nearby IDF Square, the Tarbut Movement is also establishing a creative and activity space for artists at the start of their careers.
Koten, who is married and has two children, explained why the group chose to open the cafe in the abandoned square.
“We moved here last summer and saw that anyone who wanted to attack the city would come and film Hermon Square and say, ‘Look how dead this city is, everything here is closed,’” he said. “This is not only the heart of Kiryat Shmona, it is a symbol of the heart of the Galilee.”
Koten sees students at the University of Kiryat Shmona as a strategic target audience. The institution, based on the former Tel Hai Academic College, is set to begin operating with university status in the 2026-27 academic year.
“We wanted to establish a well-designed cafe here with a top-premium feel, an excellent coffee machine, comfortable and attractive furniture and innovative design,” he said.
“Kiryat Shmona is a university city. But while downtown Beersheba, for example, which has a university, is the center of activity where students go for services, social life and community, here the situation is the opposite. They find all of that in the small kibbutzim around the city. We want to create those places here. This will be a great university city.”
To help revive the deserted city center, Bank Hapoalim joined the new initiatives through its Poalim for Revival fund, donating more than half a million shekels.
Alongside the cafe and shared workspace, 12 cultural events will be held throughout the year under the title “Live Thursday in the Square,” featuring live performances and a night market with stalls run by local businesses.
“We are excited to see the vision becoming reality and life returning to the city square,” said Sharona Tarshish, Bank Hapoalim’s community relations director.
Kiryat Shmona Mayor Avichai Stern welcomed the new residents. “You chose to come here at a time when choosing Kiryat Shmona cannot be taken for granted,” he said. “You chose not only a new address, but a community.”
On the eve of the evacuation, Kiryat Shmona was experiencing growth and stood at an unprecedented turning point. Nearly 26,000 residents were evacuated in October 2023 after the outbreak of the war, and fewer than 10,000 have returned so far.
About 40% of the city’s businesses have also not reopened, while those that have are now grappling with lower revenues. Customer traffic remains relatively sparse compared with before the war, slowing the rehabilitation of the urban center and creating a barrier to the opening of new businesses.
Against that backdrop, dozens of new families, totaling more than 300 residents, have chosen to move to the city and take part in its revival alongside longtime residents. They do not see their mission as rehabilitating or saving the town, but as taking part in rebuilding it.

====================================================================================================

Twenty five years after Durban, equating Zionism with racism has become mainstream - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:23:00 UTC
12:23:00 KST

Twenty-five years ago today, representatives from around the world gathered in Durban, South Africa, for what should have been one of the most worthy exercises the United Nations could undertake: a global conference against racism.
Instead, Durban became a watershed in the modern campaign to delegitimize Israel, and helped set the stage for the attitude, language, and vitriol we see directed against the Jewish state and those termed “Zionists” nowadays.
The 2001 World Conference against Racism 2001 included a draft document equating Zionism with racism, targeting Israel alone for its right to exist. Among back-and-forth debates over the exact language used, the idea still stood out as attacking the tiny Jewish state.
The United States and Israel eventually walked out. Jewish participants encountered open antisemitism surrounding the parallel NGO gathering. Israel was accused of racism, apartheid, and genocide, while a conference intended to confront prejudice became consumed by an attempt to revive, in a new form, the old charge that Zionism itself was racism.
The final declaration of the official UN conference did not equate Zionism with racism. Attempts to insert such language were defeated, and the document condemned antisemitism.
The NGO forum was another matter, however. Its declaration accused Israel of being an “apartheid state,” spoke of genocide and racist crimes, and called for its international isolation. Outside the conference halls, antisemitic caricatures circulated, and demonstrators carried signs praising Hitler.
What makes Durban so important 25 years later, however, is that it was more than an ugly gathering. The accusations themselves were hardly new. The Soviet Union and Arab states had spent decades portraying Zionism as racism and Israel as uniquely malevolent. Durban took those ideas and gave them a new home.
The language migrated from Soviet and Arab political polemic into the world of NGOs, international law, and human rights, a trajectory we see continuing today. Accusations could now be accompanied by reports, legal terminology, boycott campaigns and the authority of organizations widely regarded in the West as guardians of universal moral principles.
The language associated with racist regime was increasingly transferred to Israel
South Africa provided a particularly powerful setting for that transformation. Apartheid had ended less than a decade earlier, and a conference there against racism should have celebrated that achievement. Instead, the language associated with South Africa’s racist regime was increasingly transferred to Israel.
Durban helped to establish the future strategy that was to be used to delegitimize Israel.
Over the following quarter-century, that strategy became steadily more familiar. Successive conflicts involving Israel brought allegations of war crimes, international investigations, and NGO reports. Boycott campaigns grew, and the apartheid accusation moved from activist circles toward mainstream political and academic discourse.
Then came October 7 and the Gaza war.
By 2026, much of what caused outrage at Durban has become routine. Israel is regularly accused of apartheid, racism, and genocide. Zionism – the movement for Jewish national self-determination – is increasingly presented as an inherently racist ideology.
More troubling still is the way the word “Zionist” itself is sometimes used. Criticism of Zionism is not inherently antisemitic, just as criticism of Israel is not. But when “Zionists” supposedly control governments, money, or the media, or when Zionists as a category are declared unwelcome in public spaces, the ancestry of those accusations is difficult to disguise. An ancient prejudice does not become respectable simply because “Zionist” has replaced “Jew.”
None of this places Israel beyond criticism. Israeli governments should be scrutinized, wars examined, civilian suffering confronted and policies challenged. Israelis themselves conduct those arguments every day.
Criticism of Israel and opposition to what Israel is
Durban’s poison lay elsewhere. It helped erode the distinction between criticism of what Israel does and opposition to what Israel is.
Durban did not invent antisemitism or anti-Zionism. Its significance lay in helping to take ideas that had existed at ideological extremes and repackage them in the vocabulary of human rights.
Twenty-five years later, we have come disturbingly close to completing the circle. Language that helped drive Israel and the United States from a UN conference against racism in 2001 no longer shocks people. Much of it has become part of the everyday vocabulary used to discuss Israel.
That is Durban’s legacy – and why, a quarter-century later, remembering what happened there is still of the utmost importance and worth fighting against.

Sen. Ted Cruz says 'unequivocal yes' to Trump’s 'mission accomplished' claim on Iran

12:22:59 KST

United States Senator Ted Cruz backed President Donald Trump’s Truth Social post declaring “mission accomplished” in the war with Iran, while going further by calling for the collapse of the Iranian regime during a Meet the Press interview on Sunday.
Host Kristen Welker asked Cruz whether he agreed with the president’s declaration, noting that the war was entering its sixth month this week despite Trump previously saying it would last only a few weeks.
Cruz responded that he agreed “unequivocally” that the president’s military objectives had been achieved.
According to Cruz, the US has eliminated Iran’s military capabilities and nearly destroyed its supply and manufacturing infrastructure for ballistic missiles and drone programs, as well as its air force, navy, and leadership.
“Their air force is in rubble on the runway. Their navy is sunk and at the bottom of the ocean. Much of their senior leadership has been eliminated. So in terms of military objectives, I think that is correct,” Cruz said.
Cruz also addressed the US blockade of Iran and its objective of imposing economic pressure on the country, claiming that Iran’s economy is in “free fall.”
“Now, if you also look at the objective of imposing economic harm, right now with the blockade that we are holding on Iran, Iran is facing $500 million a day of economic cost. That is enormous cost that is ratcheting up,” Cruz said.
Cruz supports collapsing Iran regime, arming Kurds and protesters
The senator went further, saying he supports a long-term objective of collapsing the Iranian regime and doing so by arming Kurdish forces and protesters.
“Now, I would like to see the longer-term objective be regime collapse,” Cruz said.
“The ayatollah and the mullahs are radical Islamist zealots... The Ayatollah routinely chants, ‘Death to America.’ The Ayatollah... This regime... has been the world’s leading state sponsor of terror for 47 years. So what I’ve been urging is for President Trump and the Trump administration to arm the protesters, the people of Iran. Arm the Kurds and let the protesters remove this regime,” he said.
Welker followed up by asking Cruz why US troops had not returned home if the military objectives had been achieved.
Cruz responded that while there are “occasional skirmishes,” the “active military conflict has reduced significantly,” and said the troops’ current role is focused on enforcing economic pressure through the blockade.
Cruz highlights role of Iranian protesters
Cruz said he believes economic sanctions are a powerful tool, but argued they would be even more effective with support from protesters inside Iran. He also highlighted that the conflict began after the regime killed tens of thousands of protesters.
He reiterated his support for arming protesters, saying: “Frankly, Kristen, it’s not fair to expect some Iranian protester standing there with a rock to stand up against soldiers with machine guns. I believe if we arm the protesters, particularly the Kurds, who had a long history of being effective fighters.”
Cruz said that while the US should not determine who governs Iran, it does have an interest in preventing the country from being ruled by a regime that threatens America.
“It’s not our business to determine who the government of Iran is. But it is our business to say the government of Iran should not be a radical theocrat who hates America and is trying to kill Americans,” he said.
Cruz concluded by praising Trump’s leadership, saying: “And President Trump is acting as a strong commander in chief to keep the American people safe.”

Taiwan warns of China travel risk after reported Shanghai interrogation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:11:21 UTC
12:11:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Mainland Affairs Council on Sunday urged citizens considered high-risk to assess the necessity of traveling to China after a social-media user reported that his son was questioned for about six hours after arriving in Shanghai because he had previously worked for Amnesty International.
The user, whose Threads account is identified as vincentchou08, said his son arrived in Shanghai on Saturday afternoon for a business trip and was stopped at immigration before being taken to a private room for questioning. According to the post, three plainclothes officers questioned the man extensively about his previous work with the human rights organization, per CNA.
The officers allegedly asked about his responsibilities; whether he had worked on reports or human rights advocacy involving China, Hong Kong, Xinjiang, or Tibet; the organization's sources of funding; and his contacts with Taiwanese and international politicians and human rights activists.
The man was also allegedly asked to unlock his phone so officers could examine his chat history and work-related files, according to the post. The man told his father that he had not been a decision-maker or core member of the organization and had already left his job. He also said his trip was for personal reasons and had no political purpose. The post said the man ultimately decided not to enter China and returned to Taiwan later that evening.
The account holder questioned how Chinese authorities had learned about his son's previous employment, suggesting that Chinese intelligence agencies may have compiled lists of employees, interns, and volunteers associated with international human rights organizations and major Taiwanese NGOs. The claim about such intelligence lists could not be independently verified.
The father said he was relieved that his son did not "become another Lee Ming-che (李明哲)," referring to the Taiwanese pro-democracy activist who was detained by Chinese authorities in March 2017 and later sentenced to five years in prison for subversion of state power. Lee was released in April 2022 after completing his sentence and returned to Taiwan the following day.
MAC said Sunday that the individual involved had not reported the incident to the government but that the account was consistent with other cases previously handled by the council. The council encouraged Taiwanese to share their experiences of difficulties encountered while traveling in China, saying such accounts help raise public awareness of potential risks, per CNA.
The council said China has shown intolerance toward criticism involving democracy and pluralism and has been hostile toward personnel from overseas NGOs working on issues including human rights, environmental protection, oversight of public power, labor rights, and gender diversity.
It also warned that people who were politically active in Taiwan earlier in their lives but later moved into nonpolitical fields could still face scrutiny or punishment by Chinese authorities.
The council said China's new “Revision of Exit and Entry Administration” is scheduled to take effect Sept. 15, significantly increasing personal safety risks for Taiwanese traveling to China. The council has urged Taiwanese to register their trips through its online registration system for citizens visiting China, which allows the government to contact travelers and provide emergency assistance.

No roofs, no toilets, no teachers: TOI check finds minuses in Rajasthan govt schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:05:27 UTC
12:05:27 KST

TOI reporters visited govt schools across six Rajasthan districts after the row over CJP volunteers inspecting campuses. What they found, from Kota’s coaching hub to desert villages and tragedy-hit Piplodi, was a system in which children study under tin sheds, squeeze into unsafe rooms, and sometimes find their school locked.In Kota, a primary school with 78 students operates from municipal parking kiosks and tin sheds. Three teachers run the school on deputation, with no permanent teaching posts sanctioned. A PWD survey found 61 school buildings in the district ruined and hundreds of classrooms unsafe.Across Barmer, Jaisalmer and Balotra, some schools lack buildings, while transfers have left senior-secondary streams without teachers. In Piplodi, Jhalawar, where a roof collapse killed seven children in July 2025, classes still run from a farmer’s two-room home as construction of a new school drags on.In the CM’s Sanganer constituency, 404 students at one school have been pushed into four rooms after a second building was declared unsafe.Assembly data shows 611 govt schools have no building of their own; 2,047 lack toilets; and 1,049 lack drinking water.
Another 3,768 buildings and 83,783 classrooms are classified as completely dilapidated. Rajasthan also has 7,200 single-teacher schools and 1.5 lakh vacant teacher posts.
List of Rajasthan districts TOI visited.
It has 78 enrolled students from classes I-V who study in six classrooms but there can be no building inspection at Govt Primary School on MBS Road in Kota. The school, established in 2023, doesn’t have one.Children who come to study here gather under small tin sheds created next to municipal parking ticket kiosks. Pathways to success that all of India chases are all around them. But it’ll take a miracle for anyone in this batch to one day make that short walk to one of the city’s many fabled coaching centres, where many of India’s brightest prospects in medical and engineering come to hone their skills in a widely publicised ‘topper-producing’ machinery.Kota’s higher education success, riding entirely on private enterprise, hasn’t pulled up with it the city’s own govt education system. It’s a constituency that Rajasthan’s education minister Madan Dilawar represents, but that too has made little difference to many children who have been going to ‘school’ on footpaths, cramming into single rented rooms or under tin sheds in a state that sees extreme temperatures.Last week, a Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation led by Ashutosh Ranka was chased away by a mob after it went on an inspection of a govt school in Jaipur. In Kota, though, there’s little that’s hidden behind walls about the state of primary schools. Within a day after this non-inspection, however, Rajasthan’s BJP govt led by CM Bhajan Lal Sharma pledged to spend Rs 12,000 crore on schools over three years.Shobana Gupta, the in-charge of the primary school on MBS Road in Ward 33, says, “We operate out of six municipal kiosks and from under a tin shade. We have adequate arrangements for drinking water, electricity, and basic toilet facilities available onsite. There are no sanctioned permanent teaching posts here yet. Three teachers are currently deployed on deputation to manage the classes.”At Govt Senior Secondary School in Vigyan Nagar — a designated centre for JEE and NEET — the school sits inside a Rajasthan Housing Board building that is falling apart. Nine classrooms need major repair. Two are unusable but funds haven’t been allocated yet for demolition or repairs. Mold has eaten into walls of functional classrooms and the school’s ‘smart classroom’. A part of the perimeter wall has given way. Thieves have stolen the school’s water taps and CCTV cameras worth Rs 70,000. Principal Anita Sharma is still waiting for funds.At Shiv Nagar, Govt Primary Sanskrit School has been running for eight years now out of a single rented room, reached by a muddy track that’s impassable in the rains. Enrolment has fallen to 8-10 students under one teacher in a locality of around 60,000 people.“This locality has children who want to study Sanskrit. I have repeatedly submitted memorandums, but no permanent building has been sanctioned yet,” said former ward councillor Dhanraj Gurjar Chechi.Dilawar, incidentally, publicly champions Sanskrit learning as part of Indian cultural values.
What TOI investigation found
At Govt Upper Primary School in Devripunia, Dharmpura — in Ladpura constituency of BJP MLA Kalpna Devi, roughly 10 km from Dilawar’s residence — 130-plus enrolled students share three classrooms built decades ago under Rajiv Gandhi Swarn Jyanti Pathshala scheme. The school was upgraded to upper-primary status in 2021, but the promised classroom expansion never came.On full-attendance days, children sit under trees, on the veranda, or on open ground. Drinking water comes via a temporary line from an adjoining field. Principal Chandra Prakash Meena has written to both the MLA and the minister. Days before this report, 27 students fell ill after eating their mid-day meal.A Public Works Department survey of Kota district’s 1,088 govt schools found 61 buildings entirely ruined and marked for demolition, plus two classrooms flagged as unsafe in each of 318 school buildings, and one classroom each in a further 98. Only 41 full buildings and 29 partial structures have been demolished so far.District collector Peeyush Samaria’s office has no record of any personal inspection visit to a govt school. Samaria remained unavailable for comment. Sanganer, Jaipur: The CM’s constituency
Bhajan Lal Sharma won the Sanganer assembly constituency in 2023
At Bojyawas Govt Primary School, there are toilets, but they have no water. The water tank has cracked and dense cobwebs, indicating it hasn’t been in use for some time. The school shares space with a sub-health centre, where fungus covers medicine boxes and water stains mark chairs and registers.A staff member said open defecation has become routine for her. She does her best by consciously holding off the urge to use a toilet. The school itself has 10 students in classes 1 to 5 under a single teacher.
Govt Secondary School, Kalyanpura, looks well-kept from the gate, till you learn that one of its two buildings has been shut as unsafe, leaving 404 students across classes 1–12 to squeeze into four rooms.The school runs two shifts, 7am–12 noon and 12:30–6pm, and some second-shift students sit under a tin shed outside because the classes can’t accommodate them. Washrooms don’t have regular water supply and are cleaned only twice a month, said a Class 12 student.With no security guard and a broken, low boundary wall, the campus has seen repeated thefts. As a result, each classroom door has three latches and three separate locks.At Govt Upper Primary Sanskrit School in Hasampur Basdi, 85 students from classes 1 to VIII are taught in four classrooms — one of which is assigned to a booth level officer for special intensive revision (SIR) work.
Teacher Rajendra Verma produced letters he has submitted seeking a playground, boundary fencing and a tubewell. The school has been running on tanker water for close to a year, he said.At Govt Primary School in Hasampura, there was no need to interview anyone about the school’s condition. The gate was locked at 9.30am on a weekday. Former ward councillor Ram Singh Choudhary said he has been writing to govt for three years about the school’s lack of facilities. Jaisalmer & Barmer: Studying under treesIn Rajasthan’s desert border districts, several schools have no building.In Ramsar panchayat, Barmer, Govt Upper Primary School Azad Nagar was sanctioned in the 2022–23 budget and began classes in March 2023. But its 37 students study in a hut built by villagers or under trees.“Whether it rains, there is a storm or it is extremely hot, we have to study under trees,” said a Class V student.Land for the school was allotted only in 2024, and construction funds await sanction.At the Govt Higher Secondary School in Majal village, Samdari block (Balotra district), students and parents locked the school gate after nine teachers were transferred out at once, leaving senior secondary arts, science and agriculture streams without lecturers.“When there are no lecturers in the school, how will we study? How can Grade-II teachers perform the duties of lecturers?” a student asked.The protest ended after education officials agreed to post three teachers on deputation.Assembly data, drawn from UDISE 2025-26 figures, shows both districts have building-less schools: 36 in Barmer and 25 in Jaisalmer. Jaisalmer also features among districts hit hardest by a separate supply failure — a shortfall in the milk powder needed for the state’s Pannadhay Bal Gopal Yojana. Jhalawar: After 7 deaths, wait on for a new buildingOn the morning of July 25, 2025, the roof of Govt Upper Primary School in Piplodi, a tribal village in Jhalawar, collapsed during class hours. Seven children died; 21 were injured.A year on, Piplodi has visibly changed — better roads, more power connections, regular health camps, rising enrolment — but the one thing it still lacks is a functioning school building.Classes at the school have run since last August out of the two-room house of Mor Singh, a 60-year-old farmer and shepherd who vacated his own home so children would not lose another year of school.A new school building — eight classrooms, an anganwadi centre and a kitchen — is under construction, originally due by July 24, 2026. It has since been delayed after villagers raised concerns about construction quality when work began last November. Officials demolished the substandard work and restarted.“Construction of the school is taking longer than expected as villagers raised concerns about the quality of construction,” said Jhalawar collector Ajay Singh, adding that surprise inspections are now held every few weeks and the building should be ready by October.
Among Rajasthan’s blocks, Jhalawar has the highest concentration of building-less govt schools. District-wide, 81 schools lack toilets.Assembly data show 611 govt schools statewide with no building of their own, including 10 girls’ schools, 2,047 schools with buildings that lack toilets, and 1,049 that lack drinking water. It’s not that govt doesn’t spend on educationRajasthan’s 2026–27 budget allocates Rs 64,205 crore to school and college education. Of this allocation, around 75% goes into staff salaries and only 10–15% goes infrastructure.The state employs the second-highest number of teachers in the country, at 7.93 lakh, second only to UP. Yet, it has 7,200 single-teacher govt schools serving over 1.5 lakh students. Around 1.5 lakh sanctioned teacher posts remain vacant.The state’s own infrastructure data lays out the scale of the problem: 3,768 school buildings, 83,783 classrooms and 16,765 toilets are classified as entirely dilapidated while another 2,19,902 classrooms and 29,753 toilets need repair.Over the past two years, govt says it has spent Rs 2,723 crore building 179 new school buildings and 7,945 new classrooms to replace dilapidated ones.With govt funds in scarce supply, state-run schools increasingly lean on voluntary and community money. Statewide, philanthropic donations for school development totalled Rs 138 crore in 2024 and Rs 140 crore in 2025.In Pali district, a donor-led ‘Aao Gaon Chalen’ campaign — connecting migrants and philanthropists to their native villages — has targeted raising Rs 300 crore for infrastructure work.“There are around 23,000 such teachers in the state who are posted in a school where they are not needed, and their posting should be in another school, but they have not accepted their new posting. For instance, in an English-medium school, a Hindi-medium teacher who was earlier posted does not accept their new posting after a transfer, and the Hindi medium school, where the teacher is needed, students are suffering in that school,” said Mahendra Pandey, chief general secretary of Rajasthan Primary and Secondary Teachers Association.
TOI Special Report from Rajasthan
Gen Z, Gen alpha protestsThe consequences have spilled onto the streets.In Sikar, Class 12 students protested dilapidated buildings that force school closures every time it rains, alongside a shortage of subject teachers.In Gangapur City (Sawai Madhopur), girls locked the gates of the Mahatma Gandhi English Medium School in Meena Badoda, Wazirpur, after the principal was pulled onto local-body election duty, compounding an existing teacher shortage.At Govt Senior Secondary School in Majal village in Balotra district, students locked the gates after nine teachers were transferred simultaneously.A Class XII student at Govt Higher Secondary School at Majal in Balotra said: “If we had to study without teachers, then we could have studied at home. What is the need to come to school? If a school is operational, teachers must be posted.”
TOI Ground Report
The infrastructure debate has become an open political fight.A civic campaign, ‘School Thik Karo’, backed by CJP, has sent volunteer teams to inspect schools across nine districts — Jaipur, Ajmer, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Dholpur, Bharatpur, Kota, Barmer and Hanumangarh — after receiving what it says are public requests.“It has been over a year since the school collapse tragedy in Jhalawar, and the education minister has still not shared a concrete plan on how over 80,000 classrooms in dilapidated conditions will be fixed. Students are being forced to study in unsafe buildings, risking their lives,” said CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.One inspection, in Jaipur’s Bagru constituency, found a school that had been operating out of a buffalo shed for two and a half years after its own building was declared unsafe; it was shifted to a house only after drawing media attention.
The state education department has now issued an order requiring prior permission for any outsider to enter school premises, and barring photography, videography, interviews or livestreaming involving students without the principal’s consent.
Opposition leader Tikaram Jully called it an attempt to hide failures: “Instead of fixing schools, if you introduce ‘no entry’ measures just to hide your own failures, how can such accidents be prevented? A useless ‘double-engine’ govt,” Jully said.Additional reporting by Vimal Matta, Suparna Roy, Somdutt Trtpathi, Suntl Parmuwal & Shoeb Khan

U.S. Strikes Iran in First Military Action in a Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:05:16 UTC
12:05:16 KST

U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, according to the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), marking the first publicly confirmed strike on Iran in weeks.
CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed in a statement to TIME the strikes on the launchers on Larak Island, adding that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the strait.
Last week, U.S. forces finished clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
“U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” Hawkins added.
Iran attacks US bases in Jordan
Axios later reported, citing a U.S. official, that Iran launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan in retaliation for the strikes. Jordan’s armed forces said it intercepted eight missiles that entered the country’s airspace early Monday morning.
Iranian state news agency IRNA carried a statement from the Revolutionary Guards issued soon after the U.S. strikes saying that Iran will respond to the attacks on Larak Island “with punishment for the aggressor”.
In a statement, CENTCOM rebuffed the Revolutionary Guards’ claims, describing the Sunday attack as “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat” to the strait.
Before the Sunday strikes, the last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, announcing a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including command centers, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defense sites.
On Aug. 1, President Donald Trump said that he agreed to “hold off” strikes in Iran at the request of the U.S.’s regional allies in the Middle East.
How the U.S.-Iran war began
The strikes mark the latest escalation in the war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched a wave of attacks across Iran. Trump described the operation as a “massive and ongoing” campaign intended to eliminate what he called imminent threats from the Iranian regime and openly encouraged Iranians to overthrow their government.
The attacks came after U.S.-Iranian negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program failed to produce an agreement and amid the Iranian government’s deadly crackdown on nationwide protests. Trump had accused Iran of rebuilding its nuclear capabilities following U.S. and Israeli strikes on three major Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025. Iran has consistently denied seeking a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening salvo of the Feb. 28 campaign. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at Israel, U.S. military bases and other sites across the Middle East, widening the conflict throughout the region.
The war also led Iran to militarize and largely close the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy transit routes, through which about a fifth of global oil production typically passed before the hostilities.
A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports was lifted under a June agreement, but Trump reimposed it after that deal and its accompanying cease-fire fell apart.

Without additional $6.75 billion, Ukraine unable to pay its military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:02:57 UTC
12:02:57 KST

MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Ukraine will run out of funds to pay its servicemen in mid-October if it fails to adopt budgetary amendments to secure at least $6.75 billion in additional financing for its armed forces, according to TASS calculations based on data from the country’s Finance Ministry.
In the first months of 2026, the Defense Ministry of Ukraine was forced to tap into funds allocated for the end of the year, including money earmarked for military salaries. The ministry needs at least $6.75 billion to compensate for these expenses. However, maintaining combat operations at the current level will require roughly three times that amount, or around $20 billion.
Kiev needs approximately $2.7 billion every month to pay military salaries, or approximately $8.1 billion between October and December 2026. Consequently, without supplemental funding, money for these disbursements will be depleted by mid-October.
As a result, Ukraine will need to urgently amend its budget in September. At the same time, external borrowing is being considered as its only source of financing.

China Focus: Centuries-old artifacts bear witness to vibrant Sino-Italian cultural exchanges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:01:34 CST
12:01:34 KST

A visitor takes photos during an exhibition titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy" at the Tianjin Museum in north China's Tianjin Municipality on July 2, 2026. (Xinhua)
TIANJIN, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Chinese silk and decorative motifs found their way into the art of 18th-century European courts, while European tastes and designs came into contact with Chinese porcelain.
At an exhibition at the Tianjin Museum in the northern Chinese metropolis, more than 150 Italian artifacts offer a vivid glimpse into the rich cultural exchanges between China and Italy centuries ago.
Jointly presented by the Tianjin Museum, the Tianjin Digital Art Museum and the Turin City Museum of Ancient Art in Palazzo Madama, the exhibition, titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy," ran from Feb. 10 to Aug. 31. The exhibition showcases centuries-old treasures from the House of Savoy, one of the most influential royal houses in Italy in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Rather than simply showcasing the splendor of the Italian royal court, the exhibition traces how Chinese art and craftsmanship influenced European tastes and how Chinese artisans, in turn, responded to European demand, providing a window into the cultural interaction between East and West.
A French court gown from the collection of Palazzo Madama is among the highlights at the exhibition.
According to Li Jun, deputy director of the artifacts research department at the Tianjin Museum and curator of the exhibition, the gown incorporates Chinese silk and embroidery techniques, offering evidence of the popularity of "chinoiserie" at the time. By the mid-18th century, the style had become a hallmark of European aristocrats and the wealthy bourgeoisie.
Another exhibit, a men's robe with decorative patterns, provides further evidence of the influence of Chinese craftsmanship.
According to scholars, the ivory-colored robe with floral patterns was made from precious Chinese fabric. The silk was produced using a combination of weaving, block printing and hand painting techniques.
Such oriental-style fabrics became highly fashionable in European society in the second half of the 18th century. They were used not only for luxury garments but also extensively in interior decoration, becoming an important carrier of the "chinoiserie" aesthetic.
In the 17th and 18th centuries, Chinese porcelain, silk, lacquerware and other goods featuring distinctive oriental aesthetics became increasingly popular in Europe. Travel accounts, images of exotic people and landscapes, and Chinese-inspired decorative motifs further shaped European perceptions of the Orient.
The 18th century also witnessed the Enlightenment in Europe, with thinkers challenging feudal autocracy and religious constraints.
The thoughts of Chinese philosophers emphasizing openness and rationality resonated with some Enlightenment ideas, said Yan Guodong, dean of the School of Foreign Languages at Nankai University and an expert in the history of cultural exchanges between China and foreign countries.
Against this backdrop, an unprecedented craze for Chinese-style art and design, known as "chinoiserie," swept across European society and courts, leaving a lasting imprint on Western art and aesthetics.
The influence of cultural exchanges is even more vivid in the exhibition's "East Meets West" section, where Chinese-style porcelain, round fans and bird-and-flower paintings evoke interactions between Chinese and European artistic traditions.
A Qianlong-period Guangcai porcelain plate with a Swedish coat of arms from the Tianjin Museum's collection is one example.
Li said the piece was commissioned by Count Carl Gustaf Tessin, a prominent European art collector of the 18th century.
"Its value goes far beyond an ordinary commercial transaction. It represents a profound cultural dialogue between East and West based on mutual aesthetic appreciation and romantic imagination," Li said.
Such exchanges were by no means one-way, as Chinese kilns also accepted bespoke orders from European aristocrats, producing armorial porcelain tailored to Rococo tastes, Li added.
Yan said European consumers regarded the patterns on Chinese porcelain, silk and lacquerware as representations of life in China, while Chinese artisans sought to cater to European tastes in the selection and design of porcelain motifs.
"These exchanges were not simply the movement of commodities, but also the interaction of aesthetics, craftsmanship and cultural imagination," Yan said.
The exhibition has so far attracted more than 24,000 visitors.
"I was amazed by the material culture and artistic achievements of the House of Savoy, and even more struck by how some of the pieces ingeniously incorporated traditional Chinese craftsmanship, vividly recreating the 'chinoiserie' craze in 18th-century Europe," said a visitor surnamed Wang in Tianjin.
The artifacts, he added, bear witness to cultural exchanges between China and Italy along the Maritime Silk Road.
For Giovanni Carlo Federico Villa, director of the Turin City Museum of Ancient Art in Palazzo Madama, the journey of these artifacts across mountains and seas to China tells a story that extends far beyond artistic beauty.
"These artifacts not only allow us to look back on exchanges between ancient civilizations, but also provide a historical reference for contemporary cultural cooperation between China and Italy, further strengthening the bonds between our peoples," Villa said.
Massimo Ambrosetti, Italian ambassador to China, said the exhibition reveals the profound influence of Chinese art on European "chinoiserie" aesthetics and the porcelain industry in the 18th century, demonstrating the mutual enrichment of Chinese and Italian cultures and arts.
He expressed hope that cultural exchanges between China and Italy will continue to deepen and deliver lasting benefits. ■
People visit an exhibition titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy" at the Tianjin Museum in north China's Tianjin Municipality on July 2, 2026. (Xinhua)
