====================================================================================================

GLP-1 drug prescribed to woman with eating disorder via telehealth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:12:55 UTC
11:12:55 KST

GLP-1 drug prescribed to woman with eating disorder via telehealth sparks calls for regulation
In short:
An Australian woman with a history of anorexia nervosa has been prescribed an Ozempic-like drug through a telehealth provider.
Experts say they are concerned but not surprised by the incident, which highlights the need for more oversight of the industry.
What's next?
There are currently no endorsed national standards that telehealth-only clinics must adhere to in Australia, although there are some in development that are expected to be introduced late next year.
Experts are calling for greater oversight of telehealth clinics after an online clinic prescribed injectable weight-loss medications to a patient with a history of anorexia nervosa.
Kate (not her real name) was last hospitalised in 2022, and since then had been managing her condition with a GP and wider healthcare team.
But late last year the 25-year-old heard about a class of drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists from a colleague at work.
These drugs, sold under brand names Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro, can help with weight regulation and have a positive impact on chronic health conditions, reduce risk of obesity-related cancer and improve quality of life.
But health experts are concerned they can be used by people to fuel and maintain eating disorders, leading to serious nutritional deficits and complications including death.
Loading...
Shortly after researching the drugs, Kate said she was targeted on Instagram by an ad from a telehealth clinic, which the ABC has chosen not to name, and made an online appointment.
While direct advertising of prescription drugs to consumers is not allowed in Australia, weight-loss companies can run "disease awareness" campaigns suggesting potential patients contact a doctor.
These advertising campaigns have previously been criticised by health experts as "unethical" with the potential to lead to worse outcomes for people with eating disorders.
Kate said she was not screened for an eating disorder by her telehealth practitioner.
"I booked my initial consultation and after that appointment it was criminally easy to access the medications," she said.
Kate admitted she lied about her health details during the phone consultation and then told the clinic she was interested in using GLP-1 medications.
After having a blood test, she was prescribed the weight-loss drug during a second phone appointment.
'Urgent need' to regulate telehealth
In Australia, it is estimated more than 1.1 million people are living with an eating disorder, with women twice as likely as men to experience one.
Eating disorders are complex and potentially life-threatening mental illnesses in which people have an unhealthy relationship with food, eating, and/or body weight and shape.
Experts have previously raised concerns over the misuse of GLP-1 drugs and eating disorder risks, and called for increased screening.
But Sarah Trobe, clinical psychologist and national director of the National Eating Disorder Collaboration (NEDC), said screening for eating disorders "for the most part was not happening" and she was not surprised to hear Kate's story.
"We know that the eating disorder voice is seeking that; anorexia will try and get access to a GLP-1," she said.
"And we need to think about all people with eating disorders … and how we keep them safe in this process."
In Australia, there are currently no endorsed national standards for virtual care, although the federal government has recently tasked a committee with developing some.
These standards are not expected to be introduced until the end of next year.
Independent member for Kooyong Monique Ryan, who worked as a paediatric neurologist and medical researcher prior to politics, said 2027 would be too late.
"There's an urgent need to regulate telehealth services in Australia more quickly and effectively,"
Last week, Dr Ryan wrote to Federal Health Minister Mark Butler, asking for an inquiry into telehealth services, which could cover prescribing-pattern oversight for high-risk medicine classes such as peptides, GLP-1 agonists, stimulants and medicinal cannabis.
In a statement to the ABC, she said commercial telehealth companies screened "inadequately for eating disorders" and bypassed "the normal GP relationship".
"They largely operate outside Medicare and the PBS, so there's no systemic data on what they're prescribing and their patient outcomes.
"There's no requirement on them to screen for eating disorders before prescribing GLP-1 weight loss drugs. And the fact that they dispense prescribed medications themselves is a conflict of interest which is illegal in other forms of medical care."
Mr Butler's office was contacted for comment, which passed the request on to the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing.
A department spokesperson pointed out that virtual care standards were in development, but did not respond to questions about an inquiry.
Not-for-profit advocacy group Patients Australia has its own set of telehealth standards, developed in collaboration with providers.
'You're eating the wrong things'
In a subsequent phone appointment for a repeat script, Kate said she asked for the medication dose to be increased.
In response, she said the clinic asked about her food intake and exercise and provided advice that she said she found "forceful" and "intimidating".
"They basically said … you're eating the wrong things, you're eating too much," Kate said.
"Hearing that specifically in terms of my food was quite jarring for the eating disorder."
Trevor Steward, an associate professor at the University of Melbourne and director of the Brain and Mental Health Hub, said conversations about eating disorders needed to be sensitive.
"Patients won't always raise their own history with an eating disorder without being prompted and it should be explored before deciding to begin taking these medications," he said.
The ABC contacted Kate's telehealth provider about their process for screening and how they protected patients from harm when prescribing weight-loss drugs, but did not receive a response.
A spokesperson for the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) said it expected all practitioners to undertake a comprehensive and holistic assessment of all patients to properly assess that any recommended or prescribed treatment was appropriate.
"This includes assessment of any increased potential for vulnerability before proceeding with treatments," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Specifically in relation to weight-loss medications, the spokesperson said prescribers should consider whether patients had disordered eating, self-image or body image concerns.
"Practitioners should recognise that telehealth is not appropriate for all consultations as the lack of in-person interaction can limit the ability to provide safe and effective care," they said.
More education needed for GPs
Dr Trobe said telehealth prescribing might not be the best model for prescribing weight-loss medications.
"We can't have this low-touch model where people are having a phone call without adequate assessment, without sighting the individual and then no ongoing monitoring … to ensure this person is safe."
Kristi Griffiths, a senior research fellow at the InsideOut Institute at the University of Sydney, agreed that screening and evidence-based eating disorder care should be used when indicated.
"There also needs to be policy-level changes to online prescribing. For instance, requiring at a minimum a video call to help validate self-reported weight," Dr Griffiths said.
Separate to the standards in development, Dr Trobe said the NEDC was making recommendations to government about obesity management and treatment pathways, which she hoped would lead to safer prescribing of GLP-1 drugs.
These included prescribing by practitioners who were informed about the drugs and their usage and had kept up with the evidence, rather than by people who were "working outside the scope of their practice".
Kate has stopped using GLP-1 drugs with the help of her regular GP and is speaking out to help others.
"Knowing how easy it was to access for me and knowing how many people struggle with an eating disorder, it actually made me scared at the same time,"
Preeya Alexander is a practising GP and credentialed eating disorder clinician. She is working with the National Eating Disorders Collaboration (NEDC).

A 29-year-old doctor from the southern city of Rahat was indicted Sunday on weapons and other charges after police said a traffic violation led officers to discover ammunition and components of an M16 rifle in his vehicle.
The Northern District Prosecutor’s Office filed the indictment against Sami bin Khalil Atalka, accusing him of illegally transporting a weapon, obstruction of justice, reckless driving and interfering with a police officer. His trial is set to take place in Nazareth District Court.
Police Master Sgt. Mohsan Daghsh, head of an investigations team at the Kafr Kanna police station, said officers had set up a random vehicle checkpoint near Hamovil Junction in the Lower Galilee when they noticed a car driving on the shoulder to bypass traffic.
“It was a traffic violation,” Daghsh said. “The officers signaled the driver to stop, but he continued driving recklessly and bypassed the checkpoint.”
Police alerted another patrol car to block the fleeing vehicle, but Daghsh said the driver struck the police car before he was stopped.
“He then threw a bag from the vehicle, and officers rushed toward the bag while another officer jumped toward the vehicle and apprehended the suspect,” Daghsh said.
Police said the discarded bag contained a coupled magazine loaded with ammunition for an M16 rifle. A search of the vehicle uncovered another coupled magazine as well as a bolt carrier assembly and charging handle, according to police.
Meanwhile, police received a report from a woman in the Lower Galilee who said she had found a bag containing an M16 rifle on the road. She told police she had accidentally driven over the bag before stopping.
Daghsh said the bag had been dragged by her vehicle for a few miles during more than 15 minutes of driving.
The rifle found in the bag was missing its bolt carrier assembly and charging handle, police said. The recovered items were sent to Israel Police national forensic laboratories in Jerusalem, where investigators determined that the components found with Atalka matched the rifle found by the woman, according to Daghsh.
Atalka denied the allegations, Daghsh said, telling investigators that he had recently completed medical school, wanted to become a doctor and feared the arrest would ruin his life.
“Unfortunately, even doctors break the law,” Daghsh said.
Attorney Adel Buirat, who represents Atalka, said his client denied all charges.
“My client completely rejects every count in the indictment,” Buirat said. “He is an entirely law-abiding citizen.”

Tunisia swelters as power cuts disrupt water supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:11:35 UTC
11:11:35 KST

Tunisia swelters as power cuts disrupt water supplies
Temperature nearing 50°C is driving record electricity demand, disrupting water supplies and straining health services.
Tunisia is facing another spell of extreme heat, with temperatures reaching 49.8 degrees Celsius (121.6 Fahrenheit) in the central city of Kairouan on August 27.
The heat has coincided with electricity cuts and water shortages in parts of the country, while doctors have warned of mounting pressure on emergency departments.
The electricity and water disruptions are linked in some areas, but they have different underlying causes.
How hot has it become?
Kairouan reached 49.8°C on August 27, according to the Tunisian Observatory for Weather and Climate. The observatory said Kairouan was the second-hottest location among those monitored worldwide that day, behind Mehran in Iran, which reached 50°C. Six Tunisian cities were among the world’s 20 hottest monitoring stations.
The reading was also close to Tunisia’s national temperature record of 50.3°C, recorded on August 11, 2021.
The extreme temperatures have pushed up electricity demand as households and businesses use more air conditioning. Water demand also rises during periods of extreme heat, adding pressure to a system already facing longer-term shortages.
Why is Tunisia cutting electricity?
The Tunisian Company of Electricity and Gas (STEG) has introduced rotating power cuts in several regions.
The immediate pressure on the electricity system has come from exceptionally high demand during periods of extreme heat, particularly because of heavy use of air conditioning.
STEG officials said electricity demand may have reached a record 6,000 megawatts in July, after reaching 5,600MW only days earlier.
STEG has said the rotating cuts are intended to protect the safety and continuity of the electricity system.
Where are the cuts happening?
The outages have affected areas across Tunisia rather than a single region.
STEG has introduced temporary cuts in several parts of the country as it manages pressure on the network. The timing and duration have varied, with some residents reporting interruptions lasting several hours.
Why are water supplies being affected?
Parts of Tunisia’s water-distribution system depend on electrically powered pumping stations. When electricity is interrupted, those stations can stop operating, disrupting the movement and distribution of water.
There is a clear recent example. On August 24, an electricity interruption stopped the main Kerker pumping station, disrupting drinking-water supplies in several areas of the Mahdia and Sfax governorates, according to Tunisia’s National Company for Water Exploitation and Distribution (SONEDE).
The incident shows how a disruption to electricity at a pumping station can quickly affect water supplies.
But that does not mean every water shortage is caused by a power cut.
Was Tunisia already facing water shortages?
Yes. Tunisia has been dealing with structural water scarcity and recurring drought for years. The World Bank describes the country as facing growing water scarcity and climate pressures and is supporting projects to improve the reliability and resilience of drinking-water services.
The current electricity cuts are therefore adding pressure to an existing water problem rather than creating Tunisia’s water crisis from scratch.
Water interruptions can have several causes, including shortages, infrastructure problems, maintenance and disruptions to pumping and distribution.
What is happening to bottled-water supplies?
The heat and electricity disruptions have also affected bottled-water supplies.
The Associated Press reported that power rationing disrupted factory operations as demand for bottled water increased during the heatwave. Production was also affected by shortages of raw plastic materials.
The shortage therefore cannot be attributed to electricity cuts alone.
What does a power cut mean for households?
During a heatwave, losing electricity means more than losing lights.
Air conditioners and fans stop working. Refrigerators and freezers stop cooling. If an outage lasts for several hours, households may struggle to keep perishable food safely refrigerated.
For businesses, prolonged outages can mean lost refrigerated stock and disrupted operations.
And when a power interruption affects water-pumping infrastructure, households can face two basic-service disruptions at once: less electricity and less reliable access to water.
What is happening in hospitals?
The heat is also putting pressure on emergency departments.
On August 29, the Tunisian Organization of Young Doctors said emergency departments were experiencing an “unprecedented” increase in deaths and hospital admissions associated with heatstroke and extreme temperatures.
The organisation called for the government to declare a health emergency and said doctors and nurses were under severe pressure.
Wajih Dhakkar, head of the organisation, said 13 people had died within 24 hours at Habib Bourguiba Hospital in Sfax.
That figure comes from the doctors’ organisation and is not an official nationwide death toll.
The Health Ministry said on August 29 that 633 cases requiring medical consultation and healthcare management related to the effects of the heatwave had been recorded between July 1 and August 29. It also said health services had continued without interruption and that medical and technical resources had been mobilised.
The ministry did not provide a nationwide death toll.
What about patients who depend on electricity?
Power cuts can create particular difficulties for people who rely on electricity-dependent medical equipment at home.
Oxygen concentrators, for example, require electricity to operate.
There have been reports in Tunisia of difficulties for patients whose home medical equipment was affected by electricity interruptions. But individual deaths attributed directly to a power cut require confirmation from medical professionals or authorities.
There is also not enough reliable evidence to say that surgeries across Tunisia are being cancelled because of the electricity cuts.
Is the heat the only reason for the electricity and water problems?
No. The heat has sharply increased electricity demand, particularly because of air-conditioning use. That has put additional pressure on the electricity network.
But Tunisia’s water problems predate the current heatwave. The country faces structural water scarcity, drought and infrastructure challenges.
Water interruptions can therefore have several causes, including shortages, infrastructure problems, maintenance and disruptions to pumping and distribution.
What does President Kais Saied say?
President Kais Saied has offered another explanation for some of the recent disruptions.
On August 27, Saied said investigations had shown that water and electricity disruptions were not the result of routine technical failures but rather what he described as deliberate acts of sabotage intended to stir tensions and spread rumours. He did not identify those he said were responsible.
That remains the president’s claim and should not be presented as an established explanation for the outages as a whole.
There are documented technical explanations for at least some disruptions. STEG has said its temporary electricity cuts are intended to protect the stability and continuity of the power system, while SONEDE has documented a case in which an electricity interruption stopped a water-pumping station.
Why has the crisis become political?
Repeated interruptions to electricity and water have added to public frustration and have become a focus of protests against the government.
A protest in Tunis organised by the Nafas movement on August 20 included demands for better access to water and electricity, alongside concerns over living costs and political freedoms.
For households, the immediate impact is practical: a power cut during extreme heat means no air conditioning and less reliable refrigeration. If the interruption affects a pumping station, it can also mean less water.
For some patients, it can create difficulties if they depend on electricity-powered equipment.
What happens if the heat continues?
As long as temperatures remain high, electricity demand is likely to remain elevated, particularly while households and businesses rely heavily on air conditioning.
That keeps pressure on the electricity network. Further power cuts could affect water pumping, refrigeration and electricity-dependent medical equipment.
The current crisis shows how closely Tunisia’s electricity and water systems can be linked — but also why they should not be treated as the same problem.
Extreme heat is putting immediate pressure on the electricity network. Power cuts can then disrupt parts of the water system. But Tunisia’s underlying water crisis is older and broader, rooted in long-term water scarcity and infrastructure challenges.

John Ternus to lead Apple into the age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:04:00 UTC
11:04:00 KST

John Ternus to lead Apple into the age of AI
- John Ternus becomes Apple’s CEO on Sept 1, focusing on hardware innovation and leading the launch of the first foldable iPhone at the Sept 9 event.
- Ternus faces challenges balancing Apple’s heavy reliance on China amid US political pressure and must learn global geopolitical leadership.
- Tim Cook shifts to executive chairman, handling global policy engagement, allowing Ternus to concentrate on product engineering and company innovation.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – John Ternus takes over as Apple’s chief executive on Sept 1, inheriting a company that towers over the smartphone market but trails its rivals in artificial intelligence.
One of his biggest challenges will be balancing the company’s dependence on China while parrying acute political pressure from the White House.
The handover ends Tim Cook’s 15-year run, replacing the operations specialist who built Apple’s supply chain with the engineer who built its hardware.
Ternus, 51, joined Apple’s design team in 2001 and worked his way up to senior vice-president of hardware engineering, reporting to Cook.
He leads the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product line-up, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue.
He gets barely a week to settle in, with Apple holding its annual iPhone event on Sept 9, where it is expected to unveil its first foldable handset.
“Tim Cook left the house in phenomenal order,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co. “But now, it’s about Ternus defining the AI chapter.”
Ives expects the new CEO to lean into what he knows. “There’s no reason to fix what’s already working,” he said, predicting Ternus will concentrate on hardware innovation while leaving Cook’s supply chain intact.
Some analysts had argued software chief Craig Federighi was the more logical pick for a company scrambling to catch up on AI.
Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies, said that misreads how consumers actually adopt technology.
“Consumers are still buying hardware first, and it’s going to be like that for a long time,” she said. “You’re not going to discover the value of AI if you’re not interested in the hardware.”
Ternus earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and worked as an engineer at Virtual Research Systems before joining Apple.
Inside the company, he is credited with driving a push to make products more durable, reliable and resilient, and with design work that cut their carbon footprint.
The harder question is what kind of leader he becomes. “Even people that know him now don’t know him as a CEO,” Milanesi said. “You might know him as the head of engineering, but once you’re CEO, things change. Your responsibility is bigger; your power is bigger. You’re dancing a different kind of dance.”
‘Learn on the job’
Nowhere is that gap wider than in the geopolitical role Cook excelled at, courting both Beijing and US President Donald Trump’s White House to protect a supply chain that runs largely through China.
Apple’s manufacturing operation is among the most complex in corporate history, a web of hundreds of suppliers and assembly lines that Cook painstakingly built over decades.
Cook in recent years began shifting some of the work elsewhere – iPhone assembly to India, other production to Vietnam – but the diversification has been gradual with China, one of Apple’s biggest consumer markets, still anchoring the system.
Complicating matters, Trump has repeatedly demanded Apple build iPhones on American soil, threatening tariffs on those made overseas.
Cook avoided the heaviest blows of Trump’s trade war by cultivating the President directly, making US investment commitments and political donations – all while also keeping Beijing onside.
The tricky political terrain will be new for Ternus.
“He knows Apple Park like the back of his pocket in terms of hardware,” Ives said of Ternus. “But on the global stage – that’s probably one of the biggest areas where he’s going to have to learn on the job.”
Cook is not going far. He becomes executive chairman of Apple’s board on the same day, with a mandate the company has said includes engaging policymakers around the world.
“That was really clever,” said Milanesi, arguing the arrangement frees Ternus from a role Cook has handled alone for years.
The Sept 9 iPhone event will be the first public measure of the handover.
A foldable iPhone would be the most significant redesign in years, and Ternus will be its face – eight days into the job.
“This is a moment that they created for him,” Milanesi said. AFP

The Trump-shaped problems awaiting Andy Burnham, ranked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

LONDON — Andy Burnham spent most of his first 42 days as prime minister in his comfort zone, talking about jobs, living costs, homelessness and shifting power out of London.
Now he’s got to look beyond his own borders. As parliament returns from its six-week summer break on Tuesday, Britain’s new leader faces a towering in-tray of decisions that will affect his relations overseas, especially with Donald Trump.
British officials are preparing for the prospect of his first face-to-face meeting with the U.S. president in late September after Burnham confirmed his intention to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Downing Street is privately exploring the possibility that he visits the White House on the same trip, depending on Trump’s availability.
Advertisement
Burnham has played down the jeopardy, but he also promised to “say what I feel.” He has the advantage of having seen his predecessor Keir Starmer try to please Trump, only to be hectored relentlessly on Truth Social. Like Italy’s Giorgia Meloni or Canada’s Mark Carney, Burnham may sense a political advantage in not kissing the ring.
A visit will still tie him up in diplomacy, however; tricky for a man who wants to keep his focus at home rather than engaging in the geopolitical wrangling for which voters gave Starmer little credit. It will also come days before his first Labour conference as leader, where some of his party faithful oppose oil and gas drilling and want him to take a harder line against Israeli settlements.
POLITICO runs through a few of the Trump-shaped headaches awaiting Burnham, informed by conversations with more than a dozen U.K. government political aides, civil servants and ministers who were all granted anonymity to speak frankly.
Oil and gas drilling
The U.K. is inching closer to a politically fraught decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in two of the North Sea’s last major untapped fields.
An oil rig is seen through the mist on the Cromarty Firth on the north-east coast of Scotland on April 24, 2026. | Andy Buchanan/AFP via Getty Images
The Jackdaw gas field received initial approval in 2022, while the Rosebank oil field was green-lit in 2023. Further consultation due to a legal tussle over their environmental impacts ended in mid-August and Whitehall and industry officials expect a final decision in September. Jackdaw operator Adura has claimed gas could start flowing from Oct. 1.
Burnham — who pledged to give voters “breathing space” on the cost of living, yet is watching unrest in the Middle East push up energy bills — has spent his summer dropping positive hints about the projects, painting North Sea drilling as a “bridge to a renewable future.” He indicated similarly to Trump, who has repeatedly urged Britain to get drilling.
Advertisement
Yet the Green Party surged in opinion polls earlier this year and almost three quarters of England is in drought, after a summer that is on track to be the U.K.’s hottest on record.
A person with knowledge of the planning said the North Sea decision, which will be taken on a quasi-judicial basis by Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, is not expected this week. (One senior figure close to Burnham insisted the timing was “definitely not” tied to the optics of the dry summer, despite some MPs suspecting as such.)
When it does come, the U.S. president is likely to see it as a test of Britain’s priorities. One U.K. official said senior figures in Trump’s administration “really don’t understand” the hesitancy.
Trump Danger Rating: 4/5
Defense spending
Burnham’s new finance minister John Healey quit as Starmer’s defense secretary to demand that military spending accelerates to 3 percent of GDP by 2030 (on the road to hit a Trump-pleasing 3.5 percent by 2035).
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey plays a game of table tennis on a visit to Kiln Park Holiday Centre on August 27, 2026 in Tenby. | Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
Now he has the job of chancellor, Healey has refused to make that guarantee — and will leave the issue dangling well into next year. Healey will not set a target date for reaching 3 percent in his Oct. 28 budget, a British government official confirmed, and will instead name it as part of a cross-government spending review in 2027.
Advertisement
Conservative opponents seized on Healey’s indecision Friday, arguing he “is backtracking on the very pledge which sealed the fate of the last PM.” Whether Trump will choose to single out Britain is another matter; the president has taken a fairly equal-opportunities approach to berating NATO allies over their spending and many other nations rank below the U.K.
Healey is attending this week’s meeting of G20 finance ministers in the U.S., which could prove an early test of whether the issue is cutting through.
Trump Danger Rating: 3/5
Israeli settlements
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has promised a “comprehensive” U.K. response to Israel’s E1 settlement in the West Bank, risking a confrontation with the U.S. administration.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband listens as he meets with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Department of State in Washington on August 5, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
Two officials said Miliband is expected to make a statement to parliament in the next two weeks on the E1 project, which he has branded “unacceptable and destructive.” One senior Labour figure said they expected him to announce sanctions on Israeli settlements, though the Foreign Office has declined to comment on any future action. Miliband is separately due at regular questions in parliament on Tuesday.
His intervention will be fresh for two audiences: UNGA and then the party conference in Liverpool, at which grassroots members call for Labour to go further.
Advertisement
One minister said Burnham would want to “put his stamp” on foreign affairs due to the political salience of the Middle East. The senior Labour figure quoted above argued Miliband should wait six weeks until Knesset elections on Oct. 27, but one of two U.K. officials quoted above said: “They don’t want to go into Labour conference with this hanging around.”
A hostile reaction from Israel is inevitable, but it’s less certain how Trump will respond. The U.K. has consistently gone further than the U.S.; Starmer used UNGA last year to recognize a Palestinian state.
Israeli soldiers arrive at the scene where Israeli settlers occupy a Palestinian building under construction in the village of Qusra, south of the city of Nablus on August 29, 2026. | Jaafar Ashtiyeh/AFP via Getty Images
Burnham picked Ukraine for his first foreign trip, saying it “particularly” affected his intention to travel to UNGA, and will meet French President Emmanuel Macron in London this week. The prime minister is considering a meeting of European and other non-U.S. leaders in the “Coalition of the Willing” to coincide with the New York summit.
The new PM is not trying to be a global fixer like Starmer but he faces the same challenges. Burnham said he wants to help solve Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors, many of which are being hoovered up by the conflict between the U.S. and Iran.
Advertisement
Britain has little to fear about Trump’s rhetoric or actions against the U.K. itself, but the president’s actions in both volatile conflicts will have knock-on effects for Britain’s economy. One person who works on U.K. foreign policy said civil servants believe “the Ukraine trip was a bit of an awakening” for Burnham, while a U.K. official claimed Burnham’s team “appear a little blindsided” by the scale of the Iran conflict’s impact.
Some Whitehall officials had low expectations that Burnham would attend UNGA — Conservative PM Rishi Sunak skipped the summit in 2023 — until he told reporters last Monday that he was “likely” to go. At that moment the intensity of planning ramped up, said two Whitehall officials.
Supporters and members of the British Indian Ocean territory Chagos Archipelago hold placards and the territory’s flag outside the Houses of Parliament in London on January 7, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images
The story of both wars has been one of Britain and its allies forming coalitions to nudge the U.S. to a more favorable position, with only mixed success and, as yet, no resolution. Britain’s position is not entirely comfortable in the meantime; Burnham has continued a policy (agreed under Starmer) of allowing the U.S. to use British bases to launch “defensive” strikes on Iran.
Trump Danger Rating: 4/5
Chagos Islands
Burnham has inherited a controversial deal, agreed under Starmer, to hand the sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius — while leasing back a U.K.-U.S. joint military base on the Indian Ocean archipelago.
Three U.K. government officials said the deal itself — negotiated and backed personally by No. 10 national security adviser Jonathan Powell — is unlikely to change to appease Trump, leaving it in limbo unless the president changes his mind. “If there were easy additional baubles to provide, they would have been found by now,” said one of the three officials.
Yet this hold-up is causing tension with Mauritius, which was due a windfall in the deal and could press the U.K. to move at UNGA. It also affects wider diplomatic relations since the deal is backed by India, whose trade deal with Britain took effect a few weeks ago.
Trump Danger Rating: 2/5
Tech and trade
Burnham has inherited a complex web of deals that Starmer’s government secured (and in some cases, later un-secured) with the U.S.
These include the “economic prosperity deal” announced in May 2025, which secured lower tariffs for the U.K. than some other countries, including on steel and cars. But elements which had been due for negotiation at a later date remain in the ether. Those include the implementation of a U.K.-U.S. deal on pharmaceutical trade, which has implications for NHS spending on drugs (Britain agreed to spend more in order to get the deal over the line).
Less advanced is the “tech prosperity deal” that both sides hailed in 2025 but was then paused by the U.S. administration. Talks over nuclear fusion energy have resumed while separate tracks on AI and quantum co-operation remain stalled.
Advertisement
One U.K. official said talks could continue at an official level with little involvement from Burnham and Trump. “There is more to do” on both the trade deal, which is “imperfect but better than anyone else’s,” they said, while the tech prosperity deal gave a framework to build on. They added: “It’s a different phase of the relationship. It’s less shuttling over to Washington all the time … it’s not the same sort of theater, needing to be in the Oval constantly, in the way that Starmer had to be.”
One stumbling block: the U.K.’s digital services tax, which has drawn Trump’s repeated ire and raised more than £1 billion last year, much of it from U.S. tech firms. A spokesperson for Burnham’s government said “we remain open to discussing U.S. concerns,” but the U.K. has reiterated its commitment to the tax until a multilateral solution can be found.
Another stumbling block: Burnham wants closer ties with the EU ahead of a summit between Brussels and London this fall. British alignment with EU food standards has previously caused tension with the U.S. administration.
Trump Danger Rating: 3/5
Miliband on the world stage
A wild card in all this is Burnham’s pick for foreign secretary: Ed Miliband.
An outspoken former Labour leader who missed his shot at becoming prime minister in 2015, Miliband had coveted Healey’s job of chancellor. Instead he is set to use the foreign office to press Britain’s economic case on the world stage. That inevitably includes his long-held support of net zero, which rankles some in the U.S. administration.
Advertisement
He has personally taken the U.K.’s seat on the World Bank board, instead of a junior minister, and officials believe he would likely attend New York Climate Week (at the same time as UNGA), along with the COP31 climate summit in November. Trump has a habit of deciding individual politicians are beyond the pale. So far, though, the relationship appears to be functioning well enough; he met U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 90 minutes of talks in early August in Washington D.C.
Trump Danger Rating: 2/5
Reparations
One summit looms in November without the U.S.: the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), presided over by King Charles III and attended by the U.K. alongside 55 other countries, most of them former colonies.
The location of Antigua and Barbuda means calls for reparations for the slave trade — which dominated the last CHOGM in Samoa — will inevitably come up.
If Burnham were to attend, it would test how a PM who forged his politics campaigning for justice — including for victims of the 1989 Hillsborough stadium crush, and patients given infected blood products in the U.K. — responds to a call that the U.K. government has long said it cannot afford.
It’s not such an issue for Trump, though. The U.S. president might barely notice the summit is happening.

Chinese team maps South China Sea floor with ‘twice the resolution’ of Western models

Chinese team maps South China Sea floor with ‘twice the resolution’ of Western models
More than two decades of effort sees Chinese researchers develop maps of ocean terrain up to five times more accurate than global models
3-MIN READ3-MIN
12
 Listen
Zhang Tongin Beijing
China has mapped the seabed of its claimed waters including the South China Sea, with twice the resolution and up to five times the accuracy of methods used by other countries after more than two decades of effort, according to scientists involved in the project.
The importance of such work was underscored in October 2021, when the US Navy’s Seawolf-class nuclear submarine USS Connecticut struck an uncharted seamount while submerged in the South China Sea. The collision grounded the vessel and injured 11 crew members.
A subsequent investigation blamed poor voyage planning by the officers on watch, who failed to heed sonar warnings that did not match their charts.
Had detailed topographic data for that area been available, the billion-dollar advanced submarine might well have avoided its mishap.
Beneath the ocean surface lies a landscape as rugged as any mountain range on land. Knowing the outline of that terrain is vital not only for covert military operations and seabed mineral development, but also for research into ocean currents and earthquakes.

How Greeks conquered the Brussels coffee bubble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

IN THE QUEUE AT TO MELI, BRUSSELS — It’s the after-lunch coffee rush in the heart of the EU quarter in Brussels and this buzzing café is packed with Eurocrats and lobbyists donning suits in a distinctly limited array of shades of navy blue.
I inch closer to the front of the queue. Amid the murmurs of power plays and EU jargon, a familiar intonation rises as I hear the customer in front of me order coffee.
“Ena freddo espresso,” she says, “sketo.”
Advertisement
Before walking off with her iced sugar-free order, the customer falls into a back-and-forth with the staff. The chitchat has the polite familiarity of old friends bumping into each other while running errands on a Saturday afternoon. Heads preen toward the counter, as several French-speaking suits in the queue appear equal parts impatient and fascinated — perhaps even a bit jealous to not be part of the in-crowd.
I smile to myself, knowing the customer is at home — and so am I. Born and raised in Athens, I feel most comfortable at an establishment where the coffee is iced, the staff is warm and the pastries are savoury.
To Meli opened in 2019 in the heart of the mundane grid of concrete and power that connects the headquarters of the European Commission, Council and Parliament. Its name means “honey.”
An iced greek coffee, also known as freddo cappuccino. | iStock
Greek coffee houses have quietly conquered the Brussels bubble, offering a daily respite from the hustle and bustle of the corridors of power, beating local Belgian cafés, generic American chains and even the Italian barista masters on their turf.
Many of the cafés driving the Greek coffee coup — beyond To Meli, there’s Papillon, Caffeine and Cherry, to name the most popular ones — were born out of the debt crisis of the 2010s, when the country faced an economic collapse that saw unemployment top 27 percent.
The owners of To Meli originally moved to Belgium in 2013 in search of better opportunities before opening their first location six years later. Many of the staff members similarly arrived in Brussels during the crisis to find jobs. In typical Mediterranean fashion, many were spurred by family or friends who were already working in the cafés.
Advertisement
To Meli’s business has been massively successful, with revenues up almost 300 percent from 2013 to 2024, according to their financial accounts. Their neighbour, the Greek-owned Papillon, has seen its revenue climb by four times, Vassilis Tsourapis, the manager of the café, told POLITICO.
Tsourapis, like many of the staff members, ended up working at Papillon through a family relation. Another waiter at To Meli is the owner’s cousin.
Everything and nothing
Greek coffee culture is fundamentally not about speed, efficiency or even caffeine. Italians famously drink their coffee at the bar, standing up, whether it’s a shot of espresso or the longer milk-laden cappuccino.
In Greece, coffee is a decidedly social affair, perhaps the most intimate activity that involves patronizing an establishment. The act of “going for coffee,” or pame gia kafe, lets you focus on your interlocutor. It can be roughly interpreted as: “Let’s sit for several hours, sipping our freddo and talk about everything and nothing.” It’s the type of conversation that happens once the stresses of work and the city have melted away and your mind stops racing to keep up with your to-do list.
That’s not quite what happens at To Meli on a weekday, but the whiff of that ambience is what attracts the chronically overworked Eurocrats.
The coffee itself reflects this fact. The most popular drinks for warm summer days, freddo espresso and cappuccino, contain two shots of espresso – be warned – shaken, not stirred, over a lot of ice.
Advertisement
Prior to the arrival of espresso in Greece in the 1990s, the most common iced drink was a frappe, made out of instant coffee and shaken with ice and/or milk. The unique feature in all these recipes is that they come with a thick foam on top that generates more coffee as the ice melts away. They are meant to be sipped slowly, not gulped down.
The freddo is so essential to the nostalgic Greek expatriate that even on those miserably damp winter Brussels days, when the sun hasn’t shown itself for weeks, many of us will still go for the iced concoction.
A diaspora story
I have lived outside Greece for 13 years. Everywhere I’ve been, especially when the weather is hot, I always lament the absence of a freddo espresso. Other than two cafés mostly catering to London’s Greek and Cypriot community, the only time I saw a freddo espresso outside of Greece was, quite randomly, in Uluwatu, Bali, circa 2021. I picked up two for myself and made a beeline for the beach.
Little did I know upon moving to Brussels that I was landing in a place where Greek cafés are running a strong coffee game — and giving the Italians a run for their money.
During the week, they are mainly populated by EU workers, journalists and elected officials having meetings at the top of the hour. Over the weekend, the original To Meli branch at the Schuman roundabout presents a curious phenomenon. With the area around the Commission’s Berlaymont emptied of Eurocrats, the café fills up with Greeks and Cypriots leisurely sipping on their drinks. On one particular Sunday, I even saw a Greek Orthodox priest greet a group of men who took a break from their freddos to kiss his hand before buying him some pastries.
“This is a place not just for work meetings; it’s also for friends,” one Cypriot EU official who has lived in Brussels for 10 years told POLITICO. “It’s not a bubble place, it’s a Greek place.”
Advertisement
Many of the European officials POLITICO spoke to on several recent visits to the Greek cafés said they don’t necessarily think of the Greekness of the place, but they do appreciate the quality of the coffee and food, as well as the laid-back vibe.
Italian challenge
The Italians are going strong in the EU quarter. Still among the favorite spots in the Brussels bubble is Caffelatte, an Italian-owned café, which has seen a strong rebound since Covid-19 dented the hospitality sector in 2020.
As the names of Greeks’ favorite modern drinks indicate, there is an Italian connection. The freddo was invented in 1991 by a Greek coffee importer, Kafea Terra, who was trying to figure out a way to sell Italian Illy espresso to the local market in the summer months.
In the EU capital, the upstart Hellenic coffee challenge is undeniable. Once at the office, when I was glorifying the freddo espresso to colleagues, POLITICO’s Italian-born competition policy reporter Francesca Micheletti protested that it is just a “shakerato” marketed as Greek, citing a favorite summer coffee recipe in Italy.
I had spent enough time in Italy to know that it was different, but my journalistic instinct prompted me to investigate the exact shakerato formula.
The Italian invention is always made with sugar and the froth is looser, not thick enough to continue producing more coffee for hours. I told Francesca to give freddo espresso a try and get back to me. She didn’t budge.
Advertisement
Fast-forward a few months, and my competition colleague walked into the office on a hot summer day. “I tried a freddo espresso!” Francesca said. “You were right, it’s not the same — and it’s good.”
She also noted that it was much stronger than she’d expected: “I won’t be able to sleep tonight.” She clearly didn’t savor it with slow sips, I thought to myself.

====================================================================================================

Germany is poised to enter one of its most dangerous moments yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Election campaign placards for the upcoming Berlin State elections for the farright Alternative for Germany party (AfD) and the Green party hang on lamp posts near the Potsdamer Platz square in Berlin on August 20, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images
John Kampfner is a British author, broadcaster and commentator. His new book, “Braver New World: The Countries Daring to Do Things Others Won’t,” was published in April. He is a regular POLITICO columnist.
Picking up a recent issue of German weekly Der Spiegel, the cover seemed to scream. “Germany’s Most Dangerous Man,” it shouted, the bold words emblazoned below a photo of the far-right Alternative for Germany party’s (AfD) Ulrich Siegmund.
The intention was clear: A warning for both Germans and the world regarding the consequences of a far-right victory in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, as Siegmund seems poised to become his party’s first regional leader after the upcoming election there.
Advertisement
The strategy clearly backfired. Siegmund’s allies bought up as many copies of the magazine as they could, so he could sign them in front of adoring crowds. But the underlying sentiment was not wrong — what happens in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 will affect all of Germany, Europe and the wider world.
Polling at 42 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, that the AfD will emerge as the strongest force in this regional election is now beyond doubt — that’s around double the support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU). The Left party, another insurgent group, comes in third in the polling, while Merz’s coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), barely sit above the 5-percent threshold originally intended to keep out extremists, and the Greens are hovering perilously around that limit.
Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), campaigns prior to state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on August 19, 2026 in Dessau-Rosslau. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
The arithmetic is convoluted but crucial. If the SPD and the Greens make the cut, the various mainstream parties could cobble together enough seats to run the state. But if they don’t, the AfD will be able to govern either on its own or possibly with the support of the far-left social conservative grouping Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht, which is also hovering right below the 5-percent threshold.
The latter outcome would precipitate a political crisis across Germany not seen in decades.
But it doesn’t end there. Two weeks after Saxony-Anhalt, voters will head to the polls in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and in the once reliably leftist city-region of Berlin, which is showing strong AfD support as well.
This means that in the coming weeks or months, Germany could be faced with a collapsing government and even an ousted or replaced Merz — a move with little precedent in recent German history. And stuck with its stuttering economy, the country that prizes stability above all else is preparing to panic.
Advertisement
Two world leaders are watching all this with anticipation: Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Relations between Germany and Russia have sharply deteriorated since 2022’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the latest discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport has sharply increased the hostility. But despite the consensus at the top of government that the Kremlin is carrying out a wider campaign of hybrid warfare across Europe — and four decades spent under Moscow’s yoke — many voters in the former German Democratic Republic retain strong affection for the country.
The AfD is pushing that agenda hard. Although foreign policy falls under the federal government’s jurisdiction, Siegmund has been calling for an end to sanctions against Russia. He also intends to bring back Russian language classes in schools and wants Russian students to return to Germany as part of exchange programs. As for Ukrainians, he wants them designated as illegal migrants rather than refugees from war.
A resident checks his phone in a container facility for refugees and asylum seekers located in aircraft hangars of the former Tempelhof airport in Berlin on August 14, 2025. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images
Meanwhile, Trump, who has denounced Western Europe as socially reprobate, has made no secret of backing what his National Security Strategy calls “patriotic forces.” Quick to support European parties mirroring his own MAGA movement, his administration has been cultivating relationships and contacts with the AfD.
Both these leaders have a vested interest in the party’s success. They view the AfD — and Europe’s other ultra-conservative groupings — as a bridgehead. And Siegmund fits into that perfectly.
One of his party’s rising stars, the 35-year-old former salesman has a carefully curated image — riding East German-made Simson motorbikes to appeal to the young, while promising elderly voters to bring their “good, old, secure Germany back” — and the highest number of TikTok followers of any German politician.
Advertisement
His party’s 150-page program for governing Saxony-Anhalt does not lack in ambition either.
In it, Siegmund calls for Trump-style mass deportations of asylum-seekers — even though Saxony-Anhalt is one of the most ethnically homogeneous parts of the country, with only 1-in-13 citizens of migratory background.
He promises to defund public broadcasters deemed hostile and unpatriotic, ban all symbols of “woke” culture — including pride flags — in schools and, as part of his fight against “the extinction of the German people,” offer tax breaks for families consisting of “a father, a mother and as many children as possible.”
In an echo of the 1930s, the program even slams the Bauhaus art movement, which has strong roots in the region, as part of broader plans to promote “German art.”
These are all agenda items Germany’s federal states have jurisdiction over within their specific regions — education, culture, certain aspects of policing and criminal justice.
But to solely focus on these formal powers would be to miss the point. As in so many other countries, the far-right’s allure in Germany is growing, poisoning and often paralyzing the country’s mainstream parties and politics.
Postwar Germany faced — and surmounted — a series of difficult challenges during the Cold War and the collapse of the Berlin Wall. Its constitution is rigorous, and its commitment to democratic values (not least its unstinting support for Ukraine) is impressive. But it would not be an exaggeration to say, as I sign off my last monthly column for POLITICO, that the country is about to enter one of its most dangerous moments yet.
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

Putin to travel to Bishkek to attend SCO summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
01:59:16 UTC
10:59:16 KST

BISHKEK, August 31. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will spend the next two days in Kyrgyzstan, paying a "lengthy and intense" visit to Kyrgyzstan, including to take part in the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
The Russian leader’s schedule includes attending the SCO Council of Heads of States, a meeting in the SCO+ format, and a marathon of bilateral talks with his counterparts. Additionally, Putin has been invited to attend the opening ceremony of the 6th World Nomad Games to open in Bishkek on August 31.
Busy schedule
"The president’s trip will be long and busy. Two days of the SCO summit in Bishkek. A lot of bilateral meetings on its sidelines," Putin’s press secretary Dmitry Peskov told reporters before the departure.
Immediately upon his arrival to Bishkek, the president will go to a meeting with his Chinese counterpart and friend Xi Jinping. His aide Yury Ushakov described it as "a very important meeting."
It will be their second meeting this year, and the leaders will touch upon all pressing bilateral cooperation issues and acute global problems. Ushakov did not elaborate on whether the agreement on the Power of Siberia-2 pipeline will be finalized, saying only that "the topic will be discussed bilaterally."
After that, the Russian leader will meet with another key partner, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. "This will be a quite interesting meeting, since we have agreed to discuss a range of important issues," Ushakov told reporters. The talks will precede Putin’s scheduled visit to India to attend the BRICS summit in September.
The first part of the two-day marathon will conclude with talks with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The two leaders met quite recently, on July 25, during the 22nd Russia-Kazakhstan cooperation forum in Omsk. According to Ushakov, "there are issues that the leaders would like to discuss further at this meeting in Bishkek."
Nomad games
Sadyr Zhaparov, whose country holds the rotating SCO presidency this year, invited leaders to attend the spectacular opening ceremony of the 6th World Nomad Games on the eve of the summit. Although the games themselves will be held over the next week near Lake Issyk-Kul, their official launch will take place in Kyrgyzstan’s capital Bishkek on August 31. Putin is expected to attend the ceremony.
The games are a major branding project for Kyrgyzstan, aimed at promoting national culture, developing ethnic sports and tourism, and strengthening international cultural ties. The games will include competitions in 43 ethnic sports, including equestrian sports, national wrestling, archery, hunting, falconry, and intellectual games. The Russian national team will be represented by over 230 athletes from 33 Russian regions.
SCO summit
Putin’s September 1 schedule will be even denser. His day will begin with participating in SCO events. He will attend the meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State, and then the SCO+ format meeting. According to Ushakov, about 20-25 documents are expected to be signed at the conclusion of the summit, including the Bishkek Declaration. This document will reflect consolidated approaches to pressing regional and international issues, including in the sphere of economy.
Apart from that, the participants of the summit are planning to adopt a protocol to the 2002 Charter of the organization that will streamline the structure of some of its bodies,
After that, Putin will continue his marathon of bilateral meetings.
On September 1, the Russian leader plans to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and the summit’s host, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov.
However, while impressive, the list is not conclusive. As a rule, such meetings provide state leaders with an opportunity to communicate directly and without lengthy coordination. According to Peskov, it is possible that Putin will have an impromptu meeting on the sidelines of the event with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

Venezuela’s Maduro shares first photos from US detention

Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro has posted two photographs that appear to show him in a United States detention centre, where he has been held since his January abduction.

Security, investments, healthcare among priorities in 2027 budget - PM
The Polish government is set to adopt its draft budget for next year within a week, prioritising national security, healthcare, and infrastructure investment, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed ahead of a cabinet meeting on Friday.
Tusk announced that the 2027 draft budget will be officially approved during the August 28 sitting.
Describing the current fiscal situation as "objectively very demanding", the prime minister noted that Poland faces critical priorities that require substantial funding. Key among these is national security and defence, with Poland currently allocating roughly 5 percent of its GDP to military spending, on average twice as much as other NATO members.
In addition to defence expenditures, Tusk announced that the draft budget includes a PLN 17 billion (EUR 3.94 bln) increase for healthcare. The cabinet is currently drafting legislation to tighten oversight in the sector. The leader said that the primary goal of the new regulation is to ensure that healthcare contributions and public funds "are not wasted or caught up in abuses and unjustified earnings".
Outlining infrastructure and development as a third cornerstone of the budget, Tusk acknowledged concerns over state debt and a high budget deficit. He assured that decisions are being made with full fiscal responsibility to safeguard public finances without stunting national growth. The multi-billion-zloty investments will focus heavily on energy transition initiatives to lower long-term energy costs, alongside major upgrades to the country's rail and road networks.
In early June, the government adopted the forecasts for the 2027 draft budget bill, with CPI inflation at 2.5 percent, and GDP growth at 3.1 percent. (PAP)

US trains Polish special forces using lessons from Ukraine's war against Russia – AP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
04:50:00 EEST
10:50:00 KST

US trains Polish special forces using lessons from Ukraine's war against Russia – AP
US forces have begun training Polish special forces in Germany using exercises designed to "simulate many of the challenges" of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Associated Press
Details: Polish special forces are taking part in exercises designed only a few months ago which simulate breaking through enemy lines, travelling for miles through hostile territory and using drones to strike a key enemy target.
Associated Press noted that the exercises, initially developed by US Army Green Berets for American special operations units, began on Friday 28 August and incorporate and simulate many of the challenges faced by Ukrainian forces in the war against Russia.
"We're using lessons learned from Ukraine," a US Army Green Beret officer attached to the training facility said. "All of those effects that we're seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome – we're doing our best to replicate."
The exercises highlight efforts by some US military units to study the latest methods of drone warfare, which Ukraine has pioneered during more than four years of fighting to repel the full-scale invasion launched by Russia. They also demonstrate how the US, its NATO allies and Ukraine are working together to prepare for the possibility of further Russian aggression in the coming years, even as US President Donald Trump's administration has warned of troop reductions in Europe.
During the exercises in Germany, a senior soldier told AP that similar training is planned to take place several times a year.
A participant and officer involved in the exercises told AP that they expect most, if not all, NATO countries to be interested in sending troops to take part.
The exercise scenario lasts several days and takes place across a vast 3,000-square-kilometre training area in the Bavarian countryside.
The Polish special forces are expected to sneak past a US Army airborne infantry unit whose soldiers will play the role of the enemy. The US airborne unit will parachute into a restricted training area at the Hohenfels base and establish itself on the line of contact.
If the Polish troops manage to get past the US forces, they must head north, travelling about 100 km through the German countryside to another training area in Grafenwöhr, where they are expected to destroy a simulated target.
German farms and villages, private and government-operated cameras and a densely populated town lie along the route. These not only create obstacles but also increase the likelihood of the Polish troops being spotted.
A senior serviceman told AP that during earlier stages of the exercises, the Green Berets removed their uniforms "so they can blend in", adding that "blend in also means don't get seen by civilians".
AP added that local German civilians are largely unaware of the exercises and provide a useful test of how effectively special forces can blend into the local population. If they fail, reports of suspicious individuals made to the police will be passed to the military, which will use them to pinpoint the group's location.
The US Army will also use its own drones to search for the Polish units.
If they are detected, "now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you", a US soldier said.
The US Army could either send a military police unit with dogs to search for the Polish special forces or deploy additional drones to the area. In previous versions of the exercise, the US Army had more than 100 drones at its disposal, the soldier said.
As part of the exercises, servicemen may be "captured or killed".
AP noted that while the exercises demonstrate the use of drones and NATO teamwork, there have recently been differing views within military circles about the importance of cooperation and the value of drones.
Trump has caused confusion among NATO allies by repeatedly changing his position on possible reductions in the number of US troops stationed in Europe, while his administration has begun a review of US military forces to determine its next steps. Last week, the US Army's top military commander also disbanded a unit specialising in drone warfare.
Quote from AP: "But overall, there is growing interest in tapping Ukraine for its expertise on modern warfare and, specifically, drones."
Details: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Ukraine was helping five countries in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf counter Iranian drone attacks carried out during the US war against Iran. Those seeking assistance included both the US and European countries.
Meanwhile, the number of mysterious drone incursions across Europe has increased, including this month, when two drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was discovered at one of Germany's key cargo airports.
Background:
- During the Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, Ukrainian drone operators from the Nemesis unit – the 412th Brigade of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces – quickly detected and simulated strikes on vehicles belonging to a US mechanised brigade, demonstrating their superiority in the use of drones.
- The Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, held in April and May, showed that the US troops from Texas taking part were unprepared for the capabilities of Ukrainian drone operators.

What is celebrated on August 31 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31

What is celebrated on August 31 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
August 31 marks the International Day of Awareness of Overdose and the International Day for People of African Descent. According to the new calendar, the Belt of the Virgin Mary is commemorated.
On August 31, the International Overdose Awareness Day and the International Day for People of African Descent are observed. On the last day of summer, believers celebrate the Feast of the Placement of the Precious Sash of the Most Holy Theotokos, writes UNN.
International Overdose Awareness Day
A global initiative aimed at overcoming social stigma surrounding drug addiction and honoring the memory of overdose victims.
International Day for People of African Descent
An official UN day established to celebrate the contribution of the African diaspora and combat all forms of racism.
Traditional African Medicine Day
Observed with the support of the WHO to promote the integration of traditional healing methods into modern healthcare systems.
Blog Day
An unofficial celebration of the online community. The date was chosen because of the visual resemblance between the numbers 3108 and the word "Blog"; traditionally, on this day, authors exchange links to new resources.
Distance Learning Day
A themed date on the eve of the start of the academic year, dedicated to promoting online educational technologies.
Eat Outside Day
An international initiative calling on people to spend the last day of summer at picnics or on outdoor terraces.
Love Litigating Lawyers Day
A specialized observance honoring the difficult work of lawyers in court proceedings.
The Placement of the Precious Sash of the Most Holy Theotokos
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic Christians celebrate the Feast of the Placement of the Precious Sash of the Most Holy Theotokos. The feast honors one of the main Christian relics, which belonged to the Virgin Mary.
According to the old calendar, it is the day commemorating the martyrs Florus and Laurus. In popular tradition, these early Christian saints were considered the patrons of horses, so on August 31, animals were strictly forbidden from being used for agricultural work.

Greece moves ahead with $3.6B Israeli air defence deal despite Gaza genocide

Greece has moved to sign a $3.6 billion agreement to acquire three Israeli air defence systems, according to Israeli and Greek media reports, proceeding with the major arms deal despite widespread international condemnation of Israel's aggression in the region.
The Jerusalem Post reported that a Greek delegation will sign the accord with the Israeli Defence Ministry in Tel Aviv following nearly three years of negotiations.
The agreement covers David's Sling, Spyder, and Barak MX systems, which will be integrated into Greece's planned multi-layered "Achilles Shield" air defence network.
Israel's Rafael is expected to secure the largest share of the contract to supply David's Sling—designed to counter ballistic and heavy missiles—alongside mobile Spyder systems for drones and airborne targets.
Israel Aerospace Industries will supply the Barak MX system for aircraft and missile interception.
Command network
The project includes an AI-enabled nationwide command-and-control network linking sensors and radar arrays to classify threats and coordinate interceptions.
Spyder batteries are expected to be deployed across Greek islands, with Greek defence manufacturers set to receive approximately $820 million in subcontracts.
According to Israeli financial daily Calcalist, the project will be implemented over roughly 35 months.
Up to 12 Greek firms will account for at least 25 percent of the project following demands by Athens for domestic participation, technology transfers, and access to software source codes for autonomous maintenance.
Greek daily Kathimerini also confirmed the deal is expected on Monday.
If concluded, the transaction will surpass Israel's $3.5 billion sale of the Arrow 3 system to Germany in 2023.
Deal proceeds amid genocide
Athens is moving ahead with the acquisition despite Israel facing deepening global isolation, international legal scrutiny, and widespread condemnation over its genocidal war in Gaza, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians.
The Greek acquisition also unfolds against a fractured international arms landscape, where several Western governments have moved to restrict military sales to Israel over the Gaza genocide.
Britain has suspended 30 arms export licences over international humanitarian law concerns, while Italy and Spain halted new weapons contracts post-7 October, with Madrid additionally banning arms-laden ships from its ports.
Canada and Belgium have similarly moved to restrict or halt future arms transfers, and a Dutch court blocked direct exports of F-35 parts.

South Korea plans to become the first country in the world to provide AI to all citizens free of charge
Kyiv • UNN
The AI for All program is intended to provide citizens with free access to the premium features of local chatbots. Seoul seeks to reduce its dependence on the United States and China.
South Korea plans to provide the entire population with free access to generative artificial intelligence, effectively making such technologies universally available digital services. The government wants to promote its own AI models and reduce the country's dependence on American and Chinese developments, The Wall Street Journal reports, according to UNN.
Details
As part of the "AI for All" initiative, citizens are to receive free access to the premium features of South Korean chatbots. The state will cover the costs of their use.
According to estimates by South Korean officials, more than 20 million residents of the country currently use free versions of generative AI. The new program is intended to significantly expand the use of national platforms specifically.
Seoul is betting on "sovereign AI"
The initiative is part of South Korea's strategy to create its own artificial intelligence ecosystem. Seoul wants critical AI services not to depend exclusively on the technologies of foreign companies.
According to the WSJ, users are to be offered an unlimited number of tokens, allowing them to actively work with local models without having to pay for premium subscriptions themselves.
Thus, South Korea could become the first major power to provide its population with premium generative AI nationwide as a digital service accessible to everyone.

More than 22,000 ancient artefacts seized in Florida
Johnny Diaz
- More than 22,000 ancient artefacts, some up to 5,000 years old, were seized in Florida to disrupt smuggling networks, including items from Egypt and Greece.
- The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency stated the seizure is one of the largest by its Homeland Security Investigations unit, aiming to preserve civilisation history.
- Identification and authentication will take time and involve experts, with efforts focused on returning artefacts to their countries of origin.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – More than 22,000 ancient artefacts from around the world, some of which date back 5,000 years, were seized by officials in Florida, to disrupt criminal networks involved in smuggling cultural property, the authorities said.
The items include vases, weapons, jewellery and mosaic picture frames, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said in a statement on Aug 28.
The agency said the seizure was among the largest of its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit.
The artefacts also include Egyptian statues and Byzantine glass vessels, as well as ancient Greek and Roman coins, the statement said.
“The artefacts in this case that are determined to be genuine will be one of a kind, and HSI wants to take every step necessary to ensure a civilisation’s history is preserved for generations to come,” Mary Cook, a senior adviser in the unit’s cultural property, art and antiquities programme, said in the statement.
Initial assessments indicate that some objects may have originated from civilisations from 1,000 to 5,000 years ago and come from sites in Europe, Africa and the eastern Mediterranean, according to ICE.
The authorities did not say where or when the recovery took place and did not provide details about any arrests or charges.
ICE did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Aug 30.
The agency noted that the identification of the artefacts would take time because “unlike narcotics, there is no field test for antiquities”.
The agency added that officials would work with experts from universities to help identify and authenticate the items.
Officials said these types of investigations aim to preserve artefacts and return them to their countries of origin. NYTIMES
