G-20 countries should consider more trade barriers with China to cut imbalances, Bessent says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
00:08:00 UTC
09:08:00 KST

G-20 countries should consider more trade barriers with China to cut imbalances, Bessent says
- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urges G-20 countries to reconsider trade policies with China to reduce the country's large trade surplus and encourage economic rebalancing.
- China's economy is weak and relies heavily on exports, which Bessent says is unsustainable and needs to shift towards domestic consumption.
- The US has imposed tariffs and bans on many Chinese exports, pushing China to increase exports to Europe and Latin America, prompting a call for other countries to act.
AI generated
ASHEVILLE, North Carolina – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Aug 30 that he will encourage Group of 20 (G-20) members to re-examine their terms of trade with China to shrink global imbalances and press Beijing to rebalance its economy away from exports and towards domestic consumption.
Bessent said in an interview ahead of a G-20 finance leaders’ meeting that the current flood of exports from China was unsustainable, even though the US direct trade position with China was “rapidly improving”.
“The world cannot have a China with a US$1.2 trillion (S$1.53 trillion) trade surplus,” he said. “In China, the economy is quite weak and they are trying to export their way out of it, and they need to rebalance their economy.”
Bessent’s push to mobilise a coordinated trade response to China comes as legal setbacks force the US to rebuild its tariff policy, which had sharply reduced imports from China but led to an influx of Chinese imports elsewhere, especially in Europe and Latin America.
The US has walled off its economy from many Chinese exports with high tariffs and outright bans on some Chinese products, including cars.
Bessent said he told other industrial economies in 2025 they would face pressures from the China import surge and that “now they are confronted with some very stark choices”. He said it will be up to other countries to give China an incentive to shift away from exports and strengthen its chronically weak domestic demand.
“The rest of the world is going to have to examine their terms of trade with China,” he said.
The US is pushing for a G-20 joint statement on reducing trade and current account imbalances.
China’s embassy in Washington could not immediately be reached for comment on its view of the effort.
Tariffs imposed since US President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025 have helped cut the US trade deficit with China for the first six months of 2026 by a third from the same period of 2025, to US$73.9 billion, according to US Census Bureau data.
Some acceleration of Chinese imports occurred in January 2025 as importers tried to beat anticipated tariffs.
Although some economists and European leaders have called for a coordinated effort to strengthen China’s renminbi, Bessent questioned the effectiveness of such a move.
The International Monetary Fund has assessed the renminbi to be undervalued by as much as 21 per cent.
Bessent said suggestions that a new “Plaza Accord” – the 1985 agreement to strengthen currencies against the dollar – would be the answer to reducing imbalances are misguided.
He called it “an easy way to get around dealing with the real trade problem”, which he said was excessive Chinese industrial subsidies and weak domestic demand.
Next US-China summit
Bessent said it was unclear if he would meet his Chinese counterpart, Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, in person ahead of a White House meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping slated for late September.
Ahead of the summit, US and Chinese officials will press forward with dialogues on potential tariff reductions on non-strategic goods and artificial intelligence guard rails aimed at keeping powerful AI models from falling into the hands of non-state actors, Bessent said.
“I think that there probably are US$30 billion of non-strategic, non-critical goods on each side that we could take the tariffs off,” he added.
The September summit comes as the US has been rebuilding the tariffs after the US Supreme Court struck down broad duties imposed under an emergency law, including a 20 per cent tariff on Chinese imports.
The Trump administration in July imposed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chinese imports under an anti-forced labour trade investigation.
It is poised to add more tariffs related to excess industrial capacity under a separate probe.
Bessent said he planned to hold a bilateral meeting during the Asheville G-20 conference with People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng, but declined to give details. REUTERS

Dolly Parton was buried beside her husband in a private ceremony in Nashville
Kyiv • UNN
Dolly Parton was buried on August 28 in Nashville after dying of cancer. She was buried beside her husband, Carl Dean, in the presence of family.
American country singer Dolly Parton was buried on August 28 in Nashville in a private ceremony for her closest relatives, as she had requested before her death. The artist died on August 25 at the age of 80 after a brief battle with cancer, E! News reports, according to UNN.
Details
The ceremony took place at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Tennessee. Parton was buried beside her husband, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025.
The singer’s niece, Lainey Mae Parton, confirmed the details of the burial. The family had previously said that, in accordance with the artist’s wishes, the ceremony would be private.
Parton spoke about her wishes in advance
According to the singer’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, Parton wanted her final resting place to be arranged using soft cotton—as a symbol of her rural roots and a contrast to her rhinestone stage costumes.
The artist had also previously spoken about what music she would like to hear at her own memorial. Among the songs, she named the old gospel song "If We Never Meet Again," which was performed at her father’s funeral.
Parton assumed that her famous hit "I Will Always Love You," written and first recorded by her in 1973, would also be played after her death.

Iran fires ballistic missiles at US bases in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
00:01:18 UTC
09:01:18 KST

Iran said Monday it launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. bases in Jordan in retaliation for an American strike on Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking a new escalation in the months-long conflict between Washington and Tehran.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said ballistic missiles targeted U.S. forces at the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
Jordan’s armed forces said Monday they intercepted eight missiles that entered Jordanian airspace, state television reported.
The launches followed reports Sunday that Iran was attacking U.S. forces stationed in Jordan. Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst, citing a U.S. source, said there had been no significant impact and that nearly all incoming missiles had been intercepted at that point.
The Revolutionary Guards said Monday’s missile attack was retaliation for a U.S. strike Sunday on Larak Island, a strategically located Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.
A senior U.S. official said the American military struck two IRGC rocket launchers on the island that were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the Strait of Hormuz. The official said U.S. forces had finished clearing mines from international shipping lanes and were prepared to protect commercial navigation through the strategic waterway.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported preliminary, unofficial figures of two people killed and two wounded in the U.S. strike. Shortly afterward, the Revolutionary Guards vowed that the attack would be met with a response and that the United States would be punished.
The confrontation comes after about six months of fighting with Iran as President Donald Trump presses Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept U.S. terms for ending the conflict. U.S. Central Command has kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in the region for months amid the possibility of further military action.

Every bloc needs a chair capable of getting things done – and Southeast Asia watchers say that description fits no country better than Singapore.
The city state will get the chance to prove it in the bloc’s 60th anniversary year, after it takes the Asean helm from the Philippines on January 1.
Speaking at Singapore’s National Day Rally on August 22, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the world was becoming more fractured and dangerous – one that the city state would have to “endure and survive for many years to come”.
“Our response cannot be to retreat and turn inward,” Wong said, calling for the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations to deepen integration “to create a more effective single market”.
A litany of headaches stand in the way of that ambition, from Myanmar’s civil war to an unresolved Thailand-Cambodia border row, simmering South China Sea tensions and keeping a distracted United States engaged with the region.
But if any country can rise to the challenge, it is Singapore, according to Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a professor of political science and international relations at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok.

"It is a moment of extreme urgency": US senator urges House to approve Russia sanctions bill
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

02:58:00 EEST

"It is a moment of extreme urgency": US senator urges House to approve Russia sanctions bill
US Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut has urged the House of Representatives to support a Senate-passed bill imposing sanctions on Russia, describing the situation in the war in Ukraine as a "moment of extreme urgency".
Source: Blumenthal in an interview with CBS News
Quote: "It is a moment of extreme urgency, for the reason that Putin may try to escalate, but also because Putin is on his heels economically.
And this kind of sanctions bill, throttling the flow of revenue to his war machine could undercut completely his ability to wage this brutal, murderous war."
Details: The US Senate passed the bill by a wide bipartisan majority before breaking for its August recess. The initiative emerged after the sudden death of Senator Lindsey Graham, who had long advocated the measures alongside Blumenthal. The bill has now moved to the House of Representatives, which is due to return to work this week after a five-week recess. However, its prospects in the lower chamber remain uncertain.
The bill, known as the The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, would allow the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas, except for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia while also taking steps to reduce those imports. Some Democrats in the House, however, have raised concerns about giving the president additional powers.
Asked about possible opposition from Democrats, Blumenthal defended the bill, saying it was the "result of painstaking, sometimes painful, negotiations" with the US Trade Representative, the White House and lawmakers from both parties.
"It passed the Senate 86 to 11 – not many measures doing that kind of successful passage these days," Blumenthal said.
He highlighted the additional powers the bill would give the president to "impose scorching sanctions on the oligarchs" and financial institutions, as well as measures to "crack down on the shadow fleet" and the power to impose tariffs, "narrowly constrained" to the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Blumenthal said the sanctions bill could weaken Russian leader Vladimir Putin's position.
Quote: "His economy is on the verge of major crisis.
He has a deficit looming of US$125 billion, 5% of his GDP, an interest rate of 14% on his national debt."
Details: Blumenthal expressed great hope that the sanctions bill would receive enough support from Democrats to pass the House. He added that during his visit to Ukraine last week, he urged President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet with members of Congress, as the Ukrainian leader had done in the Senate.
Previously: Zelenskyy met with US senators from both parties – Richard Blumenthal and James Lankford – in Kyiv on 23 August.
Read also: This time could be different for Russia sanctions
Background: The US imposed sanctions on a number of entities within the Russian Defence Ministry as well as two Russian companies and five Russian nationals at the beginning of August.

Bessent expects new US secondary sanctions weekly, aiming to increase pressure on Iran
ASHEVILLE, North Carolina – The US Treasury Department is likely to unveil weekly new secondary sanctions aimed at increasing economic pressure on Iran, with an initial focus on banks, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Aug 30.
After imposing penalties on the United Arab Emirates branches of Egypt’s Banque Misr on Aug 28 over alleged financial links to Iran, Bessent said in an interview that the next step may be cutting off an institution entirely from the dollar-based financial system.
“You’re going to see a lot more of these every week,” Bessent said ahead of a Group of 20 finance leaders meeting.
“We’re starting with the banks, and we’re telling the banks it’s not okay to have Iranian money and to aid the regime.”
Bessent said he intends to drive the message home to G-20 finance ministers and central bank governors to cut economic ties to Iran, or face secondary sanctions.
The Treasury launched the effort, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, last week.
“There can be no leakage,” Bessent said. “You’re either with us or you’re with the Iranians.”
However, he said that he disagreed with some critics who have said that Iran sanctions will not be successful without targeting Chinese companies for secondary sanctions.
Most of China’s Iran oil purchases have been curbed by the US blockade of Iranian ports, and the amount of Iranian oil stored in tankers is dwindling, he said, adding: “Problem solved.” REUTERS

Bessent says yen moves ‘pretty contained’ and not disorderly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:50:00 UTC
08:50:00 KST

Bessent says yen moves ‘pretty contained’ and not disorderly
ASHEVILLE, North Carolina – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Aug 30 that recent yen moves were “pretty well contained”, suggesting the Japanese currency’s renewed declines were not seen as the kind of disorderly moves that led to a rare joint Japan-US intervention in July.
The yen slid below the 160-per-dollar level on Aug 28, a threshold widely seen as increasing the likelihood of intervention, drawing market attention to whether the United States and Japan will step in to prop up the currency again.
The two countries carried out a rare joint yen-buying intervention on July 31, signalling their determination to prevent a sell-off in the yen and Japanese government bonds from spilling over into global markets.
When asked whether the central bank should consider consecutive interest rate hikes to combat the declines, Bessent said he expects Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Kazuo Ueda to “do the right thing” on monetary policy with the backing of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
“I’m not going to tell them what to do,” Bessent told Reuters, when asked whether the BOJ should hike rates more aggressively. “I’m going to say that I do think that we have probably reached the end of Abenomics, which was a reflationary programme.”
Launched in 2013 under the late prime minister Shinzo Abe, Abenomics was an economic policy aimed at breaking Japan out of prolonged deflation with a mix of massive monetary stimulus, big fiscal spending and steps to boost Japan’s growth potential.
Bessent said he plans to meet Ueda on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance leaders’ two-day gathering in Asheville, North Carolina, that kicks off on Aug 31.
“I’ve known (Ueda) for 15 years. He’s a great economist. I think he’s under-rated in how savvy he is on markets,” Bessent said.
When asked whether the yen was still making disorderly moves, Bessent said: “Oh, no. I think it’s pretty well contained.” The remarks contrasted with his comments a month earlier, when he said the joint US-Japan intervention was aimed at countering “disorderly” moves in the currency.
The weak yen has become a headache for Japanese policymakers, pushing up import prices and driving broader inflation.
It has been blamed in part for the slow pace of BOJ rate hikes, which has kept Japan’s rate divergence with the US wide.
Bessent’s remarks on the BOJ came ahead of the central bank’s upcoming policy meeting on Sept 17 and 18.
Sources have told Reuters the BOJ is set to raise rates as soon as September and is considering hiking more aggressively thereafter than the current pace of roughly two times a year.
Bessent’s repeated calls in the past for the BOJ to raise rates have been among the factors that led markets to nearly fully price in the chance of a September hike, which would follow one in June.
Hiking in September, rather than October, could fuel market bets that the BOJ will start raising rates once every quarter, some analysts say.
Ueda in July said the BOJ will focus on mounting inflation risks and will not rule out speeding up the pace of rate increases if financial conditions were deemed too loose.
Such hawkish BOJ communication, however, has failed to put a sustained floor under the yen.
In the Reuters interview, Bessent said Japan has already “conquered” deflation and shifted to “Takaichi-nomics” under Takaichi, so the country can experience the benefits of past policies aimed at rejuvenating its economy.
Bessent said “Takaichi-nomics” is more shareholder-friendly, with substantial deregulation already implemented, especially in the workforce, meaning less government intervention.
“I think they should just sit back and enjoy the success of Abenomics and let that run,” Bessent said, when asked about his recommendations for Japan’s fiscal policy.
Known as a fan of Abenomics, Takaichi has laid out an ambitious spending programme to boost investment in growth areas and cushion the blow to households from rising living costs.
Critics say the expansionary fiscal approach contradicts the BOJ’s efforts to tame inflation with tighter monetary policy.
Takaichi’s big spending plans have also pushed the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond to a three-decade high of 2.945 per cent earlier in August, as investors grew nervous about the country’s towering debt pile. REUTERS

Algeria seeks death penalty for intentional forest fires after deadly blazes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:39:31 UTC
08:39:31 KST

Algeria's President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered the introduction of the death penalty for deliberately setting forest fires, after recent blazes across the country killed 12 people.
Tebboune issued the directive during a high-level meeting convened to address the aftermath of the fires, attended by senior civilian and military officials, state television reported.
He instructed the justice minister to submit an amendment to the penal code by September 15, providing for capital punishment for anyone convicted of intentionally starting fires in forested areas.
Legal provisions
State television reported that the capital sentence would only be carried out once all legal avenues of appeal have been completely exhausted.
The death penalty remains on the books in Algeria’s criminal code for several offences; however, the country has maintained a de facto moratorium on carrying out executions since 1993.
Under existing legislation, deliberately starting forest fires is punishable by up to 30 years in prison, or life imprisonment in certain aggravated cases.

The ministry noted that Moldova recognizes the right of foreign citizens residing on its territory to participate in elections organized by their respective countries.
"However, this right must be exercised with full respect for Moldova's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The organization of electoral processes by foreign states on the territory of the country must be agreed in advance with the constitutional authorities in Chisinau," the ministry said.
It noted that the Russian Embassy in Moldova had agreed with the country's authorities to open a single polling station in Chisinau.
"Under these circumstances, Russia's intention to additionally open 16 polling stations in the Transnistrian region without the consent of Moldova's constitutional authorities is unacceptable and constitutes a violation of the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity," Moldova's Foreign Ministry said.
Earlier, Transnistrian leader Vadim Krasnoselsky said that 17 polling stations would be opened in Transnistria in September for the Russian State Duma elections. Moldova's Bureau for Reintegration, commenting on the statement, said that opening such polling stations on Moldovan territory without the consent of the country's constitutional authorities would be illegal.
According to the Transnistrian leader, 220,000 Russian citizens live in Transnistria.

UAE to probe Banque Misr branch after US cites Iran links
DUBAI - The United Arab Emirates’ central bank said it will investigate Banque Misr after the US Treasury Department moved to cut off the Egyptian bank’s UAE branches from the US financial system as part of sanctions against Iran.
The UAE central bank said in a statement it “has decided to conduct a special and urgent examination” of the bank’s transactions during a more than two-year period referenced in the US announcement on Aug 28.
The US Treasury Department called Banque Misr UAE “a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to US dollars” and estimated it processed about US$1.8 billion between January 2024 and June 2026 for 103 companies “that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks”.
The Central Bank of the UAE said its investigation “includes a forensic/in-depth lookback covering the period referred to in the statement issued by the US authorities, with a focus on banking transactions of the companies mentioned in the statement”.
Banque Misr issued a statement saying that it “affirms its full respect” for the process and the laws and will fully cooperate with the probe. It added that it would continue to provide banking services to customers.
The central bank “expects banks licensed in the UAE not to expose the UAE’s financial system to reputational risks,” according to the statement. 
The central bank said it is looking at options regarding Banque Misr’s status if the US measure takes effect, while taking into consideration the bank’s obligations to customers in the UAE. BLOOMBERG

The online privacy change that could give Australians more control over their data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:20:03 UTC
08:20:03 KST

In brief
- The Australian eSafety Commissioner has recommended changes to how smart glasses operate.
- Further new protections will overhaul Australia's privacy laws related to social media, AI and smart glasses.
People's faces should automatically be blurred when being filmed by smart glasses as part of greater privacy measures, the online safety watchdog has urged.
In advice to industry, the eSafety Commissioner has called for extra protections to be put in place for smart glasses, or glasses with cameras attached to them.
The growing uptake of the technology, prompted by cheap versions of the products being sold in outlets such as Kmart, has increased concerns about privacy and people being filmed without their consent.
The commissioner said faces of people being filmed should be blurred by default if they have not given consent, with clearer indicators being given for when the glasses are recording video.
"Companies selling smart glasses must balance the benefits of the technology with the need to protect users and the public," the commissioner said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"As smart glasses become more common, they may create new ways to perpetrate harms."
The eSafety Commissioner said the rapid evolution of the technology meant there was still a chance for extra safety features to be baked into the products before harms became more widespread.
"They may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content," the advice said.
"The harms linked to covert recording are not hypothetical. They are real and already occurring."
Among the concerns listed by the commissioner was how the glasses could be used by "pick-up artists" who use the glasses to film women without their knowledge.
"Most of the women do not realise they are being filmed. These posts often attract misogynistic comments, compounding the harm," the commissioner said.
"Used in this way, smart glasses can reinforce and normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge."
The commissioner has also called for livestreaming from the glasses to operate on a delay, as well as for recording to be disabled when the glasses are not being worn.
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland wrote to the privacy commission earlier this month to investigate whether extra regulations for smart glasses were needed.
The Greens have called for a 12 month ban on the importation of smart glasses.
Under changes the minor party will bring to parliament, the filming, storing or sharing of footage from the glasses without consent would be a breach of privacy laws.
Social media and deletion requests
Rowland is also set to outline further changes to privacy laws, including the right to erasure, on Monday.
The policy would mean social media users can ask tech companies to delete their personal information published online or held by the platforms.
The draft laws will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles.
Rowland said the privacy laws were needed to keep up with technology changes.
"The right to erasure will help put more control in the hands of Australians, allowing personal information to be destroyed from large digital platforms," she said.
"We must ensure appropriate safeguards are placed around technology and stop the erosion of our privacy protections."
The federal government will also roll out extra protections for identity documents online.
A service called IDLock will allow people to block or unblock the use of identity documents such as passports.
IDLock will be made available through the government's MyGov platform from 2027 after a small-scale trial in late 2026.
"Australians deserve to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online," Rowland said.
"As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia's approach must evolve with them."
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

WELLINGTON – At least five heads of government were absent from talks at the annual Pacific Island Forum that began on Aug 31, as China-Taiwan tensions weighed heavily over the meeting that was intended to demonstrate regional unity.
The prime ministers of Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa and the Solomon Islands’ prime ministers and the president of Kiribati will not attend the summit in Palau, an archipelago of over 500 islands that has maintained diplomatic ties with Taiwan. The absent leaders are expected to be represented by ministers or senior officials.
China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, has gradually whittled away the number of Pacific island countries with formal ties to Taipei, with only three remaining – Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It questioned Palau’s inclusion of Taiwan in the gathering, saying it had “no qualifications” to take part in the forum.
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung was invited for meetings and side events held alongside the forum. Taiwan is not a formal dialogue partner like China but instead is a development partner.
Beijing issued a travel advisory in July declaring Palau “unsafe” for tourists.
In response, the US embassy in the capital Koror said in a statement that it “opposes any attempts by China to weaponise tourism to coerce Palau”.
Dialogue partners including the US, China, Japan and Singapore will return to the forum after being excluded from the 2025 meeting in Honiara. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and China’s Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo are among those expected to attend.
Solomon Islands’ Matthew Wale was due to attend but left Palau to face a no-confidence motion at home. He was elected prime minister in May, replacing a leadership that had deepened ties with Beijing and signed a security pact with China that alarmed the US and its allies. Kiribati said President Taneti Maamau was unable to travel because Parliament was sitting and flights were limited.
The meeting, hosted by Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr in Koror through Sept 4, is being held under the theme B.E.L.A.U. – Building Economies: Life. Action. Unity. “The theme reflects a simple but important conviction: that building stronger economies is not an end in itself,” Whipps said while opening a meeting of the Smaller Island States, the first gathering of leaders for the week.
“It must elevate the livelihoods of our people, create tangible and sustainable opportunities for our economies, and unite us in our ongoing efforts to deepen regionalism through integration.”
New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said Pacific countries wanted tangible outcomes. “We want more doing, less hui (meeting),” he told reporters on Aug 30, using the Maori word for meeting. He said oil supply disruptions were among the region’s most pressing concerns and foreshadowed an announcement on relief measures that could come soon.
Regional security is also expected to feature after a Pacific Island foreign ministers’ meeting in Suva earlier this month failed to agree on a collective response to a Chinese missile test in the Pacific. Peters said it was unclear whether leaders would reach a common position in Palau, adding that the time elapsed since the test raised questions about the value of a response now. REUTERS

Vote count starts in Guinea-Bissau referendum on strengthening presidency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:08:01 UTC
08:08:01 KST

Vote count starts in Guinea-Bissau referendum on strengthening presidency
Ten months after a coup, military leaders say the referendum is designed to stabilise future civilian governments.
Ballot counting is under way in a referendum in Guinea-Bissau that could significantly boost the presidency’s power.
Citizens of the West African nation took to the polls on Sunday to vote on a new constitution that would reform the country’s political system ahead of elections later this year.
Turnout “exceeded” 55 percent and the poll took place “without any incidents that would call into question the credibility of the vote”, Idrissa Djalo, executive secretary of the National Electoral Commission, told a news briefing on Sunday.
Results are expected on Tuesday.
The referendum comes less than 10 months after the military seized power in a coup.
The military government says it seeks to stabilise institutions before presidential and parliamentary elections, scheduled for December 6, designed to hand power back to a civilian government.
The new constitution, which citizens were asked to approve on Sunday, would switch Guinea-Bissau’s political system from a parliamentary to a presidential one.
It would abandon the system by which prime ministers came from the parliamentary majority, an approach that has led to uncomfortable power-sharing.
The new system would also allow the head of state to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and members of the government, and to dissolve parliament.
On Sunday, voters answered “yes” or “no” to the question: “Do you agree with the entry into force of the new constitution approved by the National Transitional Council?”
“What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance,” military leader and transitional President General Horta Inta-A Na Man said.
Under the transitional charter he upholds, Inta-A Na Man is barred from running in elections.
The referendum follows years of political instability. In the November 2025 presidential election, both candidates declared victory and accused each other of electoral interference. The coup happened one day after.

Israel banned Palestine 36, then it landed on an Oscars shortlist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:03:31 UTC
08:03:31 KST

Annemarie Jacir's film Palestine 36 was banned. Then it landed on an Oscars shortlist
There's one scene director and writer Annemarie Jacir fought tooth and nail for in her latest movie, Palestine 36.
The historical epic encapsulates the 1936 Palestinian revolt against British colonialism, and contains lavish sets, gunfire battles and grand explosions.
But the scene Jacir needed to include in her vision is of a little girl, running along the walls of Jerusalem; an arresting shot that came within a hair's breadth from not existing at all.
In 2023, weeks before Jacir and her crew were to begin filming in her home country, the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel shut production down.
"I was getting a lot of location images of Cyprus, of Greece, of Malta, old cities. Many, many places have old cities and old city walls," Jacir tells ABC Arts.
"The producers were like, 'You just really need to think at this point with what's happening, that this is what we have to do.' I kept saying, 'I'm not going to film anywhere except Jerusalem. It really means something to us. It might look like another old city to you, but to us, it's not another old city.'
"A lot of things I had to compromise because of the political situation and what happened to us. But there are certain things I wouldn't compromise. That was one of them."
Jacir was committed to her vision, relocating to Jordan to complete additional scenes before being allowed back into Palestine a year later to wrap shooting.
"I think in a way it was a survival mechanism, like we just have to keep doing it. We all felt that way. It felt more important, though.
"It was already important, but then suddenly, it just had a different meaning. All of it had a different meaning."
Going back
Palestine 36 is the only feature film to be shot in the country in the past two years, and one of just a few films to put 1930s Palestine on the big screen.
Bubbling over three years from 1936 to 1939, the uprising marked a violent time in the country's history as Palestinian Arabs sought to gain independence from British colonial rule which saw locals pushed out of their land and homes, alongside an influx of European settlers escaping the horrors of World War II.
Tens of thousands of people were killed or wounded, with the uprising providing important context for the current Israel-Gaza war.
"It's surprising how few people know about it. It's so critical to understand and talk about this period if we are to talk about anything else that comes afterwards, the Nakba and [the war in] 1948" Jacir says.
"It's very hard to do that without understanding what happens here in '36."
Jacir's movie is not a single story but an amalgamation of many: the young Arab pulled into an armed rebellion; the farmers of the local village who find themselves under siege; the Oxford-educated journalist bound by truth; the British representative torn between duty and morality; the Palestinian children born into violence.
Jacir says she felt the pressure in balancing her duty as an artist to create a story and her responsibility as a Palestinian to educate others.
"We're putting something on screen that hasn't been put on screen before. It's our story and we have to honour it," she says.
"Everybody on the film had a family member that was alive during '36. The cast, they thought about it a lot. Saleh Bakri, who plays Khalid, brought to me a picture of his grandfather who worked in Yafa on the docks, actually, as Khalid does [in the movie].
'He said, 'I want to look like him. Can I look like him?' So we modelled his look after his grandfather."
Coming back to Palestine to film was a sobering experience for the cast and crew with deep roots in the region.
"It was very difficult and very painful and I think you see that on screen. I think you see that the cast is in pain because we're performing acts of violence while there was real violence happening around us," Jacir says.
"We were already trying to get through checkpoints every day and we were getting stopped by settlers but we already had this mentality that nothing was going to stop us."
Rebel, Rebel
Palestine 36 premiered to a 20-minute standing ovation at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival.
It then picked up Best Film at the Tokyo International Film Festival, and by December had secured a spot on the prestigious Best International Feature Film shortlist for the 2026 Academy Awards.
A month later, Jacir and her team released a statement saying a screening of Palestine 36 at Yabous Cultural Centre in Jerusalem had been shut down by Israeli police, and that an "an official notice prohibiting any future screenings of the film" had been issued.
"Honestly, I wasn't expecting that because there are no Israelis in the film," Jacier says.
"It's about a Palestinian village and the brutality of the British. Yes, there's political Zionism and we understand the whole political context that's happening in the film.
"But it's a really a pity that the film was robbed from its audiences, and it is really interesting and telling that they put a notice on the door saying the film is forbidden from being seen because it violates some anti-terrorism law."
Despite being one of the most difficult films she's worked on, Jacir is proud to bring the story of the 1936 rebellion to cinemas around the world.
"It's important that we remember as people in the world that we have a voice … we have agency and that is something even though these are the darkest times," she says.
The power of a unified people is the reason Palestine 36 has no main characters, but is instead a "collective story", Jacir says.
"That's why the British started the idea of collective punishment; there's power in the collective," she says.
"That was our superpower, that is our superpower."
Palestine 36 is in Australian cinemas now.

Hong Kong WhatsApp hijacking scams surge 170% to nearly 2,000 cases
Police say victims lost HK$146 million in first seven months of 2026, with some suffering individual losses exceeding HK$10 million
WhatsApp account hijacking scams in Hong Kong surged by nearly 170 per cent to almost 2,000 cases in the first seven months of this year, with one victim losing as much as HK$12.2 million (US$1.55 million).
Police said the 1,993 cases logged from January to July represented a 169.7 per cent increase from the 739 cases recorded over the same period last year. The figure also surpassed the 1,669 cases recorded in all of 2025.
The cases over the first seven months resulted in losses of HK$146.3 million, down by 22.7 per cent from HK$189.2 million over the same period last year.
Despite the lower total loss, police warned that the threat was far from subsiding, noting that some victims lost between HK$1 million and more than HK$10 million.
“The rise in cases was related to the habits of our residents using these social media or instant messaging platforms,” said Superintendent Hui Yee-wai of the force’s cyber security and technology crime bureau.
“On the other hand, we have also seen that artificial intelligence is a factor. Every scam involved fake websites, while AI has made generating these fake websites significantly easier.”

Citi’s China-US corridor thrives as mainland firms hedge risks amid trade turbulence

Because North America remained a vital market, Chinese enterprises increasingly turned to international banks to execute foreign exchange hedging, manage trade exposure and reconfigure capital flows, Zhang said.
The resilience comes as Chinese corporate expansion enters what Citi describes as a “Going Global 3.0” phase.

While staff departures are typical before midterm elections, the departures of key aides such as White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in August took some in the White House by surprise, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The senior staff exodus comes at an already tumultuous time for Trump, who is struggling with foreign and domestic challenges – including some of his own making.

As he enters the last two years of his final term, Trump faces historically low approval ratings, a shaky economy and an unpopular war in Iran that has roiled global energy markets.

The string of departures threatens to create a vacuum in Trump’s inner circle and finding replacements will not be easy.
“If your vetting process the first go-round mandates that you have to claim that the 2020 election was stolen, then the pool of candidates was probably already small and getting smaller now,” said Marc Short, who served in the first Trump administration.

Scheffler wins PGA Tour Championship, Min Woo Lee ties fourth

In short:
World number one Scottie Scheffler carded a final round of four under to win the PGA Tour Championship by three shots.
Australian Min Woo Lee carded a final round of two under par to finish tied for fourth, five shots behind Scheffler.
Adam Scott, who won the tournament in 2006, was two over in the final round and finished in a tie for 11th, six shots behind Scheffler.
Adam Scott has had to settle for yet another cool milestone as Scottie Scheffler surpassed Tiger Woods as the PGA Tour's all-time leading prize money earner with his second season-long FedEx Cup crown.
Scheffler once again underlined his undisputed status as the world number one with a decisive three-shot triumph at the $US40 million ($56 million) Tour Championship in Atlanta.
The 2024 champion fired a closing four-under-par 66 to reel in third-round leader Viktor Hovland and join grand slam greats Rory McIlroy (2016, 2019, 2022) and Woods (2007, 2009) as only the third player to win the showpiece finale multiple times.
In pocketing the monster $US10 million winner's cheque, Scheffler also surged past Woods ($US120,999,166) with a mind-blowing $US130,390,661 in career on-course earnings in only his seventh season on the PGA Tour.
After starting three shots behind Hovland and alongside Scott in joint third, Scheffler surged clear to finish at 16-under for the tournament.
Hovland, the 2023 winner, was the outright runner-up despite a Sunday slip-up, a 72 as the Norwegian fell short in his own bid to win a second FedEx Cup.
American Ryan Gerard was third at 12-under following his own faltering 72.
With a closing 68, Min Woo Lee wound up one shot ahead of Scott, finishing as Australia's top finisher in an impressive seven-way tie for fourth on his Tour Championship debut.
Lee finished at 11-under with England's Alex Fitzpatrick (66), Americans Jacob Bridgeman (68), Russell Henley (68) and Chris Gotterup (71), McIlroy (69) and Swede Ludvig Aberg (71).
At 46 years, one month and 14 days, Scott was striving to become the oldest FedEx Cup champion, with Vijay Singh more than a year younger when he won in 2008.
Alas, it was not the former world number one's day.
Scott was in third spot for much of the afternoon, even pulling to within two shots of the lead early on the back nine.
But, unable to buy a birdie putt, Scott's bold challenge ended with a bogey on the par-4 16th hole after he hooked his drive wildly off the tee and hit a sloppy drop shot on number 17.
He eventually signed for a 72 to finish at 10 under with England's 2025 champ Tommy Fleetwood (67) and American world number three Cameron Young (70).
Still, Scott's share of 11th, 20 years after winning the Tour Championship, earned the veteran a tidy $US660,000.
That was enough to push Australia's 2013 Masters champion one up to seventh, above Justin Thomas, on the PGA Tour's all-time money list with $US74,880,596 in prize money.
Only Scheffler, Woods, McIlroy, Phil Mickelson, Justin Rose and Dustin Johnson are now above Scott.

The US Treasury Department denied credentials to reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg for a G20 finance meeting in North Carolina, the latest restriction on media access under US President Donald Trump. The US Treasury Department is preventing certain journalists from covering a finance meeting among the world's most powerful countries, in the latest move by US President Donald Trump's administration to restrict media access.
Individual reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg were not granted credentials to the Group of 20 (G20) finance ministerial in Asheville, North Carolina, the Times reported.
The Treasury has not explained the decision. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the Associated Press (AP) in an interview Sunday that “it has nothing to do with point of view.”
The reporters who've been denied access include the Times' Alan Rappeport, who has covered such meetings and the Treasury Department since 2017. However, another reporter for the Times, Berlin bureau chief Jim Tankersley, has been allowed to attend.
The Times said in a statement that denying American journalists access to an event in the US is “not just another disturbing effort by the administration to undermine independent journalism, but a blatant attempt to evade public scrutiny.”

“With the war in Iran, sanctions, the bond markets, and inflation on the agenda for the G20 finance ministers, the stakes of this gathering are significant for the global economy and the American people,” the Times said. "Excluding specific reporters and entire news organisations is a disservice to the public and an assault on press freedoms that we strongly condemn.”
Bloomberg News said denying access to the meeting “undermines media freedom and public accountability.”
The Wall Street Journal declined to comment.
Bessent is hosting the G20 meeting, which runs Saturday through Tuesday. It includes finance ministers, central bank governors and senior officials from the world's top economies. This year's G20 summit, which involves heads of state, is being held in December at Trump's golf club in Doral, Florida.
Tensions have been escalating between the US media and the second Trump administration, playing out both in the public arena and at times in the courts.
For example, the Defense Department declared earlier this year that its press office had become a classified space inaccessible to journalists. The ouster came after the Pentagon demanded that reporters agree to government-imposed restrictions on their work, prompting most news outlets to leave the building last fall.

Putin Looks To Set Russia As Counterweight To West At Bishkek Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:43:24 UTC
07:43:24 KST

Facing increasing confrontations with the West, Russian President Vladimir Putin is looking eastward to restore his country's standing in the region at a major summit in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz capital.
It comes at a time of increased difficulties for the Kremlin leader, with Russia's economy in tatters due to Western sanctions and Ukrainian drone strikes, ally Iran battered in war, and the leaders of former client states such as Syria and Venezuela ousted amid a muted Moscow response.
Putin is set to hold bilateral meetings with at least nine world leaders, including Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian, starting on August 31 on the sidelines of the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which is celebrating its 25th anniversary.
On the first day, the Russian leader met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Xi focused on bilateral issues and only discussed the war in Ukraine "marginally...essentially there was no discussion." Western nations have called on China to use its influence to pressure the Kremlin into ending its war on Ukraine.
Russia's Interfax news agency reported Modi told Putin that India supported "every peace effort" to end the war in Ukraine, without providing further details.
Putin is also expected to hold bilateral sessions with leaders of non-SCO nations, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, who has angered the Kremlin by seeking closer ties to the West for his small Caucasus nation.
United Front
Putin and Xi have often used SCO gatherings to put up a united front against Western influence in the region. Xi arrived late on August 30 and held his first meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, who will serve as host of the summit.
Along with Russia, Iran, India, and China, the SCO grouping consists of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. Not all members are allies, of course, with nuclear powers Pakistan and India often on the brink of war with each other.
The organization began as the "Shanghai Five" in 1996 but began expanding to other regional nations starting in 2001.
Moscow and Tehran are both under crippling Western sanctions -- Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and Iran for a multitude of issues, including its support for extremist activity in the Middle East and its alleged pursuit of a nuclear weapon.
Kyiv and the West have demanded Iran cease from providing deadly Shahed drones to Russia for use in the Ukraine war, while US officials told RFE/RL that Russia is providing Iran with targeting information to attack US troops and military assets in the Middle East, confirming a Washington Post report.
'Key Subjects'
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said "one of the key subjects" in the talks between Putin and Pezeshkian will be the Middle East crisis.
"You know how relevant this meeting is in light of the current uneasy atmosphere in the Middle East and the situation surrounding Iran," he added.
Also on the agenda will be the $25 billion agreement signed by Tehran with Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom to build four nuclear power plants in Iran.
Naser al-Tamimi, a UK-based analyst and founder of MidEast Strategia, wrote on X that the SCO can help largely isolated Iran, "but only to a point."
"The SCO offers Iran broader political cover, helps reduce its international isolation, and expands opportunities for trade and settlements in yuan, rubles, and other national currencies. In doing so, it can modestly reduce Tehran's dependence on the Western financial system."
"But the SCO is not an economic shield against US sanctions. It lacks a fully developed alternative financial architecture, provides no reliable protection for major banks and companies exposed to secondary sanctions, and cannot compel China or India to absorb high economic costs on Iran’s behalf."
Potentially Tense Armenian Meeting
Along with Turkey, other nonmember nations and others participating and observing will include Armenia, Azerbaijan, UN chief Antonio Guterres, and heads of several Moscow-oriented international organizations.
Putin is scheduled to meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, whose country has long been an ally of Russia but which has angered Moscow by seeking to move closer to the West.
Tensions heightened between the two countries after Armenian police on August 25 arrested former President Robert Kocharian, now leader of the country's second-largest opposition party, amid accusations of corruption-related offenses.
Kocharian, 71, served as Armenia's president between 1998 and 2008. He currently leads the Armenia Alliance, which is considered pro-Moscow and finished third in recent parliamentary elections in June.
Yerevan has also angered Moscow by expressing its ambition to eventually join the European Union.
"We will insist that Armenia cannot aspire for EU membership while hugely benefiting from cooperation within the European Economic Union (EEU)," said Ushakov, referring to the five-member trade bloc that also includes Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan.
Following the Bishkek event, Putin is scheduled to travel to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum on Russia's Pacific coast from September 1-4.
He is also set to meet with leaders of several other countries there, including the Indonesian president and Mongolian prime minister.

Aside from court sketches depicting him thinner and with grayer hair, these are the first images of the former leader since the early January raid that whisked him and his wife, Cilia Flores, out of Caracas to face federal charges in the US.

While President Donald Trump touted the agreement as securing US majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, Rodríguez defended the pact as a sovereign mechanism projected to net the Venezuelan state roughly US$209 billion (S$266.45 billion).
The realignment triggered an immediate domestic backlash.
Rodríguez is facing intense crossfire from hardliners both within the ruling socialist party and an opposition wary of the sweeping terms, making her political tightrope increasingly precarious.

Today, those billboards have been replaced by imagery thanking emergency responders.
Only a scattering of “#FreeMaduro” and “#FreeCilia” graffiti remains, jostling for space alongside slogans declaring “Trump out” and “Vote or street,” a reference to either voting or protesting in a sign of a fractured society.

NPS added that debris and metal structures entered the Colorado River following the flash flood, leading to the river being "closed to river traffic until further notice."
"Additional thunderstorms and heavy rainfall are possible Sunday and Monday, which could result in additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall, and changing trail and river conditions."

Winter, Smotrich cross electoral threshold at expense of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, Kan poll shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:36:54 UTC
07:36:54 KST

A new Kan election poll published Sunday shows Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party crossing the electoral threshold, gaining support at the expense of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit.
The poll, Kan’s first since the reestablishment of the Joint List, showed the Joint List overtaking Otzma Yehudit in projected Knesset seats.
According to the survey, Likud fell by one seat compared to Kan’s previous poll, dropping to 21 seats, and has lost three seats since the beginning of the month. Otzma Yehudit also declined, falling to seven seats.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Naftali Bennett’s B'Yachad party remained stable, with 24 and 21 seats respectively.
Within the opposition bloc, Yair Golan’s Democrats party and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu each lost one seat, falling to nine and eight seats respectively.
The bloc breakdown showed the opposition bloc declining from 57 seats to 55, while the coalition bloc rose slightly from 51 seats to 52. The Arab parties increased their projected representation to 13 seats.
Netanyahu continues to hold a slight lead over Bennett on suitability to serve as prime minister, with 37% choosing Netanyahu compared to 36% for Bennett. However, Eisenkot leads Netanyahu on the same question, 40% to 37%.
Kan News polls right-wing mergers
The Kan News poll also examined possible right-wing mergers. A merger between Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, which is supported by 57% of coalition voters, would actually weaken their combined support to 10 seats, compared to 12 seats if they ran separately. In that scenario, Winter’s party would rise to five seats.
If Smotrich were to unite with Moshe Feiglin’s party, Religious Zionism would rise to seven seats, tying Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, at Winter’s expense. In that scenario, Winter’s party would fall below the electoral threshold. In all scenarios, Benny Gantz, Gilad Erdan, and Matan Kahana’s parties fail to pass the threshold.
The poll also examined public opinion regarding security arrangements for political figures. Forty-one percent of respondents said the Shin Bet should provide security for Eisenkot, while 29% opposed. Regarding Yair Golan, the results were reversed, with 43% opposing Shin Bet protection and 30% supporting it.
Netanyahu addressed right-wing bloc challenges on Channel 14’s 'The Patriots'
During an interview with Channel 14’s The Patriots program Sunday evening, Netanyahu addressed the political challenges facing the right-wing bloc and the battle for right-wing votes, including divisions between Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism and the challenge posed by Winter’s People of Israel party.
The prime minister criticized Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir’s opposition to a merger with Religious Zionism chairman Bezalel Smotrich, saying: “He is coming out with great anger; I do not understand why. When Smotrich was high, and he was low, Ben-Gvir called on him to put his ego aside and unite, and Smotrich did the responsible thing. Today Ben-Gvir needs to do the responsible thing.”
Netanyahu urged the two parties to merge, saying: “There is about a week to allow for a merger. It is very possible that everyone can unite.”
Netanyahu also addressed Winter’s party and expressed concern that its independent run in the election could harm the right-wing bloc.
“I am worried that this [People of Israel] party could do one of two things: either waste votes or cause one of the parties I mentioned to fall,” Netanyahu said.
Winter responds to Netanyahu
In response to Netanyahu’s remarks, Winter rejected claims that his party threatens the right-wing bloc, arguing that other issues pose a greater danger.
“What endangers the right-wing camp and the entire people of Israel are kites from Gaza,” Winter said, also pointing to the entry of aid trucks into Gaza, Hamas’s Nukhba forces, and the failure to enlist haredim into the IDF as threats facing Israel.
Winter said real change would require new leadership rather than the same political figures.
“There is only one real possibility for change in the right-wing camp and in general: new people, who were not part of the failures of October 7,” he said, adding that his party is “part of the right-wing camp, but we do not work for anyone, only for the people of Israel.”

====================================================================================================

US Strike On Iranian Launchers Signals Resolve To Keep Hormuz Open, Experts Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:36:24 UTC
07:36:24 KST

WASHINGTON -- US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz after the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) was observed preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the vital waterway, a US official confirmed to RFE/RL.
The August 30 strikes mark the first publicly reported direct US attack on Iranian military positions in more than a month and come as Washington seeks to restore shipping through one of the world's most strategically important maritime chokepoints.
The US official said IRGC forces were preparing to launch the rockets with sea mines into the strait. Last week, US Central Command said American forces had completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes and were keeping a close watch on activity there.
"US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway," the official said.
US Central Command said that "US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC mine-laying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz. In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce."
Iran's hard-line IRGC vowed retaliation. In a statement carried by Iranian state media, it acknowledged "the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots" and said the attack would "result in the punishment of the aggressor."
The IRGC later said it fired ballistic missiles at two bases housing US forces in Jordan in retaliation. Jordan, a close US ally, said it intercepted eight incoming missiles that entered its airspace early on August 31.
A Warning Over Hormuz
Experts interviewed by RFE/RL said the US strike is less significant as an isolated military action than as a demonstration that Washington is prepared to use force to prevent Iran from restoring its ability to threaten shipping through Hormuz.
Alex Plitsas, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council and a former Pentagon official, said the latest exchange began after Iran struck a ship off the coast of Oman.
"Today's tit-for-tat strikes began after Iran struck a ship off the coast of Oman and then was attempting to launch a small number of mines into the strait," Plitsas told RFE/RL. "The US struck the launchers."
Plitsas said he believed Iran's attack on the ship was "in direct response to US statements about increased oil flows out of the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks," intended to demonstrate that Tehran could still strike maritime targets and increase the risk level for shippers.
The distinction between a physically blocked waterway and a waterway made too dangerous for commercial traffic is crucial, he said.
"The strait itself is physically open," Plitsas said. "Reduced flow at this point is largely due to the risk of an Iranian attack on a ship."
That means clearing mines and destroying identified launch sites may not be enough to restore normal traffic. Iran can continue using missiles and drones to threaten vessels, and the US cannot eliminate every potential launch site or weapon.
"It'll be virtually impossible to strike every Iranian missile or drone, so the Iranians can continue to harass ships and keep the strait held at risk for some time," Plitsas said.
He said the current situation could persist in the absence of a return to large-scale combat, until pressure on Iran produces a negotiated settlement.
The result is a difficult test for Washington. The military objective is to protect the waterway, but commercial operators must also be convinced that the risk of sailing through Hormuz has fallen enough to justify resuming regular traffic.
Not A New Phase Of War
Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran, said the strike was a signal that Washington would not allow Iran to reverse what he described as American gains in recent weeks in ensuring freedom of navigation in Hormuz.
"Today's strike is a signal from the US that it is not going to allow Iran to reverse the American gains in recent weeks over ensuring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," Brodsky told RFE/RL.
But Brodsky cautioned against portraying the attack as the beginning of an entirely new phase of the conflict.
"It's not a decisive shift to a new phase of the war," he said. "Rather it is a reminder that the US has the will to police the Strait of Hormuz."
The more consequential development may be Iran's response. Speaking before the report of the IRGC's retaliatory strikes, Brodsky said Tehran is expected to lash out as it suffers economically, and that US policymakers understand the dynamic.
"How the US responds to any Iranian attacks will matter most," he said. "A decisive American response will be required to demonstrate that the US has the endurance to continue the blockade for as long as Iran refuses to submit to US demands."
That could create a cycle in which Iran seeks to impose costs on US forces or shipping without returning to full-scale war, while Washington responds whenever it determines that Iranian actions threaten navigation.
Hormuz Open, But Traffic Severely Constrained
Ian Ralby, head of the maritime-security firm Auxilium Worldwide, said the US strike underscores that the conflict between the US and Iran remains unresolved.
"Today's strike indicates what any serious observer has known all along, which is there remains an international armed conflict between the US and Iran," Ralby told RFE/RL. He said the attack showed there are "a number of unresolved issues that do not have any clear timeline for their resolution."
The continued weakness of shipping through Hormuz illustrates the problem. Ralby said traffic is among the lowest seen during the conflict, with about five vessels a day traveling in either direction and some days with no traffic at all.
For Ralby, that demonstrates that Washington remains "poised and ready and willing to use force against Iran -- both at sea and in its sovereign territory -- in order to accomplish its goals."
But military action alone cannot remove the risks facing commercial operators. Even an attack that does not close the waterway can deter ships, increase insurance costs and push companies toward alternative routes.
The next Iranian moves will therefore be critical. Tehran's pledge to punish the aggressor came as the IRGC reported casualties in the Larak Island attack, creating pressure on Iranian leaders to demonstrate that US attacks will carry a price.
Ralby cautioned that any escalation may not remain confined to Hormuz. He said the region has multiple potential flashpoints and warned that frustration with the status quo could lead one of the parties to act in a way that triggers renewed violence.
"The situation in Hormuz is unlikely to be resolved anytime soon," Ralby said. "There are short tempers and short fuses among a number of the players."
Iran has often attacked US bases across the region, Ralby noted, while the involvement of the Houthis and piracy incidents create additional opportunities for violence. The next escalation could therefore spread "well beyond the geographic confines of the strait of Hormuz."
He also pointed to Lebanon and Gaza as flashpoints where continuing violence could prompt Iran or the Houthis to attack in new ways.
"So this thing could spiral further out of control than it has at any moment," Ralby said.
Global Economic Stakes Rise
The consequences of a prolonged disruption in Hormuz would extend well beyond the military confrontation. Ralby said the global economic picture is becoming increasingly concerning as the Northern Hemisphere approaches winter and heating-oil demand is expected to rise.
He warned that the problem could shift from higher energy prices to questions of physical supply and potential shortages, depending on the severity of the winter.
"We become closer and closer to the winter period for the northern hemisphere with a demand for heating oil will start to spike in the next two months," Ralby said, raising concerns about "not just price but supply and then overall shortage."
China could add another layer of uncertainty. Ralby said Beijing has been artificially decreasing its demand for oil, but a renewed increase in Chinese consumption could send oil prices higher and deepen the economic effects of the standoff.
He warned that such pressure could also encourage more states to conduct transactions with China outside the dollar-based financial mechanisms that have helped underpin US economic influence for decades.
A Fragile Status Quo
For now, the central question is whether the August 30 strike and the IRGC retaliation remain isolated exchanges or become the start of another cycle of escalation.
Washington has shown that its effort to protect navigation extends beyond clearing mines from shipping routes. It is also prepared to strike Iranian military assets when it believes they are being used to threaten the waterway.
Iran, meanwhile, retains the ability to keep commercial shipping at risk without necessarily attempting a conventional blockade. That leaves Hormuz in an unstable middle ground: physically open, but with traffic severely constrained by the threat of attack.
Plitsas said that status quo could persist for some time if neither side returns to large-scale combat. But Ralby's warning about regional flashpoints and the economic pressure building around Hormuz underscores how difficult it may be to contain the conflict indefinitely.
The immediate test will be how Washington responds to the latest Iranian retaliation in Jordan. The longer-term challenge is whether the US can make the waterway sufficiently secure for commercial operators without triggering a wider war.

One dead, more than a dozen unaccounted for after Grand Canyon flash flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:34:46 UTC
07:34:46 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The National Park Service recovered the body of a 46-year-old man after a significant flash flood in the Grand Canyon on Saturday.
The man’s identity has not yet been released, and the agency said Sunday night it was still searching for about 15 other people. Earlier Sunday, the park service had asked for the public’s help finding as many as 20 people. The body was recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, and the Coconino County medical examiner’s office is on site as the search for more hikers continues, according to the park service.
“If you know of hikers or backpackers who were in the Bright Angel Creek corridor on August 29, or if you had a campground reservation in the affected area, please contact the NPS Investigative Services Branch,” the agency wrote in a news release and social media posts on Sunday afternoon.
This includes people who may have been traveling along the North Kaibab Trail from the trailhead to Phantom Ranch, staying at Bright Angel Campground or traveling or staying in the area known as “the Box” north of Phantom Ranch, officials said.
The park service said the flash flood happened around 2:30 p.m. Saturday and resulted in “significant impacts” to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon. Nearly all footbridges were destroyed, eliminating hiker access to the creek. The flooding widened the creek bed and created what appeared to be a new river rapid.
Dozens of people were evacuated as the flooding swept large boulders, metal structures and other debris into the Colorado River, which runs through the Grand Canyon, the National Park Service said. Flooding also knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents at the national park, officials said late Sunday.
Sixty-two people were evacuated from the area Sunday morning, and additional evacuations were underway from Cottonwood Campground, Phantom Ranch and other nearby sites.
Evacuees have been transported to the Maswik Lodge Cafeteria on the South Rim, where the American Red Cross is coordinating assistance.
Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, the Phantom Ranch Canteen and cabins, and the entire North Kaibab Trail from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch are closed until further notice, the park service said.
The Black Bridge and Silver Bridge crossing the Colorado River are also closed until further notice, with no estimated reopening date.
Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with a group of fellow physicians and a park ranger when the downpour started.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” said the hiker, who was later rescued by helicopter.
A flash flood watch remains in effect in the Grand Canyon area through Monday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms in the forecast, according to the National Weather Service.
“Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas,” the agency warned. “Raging killer currents will be possible in side canyons and narrow slot canyons. Low-water crossings may be flooded.”
Anyone with information is asked to contact the National Park Service Investigative Services Branch Tip Line at (888) 653-0009 or nps_isb@nps.gov.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Lake Ontario now called ‘Lake America’ on Google Maps for US users after Trump order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:34:36 UTC
07:34:36 KST

Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
Canadian users continue to see the original name as the tech giant rolls out location-based labelling
Google has updated its maps application to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the United States, reflecting a recent order by US President Donald Trump that changed the name of the lake, the global technology giant said.
The Google Maps update comes days after Trump’s order amid an escalating trade war with Canada that has led both countries to impose billions of dollars in added tariffs on each other’s goods. It echoes what Google did in 2025 when Trump issued an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
Google said in a blog post on Saturday that the decision was based on its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System, also known as GNIS.
“People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America’, those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’, and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.”
Trump’s decision on Thursday to rename the lake was met with mockery and indifference in both Canada and the United States. On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Trump’s order with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shore: “Lake Ontario. Now and forever”.
The White House, the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford’s office did not immediately comment on Sunday on Google’s decision.

800 Russian jet-powered drones launched over 4 days as attacks enter 5th straight day
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 30 that around 800 Russian jet-powered drones were launched over the last four days amid prolonged waves of attacks on Ukrainian cities that have now entered their fifth straight day.
The president's latest report comes amid an ongoing Russian drone attack on the capital with explosions heard in central Kyiv beginning around 12:30 a.m. local time overnight on Aug. 31, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. No information was immediately available on the aftermath of the latest attack.
In a shift in tactics, Moscow has increasingly launched daytime kamikaze drone attacks against Kyiv over the past week, keeping the capital in a perpetual state of alert, with air raid alarms constantly turning on and off. Homes, businesses, and other civilian infrastructure have been hit, the president wrote.
Russia is increasingly using jet-powered drones, which can travel up to 600 kilometers per hour, more than three times faster than piston-powered Shaheds.
"Right now, Russia’s tactic is to wear down Ukraine and Ukrainians – first and foremost, our people," Zelensky said in his evening address, noting that Moscow's forces launched nearly 1,500 drones over the last four days.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
"The most difficult task is intercepting the jet-powered ones. Now, it is mainly our combat aircraft that protect against them," the president added.
As Ukraine continues to search for effective defense against the jet-powered drones, Ukraine's new Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara told reporters on Aug. 29 that Ukraine has tested four potential interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
"Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology," Zelensky concluded in his evening address. "This fall, we need to deliver a response and bring the interception rate to well above 90%."
Over the past week, Russia launched nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 glide bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, against Ukraine, marking an uptick in attacks.
