What Is Trump’s U.S. Space Academy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:00:47 UTC
05:00:47 KST

President Donald Trump last week signed an executive order creating a commission to develop plans for the United States Space Academy, which is intended to “educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”
The initiative was first announced when Trump visited the Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, on Aug. 28 to present the crew of Artemis II with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor. The crew was recognized for their 10-day lunar flyby in April, which took them farther from Earth than any human had ever traveled.
“Given the rapid growth of the Space Force and the commercial space industry and the expansion of our ambitions to the moon and far beyond the moon,” Trump said while giving remarks at the ceremony, “it’s clear we will need to educate and train an entire generation of skilled service members, engineers, and civil operators.”
The proposed academy is envisioned as serving the military, civil government, and broader space industry. However, the exact admissions requirements for Space Academy—which will help characterize who it serves and how—are yet to be determined. Future Space Force officers currently attend the U.S. Air Force Academy.
“The Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the executive order said. “Achieving this goal requires us to recruit, train, and retain America’s best and brightest from across the Nation.”
At the ceremony, Trump also acknowledged the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named for one of the forebears of modern space science, which was launched Sunday aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. With surveying capabilities over 1,000 times faster than its predecessor, the Hubble Space Telescope, Roman seeks to explore dark matter, uncharted corners of the cosmos, and questions about the expansion of the universe.
What do we know so far about the Space Academy?
The first step in establishing the new academy is forming a Presidential Commission to develop recommendations for it. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will chair the new commission, according to the executive order, and it will also include War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink, or their designees, among other federal representatives.
The commission has 120 days from Aug. 28 to submit its report to the President. It must include a governance framework, an academic and leadership curriculum, prerequisites for students, a service obligation for graduates, and a plan of implementation, legislative and otherwise, for all of the included components to take effect.
The White House also released a fact sheet, which described the proposed Space Academy as a “NASA-led federal academy dedicated to combining rigorous technical education with leadership development, discipline, and a durable commitment to public service.”
The fact sheet organized the administration’s case for the academy under three headings.
“Building the Next Generation of American Space Leaders” covered the convening of the commission and how the commission’s subsequent recommendations will be implemented.
“Advancing American Space Superiority” established that intensifying competition in space requires the United States to encourage more students to pursue cutting-edge technical fields.
Finally, “Building American Strength and Driving Achievement” explained Trump’s commitment to the space industry, from signing the legislation that formed the Space Force in 2019 to this month’s National Security Presidential Memorandum, which calls for U.S. ranges to support “more than 1,000 launches and reentries every year” by 2030.
“Access to, from, and within space is a vital national and economic security interest,” the Aug. 20 memorandum stated.
The fact sheet also linked the Space Force to the military’s preparation for future warfare, saying: “The Space Force is critical to preparing the Department of War for evolving warfighting conditions and expanding our capabilities.”
Where will the Space Academy be located?
The future location of the Space Academy has not yet been determined. Trump said that the White House would be accepting proposals. At the Congressional Space Medal of Honor ceremony, he said, “I’m going to be choosing a location very shortly.”
Joking that Sen. Ted Cruz was already interested in hosting the new academy in Texas, Trump continued: “Everybody wants it because it’s the hot thing. Space is the hot thing.”
Trump compared his ambitions for the academy to other prestigious military education institutions.
“So you think of West Point and you think of Annapolis and you think of the Air Force Academy and you think of the Coast Guard Academy. It’s great. They’re all great,” he said. “But we’re going to have now a Space Force [academy].”
Those are based in New York, Maryland, Colorado, and Connecticut, respectively.
“But I said this has to be comparable to [those schools],” he explained. “You know, we don’t want to do it in any other way, and it’s going to be, even architecturally, it’s got to be beautiful. It’s got to be the top. It’s going to be as good as it can get.”

How Palestine is becoming a fault line in French elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:56:43 UTC
04:56:43 KST

Breadcrumb
How Palestine is becoming a fault line in France’s 2027 presidential race
France is preparing for its presidential election in eight months, with analysts telling The New Arab that Palestine has become an increasingly important domestic litmus test in the battle for political power.
With President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, the 2027 race is more open than it has been in years.
From left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, whose pro-Palestine rhetoric has helped bolster his support, to National Rally (RN) figures seeking closer ties with Israel, analysts said Palestine could emerge as not only a major foreign policy issue but also a defining electoral fault line during the campaign.
The Palestine question has gained greater prominence in French politics following Paris's public response to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and developments in the occupied West Bank, with Macron's government adopting a more critical stance towards Israeli actions while, at the same time, maintaining diplomatic ties with the country.
This has included France's landmark recognition of Palestine in September 2025 and public condemnation of Israeli officials including far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
"Unlike in 2022, Israel-Palestine can no longer be kept at the margins of French presidential debate. It has repeatedly ranked among French voters' top concerns since October 2023, spiking again with each escalation (Gaza, Lebanon, Iran)," Julia Amoura, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), told The New Arab.
She argued that the decision to recognise an independent Palestinian state "has turned the issue into a marker of presidential leadership rather than a peripheral foreign-policy question," and predicted that it was likely to become an even bigger foreign-policy dividing line as the campaign advances.
"France's recognition of Palestine has already forced every major candidate to state a clearer position, and the situation on the ground remains volatile: the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire is fragile, with continuing strikes, a US-brokered disarmament plan rejected by Netanyahu, and UN warnings of a possible return to full-scale hostilities," Amoura said. "Any renewed escalation before April 2027 would likely reopen the debate at moments candidates can't control."
Melenchon's polling position
This comes as Mélenchon, leader of La France Insoumise (LFI), has emerged as a serious contender for the second round of the presidential election in several polling scenarios.
He could face the far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen, who is polling at historically high levels and is projected to lead the first round in several potential candidate line-ups next spring.
A recent Harris Interactive–Toluna poll, reported by Politico, put Mélenchon on 16 percent in one scenario, ahead of former prime minister Édouard Philippe on 14 percent and former prime minister Gabriel Attal on 8 percent. Le Pen was well ahead on 35 percent. In scenarios without Attal, Mélenchon and Philippe were tied on 17 percent, underlining that the contest for second place remains open.
Analysts have linked part of Mélenchon’s appeal to his outspoken pro-Palestine stance and his effort to mobilise voters around a vision of a “New France”, centred on younger and more diverse voters who may previously have felt alienated from electoral politics.
LFI has also recorded local breakthroughs, including victories in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, and Roubaix in northern France during the 2026 municipal elections.
"Gaza resonates strongly with younger and urban minority voters, which is why LFI centred its 2024 European campaign on it and why RN has worked to reassure French Jewish voters," Amoura told The New Arab.
"Both communities have also been directly affected by a sharp rise in religiously motivated hate. In 2025, France recorded 1,320 antisemitic acts — a 16 percent year-on-year fall, but still a historically high level — while anti-Muslim acts rose 88 percent to 326 incidents."
She added: “For many French voters, this is not an abstract foreign-policy debate but one intertwined with domestic security and communal anxiety, a combination likely to keep the issue emotionally charged throughout the campaign.”
RN's pro-Israel shift
The issue’s growing prominence is also evident in the RN’s attempt to distance itself from its historic associations with racism and antisemitism while adopting a more openly pro-Israel position.
The party’s promotion of the 28-year-old Jordan Bardella has coincided with a broader rapprochement between Israel and parts of the European far right.
French political analyst François Burgat told The New Arab that growing pro-Israel sentiment in sections of the French far right rests partly on hostility towards Palestinians, whom he said Le Pen views as among the "decolonised" peoples. He linked this to the RN’s longstanding support for restrictive immigration policies and its portrayal of France as threatened by "Islamisation".
"The sympathy the State of Israel garners in France is not directed at the Jewish people as such, but rather at an anti-Muslim people — one with whom those nostalgic for the colonial era easily identify, and one that does not shy away from the extreme violence it is currently deploying in Gaza," he said.
“The question of Palestine will therefore be central to the presidential debate for several reasons, but above all because support for Israel serves as a way to stigmatise France’s Muslim community — a group whose existence and growing assertiveness have come to dominate public discourse.”

'Almost dystopian': Should AI be used to write work emails?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:54:38 UTC
04:54:38 KST

Should artificial intelligence be used to write work emails? Australia's workplace tribunal ruled against
The first email was sent in 1971 as an experiment to see if two computers could exchange messages.
Since then, the communication tool has become commonplace in businesses, but with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), those exchanges have become even less human.
Griffith University's Mai Nguyen said it was now the norm for workers to use AI to sound more professional and use the right grammar.
But the business school senior lecturer warned that using the wrong "prompt" in an AI generator could exaggerate facts and make the text's tone inappropriate.
'Couched in accusatory language'
The widespread use of AI had recently prompted Australia's workplace tribunal to order an employee and their workplace to cease using the technology in all future correspondence.
The order was handed down in a bullying complaint before the Fair Work Commission in late July.
An employee working as a caretaker for a Queensland body corporate submitted to the tribunal that the workplace repeatedly refused to clarify their duties, provided confusing and shifting directions, and made several other allegations.
Commissioner Sarah McKinnon ruled that the employee had been bullied.
But she noted emails from the employee and the workplace and found the caretaker's correspondence was "unhelpful" and appeared to have been prepared with the use of an AI tool.
Commissioner McKinnon described the communication as "lengthy, wide-ranging, replete with generalisations, repetitive, and often couched in accusatory language".
She said it was "unsurprising" that the workplace "eventually chose not to engage" with the employee.
"Unfortunately, its choice to 'disengage and dig in', my description, had the result that it did not engage in any meaningful way with many of the concerns [the employee] was raising," Commissioner McKinnon said.
"This was to the detriment of all parties."
To prevent further bullying of the employee, Commissioner McKinnon ordered all future communication between the parties be "accurate and respectful".
"There is to be no use of artificial intelligence tools in the preparation of correspondence between the parties," she said.
"Parties should endeavour to keep their communications brief and to the point."
The order was to take effect immediately.
Digital communication Professor Daniel Angus said it was an interesting case.
The Queensland University of Technology professor said there was a "natural appeal" to want to use the technology to make text more "forceful or persuasive".
He said someone could use it to overwhelm "an opponent within a debate in this kind of adversarial environment".
Should you disclose an email has been written with AI?
Professor Angus said we need to normalise disclosing the use of AI "a lot more" but conceded it was "a really tricky topic".
"What we're seeing is that there are some folks who are vehemently opposed to the use of AI," he said.
"You can understand why people don't want to be forthcoming about their use of AI."
Law research fellow Guzyal Hill, from the University of Melbourne, said very few organisations had AI policies but said there was a growing push for it.
"It's difficult to avoid AI in terms of large language models in the modern society," she said.
"Australia does not have an AI Act, so each organisation has to develop its own AI Strategy/AI Policy."
The AI Governance Chair at HWLE Lawyers said there wasn't much "harm" in using AI for emails as long as it was used skilfully, in line with legislation and internal work policies.
But she said it should be "discouraged" if private and confidential information was being put into the AI generator.
"The caution is always about the way it's used," Dr Hill said.
Can you tell if AI wrote an email?
Professor Angus said there were "telltale signs" when AI has written texts, but that humans were "notoriously" bad at picking it up.
"I often think about the maligned em-dash (—), which is a real victim of the AI moment," he said.
Professor Angus said the tone of voice was another revealing sign of the AI.
"You could read something and think, 'Well this doesn't sound like them,'" he said.
Professor Angus warned about the increasing outsourcing of emails and other forms of communication to AI agents.
He said that would put workplaces in a "really weird and almost dystopian position" where it is just "a bunch of AI agents talking to each other" while the workers are "seemingly unaware of what they're talking about".
Dr Nguyen reads up to 30 emails each day, and she suspects about 80 per cent of them are AI-generated.
"Especially the long emails, I can predict that [they] come from some sort of AI," she said.
If using the technology for emails, Dr Nguyen advised double-checking that the text is clear, precise, and what you intended to send.
"At the end of the day, the email comes from the name of the sender,"

Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:53:00 UTC
04:53:00 KST

Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview
August 30, 2026
As part of an annual tradition, Chancellor Friedrich Merz sat down with public broadcaster ARD on Sunday evening for a wide-ranging summer interview. Amid drooping poll numbers, Merz tried to use the interview to tout his government's work on economic, migration and energy policy.
At the same time, Merz made a number of misleading claims, often overstating his administration's work and misrepresenting climate science.
DW Fact check, in collaboration with colleagues across the ARD fact-checking network, reviewed Merz's interview live.
Did Merz cut asylum numbers by 60%?
Claim: "One of the main issues in the last federal election campaign was the migration crisis, and together with the federal government, we've been able to reduce the numbers by over 60% in just over a year."
DW Fact check: Misleading
This is misleading for several reasons — it is both questionable what exactly Merz meant by migration, and also not clear to which period he is referring.
The number of asylum-seekers in Germany has fallen significantly, but not to the extent Merz said. According to the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), a total of 56,547 asylum applications were filed in the first half of 2026, including 39,646 first-time applications. Compared with the same period last year, the number of first-time applications fell by 35.4% — significantly less than the figure cited by Merz. Comparing the number of initial asylum applications for the second half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 with the same period of the previous year, the number of initial asylum applications fell from 169,671 to 91,546 – a decrease of 46 percent.
Comparing individual months reveals significant fluctuations: In July 2026, the number of initial asylum applications, at 4,311, was even around 48 percent lower than in the same month of the previous year. A decline of almost 60 percent was recorded only once, inAugust 2025 compared to August 2024, when looking at individual months since Merz took office .
In addition, the downward trend began even before the Merz government took office in May 2025. After the fall of Syrian ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, the number of asylum-seekers in Germany declined. At the European level, the number of asylum applications also fell in the first half of 2025.
Official statistics also show a decline in general migration. According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 235,000 more people immigrated to Germany in 2025 than emigrated. This means that net immigration was 45% below the previous year's figure of 430,000 people. But that's mostly due to the number of arrivals falling, while the number of departures remained almost stable.
Germany's debt, in context
Claim: "We are still one of the least indebted countries in Europe. We are still a country that has by far the best credit rating of any European nation. No one doubts the debt sustainability of our country or our economy; we are operating within reasonable limits here."
DW Fact check: Misleading
There are three important ways to measure how much debt EU countries hold: debt-to-GDP ratio, deficit spending and credit rating.
On the first — debt-to-GDP ratio, or how a country's total debt compares to its annual economic output — Germany receives a failing grade. The eurozone requires countries to keep this ratio below 60%. Germany and 11 other countries are above that limit, versus 15 countries which are in compliance, putting Germany smack in the middle of the eurozone.
On the second — government deficits, or a country's net borrowing — Germany is just scraping by. The eurozone asks its members to keep this figure below 3%. Germany's net borrowing is at 2.7%, joining 16 other countries that are also below the limit. Of the 17 countries that meet that requirement, Germany comes the second closest to hitting the 3% limit.
As for credit rating — a grade from investors on how likely a country is to repay its debts — Germany does indeed earn the highest marks possible. But it shares that grade with several other countries. There are only 11 countries in the world with an AAA rating from S&P: Germany joins Denmark, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland in earning the grade.
In 2009, Germany amended its constitution by adding a so-called "debt brake," mandating the government to keep deficits to 0.35% of GDP. In 2020, that restriction was suspended to deal with the COVID pandemic and then again in 2022 and 2025 to allow for an increase in defense spending.
Real CO2 balance of electric cars
Claim: "At the European level, the issue with internal combustion engines has nothing to do with CO2 emissions. We want climate-friendly and climate-neutral cars, but we don't want to dictate the technology — it's not up to politicians to decide that. What matters is how much CO2 such a car emits, and the CO2 balance of electric mobility isn't as rosy as it's often portrayed."
DW Fact check: Misleading
Battery electric vehicles produce, on average, 73% less CO2 emissions than internal combustion engine vehicles, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a US-based nonprofit think tank.
Battery electric vehicles do generate about 40% higher production emissions, mostly because of the processes involved in manufacturing the battery, though these are usually offset after about one or two years of driving.
Merz was likely referring to a new paper from researchers at the Technical University of Munich, which right-wing media seized on this week. The paper, which took an average of 19 studies, claimed that battery electric vehicles only reduce CO2 emissions by 41%, compared to traditional cars.
But there's a key issue with the TUM paper: including all those studies means older analyses with outdated electricity mixes are given equal weight. The ICCT analysis, on the other hand, uses a more current estimate.
Either way, there's an overwhelming scientific consensus that electric vehicles are better for the environment than traditional cars.
This article is a collaboration with Germany's public broadcasting ARD fact-checking network.
Edited by: Martin Kuebler

Fedorov offers drone technology to US in exchange for Patriots, seeks funding for defense tech fund
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is seeking U.S. investment for a new defense technology fund and offering to help Washington develop drone capabilities in exchange for Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine, he told the Financial Times in an interview published Aug. 30.
The proposal comes as Fedorov has begun an international trip that has included Italy and the United States after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky as defense minister.
Fedorov told the FT in Washington that he is seeking backing from venture capitalists, private investors, and U.S. technology companies for a fund that would invest in Ukrainian defense startups and create new companies focused on battlefield technologies.
"This is not exactly a classic venture fund," Fedorov said in an interview. "We're writing a new history of the war."
Fedorov said the fund would initially focus on battlefield robotics, high-speed interceptor drones capable of countering Russia's newer jet-powered attack drones, and low-cost missiles equipped with artificial intelligence.
He also proposed a direct exchange with the United States, saying he would be willing to help Washington "build an army of drones" in return for Patriot interceptors to help Ukraine withstand Russian attacks this winter.
"I'm ready to make that trade," Fedorov told the FT.
Ukraine has faced a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors as Russia has intensified missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The U.S.-made systems are among the few weapons capable of intercepting Russia's ballistic missiles.
Fedorov said Ukraine had already tested high-speed drones designed to bring down Russia's jet-powered attack drones and argued that they could be produced at scale with additional investment.
"We need more jet drones, we need cheap missiles, we need missiles with artificial intelligence," he said. "You can't conduct any kind of dialogue with Putin any other way. He understands only force."
Fedorov served as defense minister from January to July before Zelensky dismissed him in a Cabinet reshuffle. His firing triggered weeks of protests across Ukraine and elevated Fedorov's profile as a potential political rival to Zelensky.
After Zelensky declined to reinstate him as defense minister earlier this month, Fedorov called for wartime elections, a move that divided public opinion.
In an interview with the FT, Fedorov defended his call for elections, saying it was not aimed at replacing Zelensky but at updating the country's governing system.
"This is not against Zelensky, it's not against some specific person," Fedorov said. "It's about the fact that we need to … update the state's operating system."
Fedorov's trip to the U.S. follows a visit to Italy, where he agreed to serve as an unpaid adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto on modern warfare technologies, his press service told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 28.
Fedorov's press service said his primary focus would remain on projects in Ukraine and efforts to attract international resources for the country's defense technology sector. During his meeting with Crosetto, the two discussed drones, autonomous systems, air defense, and the development of Ukraine's defense technology ecosystem.
The FT reported that Fedorov was also considering similar advisory roles with other partner countries, potentially including France and the United States. He declined to say whether he planned to meet with officials from the Trump administration during his Washington visit.
Fedorov also said he remained in close contact with U.S. billionaire and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, but declined to comment on whether he planned to meet him in the U.S. Ukraine has relied heavily on Musk's Starlink satellite communications system throughout the war.
Previously, Zelensky awarded Musk Ukraine's Order of Liberty on Aug. 26, as Kyiv seeks his approval to use Starlink on drones operating inside Russia.

Ukraine has four potential interceptor systems that could shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on 30 August, according to Suspilne.
Russia has sharply increased its use of the faster drones against Ukrainian cities, causing major damage to civilian infrastructure and many civilian casualties. The attacks are putting near-unprecedented strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
All four interceptor systems have undergone field testing, Khmara said. Ukraine now aims to bring them to the required level as quickly as possible and scale production to thousands of units.
“The search for countermeasures against jet-powered drones continues,” Khmara told journalists, according to Suspilne. “There are already four potential interceptors that can shoot down jet-powered ‘Shaheds.’ Field tests have already been conducted on them.”
Russia is rapidly expanding Geran attacks
Russia's Gerans are jet-powered adaptations of the Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones that Russia has produced domestically throughout the full-scale war. The faster Geran variants give Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect and engage them.
Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said Russia used more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans against Ukraine in August, up from about 1,500 in July.
He also said the drones are being launched against Ukraine almost directly from Russian factories, highlighting the rapid expansion of their production and use.
Zelenskyy calls for faster production
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made countering the Gerans a priority as Russia sustains repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities.
At a 28 August meeting of Ukraine’s military leadership, Zelenskyy said the country needed to maximize domestic weapons production, with the immediate focus on defending against jet-powered Gerans and increasing Ukraine’s own long-range strikes against Russia.
“[The] main thing is our defense against jet-powered ‘Shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said in his evening address.
He said Russia had adopted a tactic of keeping Kyiv and other cities under repeated air raid alerts, with Gerans reaching the capital as well as cities including Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.
Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies
“All our means of countering [them] are already being used,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine needs a significant acceleration in production of interceptors specifically designed for the jet-powered drones.
Khmara said the four potential interceptors are now at the field-testing stage, with the next step being to bring them into production at a scale of thousands of units.
For Ukraine, that scale is critical. The country must defend a large territory against increasingly large Russian drone barrages while also preserving limited air-defense resources for ballistic and other missiles that require more advanced interceptors.

NHAI has made Automated and Intelligent Machine-Aided Construction compulsory for highway projects longer than 20 km (AI generated image)
NEW DELHI: National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has made Automated and Intelligent Machine-Aided Construction (AI-MC) compulsory for all highway projects longer than 20 km in length and costing over Rs 500 crore, in what’s a move aimed at addressing quality issues, which have become a major concern for govt.As per an NHAI circular issued on Friday, contractors will have to use the AI-MC system while building the road from the ground up and continuously across the entire spatial footprint of the project. The technology will be used for every major layer of highway, including embankment (raised earth foundation), subgrade (compacted soil base) and Granular Sub-Base (GSB) — the first layer of crushed stone, sand and gravel laid over the compacted soil before the road surface is built.The move is aimed at improving construction quality and ensuring roads are built with greater accuracy and uniformity. AI-MC is a construction technology with on-board computers and sensors on heavy machinery such as graders, pavers, compactors and dozers. Deployment of AI-MC aims to improve the quality, durability and transparency of road construction by replacing manual monitoring with technology-driven, real-time execution and quality control.
TOI has learnt that though AI-MC was first deployed during construction of Lucknow-Kanpur Expressway, it was not used on the entire stretch and at all grades.Officials said the move is designed to minimise human errors, ensure uniform construction standards and generate digital records of every stage of construction, from earthwork to pavement laying. “The new norms make it mandatory to share real-time data with NHAI officials.
This is good for contractors and for us as well. Once the contractor gets real-time data, there will be hardly any scope for sub-contractors to cut corners,” said an official.Some of the industry players in AI-MC segment said that contractors are reluctant to share real-time data with NHAI and other highway construction agencies as this makes them accountable. “Unless NHAI and other agencies get the data in real time, the impact of using the technology will be negligible. It must not be used in a piecemeal way if govt is serious about putting things in order,” said one of them.

The US military struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces were seen preparing to fire towards the Strait of Hormuz, a US official confirmed to The Jerusalem Post on Sunday night, marking the first US strike on Iran in several weeks.

US recently began Operation Economic Outcast
This is the first US strike in Iran since the end of July. Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told foreign counterparts that the US would avoid striking Iran "for the time being," Axios reported.
The US intended to pressure Tehran through Operation Economic Outcast, sources familiar with the matter told Axios.
The Operation, which was announced by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on August 24, was described by both Bessent and US President Donald Trump as an "economic D-Day" against the Iranian regime.
"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.

Rubio didn't rule out a return to strikes if Iran attacked the US first.

Loïc was diagnosed with psychopathic traits and feels no empathy. He says harm is a choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:33:08 UTC
04:33:08 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
A man diagnosed with psychopathic traits, parents concerned about their children's violent behaviour, and guests who grew up believing they were bad. Are some of us born bad, or is harmful behaviour shaped by experience? How do nature and nurture influence our choices and morals? Watch Insight episode Born Bad? at 8.30PM Tuesday 1 September on SBS or SBS On Demand.
This article references suicide and drug use.
Loïc De Marie says he views a human as "a rock" and has struggled to understand other people's emotions from a young age.
"A little classmate died in a dramatic car accident when I was six years old … everybody was crying," the 26-year-old told Insight.
"This [was] the first time I understood that emotions are different with me [because] the look that the teacher gave me was, 'Why is this kid not crying?'"
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Growing up in Belgium, in that same year, Loïc and his little sister were playing near their backyard pool when she fell in.
"She was drowning, and I looked at her, and that was kind of troubling," he said.
He then saved her by holding out a plastic golf club for her to grab as he dragged her back to the ladder.
"And I didn't jump into the pool because I didn't want my clothes to get wet."
As he grew older, Loïc became increasingly involved in fights and would have angry outbursts.
"A guy was looking me in the eyes, some rivalry between men… and one day, I came to school with a baseball bat," he said.
"I would have smashed his head like a watermelon."
Loïc says the police arrested him on the school grounds over the incident but says he never faced serious legal consequences.
"I could have done prison for threat with weapon ... "
"But I got a lot of chances, and I always found myself okay."
Receiving a diagnosis
Three years ago, Loïc began seeing a new psychologist — having grown tired of masking his thought processes.
The psychologist diagnosed him with antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) and documented traits associated with psychopathy — including manipulation and lying, a reckless disregard for other people's safety, and a lack of remorse and empathy.
"Empathy [is like] music," Loïc said.
"Everybody in the room can understand the words of the music and the melody ... I don't hear the melody — I don't understand it."
Loïc's father, Philippe, says he used to worry his son would go down the wrong path, but receiving a diagnosis was helpful.
"It [was] good to put a name on a disorder, and then you understand a lot of things.
"We try to ... do the best we can to support him [with] a lot of communication and love."
Forensic psychiatrist Dr Rajan Darjee, who has worked in prisons, mental health hospitals and in the community, says ASPD is a broad concept describing "people who, because of personality problems, are repeatedly breaking rules".
"Psychopathy is a particularly narrow set of traits in people with personality disorder," he said.
"They're callous, they lack concern for other people, they lack empathy."
But Darjee says these traits does not mean someone is destined to cause harm.
"Just because you've got those things going on for you when you're very young doesn't mean inevitably you're going to do bad things.
"There's plenty of people who have those traits [who] will never commit a crime. And, you know, I meet plenty of people who commit murder who don't have those traits."
Darjee believes empathy is important as it is "the reason" we are social as humans.
"I always say lack of empathy doesn't cause violence; it just means that where you've got a decision whether you're going to be violent or not, it doesn't help weigh it in favour of not being violent."
'It's not being evil'
Diagnosed with ASPD and psychopathy, Loïc believes empathy to be a weakness and is "against the law of nature".
"A wolf doesn't feel any empathy for a sheep, because you need to eat."
But he believes someone doesn't need empathy to make a choice to help or not to harm, and that "even people with empathy can harm".
"People very often see empathy as morality, and they say, 'Oh, if you want to act in a good way, you need to have empathy'. No", he said.
"Morality ... I think this is something that can keep you from greatness or your full potential."
We think of cannibals, serial killers … but most of us never kill anyone.
Since his diagnosis three years ago, Loïc has been speaking publicly about his personality traits to dispel some of the myths surrounding psychopathy.
"It's not being evil ..." he said.
"We think of cannibals, serial killers…but most of us never kill anyone."
Seeking the ‘wrong'
Zac Jones, 31, doesn't have ASPD but also experienced behavioural problems from a young age after being bullied and experiencing "somewhat of a volatile home environment".
He says his outlook was affected by one of his schoolteachers once referring to him as a "bad egg".
"When you hear from an adult, ‘you're bad'. [You think] ‘oh, okay, that makes sense.' And then I wanted to explore what it means to ‘be bad'."
"I would be destructive, I would graffiti, I would steal, I would skip class; I would actively seek out things that I knew — or thought to be — wrong."
Zac says he was an "intravenous drug user" when he was 16, and by 21, drugs, alcohol and risk-taking were a regular part of his life.
In 2017, he was driving in Melbourne under the influence of drugs and alcohol with four friends in the car. He ran a red light and crashed into a nursing home. All four passengers were seriously injured.
"In that moment, I realised that there was no ‘sorries'," he said.
"All I was left with was the reality of what I'd done."
Subsequently, Zac spent two-and-a-half years in prison, which he believes saved him.
"Having to sit with the guilt and the shame of what I had done ... I had a moment where I was going to take my own life."
"But the realisation that I had was I wasn't dead yet, and that didn't have to be my story."
Zac now believes he is rehabilitated and works with young people to try keep them out of trouble.
'I decided that people can be truly evil'
Bernadette Schiller, who survived the 1983 Inland Hotel massacre, does not believe everyone can be rehabilitated.
She was injured when a local delivery driver Douglas Crabbe deliberately drove a truck into the Inland Hotel near Uluru Ayers Rock and killed five people.
"He stepped over friends that were pinned under the truck, laughed and left, didn't try to help anyone," she said.
"After that night, I decided that people can be truly evil. They actually don't show any remorse for what they've done — not genuine remorse."
Crabbe was sentenced to five consecutive terms of life imprisonment for the mass murder. Bernadette has challenged his parole bids multiple times.
"I don't think the community would be safe."
"I think people who have no remorse, they definitely should not be put back into society."
But she believes early intervention could make a difference for some children.
"I think if certain behaviours can be recognised as children to maybe get counselling or help…if that can stop that person from becoming what they become as an adult, then that is a good thing."
Can empathy be taught?
Eva Kimonis is a clinical psychologist and professor at the University of New South Wales. She works with young children with behavioural issues and says research suggests callous and emotional traits can be identified early.
"We've done research that found that we can reliably measure callous and emotional traits from age two or three.
"I think if we can address the problem when empathy is developing and it's starting to go the wrong way, then I think yes, we can teach empathy."
Dr Darjee says people can be motivated to change their behaviour for reasons beyond emotional consequences.
"If someone's fundamentally callous and lacking empathy, it's probably unlikely you're going to be able to teach that person or change them," he said.
"But what you can do with someone who's psychopathic is you can get them - for their own selfish reasons - to decide they want to aim for something that isn't screwing other people over."
'Doing the good things'
With therapy, Loïc has also been on his own journey to change his behaviour.
"You can act without empathy and do the good things," he said.
"Maybe I cannot feel empathy, but I can stop my car on the road and I can help a beautiful woman maybe to change the tyre ... You don't need empathy to do that."

What the case of a slain Australian reveals about accountability for 'mistakes'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:32:48 UTC
04:32:48 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
"Tragic circumstances" occur in war zones.
But when does an accidental killing become a criminal offence?
In the case of Zomi Frankcom, an Australian killed in a drone strike while delivering humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip in 2024, Israel's military justice system has concluded there is no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct.
It announced this month its decision to close the investigation into the death of Frankcom and six other World Central Kitchen (WCK) colleagues.
Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said there had been no intention to attack the aid workers and a "reasonable mistake" was made.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"There are tragic circumstances in a war zone and we're very sorry for the family, but that does not always mean that there's criminal liability," Newman told ABC Radio National.
Two Israel Defense Forces (IDF) officers were removed from their positions over the incident and another three were formally reprimanded.
But Foreign Minister Penny Wong has criticised the decision, noting "there are still many unanswered questions".
This decision falls far short of the accountability we expect.
The Frankcom family and WCK are demanding an independent investigation into the airstrikes, saying "the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct".
The case raises questions about whether Israel's military justice system is capable of delivering fair outcomes when its forces are accused of killing civilians, and where the line lies between a tragic operational error and conduct that warrants criminal investigation.
Michelle Burgis-Kasthala, professor of international law at La Trobe University, says there is "very compelling documentation" from many human rights organisations to suggest a "pattern of impunity" when it comes to the investigation of war crimes in Israel.
Most acts aren't investigated, but when they are, they seem to be quite perfunctory.
"A lot of the time they simply lapse and very rarely do they ever result in any form of criminal investigation, and even less likely [to result in] criminal conviction."
How often are Israeli soldiers prosecuted?
Last year, Action on Armed Violence (AOAV) looked at 52 publicly reported incidents in English-language media between October 2023 and June 2025, in which the Israeli media either reported an investigation was underway, or serious allegations of civilian harm.
The London-based charity found 88 per cent were either still under review or had been closed without any finding of wrongdoing.
So far, according to the cases examined by AOAV, only one case has resulted in a prison sentence against the accused.
IDF reservist soldier Israel Hajabi was convicted on 7 February 2025 for repeatedly beating bound Palestinian detainees with his fists, a baton and an assault rifle at the Sde Teiman military detention centre. Some of these attacks were captured on video.
Hajabi was sentenced to seven months in prison as part of a plea deal, an outcome that the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel says does "not constitute a significant deterrent".
Charges against five soldiers accused of physically abusing a detainee were dropped this year, partly due to "exceptional circumstances". This included the leaking of CCTV footage by then-Military Advocate General (MAG) Yifat Tomer-Yerushalmi, and the fact that the detainee had been released and allowed to return to Gaza.
In general, Burgis-Kasthala says Israelis are very supportive of their soldiers.
There'll actually be a huge amount of domestic pushback if there were quite high sentences issued to any Israeli soldiers.
"It's an extremely delicate situation domestically."
'Appeasing the international community?'
The AOAV found only six of the 52 cases resulted in an admission of error, although the IDF recently acknowledged alleged failures in the killing of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab.
Rajab's case prompted outrage around the world and the movie The Voice of Hind Rajab, featuring recordings of her emergency call, was nominated for an Academy Award this year.
The girl was killed on 29 January 2024 after sitting in a car with six deceased family members for hours. Two Red Crescent paramedics sent to rescue her on a route coordinated with the IDF were bombed on arrival at the scene.
The IDF told Sky News UK in a statement in 2024 that a "preliminary inspection" appeared to show that "IDF forces were not present near the vehicle", but satellite imagery indicated 15 military vehicles were in the neighbourhood.
Burgis-Kasthala says Rajab's case is one of only two cases related to the current Gaza conflict to have moved into a criminal investigation stage, and while it's possible convictions will be secured given they are such high-profile incidents, she has her doubts.
"At best we would expect some very minor type of sentence being issued," she says.
Souheir Edelbi, a lecturer in international criminal law at Western Sydney University and co-convenor of the school of law's Palestine Project, says it's good to hear Israel will investigate but would like to understand how Rajab's case met the threshold for a criminal investigation while Frankcom's did not.
"Have they followed the same process or have there been gaps?
Are they running [it] for the sake of appeasing the international community?
How Israel investigates soldiers
The Israeli system of investigating and prosecuting allegations of international crimes is concentrated in the hands of the MAG.
The MAG decides whether a criminal investigation is opened after the Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM) process conducts "factual assessments".
Approximately 150 incidents since the beginning of the current war have been reviewed through FFAM, with results sent to MAG. Three cases, including Frankcom's, have now been closed by MAG, and two will be examined by the Military Police Criminal Division as part of a criminal investigation.
The IDF says the MAG operates with full independence and is also subject to civilian oversight. Appeals can be lodged with the Israeli attorney general and the Supreme Court.
But German not-for-profit the European Centre for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) has raised concerns of a conflict of interest because the MAG also advises the IDF on the legality of operations.
Israeli not-for-profit organisation Yesh Din believes Israeli authorities have consistently avoided investigating and prosecuting soldiers who commit offences against Palestinians in the West Bank.
A data sheet it released last year looked at 219 complaints involving Israeli soldiers killing Palestinians from 2018 to 2022, before the most recent escalation in the Gaza conflict.
It found 107 investigations were opened and just one resulted in an indictment.
"The odds of a soldier being prosecuted for a complaint involving the killing of a Palestinian in the West Bank are just 0.4 per cent," the report noted.
The one soldier who was prosecuted was convicted of negligent homicide after opening fire on a Palestinian family whose car had been involved in a road accident. He also fired at people who came to the family's aid, killing one person.
The soldier was sentenced to three months of military community service as part of a plea bargain, a result Yesh Din criticised as lenient and said could contribute to a "deadly trigger-happy policy" that has claimed many Palestinian lives.
In a report released last year, the ECCHR highlighted cases prior to the current Gaza conflict where criminal investigations had not been pursued.
This included the killing of Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh on 11 May 2022, who was shot by IDF snipers while standing with a group of five other journalists, all wearing "PRESS" vests. Palestinian militants were initially blamed for the shooting until video footage of the incident was released.
After a preliminary investigation, the IDF acknowledged there was a high possibility she was accidentally hit by IDF gunfire but said it was not possible to "unequivocally determine" the source of the gunfire.
The MAG found there was "no suspicion of a criminal offence that justifies the opening of a Military Police investigation". The documentary Who Killed Shireen? released last year challenged this conclusion after identifying an Israeli soldier it claims was responsible for her death.
Meanwhile, a criminal investigation into the bombing of Jabalia Elementary Girls School, which was being used as a shelter for displaced Palestinians in 2014, remains unresolved more than 10 years after it happened, with no information available on the outcome. The attack killed 17-18 people and injured at least 90 others.
"Israel cannot be viewed as a credible avenue for accountability for these crimes," ECCHR states.
Calls for international accountability
The ECCHR noted that in cases that have attracted international scrutiny, Israeli authorities will at times open investigations in order to create what it describes as "the veneer of a functioning system". It argues these investigations consistently absolve Israeli perpetrators of any wrongdoing.
It says the International Criminal Court (ICC) and third states must intervene to investigate and prosecute crimes committed against Palestinians, which it says have consistently gone unpunished.
Burgis-Kasthala says Australia could consider legal and diplomatic options to achieve justice for Frankcom.
While Australia has placed sanctions on a number of Israeli individuals, Burgis-Kasthala believes more broad-based sanctions may be required, including potentially rethinking the Australia-Israel trade relationship, and Australia's contribution to the F-35 fighter jet supply chain.
The Australian government has previously said it does not supply weapons or ammunition to Israel and the F-35 supply chain is centrally coordinated by Lockheed Martin and the United States government.
We need to actually do something serious if our statements are going to be taken seriously.
Australia is also a member of the ICC, which has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant, alleging they were responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity in relation to the conflict in Gaza.
In recent years, the ICC has come under attack from the US, which has called it "corrupt" and issued sanctions against nine of the court's 18 judges.
Burgis-Kasthala says Australia needs to back the ICC's work, including arresting Netanyahu if he visited Australia.
Netanyahu has denied the authority of the ICC and described the order against him — including claims that he used "starvation as a method of warfare" in Gaza — as "absurd and false".
Other experts have suggested Australia could potentially join with the United Kingdom and Canada, whose citizens were also killed in the WCK attack, to launch an MH17-style joint criminal investigation.
In this case, trials were held in a Dutch criminal court without the accused being present, leading to the convictions of three people in 2022.
Questions remain
Wong says unanswered questions remain about why the drone strike that killed Frankcom and her WCK colleagues occurred in a humanitarian fire control zone, and after the brigade commander had been told not to engage the convoy of vehicles.
"Even if the first strike was a catastrophic error, two further strikes followed, each two minutes apart," she told reporters at a press conference earlier this month.
As former Australian defence force chief Mark Binskin concluded in his 2024 report on the deaths, Wong says the strikes were in violation of IDF's standard operating procedures and rules of engagement.
Drone audio has also not been released despite being requested multiple times by the government on behalf of Frankcom's family.
Edelbi says it’s difficult to assess whether a genuine investigation has been conducted because Israel has not released all the evidence and the IDF appears to be relying almost exclusively on the drone operator's interpretation of events.
Questions have also emerged around the state of mind of a senior brigade officer after it surfaced he was a signatory to a letter calling for Gaza aid to be restricted.
Edelbi says this raises further questions around the decision to launch the strikes, and whether the circumstances could give rise to criminal liability.
She says the fact that it has taken more than two years for MAG to make a decision could also be considered an "unjustified delay" that essentially shields the suspects from criminal responsibility.
Wong says the Australian government will keep pressing Israel for justice and would consult with Frankcom's family before announcing further steps.
Burgis-Kasthala says if justice is to be achieved in cases like Frankcom's, Australia needs to do more than make statements.
Simply calling this out will not do anything because Israel is used to this.
"It's very good at being able to deflect criticism, and it's learned from past practice that it's a waiting game.
"I think Israel's expecting us to forget.
"It's expecting even Australians to forget Zomi Frankcom's killing."

Joint prayer held in Kyiv to mark International Day of Disappeared
According to Ukrinform, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said this in a Facebook post.
The service was led by Epiphany, Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Ukraine and Primate of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine.
Families of Ukrainian defenders, Dmytro Usov, Secretary of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, Secretariat Head Bohdan Okhrimenko, representatives of the headquarters, military personnel, volunteers, and members of the public joined the joint prayer.
During the service, Epiphany honored all Ukrainians who are missing and thanked everyone working to find and bring Ukrainian citizens back from enemy captivity.
He also expressed unwavering faith that all Ukrainian prisoners would return home.
Representatives of the defenders' families were presented with awards from the Orthodox Church of Ukraine in recognition of their spiritual resilience and dedication.
For her part, a representative of the families thanked Epiphany for his continued attention to the families of Ukrainian defenders, regular meetings, and assistance in addressing their urgent needs. She also highlighted the OCU's consistent support for military personnel.
Following the prayer service, representatives of the Coordination Headquarters met with the families of Ukrainian defenders. The participants discussed pressing issues and further cooperation.
During the meeting, Usov assured the defenders' relatives of comprehensive support from the Coordination Headquarters and emphasized the importance of maintaining regular, direct dialogue with the families.
As noted by the Coordination Headquarters, it is critically important for the families of prisoners of war and missing persons to know that society remembers their loved ones and continues to support them as they wait day after day.

The attack Saturday by Jewish extremists on the village of Qusra was the latest in a yearslong series of violent incidents in which Jews have attacked Palestinian residents, their villages and their fields.
These incidents increased after the formation of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current government and intensified further after the October 7 massacre. Government condemnations are heard from time to time, usually in muted terms, and police sometimes respond with arrests, but these steps have not stopped the trend. The number of indictments filed against Jewish rioters remains marginal despite the toll Palestinians have paid in lives and property.
In most cases, the rioters’ aim is to make life unbearable for Palestinians. Indeed, in recent years several Bedouin communities have abandoned the places where they lived, but established villages also have come under attack. Qusra, in the Nablus district, is one of dozens of such flashpoints.
On Saturday, rioters were documented arriving there in white pickup trucks. They later barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home, threw stones and attacked journalists who came to cover the incident, but no arrests were made.
Despite the broad spread of violent incidents across the West Bank, the security establishment insists that they are led by only 70 to 100 young people, classified as “individual targets,” who in turn lead about 300 additional youths.
“These are a few dozen people who direct the others where to go,” a security official told ynet.
“They don’t care about anything. Not the State of Israel and not the IDF. They want to create a kingdom. They only want to blur the lines between Area C,” which is under full Israeli control and where the government officially permits settlement, “and Areas B and A. Some of them are already under house arrest orders and some have also been indicted. But there is still a lot of work to do. They are the engine behind the riots,” according to the official.
Nearly all of the confrontations take place in Area B, which is under Israeli security control and Palestinian Authority civil administration, far from agricultural farms but near outposts established deep inside the territory, close to Palestinian villages.
The roughly 300 youths referred to by the security official came to the hilltops in search of meaning and roam the area without being subject to any real authority.
Some of the young people were directed to farms, where there is a responsible adult and a daily routine, but the situation is very different at the outposts. There, they move from one area to another according to instructions from the hard-core group, remain at an outpost until it is evacuated, then repeat the process elsewhere.
“There really is no law there, and everyone does what is right in his own eyes,” an official in the settlement movement explained.
The profile of these young people is familiar. They are usually teenagers who have dropped out of educational frameworks, some of whom had previous run-ins with the law. On the hilltops, they receive a kind of ideological reinforcement for their violent activity, one that convinces them they are acting as pioneers for the sake of Greater Israel.
“What pioneering are you talking about?” said a senior settlement official. “We created a revolution here and they are destroying it. Every time an attack like this happens, there is enormous criticism from the Americans and it gets echoed everywhere. The settlement enterprise is flourishing and they are harming us. Farms are not being established because of them. This is not Jewish.”
Criticism of the rioters within the West Bank settlement community focuses on the damage caused to the settlement enterprise, not to Palestinians.
“The rioters should have been dealt with through the welfare system, because when they are not treated, they find fertile ground on the hilltops of Judea and Samaria (the West Bank),” another figure in the settlement movement said. “All the welfare agencies need to get involved in this with full force. They need to give them help. And those who won’t accept it — send them to the police. Look at the enormous damage they are causing us. Look at what Israel’s great friend Mike Huckabee said.”
At a joint command center established in the Israel Police’s Judea and Samaria District together with the Shin Bet and the IDF, investigators are continuing to examine the Qusra incident from the weekend. Efforts are underway to locate the vehicles and those involved, and security officials believe arrests will be made in the coming days.
Three vehicles were seized at the scene, but they are apparently “mashtubot” — vehicles that have been taken off the road and are no longer registered — so it is unclear how much evidentiary value can be extracted from them.

At least 8 die, more missing, as ferry capsizes off N. Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:16:21 UTC
04:16:21 KST

Breadcrumb
At least 8 die, more missing, as ferry capsizes off Northern Cyprus
A passenger ferry capsized and sank off Northern Cyprus Sunday, killing at least eight people and leaving more than a dozen missing, officials and media reports said, as police took the captain and seven crew members into custody.
Several rescued passengers told local media a blast had gone off at the bow of the ferry before it rolled over, and said the boat had an insufficient supply of life-vests.
The vessel capsized 6.5 kilometres (four miles) off the coast of Cyprus, shortly after leaving a Northern Cyprus port bound for Turkey's mainland.
Images broadcast by Turkish television showed the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its orange hull.
"Some people had to jump without lifebuoys or life jackets," one young man, Efe Multici, told CNN Turk. "It was literally a fight for survival."
The ferry had been carrying a total of 267 people, according to authorities, of which 161 were rescued and taken to hospital and 76 have returned home.
The official Cypriot news agency TAK, however, said 17 were missing.
Captain arrested
Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), said the ship's captain and seven crew members had been arrested.
The TRNC's transport minister Erhan Arikli said the ferry had "completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres (1,686 feet)".
"Efforts to find the missing are continuing tirelessly," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said during a public ceremony. "We hope to receive positive news from these efforts."
The TRNC is dependent on Turkey, and Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on X: "We are providing all necessary assistance to the search and rescue operations."
One rescued passenger who spoke of a blast on board told local TRNC television after he was taken back ashore: "The front part exploded, they tried to turn around. And the side windows blew out. The boat started taking on water."
The man, aged in his 50s and not named, said he spent an hour and a half in the water before being rescued. He said many people had been inside the ferry at the moment started taking on water.
"Those who could, got out," he said, adding that he saw the captain among the first to abandon ship "without organising anything".
Another witness, in his thirties, corroborated reports of an explosion. He said he had reported water leaks to the captain.
"The seats started to float, the captain kept going, and the bow exploded," he said.
Many inside
Many boats, including private ones, were involved in the rescue operation. Turkey's interior ministry said on X that six Turkish navy ships had also been despatched.
"All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services," the TRNC's health ministry said in a statement.
Hospitals in the territory had been alerted, to provide any needed medical attention, it added.
The ferry had departed from the Northern Cyprus port of Kyrenia -- called Girne Kepuveia in Turkish -- heading to the Turkish port of Tasucu.
The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.
Ankara occupied that part of the island in response to an Athens-engineered Greek Cypriot coup seeking union with Greece. The territory is served with regular air and sea links to Turkey.

Covenant is a relatively new player in the arms industry. The company was founded in 2024 and is also active in Israel.
US defence contractor Covenant plans to start producing medium-range missiles near Leipzig from 2027, according to sources, with up to 1,000 missiles a year thought to be possible.
The plans could bring a previously little-known cruise missile into greater focus in Germany. But what is actually known about the new weapon?
A reported range of more than 1,500 kilometres
The missiles are expected to have a range of more than 1,500 kilometres, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
So far, however, few other technical details are known.
According to sources, the missiles are set to cost a few hundred thousand US dollars each, making them significantly cheaper than Tomahawks, which cost around $2 million per missile, depending on the version.
Covenant is also developing a cruise missile called "Anthem," which is seen as the company's flagship project. However, it has not yet been confirmed whether this is the system that is to be produced near Leipzig.
Germany looking to build deep strike capability
Covenant's plans come as Germany addresses a growing need for long-range missiles that are relatively inexpensive and that can be produced in large numbers.
According to reports, Germany's Ministry of Defence has already sent requests for proposals to Covenant as part of plans to build up its deep strike capability.
The company is said to be planning to establish supply chains and production lines in Europe.
Although Covenant is a US company, most of the components are expected to come from Germany and other European countries. For Germany, this could mean less reliance on weapons deliveries from the US.
Who is behind Covenant?
Covenant is a relatively new player in the arms industry. The company was founded in 2024 and is also active in Israel.
The firm is backed by US investor Michael Kaufman, who previously worked for the investment firm Thiel Capital. Its backers are also said to include prominent US technology investors such as Andreessen Horowitz and the Founders Fund.
It remains unclear whether Berlin actually intends to procure Covenant's missiles and how far any talks with the company have progressed.

Roketsan Conducts First Ground Launch of ÇAKIR Cruise Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:07:38 UTC
04:07:38 KST

Roketsan has conducted the first publicly disclosed launch tests of the ÇAKIR cruise missile from a mobile ground-based launcher against land and sea targets.
Roketsan published footage of the launches on its X account.
Roketsan said two missiles were launched in two separate tests, and both hit their respective targets. The company did not disclose the launch ranges, target types or detailed configuration of the launcher.
In 2024, the company conducted launch tests of the ÇAKIR missile from a Bayraktar Akıncı UAV. At the time, the missile struck a surface target at a range of 100 kilometers.
Roketsan unveiled the ÇAKIR family of subsonic cruise missiles in March 2022 as a modular system designed for use from air, naval and ground platforms.
The ÇAKIR cruise missile was developed with a modular architecture that allows it to be adapted for different missions.
In its press release, Roketsan said the missile would be produced in anti-ship, anti-radiation and strike cruise missile variants.
The missile weighs approximately 275 kilograms, rising to 330 kilograms when equipped with a solid-fuel booster for launches from ground platforms. The warhead weighs 70 kilograms.
The stated range of the ÇAKIR exceeds 150 kilometers. Its baseline guidance system combines inertial navigation, jam-resistant satellite navigation and an altimeter. Different versions can be equipped with various types of seeker.
The missile is also equipped with a two-way data link that allows target information to be updated in flight, a decision to be made on conducting a second attack, and the mission to be canceled.
The missile is designed to use terrain masking to approach targets covertly or fly at low altitude over the sea. Roketsan has also stated that multiple missiles can be used in coordinated attacks.
According to Naval News, in July 2023, the CEO of Roketsan said an export agreement for the ÇAKIR had been signed before the missile entered service with the Turkish military but did not identify the customer. Two publicly known customers for the system are Qatar and Indonesia.
Earlier, in late March, Turkey’s SOM-J air-launched cruise missile, developed specifically for the F-35, successfully completed flight testing and entered serial production.
