Where is Gaza headed as Israel, US undergo their election cycles? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
17:35:07 UTC
02:35:07 KST

Gaza is stuck.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would have liked to have reinvaded it in early 2026 (or never to have been forced into a ceasefire with Hamas by the Trump administration in October 2025) and at almost every moment since then.
Hamas wants to limit to symbolic any concessions it makes over its control, but to remain the force behind the curtain so that when all is said and done in five to 10 years time, it remains the decisive power in the Gaza Strip.
Jared Kushner, the lead player in the Trump administration on Middle East and Gaza policy, has wanted since early 2026 for Israel to make gradual and periodic withdrawals to a much narrower security zone within Gaza (from 50 to 60% of the Strip to closer to 15%), to press forward with rebuilding it, and for Hamas to take gradual and periodic steps toward disarming.
In the long run, unless something major changes, Kushner has the upper hand over all sides because at every key moment since October 2025, Trump has backed his plans.
Netanyahu government forced to concede to ISF, Hamas
This has forced Netanyahu to approve the idea of letting an International Stabilization Force (ISF) into Gaza, compelled Hamas to approve the idea of letting a technocratic committee, the NCAG, come into the Strip to take over civil rule issues, and has made the government continue to provide massive amounts of aid to Gaza, through Hamas, even as Jerusalem watches the terror group’s power grow.
True, the ISF and NCAG actually moving into Gaza have been delayed pending Israeli and US elections in October-November.
But when one averages these trends and countertrends together, the result has been that while Netanyahu does not get to invade, neither has Israel had to withdraw much or allow much rebuilding.
This has basically maintained the status quo in place for a year, with Hamas very slowly growing stronger, but with the IDF being able to continue to strike its field commanders, and back in May, two of its military leaders.
Within this framework of a status quo which is inching forward toward the Trump-Kushner vision of the “day dfter” in Gaza, enter the slew of stories about Hamas attack balloons, the Erez crossing opening and then suddenly not opening, talks of overthrowing Hamas with local Gaza gangs, and talks of Hamas getting so strong so soon that the IDF will need to immediately invade Gaza when election season is over.
Israel, Shin Bet maintains ties with Gaza gangs
Some of what is behind these stories is real.
There are local Gaza gangs supported by Israel.
Netanyahu himself confirmed this publicly in 2025 when there were repeated reports of Israeli defense teams working with Gaza gang boss Yaser Abu Shabab.
The Jerusalem Post and other media outlets also confirmed that the Shin Bet was in charge of managing relations with these gangs.
The primary long-term purpose then and now was to build up local opposition to Hamas in Gaza to eventually lead to toppling it from within.
The short-term purpose was to use the militias for various smaller, messy, tactical missions to avoid the risk of Israeli security officials getting stuck in one type of quagmire or another.
Over the weekend, Haaretz revealed that the IDF has also been heavily involved in managing the local Gaza gangs, and that their number has expanded to six, covering nearly every major region in Gaza.
The Post got clear indications from IDF sources that while the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) is the lead Israeli player with the gangs, the military is also often involved.
This makes sense since the Shin Bet is small compared to the IDF and usually has highly trained specialists accomplishing a mission in Gaza, but accompanied by IDF forces.
Local gangs contribute, but are not primary drivers of toppling Hamas
In any event, political leaks suggesting that the local gangs have any chance of taking over Gaza from Hamas in the near or medium term are divorced from reality.
Each of these groups can only survive now with clear IDF protection and can only confront Hamas for small and limited operations.
If their numbers range between the dozens and a couple of hundred, Hamas still has thousands or more foot soldiers.
Put differently, these local gangs might contribute long-term to the fall of Hamas, but they will not be a central component of that fall.
Rather, most experts agree that either some arm of the Palestinian Authority or a hybrid of the PA, Egypt, the ISF, and some outside IDF support would be needed to overcome Hamas for the long-term.
There is also some truth in reports that Hamas is making a comeback.
Israel has made zero attempt to replace Hamas politically over the last three years, or since the October 2025 ceasefire.
This has allowed Hamas to consolidate its power in the 40 to 50% of Gaza that it governs, which contains well over 90% of the Palestinian population.
Hamas even experimented with sending balloons over the border recently to test Israel’s patience.
Israel responded by increasing the number of airstrikes against mid-level Hamas officials and Hamas weapons depots.
As such, Netanyahu and some IDF sources, mostly from the Southern Command, have been pushing for even stronger responses, including a potential invasion after election season.
They also said this could be a sign that Hamas could undertake some major offensive move.
What move? Hamas cannot even hold training exercises in public. The October 7 “surprise” came in an atmosphere when Hamas was holding constant massive military exercises, which the IDF disregarded as “just for training.” Hamas could not move a large group of soldiers now out of its territory far past the IDF’s first outposts within Gaza. At most, Hamas could possibly surprise a few outposts, but it would certainly not get into Israeli territory. And it has no rockets left, or almost none. Even the balloons they sent over the border fence this time were not fire or explosive balloons as in 2018, but just balloons.
Trump holds the cards, wants 'quiet' in the Middle East
And what Israeli invasion?
There are no signs that Trump would permit Israel to start a new invasion.
He wants quiet in the Middle East and to advance normalization deals – and none of that has happened for him whenever fighting has escalated.
In addition, the polls currently show that Gadi Eisenkot has a real chance to become the next prime minister.
There are no signs that Eisenkot would push as hard to invade Gaza as Netanyahu did, given that the former IDF chief was the first in the war cabinet to want to end the war to get the Israeli hostages back, as early as early 2024.
It has only been Trump’s deference to Netanyahu’s electoral needs that has slowed his pressure on the prime minister to move forward with allowing the ISF into Gaza as a fact, and not just a theory.
But that deference may fade as Trump may be seeking a photo op of ISF forces and NCAG technocrats actually entering and operating in Gaza before the US midterm elections.
In some scenarios, Trump could twist Netanyahu’s arm if they meet at the United Nations in New York in September; and in other scenarios he could allow Netanyahu to wait to approve the progress until the week between Israeli elections on October 27 and US elections on November 3.
All of these tangled election calculations explain the latest bizarre policy double-take this week when the Israeli National Security Council, which works for Netanyahu, told the IDF to carry out all necessary security measures to get ready to open the Erez Crossing, but then hours later, after he saw he was taking some political flak for the move, the prime minister pretended he was against the idea and stalled it.
To be clear, there had been a plan to open the crossing based on a deal with Kushner.
But without Trump going public about it, Netanyahu has now delayed implementing the deal to try to avoid paying an electoral political price for it.
Hamas could try a surprising offensive move. The local Gaza gangs could escalate against Hamas.
But most likely, other than some possible additional mild steps of progress toward the Kushner-Trump vision, the status quo will remain in Gaza at least until October 27.
After that, Trump will likely press either Netanyahu or Eisenkot to make further concessions in Gaza provided Hamas makes its own symbolic concessions.
Until then, the Palestinian people will continue to suffer under the status quo in which they have food but no proper housing or even the beginning of a horizon for a future; and Israel’s reputation in the world will continue to suffer as it will not get any credit for refraining from invading Gaza until the Strip starts getting rebuilt. This also likely means that concerns about major Hamas moves before November, and even for a while after that, are likely misplaced.

The heads of the US armed forces jointly warned US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against continuing operations in Iran, The Washington Post reported on Sunday.
According to people familiar with the matter, the heads of the army, navy, and air force, along with the commanders who head the US military’s operations in Europe, Asia, and Latin America, warned Hegseth that continuing the war in Iran risks weakening their ability to confront threats elsewhere around the world.
The warnings were detailed in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB), which is classified. The people with knowledge spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The SDOB details the worldwide availability of the US’s military assets, such as warships, aircraft, personnel, and weapons systems. It also reflects the president’s priorities for the armed forces, which the defense secretary and the branches of the military carry out.
US military heads disagree with Hegseth orders to keep troops in Middle East until 2027, still will carry it out
The orders book reportedly stated some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain there through September, while others would remain in the region until 2027, sources familiar with the matter said.
The Washington Post reported that the navy’s top admiral, along with the leaders from America’s European Command, Pacific Command, and the Southern Command, responded with “non-concur,” which means that they do not agree with Hegseth’s order, but will execute it regardless.
Leaders from the US Army and Air Force both noted that the extension of their forces comes with significant risks.
One person familiar with the matter said that US military leadership believes that the war in Iran has been “too much for too long.”
“Decisions regarding the scope and duration of specific force commitments to any Combatant Command are made based on the current threat assessment, strategic priorities established by the President, and the advice of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Combatant Commanders,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to the Washington Post.
He added that the Pentagon “does not discuss internal operational processes,” such as the SDOB, “or specific concurrences, non-concurrences, or risk assessments provided by the Services or Combatant Commands during force allocation deliberations.”

Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
Iraq is committed to a full withdrawal of US-led coalition forces by the end of September, UK-based Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat reported on Saturday, citing an Iraqi official.
US forces have been in the country for 23 years since the 2003 invasion and subsequent smaller-scale operations against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS).
Reports that US and other foreign troops could remain after September “contradict what was agreed upon between the previous Iraqi government and the US administration,” Asharq Al-Awsat cited the official as saying.
The comments followed media reports suggesting that Washington was only planning a drawdown, rather than a full withdraw by the end of the September deadline.

US President Donald Trump has previously backed reducing the US military presence in Iraq, reaffirming a withdrawal plan originally agreed in 2024 under the Biden administration. During a meeting with al-Zaidi this summer, Trump said the two countries were developing a relationship “where we don’t need the military” in Iraq.
Washington’s presence in the region has taken a significant hit during the Iran war, as Tehran has damaged or outright destroyed key US radar, communications, and other military infrastructure at bases in Gulf nations.
During the conflict, US military infrastructure in the region also faced attacks by pro-Iranian armed groups in Iraq operating outside Baghdad’s direct control.
The Pentagon is now considering whether to reduce the US military footprint in the Gulf after the Iran war ends, The Washington Post reported earlier in August, citing anonymous officials.
US allies in the Gulf have also reportedly expressed frustration over what they see as a lack of proper consultation before the US-Israeli attack on Iran, which led to bases on their territories being targeted. Regional powers have since moved to diversify their security partnerships, with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, already dubbed by commentators an ‘Islamic NATO,’ early this month.

NASA has launched the new Roman space telescope to study dark matter and exoplanets
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:28:10 EEST
02:28:10 KST

NASA has launched the new Roman space telescope to study dark matter and exoplanets
Kyiv • UNN
The Nancy Grace Roman Telescope will study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets. NASA plans to release the first images in early 2027.
NASA launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket. It will study dark matter, dark energy and exoplanets, and the telescope is expected to transmit its first images of the Universe in early 2027. This is reported on NASA's website, writes UNN.
The mission was launched at 7:26 a.m. Eastern Time on Sunday from Launch Complex 39A at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida
It is noted that the Roman telescope combines a wide field of view with sharp infrared vision, allowing it to survey vast areas of the sky and "delve deeply into the history of space." They added that the mission will help astronomers study dark matter, dark energy and worlds beyond the Solar System—exoplanets.
Roman is exactly the kind of success story we want to see across NASA. This mission, delivered ahead of schedule and within budget, is the result of more than a decade of dedicated work by NASA employees and our industry partners
The ground control team at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, began receiving telemetry data from the Roman telescope seven minutes after launch.
The Falcon Heavy rocket performed as expected and separated from the observatory at the 31st minute of flight. After separating from the central core, the rocket boosters safely returned to the spaceport for maintenance.
It is reported that the Roman mission team also confirmed the successful deployment of the observatory's lower instrument sun shield (LISS) and solar panels. Over the next few days, Roman's high-sensitivity antenna and deployable aperture cover will be deployed, ground controllers will begin the first of two midcourse trajectory corrections, and the coronagraph will also be switched on.
Several weeks after the journey begins, Roman's primary instrument—the Wide Field Instrument—will become operational. The 300-megapixel infrared camera has 18 4K detectors that collect photons of light, which will then be converted into sharp cosmic panoramas.
During the remainder of the telescope's three-month commissioning period, scientists will conduct a series of instrument calibrations and tests.
NASA plans to release the first images from the Roman telescope in early 2027.
Every day, the space telescope will transmit 1.4 terabytes of data, which is currently the highest data transmission rate among all of the administration's astrophysics missions.
Roman is the fourth major mission that NASA has launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket.

September to begin with unsettled weather across Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:26:03 EEST
02:26:03 KST

September will begin with unsettled weather across Finland, with rain expected somewhere in the country each day and weekly totals exceeding 50 millimetres in parts of Lapland, according to a forecast from Foreca.
South-westerly airflows from the Atlantic will continue to shape conditions as Finland remains within a broad area of low pressure.
Foreca expects successive rain bands and low-pressure systems to cross the country during the first week of September. The pattern will also produce dry periods and sunshine between showers.
Lapland is forecast to receive the most rain during the week. Accumulations there are expected to reach more than 50 millimetres in some areas.
Western Finland is forecast to receive around 20 to 30 millimetres. The lowest totals are expected in south-eastern Finland and areas close to the eastern border, where less than 10 millimetres is forecast for the week.
Monday will bring extensive cloud cover. A scattered area of rain will move north from southern Finland into central parts of the country, while showers are also expected across northern areas.
Daytime temperatures will range mainly from 15°C to 19°C.
The rain band will move towards northern Finland on Tuesday. Southern and central areas will see changing cloud cover and local showers. Foreca also forecasts a risk of thunderstorms in south-western Finland.
Temperatures on Tuesday are expected to remain between 15°C and 20°C across most of the country.
Wednesday and Thursday are forecast to bring the best prospects for sunshine during the week. Scattered showers will remain possible across Finland, though rainfall is expected to become less widespread than during the first part of the week.
Northern Lapland will remain cloudier. Temperatures across most areas will reach between 15°C and 20°C, while northern Lapland is expected to record 10°C to 15°C.
Conditions are forecast to change again towards the end of the week as another low-pressure system approaches Finland.
Rain and showers will become more widespread while temperatures fall. Southern and central Finland are forecast to record daytime temperatures of around 10°C to 17°C. Temperatures in Lapland are expected to fall to between 5°C and 10°C.
Foreca meteorologist Joanna Rinne said the changing conditions continue the weather pattern seen during Finland’s summer, when south-westerly airflows brought repeated periods of rain.

Senior US military commanders have warned Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that the continuing war against Iran is “unsustainable” and threatens the country’s ability to respond to global crises and defend the homeland, The Washington Post reported.
The warnings appeared in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book, a classified internal document used to direct military movements.
People familiar with the assessment said the latest edition requires certain personnel currently in the Middle East to remain there through September, while other units have been ordered to continue their deployments into 2027.
The heads of the army, navy and air force, along with four-star commanders responsible for operations in Europe, Asia and Latin America, characterised the six-month war as “too much for too long”.
The leaders of US European Command, US Indo-Pacific Command and US Southern Command, as well as the Navy’s top admiral, formally registered their “non-concurrence” with orders extending the deployment of their forces in the Middle East.
Although the move signals formal disagreement with the defence secretary’s directive, the commanders confirmed that they would still carry out the mission.
The report said the reassignment of ships and surveillance aircraft to US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, had reduced the military’s capacity for training and homeland defence.
The navy has reportedly stretched its resources to meet wartime demands, raising concerns that insufficient ship maintenance could result in fleet shortages if other conflicts emerge.
Although the Army and Air Force leadership formally concurred with the deployment extensions, they warned that the decision carried “significant risk”.
More than 50,000 US troops are currently stationed in the region.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to discuss the orders book or specific internal disagreements.
He said force allocation decisions were based on “strategic priorities established by the president and the advice of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Combatant Commanders”.
It remains unclear when the overstretched units will be allowed to return to their original areas of operation.

Venezuela’s interim president addresses US oil deal
Venezuela maintains control over its oil resources under a new agreement with the US granting Washington significant access to the country’s proven crude reserves, acting President Delcy Rodriguez said on Saturday.
US President Donald Trump claimed earlier in the week that Washington had secured “majority” control of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves “at no cost to the American Taxpayer.” In a post on Truth Social, he declared the transaction “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY,” claiming that it “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves.”
The “historic” 25-year deal with Washington provides for the development of 17 strategic oil fields holding 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven crude reserves and aims to revive the Latin American country’s energy industry, Rodriguez said in a televised address.
“Something must be made absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources while using capital, technology and operational capacity to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions,” the acting president stressed.
According to the latest US Energy Information Administration data, the US has around 46 billion barrels of proved crude oil and lease condensate reserves. Adding Venezuela’s 65 billion barrels would put more than 111 billion barrels of oil under some form of US control, although the Venezuelan crude would not technically be counted as part of US domestic reserves.
The oil deal marks the latest expansion of US control over the country’s vast oil wealth following the January 3 military raid that abducted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him to the US to face federal charges.
Shortly after the operation, Trump vowed that Washington would “run” the Latin American country while overseeing a political transition and left open the possibility of further military action if the interim leadership failed to cooperate.
Washington has also announced plans to take “indefinite” control of Venezuelan oil sales and revenues, while Trump has ordered proceeds from Venezuelan crude to be held in US Treasury accounts, subject to US restrictions.
Earlier this week, Bloomberg cited people familiar with the matter as saying that Venezuela is weighing whether to leave the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), of which it has been a founding member for more than six decades.
The latest deal has drawn criticism over Venezuela’s sovereignty, including from some normally pro-Western opposition figures. Former Planning Minister Ricardo Hausmann called it “unconstitutional,” arguing that Rodriguez’s interim government lacks the authority to surrender long-term control of the country’s oil.
Former Vice President and veteran Chavista figure Elias Jaua likewise accused Washington of stripping the nation of its sovereignty and taking control of its natural resources.
Last week, reports said some 31 tons of Venezuelan gold worth around $4 billion and held at the Bank of England could be released for June earthquake reconstruction, potentially under US Treasury control.
Earlier this year, the WSJ, citing US officials, reported that the White House had urged American investors to tap Venezuela’s gold and critical mineral reserves, potentially boosting US supplies and giving Washington leverage over the resource-rich country.

Trump threatens to report journalist Kristen Welker to broadcast regulator
The Federal Communications Commission under Trump has tried to target news outlets for spreading ‘fake’ news.
United States President Donald Trump says he will report a prominent NBC television journalist to the federal agency in charge of regulating broadcast news outlets for “rebuke or punishment”.
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump took issue with Kristen Welker’s characterisation of his endorsements of electoral candidates as having “mixed results” in the primaries leading up to November’s elections.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

“How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given public airwaves?” Trump wrote. He also posted, without any attribution of where he got the data, a chart showing 98 percent of the candidates he endorsed had won their elections.
“Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC,” the Federal Communications Commission, he said.
Welker hosted the 2020 presidential election debate between Trump and former President Joe Biden and currently hosts NBC’s weekly news programme Meet the Press.
‘Crooked networks’
In June, Welker had a one-on-one interview with Trump that ended in a heated exchange as she pressed the Republican president on continuing to claim the Democratic Party had cheated in the 2020 presidential election, in which Biden defeated Trump.
“Your elections are crooked, and you’re crooked, and Meet the Press is crooked and so is ABC and CBS and CNN. You’re one-sided crooked networks,” Trump said shortly before pulling off his microphone and leaving the interview.
Trump, who has long had a tumultuous relationship with those US television news networks, has increasingly threatened to use the FCC to target what he says is false news.
This month, ABC News’s owner, Disney, sued the FCC, saying the agency was conducting an early licence review of eight of the network’s stations, a move that it said was “retaliation” against it. ABC said the FCC was seeking “a media industry too fearful of official reprisal to report the news freely”.
The review followed a row between the network and the FCC after Trump and his wife Melania called on it to fire late-night TV host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he had made about her.
President Trump has also filed several multibillion-dollar civil lawsuits against news outlets alleging defamation. Last year, he filed a $10bn lawsuit against the BBC, which he said unfairly edited a clip of him speaking just before his supporters stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, to make it seem like he had called for violence.
Trump sued The New York Times for $15bn and The Wall Street Journal for $10bn, alleging defamation over reporting on issues such as how he amassed his wealth and his relationship to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. A judge threw out the case against The Wall Street Journal. Trump refiled the case against The New York Times after a judge dismissed the first complaint against the newspaper last year.
Attempts to compel reporters to reveal sources
The warning from Trump also comes as his administration has taken the rare step of using the courts to try to pressure journalists into giving up confidential sources for stories that have pointed out wrongdoing.
This month, The New York Times said agents from the FBI showed up at the home of one of its reporters in February to deliver a subpoena seeking cooperation for an investigation into a story that revealed how a secret US Navy SEALs mission in North Korea had ended up with them opening fire on a North Korean boat.
In July, the US Department of Justice also tried to subpoena three other journalists from the newspaper after they reported on security concerns with the president’s new Air Force One jet. Investigators were seeking phone records of the journalists but withdrew the requests after a federal judge upbraided the tactic in court, saying they were violating the First Amendment, a provision in the US Constitution that protects freedom of the press.
Reporters at The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post have also been subpoenaed in recent months for national security coverage, including for reporting on internal Pentagon warnings about the US-Israel war on Iran.
News media freedom groups like the Committee to Protect Journalists have criticised the Trump administration for targeting critical media. In April, the group Reporters Sans Frontieres, or Reporters Without Borders, said the US has fallen to a “historic low” in its annual global press freedom rankings, dropping from 57th in the world to 64th.

GUIYANG, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and Thai experts have gathered in China's Guizhou Province to explore ways to deepen comprehensive cooperation in the digital industry and artificial intelligence (AI) between the two countries.
The experts were attending the "China-Thailand Digital Economy Cooperation" exchange event, a bilateral forum held on the sidelines of the 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, which ran from Friday to Sunday in Guiyang, the capital city of Guizhou in southwest China.
According to experts at the event, digital industry cooperation between China and Thailand has entered a new stage characterized by full-chain empowerment, diversified business models, deep localization, and systematic upgrading. Digital economy and AI technology cooperation between the two countries has evolved from isolated pilot projects to a more systematic phase.
During the event, a report on China-Thailand digital economy cooperation was released. According to the report, in 2025, the digital economy became Thailand's top investment sector, attracting about 23.95 billion U.S. dollars in investment across 151 projects and securing the leading position among the country's high-tech industries.
Chinese digital investment projects in Thailand surged 42 percent year on year in the first quarter of 2026, with mega-projects rolling out in quick succession, it said.
According to the report, in 2025, bilateral digital trade volume exceeded 110 billion yuan (about 16.35 billion U.S. dollars), growing 22.3 percent year on year -- far outpacing traditional goods trade and becoming the primary driver of China-Thailand economic and trade growth.
Nirinthon Sakdiset, director of the Thailand Board of Investment (BOI) Chengdu Office, said at the event that well-known Chinese companies have already entered a wide range of sectors in Thailand.
Sakdiset noted that Chinese investment projects have grown steadily, with the fastest growth between 2021 and 2025 concentrated in the digital industry, new energy vehicles, and smelting technologies.
Moreover, the report notes that in recent years, China and Thailand have jointly established multiple national-level AI research and development centers, deepening bilateral cooperation in AI research and industrial development.
A joint laboratory established by the two sides focuses on industrial AI, unmanned systems, smart mining, medical AI and low-carbon intelligent technologies. To date, it has implemented over 70 joint technology projects, serving as a core vehicle for technology transfer, joint patent applications, and high-end technical talent development between the two countries.
Experts agreed that cooperation projects are now being implemented across multiple sectors, with China assisting Thailand's digital transformation in new energy vehicles, embodied intelligence, enterprise digitalization and factory automation. AI applications in education, healthcare, smart tourism and smart agriculture are also bringing technological benefits to ordinary Thai citizens.
Soontaree Songserm, senior executive vice president of the Big Data Institute in Thailand, said Thailand and China share a solid foundation for cooperation, with the digital economy providing an important path for establishing an even closer partnership.
Songserm expressed confidence that both countries can build on the existing foundation and deepen partnership to foster closer ties between governments, enterprises, universities, research institutions, and technology sectors on both sides, translating cooperation into more tangible outcomes.
The expo, themed "Token: A New Path to Value of Data Elements," attracted 372 domestic and international companies and over 16,000 registered guests, showcasing new technologies, products and applications in areas including the token economy, computing power, large model innovation and data element circulation.
China's data industry is sustaining its rapid growth momentum, with its scale reaching 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, up 15.7 percent year on year, according to figures released at the expo's opening. ■

NASA launches Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to study dark energy, dark matter
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
01:20:46 CST
02:20:46 KST

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched into space on Sunday, beginning an approximately three-month journey to its final orbit, where it will study dark energy, dark matter and planets beyond the solar system.
The mission lifted off at 7:26 a.m. Eastern Time（1126 GMT）aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
The ground control team at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, began receiving telemetry data from Roman seven minutes after launch.
The Falcon Heavy rocket performed as expected, separating from the observatory 31 minutes into the flight. After separating from the center core, the rocket's boosters safely returned to the launch site for refurbishment, NASA said.
The mission team confirmed the successful deployment of the observatory's solar panels and lower instrument sun shade one hour and 23 minutes after launch.
Within the coming days, Roman's high-gain antenna and visor-like deployable aperture cover will be deployed, ground controllers will initiate the first of two mid-course corrections, and the Coronagraph Instrument will be powered on, according to NASA.
Throughout Roman's three-month commissioning period, scientists will conduct a series of calibrations and tests on its instruments. NASA anticipates releasing Roman's first images by early 2027.
Roman will send back 1.4 terabytes of data every day, the highest data rate of any NASA astrophysics mission so far, according to the agency. Machine learning, artificial intelligence and citizen scientists will help sift through the data and flag significant findings for astronomers to study.
This flagship mission will help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy and worlds outside of our solar system, known as exoplanets. Its surveys will support a broad range of research extending far beyond the mission's main science goals, according to NASA.
"Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity's most profound questions about our cosmic history," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "With its large field of view and fast survey speeds, Roman will usher us into a new era of discovery and make the invisible visible, setting the foundation for humanity's search for life beyond our solar system." ■

China Focus: Mudslide rescue efforts intensify in Xizang as death toll rises to 16, with 546 missing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
01:20:33 CST
02:20:33 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Rescuers are racing against time and the odds in search of survivors after a devastating mudslide, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal, hit the border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
According to a press conference held by the information office of the regional government on Sunday, the disaster, which occurred on Aug. 26, has claimed the lives of 16 and left 546 people missing as of 6 p.m. Saturday.
Despite difficulties such as high-altitude terrain, steep valleys and volatile weather, rescuers are pushing forward into the core disaster area, carrying out road mud removal, search and rescue operations, hazard identification, disinfection and epidemic prevention, as well as clearing and restoring damaged routes.
The conditions at the heart of the rescue area are especially tough. Rescuers there told Xinhua that the site was covered in mud and scattered rocks, with turbulent water currents. The mud was about one meter deep in some places, enough to sink in up to half a person's body, and even in shallower areas, the mud was generally above ankle level. Video footage showed that the Gyirong Port building was reduced to its steel frame.
On Sunday morning, the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command mobilized an epidemic prevention team to the disaster-hit area to carry out environmental disinfection, food and water quality testing, emergency vaccinations, and routine medical rounds for injuries and illnesses.
This relief mission also included psychological support personnel, who will regularly provide psychological counseling for rescuers and the disaster-affected local residents.
So far, a total of 2,141 personnel have joined search and rescue operations, including personnel from the People's Liberation Army, the People's Armed Police Force, and China Anneng. And 269 rescue vehicles and 3,922 sets of rescue equipment have also been dispatched to the front line.
Communications have been restored at the core rescue site, as successful phone calls have been made with rescuers at the port via a newly-built base station on Sunday, according to the regional communications administration.
The first emergency base station adjacent to the border gate of the Gyirong Port was put into operation at 1:30 p.m. on Sunday. Up to now, telecom operators in Xizang have restored one damaged base station and built eight new ones near the port.
Rescuers with China Anneng are carrying out clearing and restoration operations on the damaged road sections, striving to restore the vital access route to Gyirong Port. They had pushed forward 285 meters on Sunday, leaving some 1.25 kilometers to go before reaching the port.
The barrier lake above the Gyirong Port has basically drained, forming a flowing state of the river channel, China's Ministry of Water Resources said Sunday, citing drone footage and panoramic images captured in the morning and reports from emergency response teams.
At the press conference, the regional government also noted that the mudslide was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal.
A glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters, triggering the ice-rock avalanche. The avalanche plunged rapidly to an altitude of around 4,000 meters, scouring the mountainside and developing into a massive debris flow, which surged about 22 kilometers before reaching Gyirong Port at an altitude of around 1,800 meters.
The disaster flattened an area of about 0.7 square kilometers, destroying 27 buildings and related facilities in the port area. ■

REYKJAVIK, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said on Sunday that the current government would not pursue further talks on resuming Iceland's accession to the European Union (EU), after a Saturday referendum saw more voters against the accession negotiations.
During a press conference, she said the outcome of the election will be respected and no further accession negotiations will be entered into during the term of the ruling government.
Polling results published by Icelandic public broadcaster RUV on Sunday showed that 52.8 percent of voters opposed the negotiations, with 47.2 percent in favor. A total of 225,031 votes were cast, with the voter turnout reaching 82.5 percent, RUV reported.
The prime minister said she has exchanged messages with Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, adding that the EU is aware that there is still a desire for a continued strong relationship between Iceland and the EU.
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009. Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a Eurosceptic government took office. However, according to Icelandic parliamentary documents, the European Commission has maintained that the application was never formally withdrawn.
Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir has planned to convene the Foreign Affairs Committee on Aug. 31 to discuss the "next steps". The meeting will discuss whether the membership application will be formally withdrawn, RUV reported. ■

"It has been agreed upon, and final agreement is due to be reached in the next few days with the European Union and our NATO partners," he said.
"It will be a response from Germany, but our partners in the European Union and NATO will not be taken by surprise." REUTERS

Xinhua Headlines: Xi kicks off state visit to Kyrgyzstan, hailing "golden period" of cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
01:20:25 CST
02:20:25 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan step out of the airplane cabin upon arrival in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Aug. 30, 2026. Xi landed in Bishkek on Sunday for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 and a state visit to Kyrgyzstan upon the invitation of President Sadyr Japarov of Kyrgyzstan. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
BISHKEK, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in Bishkek on Sunday for a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026.
The China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation has ushered in a "golden period" of rapid development, Xi said in a written speech delivered upon his arrival.
TIME-HONORED FRIENDSHIP
Noting that China and Kyrgyzstan share a time-honored traditional friendship, Xi said that the majestic Tianshan Mountains stand as witnesses to the millennia of friendly exchanges between their peoples.
Over the 34 years since the establishment of diplomatic relations, the China-Kyrgyzstan relationship has withstood the test of a changing international landscape, maintained sound and stable development throughout, and reached the high level of a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era, Xi said.
In recent years, bilateral trade volume and people-to-people exchanges have reached new highs, Xi said, noting that major projects including the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway have been successfully implemented, and the tangible results of mutually beneficial cooperation have broadly benefited the two peoples.
Xi said that during the visit he will have in-depth exchanges of views with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov on China-Kyrgyzstan relations, cooperation in various fields between the two countries, and international and regional issues of common concern, and draw a new blueprint for building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future.
"I look forward to attending the SCO Bishkek Summit, working with all parties to revisit the 25-year development experience of the SCO, jointly discuss cooperation plans, create the future of the organization, and promote the continuous new development of the SCO," Xi said.
HIGH-QUALITY DEVELOPMENT OF TIES
Ahead of his state visit to Kyrgyzstan and attendance at the SCO summit, Xi on Friday published a signed article titled "Jointly Opening up New Prospects for the High-Quality Development of China-Kyrgyzstan Relations" in the Slovo Kyrgyzstana and the Kabar National News Agency.
Noting that it will be his third visit to this beautiful land, Xi said he looks forward to working with President Japarov to map out a new blueprint for China-Kyrgyzstan relations and make new progress in building an SCO community with a shared future.
Describing the two countries' relations as a "golden model" of good-neighborly friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation, Sheradil Baktygulov, director of the Kyrgyz Institute of World Politics in Bishkek, said high-level exchanges have provided clear strategic guidance for the deepening of bilateral relations and closer coordination between the two countries in international affairs.
In the signed article, Xi said that China and Kyrgyzstan are good neighbors sharing weal and woe, good partners with a shared future, and good friends who help each other succeed.
"When a neighboring country is genuinely happy about your success, that sincerity is truly precious. It reflects President Xi's respect for Kyrgyzstan, its people and the development path they have chosen," said former Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Alikbek Jekshenkulov. Noting the improved understanding between the two peoples, Jekshenkulov said such mutual understanding has kept bilateral friendship enduring and vibrant, allowing it to be passed down from generation to generation.
In February 2025, Xi and Japarov reached important common understandings on further deepening the comprehensive strategic partnership for the new era and building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future defined by good-neighborliness, friendship and shared prosperity. The decision opened a new chapter of bilateral relations.
In the signed article, Xi said China and Kyrgyzstan have complementary economies and immense cooperation potential. Despite sluggish global growth, the two countries' business cooperation has continued to make steady progress.
Tolonbek Abdyrov, professor of economics and vice rector of the International Higher School of Medicine in Kyrgyzstan, said the two countries enjoy enormous potential for cooperation. "Chinese investment has not only enabled Kyrgyzstan to implement a number of major infrastructure, energy and industrial projects, but has also created opportunities to accelerate the country's modernization."
Noting that Xi's signed article provides strong guidance for the sustainable development of bilateral cooperation, Kyrgyz economist Iskender Sharsheev said: "The two sides enjoy enormous potential for cooperation in such fields as the digital economy, green energy, and artificial intelligence."
In the article, Xi also called on the two sides to solidify good-neighborliness and friendship, pursue mutual benefit and win-win results, carry forward the traditional friendship, and practice multilateralism.
Xi said China is ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to steadily advance their multifaceted cooperation, channel the streams of the two peoples' goodwill into the river of the two nations' friendship, and jointly open up new prospects for the high-quality development of China-Kyrgyzstan relations.
On the SCO summit, Xi said China is convinced that with the concerted efforts of all sides, this year's SCO summit will be a crowning success and provide fresh impetus for carrying forward the Shanghai Spirit and building an SCO community with a shared future.
Professor Almazbek Akmataliev, former rector of the Academy of Public Administration under the President of Kyrgyzstan, said in today's international environment, Xi's call for further carrying forward the Shanghai Spirit has become increasingly relevant.
HOPES FOR GREATER COOPERATION
People across Kyrgyzstan see Xi's visit as an important opportunity to deepen political trust, expand mutually beneficial cooperation, and boost people-to-people ties, which will inject new impetus into bilateral relations.
"We are witnessing one of the most meaningful and fruitful periods in the history of Kyrgyz-Chinese relations," said Jekshenkulov. Xi's visit will represent not only another milestone, but also an opportunity to elevate bilateral ties to a new level, he said.
Kanaiym Baktygulova, former Kyrgyz ambassador to China, has witnessed the development of bilateral ties at close range. She said the political wisdom and strategic vision of the two leaders have provided a solid foundation for the growth of bilateral relations and charted a clear course for future cooperation.
Baktygulova said she expected Xi to put forward new proposals for deepening mutual political trust and expanding win-win cooperation.
Noting that Kyrgyzstan is implementing its National Development Program until 2030 and China is advancing the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), Elkinbek Ashirbaev, governor of Kyrgyzstan's Chui region, voiced his hope that Xi's visit will help bring the two countries' development strategies into closer alignment.
For Kyrgyz economist Abdyrov, China's experience in infrastructure, industrial modernization and the clean energy industry is particularly relevant to his country's development needs.
Abdyrov also sees useful lessons in China's approach to long-term development. Strategic planning and consistent industrial policies can offer insights into Kyrgyzstan's pursuit of sustainable growth, he said, adding that the visit could encourage further exchanges on governance.
In recent years, people-to-people and cultural exchanges between China and Kyrgyzstan have continued to deepen and yield tangible results. Zhyldyz Bakashova, director of the State Book Chamber, said she expects Xi's visit to promote further cooperation in book publishing and translation, helping readers in both countries better understand each other's cultures.
The two countries are also working together to study and protect cultural heritage through the China-Kyrgyzstan Belt and Road Joint Laboratory on Cultural Heritage Conservation.
"By studying and protecting cultural heritage together, we have gained a deeper understanding of the histories of both countries," said Aisin Duishanalieva, the laboratory's Kyrgyz director, expecting the leaders' meeting to offer further support to that collaboration.
At a time of heightened global uncertainty, Kyrgyz-China collaboration in the United Nations, the SCO and other multilateral forums has become increasingly valuable, said Baktygulov, highlighting China's support for Kyrgyzstan's successful election in June as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.
Baktygulov said he expects the visit to strengthen bilateral communication and coordination on regional and global affairs, and promote joint efforts to maintain regional stability, enhance dialogue and seek solutions to hotspot issues. ■

The Kremlin has also rejected proposals for a partial aerial ceasefire, while U.S. and Ukrainian officials have explored new approaches to move negotiations forward. Moscow has also rejected other proposals, including an American suggestion to establish a free economic zone in Donbas.

Layan Bsharat and Rania Abushamala
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
Israeli police renewed a raid on the Qalandiya Training Center of the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in occupied East Jerusalem on Sunday, Palestinian authorities said.
The Jerusalem Governorate reported the raid in a brief statement, without giving further details.
The raid came after Israeli forces withdrew from the site two days ago after a four-day incursion, triggering a widespread wave of criticism from Arab nations and the United Nations.
Israeli forces evacuated and seized the center on Tuesday and raised the Israeli flag in its courtyard before withdrawing on Friday. Israeli authorities also installed surveillance cameras inside the center and left figures depicting soldiers in some of its facilities, while municipal work continued, he added.
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir took part in the Aug. 25 raid and said there was “no place” for UNRWA in Jerusalem or Israel.
Established in 1952, the center provides vocational and technical training to hundreds of Palestinian refugees annually.
UNRWA on Saturday condemned the Israeli measures targeting the Qalandiya Training Center, including the raid and what the agency described as unlawful activities inside its buildings.
The agency also reaffirmed its commitment to fully resuming educational activities at the center.
The new raid comes amid mounting Israeli pressure on UNRWA. In October 2024, the Israeli Knesset passed two laws restricting the agency’s operations, including one banning its activities inside Israel, which took effect in early 2025.
In October 2025, the International Court of Justice affirmed Israel’s obligation to respect the inviolability of UN premises, including UNRWA facilities, and not interfere with the agency’s property and assets.
Despite the pressure, the UN General Assembly renewed UNRWA’s mandate for another three years in December 2025, allowing it to continue operating until June 2029.
UNRWA was established by the UN General Assembly in 1949 to provide assistance and protection to Palestinian refugees across its five areas of operation: Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

Serbia on Saturday opened a facility for mass production of humanoid robots in the western city of Sabac, with the government describing it as Europe's first such production base.

The first phase of the project represents an investment of €20 million, while a Robotics Industrial Park planned in the northern city of Indjija will bring the total planned investment to €200 million, the government said in a statement.
Upon completion of the project, annual production capacity is expected to reach 20,000 humanoid robots and robotic dogs for markets across Europe and the world.
Vucic said he hoped more than 5,000 robots would initially be assembled at the facility each year, describing the project as a step into a new technological era for Serbia. He said Serbia must keep pace with leading powers.
The company plans to expand its product range in the country to include unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and advanced batteries, Qin said.
The opening follows Vucic's visit to China in May, when he toured Minth's innovation center in Shanghai and viewed demonstrations of robotic technologies.

But his approval ratings have slid, and at least 10 of Trump's picks have been defeated this cycle, according to a tally compiled by Ballotpedia. They include four US House hopefuls and six candidates for governor, among them conspiracy theorist Mike Lindell in Minnesota.
Billionaire Trump has used American media to his advantage over the years as a provocative real estate developer in New York. But as US president he has since dramatically turned against the press and what he called "fake news."

Relations between Trump and Welker have been under pressure for months. In June, the president abruptly cut short an interview with her following a tense exchange, during which he grew irritated by Welker's questioning, particularly on the war against Iran.
Experts argue the FCC lacks the legal authority to punish broadcasters or reporters for their viewpoints.
According to a 2025 paper by the Yale Journal on Regulation, the US Supreme Court has confirmed that US law "does not grant the FCC the power to ban controversial speech."

Is Germany's Laacher See volcano stirring again? Scientists detect hundreds of deep earthquakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
17:06:15 UTC
02:06:15 KST

The Laacher See volcano last erupted around 13,000 years ago. Now, deep below the Eifel, scientists are reporting signs it remains active.
Earthquakes occur in Germany again and again, but many never notice them.
That's because these tremors occur deep below the ground and often have low frequencies.
But far beneath the surface, something could be stirring. That is the suspicion of researchers who have been monitoring Lake Laach in the Eifel region in western Germany over the last few years.
Between September 2022 and August 2023, they used several monitoring stations to record more than 500 micro-earthquakes beneath the lake - which formed in the crater of a volcano that last erupted around 13,000 years ago.
Germany's most powerful volcano
That last explosion was so powerful that ashfall was carried as far as Sweden and Italy, and experts still call for continuous monitoring of the site today.
Several studies show that there is still activity underground. In October 2025, a renewed increase in seismic activity was reported in the Eastern Eifel, most recently confirmed by a study published in 2019.
Researchers refer to these movements as deep low-frequency earthquakes, or DLF for short. These DLF quakes are seen as a sign that the Laacher See volcano could one day erupt again.
The focus of investigations is Lake Laach in Rhineland-Palatinate, the largest lake in the federal state.
The region is known as the Volcanic Eifel for good reason - the Eastern Eifel alone is home to a volcanic field with around 100 volcanoes.
"DLF earthquakes are regarded worldwide as an indication of the movement of magmatic fluids at great depth," explains Torsten Dahm, head of the Earthquake and Volcano Physics section at the GFZ, referring to a study from 2019. "Under active volcanoes, for example in Iceland, Japan or Kamchatka, such earthquakes can be observed regularly."
According to the study, magmatic fluids appear to accumulate at depths of about 12 to 14 kilometres. Magmatic fluids can be water, oxygen, sulphur compounds or halogens. They are released from molten rock and play a key role in determining how explosively a volcano erupts. Their movement can also trigger earthquakes in the subsurface.
These magmatic fluids could rise from the upper mantle into the Earth's crust. According to the Helmholtz Centre Potsdam GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, they would ascend along the Ochtendung fault zone - evidence that the volcanic system at Lake Laach is still active.
They also indicate that magma chambers exist in the Earth's crust beneath Lake Laach and may be slowly filling.
On the night of 10 October 2025, there was an unusual earthquake swarm with around 92 small microquakes within twelve hours. The strongest quake had a magnitude of just 0.9.
"In total, four spatially confined clusters of such DLF earthquakes have been detected in the Eastern Eifel over the past five years," said lead author Martin Hensch from the Association of State Seismological Services in 2019.
However, researchers do not expect any volcanic activity in the near future. Dating of the magma produced when the volcano last erupted suggests that it may have taken around 30,000 years for the upper magma chamber beneath Lake Laach to fill before the eruption eventually occurred, according to a GFZ statement.
"The ascent of magma into the shallow crust is almost always accompanied by high-frequency earthquake swarms. Such activity has not yet been observed in the Eastern Eifel," said Joachim Ritter from the Geophysical Institute (GPI) at KIT.
"Moreover, there is no evidence of uplift of the Earth's surface, which would have to be clearly detectable in the event of massive magma ascent," adds Dahm.
In addition to the small quakes and, most recently, a so-called earthquake swarm, there are further signs of ongoing CO2 degassing from the mantle.
In 2024, the GFZ carried out RMT measurements at two locations around Lake Laach. At both sites the emission of CO2 gases of magmatic origin was detected. Taken together, all these activities ultimately indicate that underground processes are active.
From September 2022 to August 2023, geologists recorded more than 500 local micro-earthquakes in a study published in 2026. In the process, the rock is hydraulically fractured; the researchers describe this as an example of natural hydraulic fracking.
They also found that there is likely a reservoir structure, such as a possible magma chamber, at a depth of around 12 to 14 kilometres. It extends horizontally over 15 kilometres beneath the active earthquake zone.
Ice Age eruption
During the Ice Age, the volcano in the Eifel erupted. Recent studies have redated the eruption: it is now thought to have occurred 13,084 years ago, around 184 years earlier than previously thought.
The eruption was enormous. Volcanic ash is thought to have risen into the stratosphere and probably reached an altitude of 30 kilometres. Winds are believed to have transported the ash over thousands of kilometres - north as far as Sweden and south as far as northern Italy. Today, its explosive power is estimated to be equivalent to around 500 Hiroshima bombs, according to the website of nearby Maria Laach abbey.
Volcanic ash and pumice formed a seven-metre-thick layer in the Rhine valley. Near the volcano, this layer is thought to be around 60 metres thick. In what is now the Cologne-Bonn region, volcanic ash accumulated to a depth of up to one metre.
It was only after this that Lake Laach formed. The eruption lasted for 10 days, interrupted by several periods of relative calm. Hot gases, which shattered the basement rock and ancient lava flows when they came into contact with groundwater, cleared a path for magma rising from below.
To date the eruption precisely, a research team from the universities of Mainz, Frankfurt and Heidelberg searched for sulphur deposits in various natural climate archives. They found evidence both in an ice core from Greenland and in a stalagmite from a cave in the Westerwald, with the sulphate concentration proving key.
The volcanic rocks produced during the eruption were later used, among other things, as building material in the 19 Century.

Former Assad-era Syrian commander killed in Tartus security raid
Syrian forces killed a former Assad-era commander during a security operation in Safita, east of Tartus, authorities said on Sunday, as the government intensifies its campaign against armed groups it says are linked to remnants of the former Assad regime.
Firas Abdul Karim Hammoud, known as "al-Khal", was the former commander of special forces in the unit once known as the 25th Division, the Syrian Interior Ministry said in a statement.
The ministry said Internal Security forces raided Hammoud’s hideout in the town of Safita in Tartus province after tracking his movements across several areas.
It said Hammoud opened fire on the forces during the operation, prompting officers to return fire, killing him. Authorities said he had also fired at security personnel during an earlier attempt to arrest him three days before the raid.
Hammoud had served as special forces commander in the 25th Division under former president Bashar al-Assad. The unit was later referred to as "Fajr" after the fall of the Assad regime.
The Interior Ministry accused Hammoud of helping lead armed groups linked to former regime forces in Syria’s coastal region, including in Tartus and neighbouring Latakia.
It alleged that he was involved in armed unrest targeting government and security sites, which it said killed members of Syria’s security forces and army and led to the detention of others. Hammoud was also accused of taking part in negotiations over detainees during those incidents.
The ministry further alleged that he was seeking to organise armed groups to target state institutions and civilians, though it did not provide further details about the alleged cells or attacks.
Sunday’s operation comes amid a wider security campaign by Syria’s new authorities against armed groups and figures accused of links to the Assad regime.
Syria’s coastal provinces, particularly Tartus and Latakia, have seen recurring tensions and clashes in recent months, with authorities accusing armed groups described as former-regime remnants of carrying out attacks against security and military personnel.
Damascus says it is pursuing those responsible for attacks on state forces and seeking to bring weapons under the control of official institutions. Critics, however, have warned that sweeping security measures in the predominantly Alawite coastal region risk deepening communal tensions unless arrests and military operations are conducted transparently and with due process.
The security crackdown follows a wave of sectarian killings in the Latakia region in March 2025, when hundreds of civilians, many from the Alawite community, were reported killed amid clashes and retaliatory attacks involving government-aligned forces and armed groups linked to the former regime.

Iceland’s government said Sunday it will respect a referendum in which voters rejected resuming talks on joining the European Union, while pledging to keep close ties with Brussels through existing agreements.
Final results released by public broadcaster RUV showed 52.8% voted No and 47.2% Yes. Turnout was 82.5%, higher than the 80.2% recorded in the 2024 parliamentary elections.
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir welcomed the strong turnout at a news conference in Reykjavik and said her government would honor the result. She added that the narrow margin makes it important to respect both sides.
“We will continue to actively defend Iceland’s interests. I do not see this as a step backwards. If anything, it is a step forward, as it has confirmed the will of most parties in Parliament and the public to continue cooperating with the European Union,” she said, according to RUV.
Frostadottir said the issue of EU membership would not return under the current government and that it would instead focus on strengthening cooperation with the EU under existing agreements by bolstering Iceland’s position within the European Economic Area.
The government did not indicate whether it would formally withdraw Iceland’s 2009 EU membership application after the referendum. "We will consult with Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee on the best way to close this chapter. We are not making any firm decisions on that at this point,” the prime minister said.
Foreign Minister Katrin Gunnarsdottir said EU membership was never the goal in itself, but a means to greater prosperity and economic stability. She asked the Foreign Affairs Committee to meet Monday to review next steps and said Iceland would continue to meet its international commitments, deepen Atlantic cooperation and strengthen national defense.
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009 after its banking system collapsed during the global financial crisis. Accession negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended three years later when a euroskeptic government took office. The talks have remained frozen since then, though Iceland never formally withdrew its application.

Rescuers search for missing workers as Nepal-China death toll nears 800
Specialised search-and-rescue teams join recovery operations in Nepal and China as floodwaters and severe weather hamper search efforts.
Rescuers in Nepal are scrambling to save more than 900 workers believed to be trapped underground at hydropower projects following last week’s devastating floods, the country’s disaster management authority has said.
At least 933 workers are understood to be stuck in tunnels at about six hydropower projects, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Aerial video shows devastation in flood-hit Nepal
- list 2 of 3Photos: Nepal issues alerts as region’s flash flood death toll nears 800
- list 3 of 3Road collapses in Nepal landslide four days after floods
At least 797 people were killed on the border of Nepal and the Chinese territory of Tibet after part of a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas on Wednesday at an altitude of roughly 5,200 metres (17,000 feet) and plunged approximately 1,200 metres (3,900 ft), gathering rock and debris before slamming into the Lhende River in Tibet.
The descent and plunge sent water and debris surging downstream into Nepal, creating a lake across the border that overflowed through the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river corridors, destroying several villages.
About 3,048 people remain missing.
Nepal said on Sunday that at least 781 had been killed on its side of the border, with 2,502 people missing, including 592 foreign nationals. In China, state broadcaster CCTV reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing, including 261 foreigners.
The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change.
Rescue operations have been suspended repeatedly since Friday due to poor weather and fears of fresh flooding.
In Nepal, rescue efforts have increasingly focused on hydropower projects inundated by the floods, including the Upper Trishuli complex, where authorities said on Friday they received information that about 350 people could be trapped inside a tunnel. About 10,000 Nepali troops have been deployed alongside specialist teams from China and India.
Troops and engineers drilled through debris on Sunday towards workers believed trapped in a tunnel at one of the sites in the Himalayan river valley after successfully inserting a pipe into the passage.
Workers who managed to get out described horrifying scenes when the disaster struck.
Surendra Dowluri, 33, from India’s Andhra Pradesh state, said that raging water swamped the Upper Trishuli-1 site, where he was working.
“We heard a very loud sound… and saw that the turbine floor was submerged with slush, and six workers were stuck in that,” Dowluri told the AFP news agency in the Nepali capital, Kathmandu, after his rescue four days into the disaster.
“We managed to rescue five of them, but one person lost his life,” he said, describing how some workers reached higher ground or construction areas out of reach of the torrent.
Specialised teams from India, China, and South Korea have joined the search-and-rescue efforts. Malaysia is also deploying its Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance Search and Rescue Team (SMART) and contributing $1m in recovery assistance.
International funding has begun to arrive, with the European Union promising $2.3m on Friday. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has allocated more than $1m and launched an emergency appeal for $31m.
Burials start
Authorities in Nepal began burying some of the victims on Sunday after taking DNA samples to allow for future identification. Many bodies were carried away by the floodwaters, leaving families unable to locate and identify their relatives. Mass burials for hundreds of unidentified victims are taking place in Nepal’s scenic Chitwan district, known for its forests and rivers.
Distraught families have packed rescue stations and hospitals in search of their missing relatives, while others have faced the grim task of identifying bodies at overflowing morgues.
Survivors were also faced with the daunting prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” resident Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.
“There is nothing left.”

Up to half the price of the product: marketplace commissions and logistics costs have surged in Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:59:30 EEST
01:59:30 KST

Up to half the price of the product: marketplace commissions and logistics costs have surged in Russia
Kyiv • UNN
In Russia, marketplace commissions and logistics costs have exceeded 40% of the product price. Sellers’ profitability has fallen to 5–8%.
Russian marketplaces have sharply increased commissions and logistics costs for sellers. This is reported by UNN , citing data from Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service and Russian market participants.
In the second quarter of 2026, the overall burden on sellers on the largest online marketplaces exceeded 40% of the value of goods, while at Ozon, under certain operating models, it reached approximately 55%.
Details
According to participants in the e-commerce market, in the second quarter of 2026, commissions and basic logistics costs on Ozon averaged 47.8% of the value of goods. By comparison, a year earlier this figure was estimated at 18.6%.
At Wildberries, the overall burden on sellers increased from 31.9% to 42.7%, while at Yandex Market it reached 40.1%, rising by approximately 15 percentage points year-on-year.
At the same time, for Ozon sellers operating under the FBO model, in which goods are stored and processed in the marketplace’s warehouses, costs, according to market participants’ estimates, may already reach approximately 55% of the value of the goods. For Wildberries, the comparable figure is estimated at approximately 42%.
The situation may deteriorate further after another revision of tariffs. Starting August 28, Ozon increased logistics costs for most FBO and FBS routes and also raised its sales commission for a significant share of product categories.
According to marketplace analytics services, the changes affected the vast majority of product categories, while rate increases ranged from approximately 5 to 14 percentage points, depending on the segment.
In addition, starting August 30, Ozon reduced the commission discount for local sales under the FBO model from 6 to 3 percentage points. For a number of regions, including Moscow, the Moscow region, St. Petersburg, and Russia’s Northwest, this discount no longer applies at all.
Wildberries also revised its tariffs over the summer. Following the July changes, the basic commission, according to analysts’ estimates, increased for approximately 90% of the comparable product items. On average, the increase was about 5 percentage points, although under certain operating schemes it was significantly larger.
At the same time, the marketplaces themselves emphasize that the actual burden on each seller varies depending on the product category, operating model, logistics, discounts, and additional services.
In addition to the sales commission, sellers pay for delivery, storage, receipt of goods, returns, acquiring, and other marketplace services.
Sellers’ profitability is falling
Against the backdrop of rising payments to marketplaces, the profitability of Russian sellers is declining sharply.
According to market participants’ estimates, the average profitability of sellers may have fallen over the year from approximately 15% to 5%. Other experts estimate its current level at 5–8% and do not rule out a decline to 3–6% by the end of 2026.
At the same time, the number of active sellers is declining. As of the end of June, approximately 1.1–1.2 million sellers were operating on the three largest Russian marketplaces, 6–14% fewer than a year earlier. The number of new registrations in the first half of the year also fell by approximately one-quarter.
Market participants do not rule out the possibility that, due to further tariff increases, as many as 15–20% of small sellers may leave the marketplaces.
Costs are passed on to buyers
Higher commissions and logistics payments are gradually reflected in product prices as well.
In the second quarter of 2026, consumer prices on Russian marketplaces increased by approximately 1.8% year-on-year, showing noticeable growth for the first time in the past three years.
In some categories, sellers have already raised prices by 5–10%. Market participants forecast that, by the end of the year, price increases for goods on Russia’s largest online marketplaces may amount to 8–15%.
At the same time, the marketplaces themselves are reporting improved financial results. In particular, in the second quarter of 2026, Ozon reported net profit of 10.1 billion rubles, compared with 359 million rubles a year earlier. The company’s revenue increased by 47% to 334.2 billion rubles.

Ukraine’s long-term advantage lies in its ability to adapt quickly to changes on battlefield — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:59:00 UTC
01:59:00 KST

Ukraine’s long-term advantage lies in its ability to adapt quickly to changes on battlefield — expert
This view was expressed by Can Kasapoğlu, a senior research fellow at the Hudson Institute, in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Three features of Ukraine’s defense technological and industrial base have impressed me. First is adaptive velocity. At occupied Ukrainian Sevastopol, Russia reinforced Soviet-inherited marine-mammal defenses against divers yet failed to anticipate robotic naval attack. Eight months after the full-scale invasion, an early USV struck the heart of the Black Sea Fleet. Apart from its warhead, nothing was military-grade: commercial satellite communications, a jet-ski power pack that one can find and buy online, and a simply workshop-built hull. The same logic drove the FPV revolution—recombining components faster than the enemy adapts,” Kasapoğlu noted.
The expert cited Ukraine’s information architecture as the second key advantage, particularly the Delta system, which, he said, was developed directly in the context of war.
“Fusing commercial LEO imagery, tens of thousands of air, land, and maritime sensors, and acoustic warning networks converts data into information superiority. Russia retains advantages in manpower, industry, and authoritarian partners; Ukraine compensates through a higher-quality picture of the battlespace,” Kasapoğlu emphasized.
The expert identified combat data as the third distinctive feature of the Ukrainian defense sector, noting that it has become a strategic asset.
“Secure data rooms and AI infrastructure turn battlefield experience into military-grade datasets and data into defense diplomacy,” the expert stressed.
In his view, after the war, Ukraine must maintain the mechanism of interaction between the front lines and the defense industry, protect the accumulated combat data sets, diversify the supply of components, and develop long-term joint ventures with allies.
“Ukraine’s enduring advantage is not any single drone, but the ecosystem that learns faster than its adversaries,” Kasapoğlu concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, Can Kasapoğlu believes that Ukraine is providing NATO countries with invaluable lessons—ranging from the effective use of low-cost technologies on the battlefield to building national resilience and preparing for protracted wars.
