Israel must give Ethiopian Israelis a real seat at the table - starting at the UN - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:58:23 UTC
01:58:23 KST

For generations, in the highlands of East Africa between the Blue Nile basin and the Red Sea world, Ethiopian Jews observed Shabbat, preserved ancient biblical traditions, prayed toward Jerusalem, dreamed of returning to Zion, and sometimes died attempting to reach it.
During the annual holy day of Sigd, Beta Israel prayed for a return to Zion and renewed its covenant with God and the Torah. In 1862, a Beta Israel group led by the spiritual leader Abba Mahari attempted to reach Jerusalem decades before Theodor Herzl published The Jewish State.
We did not need European Zionism to teach us to long for Jerusalem because Zion lived in our prayers before modern political Zionism acquired a congress, a flag, or a diplomatic office.
Yet now that we have reached the Jewish state, served in its military, joined its religious institutions, and voted for its political parties, we are still too often invited to demonstrate loyalty without being trusted to exercise power.
This history does not mean every Ethiopian Israeli holds the same political beliefs. No community is politically uniform. But it helps explain why many feel a natural affinity with religious Zionism and the Israeli right.
It has to do with a reverence for Jewish tradition, an attachment to Jerusalem, a belief in Jewish sovereignty, a respect for military service, and an understanding that Jewish survival requires strength.
On October 27, Israelis will democratically elect the 120 members of the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Israelis do not vote directly for congressional-style district representatives. They vote for national party lists, and parliamentary seats are distributed proportionally. The parties represent Jewish, Arab, religious, secular, liberal, and conservative constituencies.
A candidate’s position on a party list can therefore determine whether an internal-primary victory produces actual power.
That distinction explains why Ethiopian Israeli Gabi Gebre Worku’s victory matters. Worku entered the Likud’s 2026 primaries alongside ministers and lawmakers. He traveled, organized, addressed party members, and asked voters to judge his work.
In the direct contest for the position reserved for a new immigrant, he defeated six other candidates and received 3,159 votes. He won, but was then placed at No. 43.
That position is outside the Likud’s practical electoral range. Worku competed and prevailed. Leaving him at No. 43 would indicate to Ethiopian Likud members that their participation is welcome, but their democratic decision is expendable.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should use one of his leadership-controlled positions or any remaining lawful mechanism to move Worku up so that he will be situated among the top 23 candidates.
This would not be charity or tokenism; it would respect a candidate who entered the Likud’s democratic process and won.
Another possibility has raised hope. An Israeli publication reported advanced discussions between Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Yaakov, an Ethiopian-Israeli right-wing strategist and Channel 14 panelist, about a possible reserved place on the party’s Knesset list.
Channel 14’s Bezalel Yaakov considers joining Ben-Gvir’s party
No final commitment has been confirmed. Yaakov represents a young, Hebrew-speaking and unapologetically Zionist Ethiopian generation. His inclusion would be encouraging. But hope must not again become a photograph, a campaign slogan, then silence once the final list is submitted.
Ethiopian Israeli representation in the Knesset is important. Nevertheless, none of us has led Israel at the highest levels or headed its mission to the United Nations, a consequential diplomatic appointment.
I have asked why Ethiopian Israelis are rarely invited to speak seriously about Israel, Zionism, or the Jewish future. Why has no qualified Ethiopian Israeli been seriously considered to become Israel’s permanent representative to the United Nations?
During Danny Danon’s first term, from 2015 to 2020, he became the first Israeli elected to chair a principal UN committee, the General Assembly’s Sixth Committee on legal affairs. He began a second term in August 2024, making him the only Israeli to hold the ambassadorship twice. He has represented Israel and deserves recognition for his service.
In September 2025, the UN General Assembly endorsed a declaration on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict by 142 votes to 10. No single envoy alone controls such outcomes, and the UN’s institutional hostility toward Israel long predates Danon’s. 
But that overwhelming margin demonstrates the limits and ineffectiveness of repeating the same strategy with the same political messengers. 
After nearly seven years across two terms, Israel should prepare new leadership not because Danon’s service was worthless, but because forceful rebuttals alone and the current method have not reversed Israel’s diplomatic isolation.
I am not raising this issue only in the abstract. I would be honored and humbled to be considered to lead Israel’s mission to the United Nations.
I am a proud black African; an Ethiopian-born Israeli American Jew; a Modern Orthodox; a right-wing but inclusive educator; a student of the Baron Rabbi Jonathan Sacks; and a specialist in moral diplomacy, conflict resolution, and restorative justice.
I earned a doctorate in educational leadership from Yeshiva University and a master’s degree in community leadership and philanthropy from Hebrew University. I also spent two decades working in New York’s court system and have experience in Israeli and Ethiopian public affairs.
These qualifications do not entitle me to an ambassadorship. They do entitle other Ethiopian Israelis and I with comparable records to serious consideration.
A black Jew at the UN might achieve what others could not
I cannot promise to transform UN voting overnight. No honest diplomat can. But I would bring a broader moral-diplomacy strategy.
This would encompass cultivating relationships with African and other Global South delegations before a crisis erupts; engaging black, Christian, Muslim, and Jewish audiences; and explaining in English, Hebrew, and Amharic that the Jewish return to Israel was never exclusively European.
Imagine a black Ethiopian Jew, a descendant of an ancient East African Jewish community that prayed toward Jerusalem for centuries, addressing the UN General Assembly. That envoy would be more than a symbol. They would be living evidence against the accusation that Israel is a white colonial project.
Gabi Gebre Worku competed and won. Bezalel Yaakov may be approaching an opportunity. Qualified Ethiopian Israelis are prepared to serve and represent Israel internationally, including at the UN.
The writer is an international educator, community activist, and diplomacy expert. He has served in New York City as an Investigation Officer for the Supreme and Family Court, and represented the Israeli Knesset in international public affairs.

Finland, Israel quietly extend defense agreement for 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:57:55 UTC
01:57:55 KST

Finland and Israel have extended a memorandum of understanding (MoU) for defense cooperation over the next decade that will include research and development (R&D), cooperation, and procurement of defense equipment.
Finland’s public broadcaster YLE reported that the MoU was approved by Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen in early 2024, despite strong criticism due to the ongoing war in Gaza. The agreement, set to last until 2034, was not made public until the report by YLE.
According to the report, the MoU was drawn up in 2013, but with its validity about to expire, Helsinki proposed to Israel that the protocol be extended in early 2024. Finland proposed extending the agreement to 10 years rather than the previous five years, which Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram, director general of Israel’s Defense Ministry, agreed to.
“On behalf of the IMoD, I hereby accept the extension of the MoU in the form suggested by the Finnish side, for 10 more years. We appreciate our fruitful cooperation and wish for mutual projects and activities,” read a letter sent by the IMoD to YLE.
Major Israeli companies already have subsidiaries in Finland, as well as significant cooperation with local Finnish firms.
Defense & Tech understands that while Finnish purchases from Israeli defense industries may have been just a few million dollars a few years ago, they currently total hundreds of millions of dollars a year and are continuing to rise.
The largest single acquisition was the David’s Sling air defense system, purchased in 2023 for €316 million. Rafael also provided the Finnish Army with Spike anti-tank missiles in 2022 for €213m. The third largest purchase was the Gabriel anti-ship missiles bought by the navy in 2018, priced at €162m.
There are currently some 20 defense projects ongoing between the two countries.
The MoU was likely signed during the visit of the Commander of the Finnish Defense Forces, General Janne Jaakkola, who visited Israel from August 3-6th. According to a press release by the Finnish armed forces, Jaakkola and his Israeli counterparts discussed the evolving security environment as well as multi-layed air defenses.
“We are moving towards a capability using which Finland will no longer rely on single, point-by-point solutions, but, instead, build a multilayered, networked and scaled air defense system. The aim is to be able to respond to both rapid and wide-scale air and missile threats” Jaakkola was quoted as saying.
The signing of the extension was strongly criticized by the opposition, with Green League chair Sofia Virta quoted by the Helsinki Times as calling it a “historic shame.”
“When we demanded pressure on Israel, the government tightened cooperation. When we demanded that dependencies on Israel be reduced, the government deepened them,” Virta said in a party statement.
Häkkänen was quoted by YLE as defending the extension of the MoU as standard practice, saying that it was “not some dramatic new policy” as it was part of the implementation of existing air-defense and procurement agreements.
Close cooperation
As part of the MoU, the countries agreed on the establishment of a joint coordination group for Finland and Israel, which meets once a year to discuss bilateral defense ties
In May, Defense Ministry’s International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT) led a delegation of 32 Israeli defense companies to the second Finnish-Israeli Defense Industry Seminar.
The delegation to the seminar was held in the capital, Helsinki, and led by SIBAT Director Brig.-Gen. (res.) Yair Kulas.
It spanned the full spectrum of Israel's defense industry, specialized across a wide range of domains, with particular focus on air defense, unmanned aerial systems (UAS) and counter-UAS technologies, and border protection, alongside autonomous systems, advanced munitions, C2 and communications, electro-optical solutions, HLS, and cyber intelligence.
It included seven new defense tech start-ups under the ministry’s Directorate of Defense Research and Development (DDR&D)’s Mafat for Start-ups (MFS) program, along with larger defense companies, such as Israel Aerospace Industries, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Elbit Systems Tomer, UVision, Xtend, TSG, and Aeronautics.
Some 30 Finnish defense companies also attended the seminar, which was co-organized with the Finnish Ministry of Defense and the Finnish Defense and Aerospace Industries Association (PIA). 
Finland’s deputy chief of staff, the head of its defense procurement administration, and its chair of the defense industry association, Tuija Karanko, also attended the seminar.
Following the event, an IMoD official told D&T that the biggest interest at the seminar was air defense and counter-UAS technology.
“Markets are important,” the IMoD official said. “Finland gives us a gateway into NATO and the broader European market, including potential manufacturers who are up to NATO standards.”
Finland, which recently joined NATO, is facing a menacing Russian neighbor and has suffered drone incursions both from Ukraine and Russia. The country shares 1,340 kilometers of border with Russia and is considered a key northern flank against Moscow.

Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’

Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’
Tech giant says name to remain Lake Ontario for Canadian users, change reflects decision by US government agency.
Google has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on its maps in the United States after an order by US President Donald Trump to rename the body of water as trade tensions escalate with Canada.
The tech giant said in a statement on Saturday that the name of the lake will be updated for US users but still appear as Lake Ontario in Canada. People outside the US and Canada will see both names.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3With the US and Canada locked in a trade war, fears of a recession lurk
- list 2 of 3Ontario’s Doug Ford prods Trump with sign rejecting ‘Lake America’ name
- list 3 of 3Canada unveils huge new Lake Ontario sign in snub to Trump
Google said the decision reflects the change made by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).
“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” the company added.
Users in the US started reporting the update on Sunday.
Google followed a similar policy when Trump unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America last year.
Apple Maps, which abided by Trump’s name change for the Gulf of Mexico, still shows the lake as Lake Ontario for users in the US as of Sunday.
The Trump administration on Thursday renamed the lake, which sits between the Canadian province of Ontario and the US state of New York, as a slight to Canada.
The US president had threatened to change the name of the lake as a retaliatory measure against Canada. Earlier this month, Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian products after the two countries failed to reach a trade agreement. Canada retaliated with similar levies.
On Wednesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney invoked the Indigenous roots of the name Ontario.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,'” he wrote in a social media post. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”
Carney added that while the US is changing its trade relationships, foreign policy and names of its bodies of water, “naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Over the past few days, Trump has shared several social media posts celebrating the name change.
He shared an AI-generated video on Saturday showing a flock of Canadian geese with his blond comb-over hairdo holding machineguns and patrolling “Lake America”. The post ends with the ducks firing their rifles in the air.
Trump’s critics have mocked the policy, arguing that the US is focused on trivial issues instead of tackling real problems that the country is facing, including the rising cost of living.
On Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump’s order to rename the lake “was something out of Saturday Night Live”, a US comedy show created and produced by a Canadian.
“No one’s going to call it Lake America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue to be Lake Ontario,” Ford told the US network ABC News.
The controversy over the name of the lake came after the latest episode in the trade war between the US and Canada.
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has been using tariffs to increase the price of imports from foreign countries as he seeks to remedy what he sees as an unfair imbalance with Washington’s trading partners.
Canada has historically been one of the closest allies of the US. But as the third largest exporter to the US, Canada has become one of the most persistent targets of Trump’s trade wars.
Beyond trade woes, Trump has repeatedly questioned Canada’s status as a sovereign country.
In the first months of his second term, Trump referred to then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau as governor, suggesting he was leading a US state, not an independent country.
Carney succeeded Trudeau in March 2025 with a platform focused on pushing back against Trump and helping Canada adjust to its changing relationship with the US.

Ukraine Tests Four Interceptors to Counter Jet-Powered Geran Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:56:35 UTC
01:56:35 KST

Ukraine has conducted field tests of four interceptor drones designed to counter jet-powered Geran drones.
LB reported on this, citing Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
“The search for ways to counter jet-powered drones is ongoing. There are already four potential interceptors that can shoot down jet-powered Shaheds,” the Minister shared.
According to him, the immediate task is to bring these solutions to the required level as quickly as possible and scale up production to thousands of units.
Recently, it was reported that production of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type kamikaze drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, had surpassed production of Geran-2 strike drones equipped with conventional internal-combustion engines.
This was likely achieved by redirecting part of Russia’s production capacity to manufacturing jet-powered drones.
A substantial and gradual increase in Russia’s use of jet-powered drones began to be recorded in early 2026. By April, 15–20% of the Shaheds Russia launched were equipped with jet engines.
As of early June, Russian forces had launched 1,400 jet-powered UAVs, compared with only 180 such cases recorded by Ukraine’s Defense Forces throughout 2025.
However, since the first weeks of summer, the Defense Forces have recorded a significant increase in Russia’s use of jet-powered Shaheds, substantially increasing the burden on Ukrainian air defense units and aviation.
It was recently reported that the jet-powered Alexa Spatium interceptor had been accepted into service with Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones are among the newest members of this Russian family. Despite sharing the same designation, their designs differ substantially.
The Geran-4 builds on the concept of the Geran-3 jet-powered drone. Its fuselage is optimized for higher-speed flight, and the drone has a more powerful engine.
The drone has a wingspan of about 3 meters and a length of 3.5 meters, matching the previous version’s dimensions. At the same time, its maximum takeoff weight has increased from 350 to 450 kilograms.
The Geran-4 is equipped with a Chinese turbojet engine producing 160 kgf of thrust, twice that of the Chinese Telefly JT80 engine installed on the Geran-3. This has increased its cruising speed from 280-330 to 350-500 km/h and its range from 600 to 850 kilometers.
The drone can fly at altitudes ranging from 100 to 5,000 meters, with an endurance of about 2.5 hours. Its warhead weighs at least 50 kilograms.
The Geran-5 has a fundamentally different design. Its developers abandoned the aerodynamic configuration characteristic of earlier models.
The fuselage shape makes the new aircraft resemble a cruise missile more than a Shahed-type drone with a delta wing. The drone is equipped with a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A jet engine producing 200 kgf of thrust.
The Geran-5 carries a 90-kilogram warhead, while its stated strike range is about 1,000 kilometers.

Iran rebuilds defense-industrial capacity after recent conflicts:  Defense Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:56:03 UTC
01:56:03 KST

Iran rebuilds defense-industrial capacity after recent conflicts: Defense Ministry
TEHRAN — Iran is moving to replenish strategic weapons stocks and expand its defense-industrial capacity following two recent conflicts, with the Ministry of Defense focusing on production resilience, indigenous technology and lessons learned from combat, Defense Ministry spokesman Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik said.
Speaking to IRNA, Talaei-Nik said the government had provided sustained support to the Armed Forces throughout the conflicts. The support covered weapons, ammunition, equipment and other military materiel while efforts were made to maintain essential civilian supplies.
Talaei-Nik said attacks had affected around 25 provinces to varying degrees. He described the confrontation as asymmetric, with Iran facing opponents possessing significantly greater military resources and access to regional logistical and operational support. Despite this disparity, he stated, Iran’s adversaries failed to achieve their objectives.
According to Talaei-Nik, Iran’s pre-war accumulation of strategic stocks of weapons, equipment and ammunition enabled the Armed Forces to sustain operations during the fighting. The consumption of those reserves has now created a requirement for replenishment.
The spokesman also highlighted the resilience of Iran’s defense-industrial supply chain. Around 9,300 companies are involved in the country’s defense-production network, he said, with knowledge-based and private-sector firms accounting for roughly two-thirds of the industrial base in areas including components, raw materials and subsystems.
This distributed production network, Talaei-Nik said, helped maintain output even after some defense facilities were damaged.
He added that production of some weapons, equipment and ammunition had more than doubled between the 12-day war and the subsequent conflict (Ramadan war).
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s defense industry is undergoing a technological expansion, particularly in ballistic and cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). He said that domestic capabilities in several fields have moved beyond reverse engineering towards independent design and production.
The ministry is now rebuilding and expanding its industrial capacity based on operational lessons from the recent conflicts, assessments of future threats and input from scientific and research institutions.
New weapons, equipment, technical capabilities and tactics have also been prepared for potential future contingencies, Talaei-Nik said, although details would remain undisclosed to preserve operational surprise.
He argued that one of the key lessons of the conflicts was a miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries regarding the country’s ability to withstand sustained military and economic pressure.
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s core defense doctrine remains centered on “both integrated and asymmetric defense,” while operational and tactical methods are adjusted in response to changes in the battlefield and regional security environment.
The approach integrated defensive objectives with offensive operational measures intended to prevent an adversary from gaining the initiative, he said. The spokesman also pointed to improvements in Iran’s air-defense capabilities, particularly systems designed to counter advanced UAV threats.
He added that Defense Ministry personnel fatalities during the longer “Ramadan war” were approximately half those recorded during the earlier 12-day conflict, attributing the reduction partly to improved defensive capabilities and lessons learned from previous combat.
Talaei-Nik said foreign demand for Iranian defense products had been increasing before the recent conflicts. However, he stressed that replenishing domestic military stocks is now the priority, with exports dependent on production surpluses.
The spokesman said Iran manufactures more than 1,000 types of weapons, equipment and ammunition and has achieved more than 90% self-sufficiency in defense production, according to the ministry’s assessment.
He also highlighted efforts to lower production costs, stating that some Iranian defense products cost between one and 20 times less to manufacture than comparable foreign systems.
For Iran’s defense establishment, the post-conflict priority is therefore twofold: restoring stocks consumed during combat while using battlefield experience to accelerate technological development, strengthen industrial resilience, and improve operational readiness for future contingencies.

IISc eco-friendly foam moves from lab to market; TOI story drew industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:51:10 UTC
01:51:10 KST

BENGALURU: An eco-friendly bio-based foam developed by researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), is moving from the laboratory towards commercialisation, with Absolute Cold LLP working on its use in cold-chain and temperature-controlled packaging.The foam, developed by Prof Suryasarathi Bose and Prof Subodh Kumar, along with the team comprising Sampath Parasuram, Akshay Sunil Salvi, Supriya H, Sandeep Kumar Singh and Amit Malakar, is an alternative to conventional polyurethane (PU) foam, which is widely used for insulation but is difficult to recycle after use.The IISc material was designed to combine the properties needed for insulation with a more sustainable approach to what happens to the material at the end of its life. The journey from laboratory to industry also had a link to TOI.Bose said a report on the development published by TOI on Nov 11, 2024, helped bring a potential industry partner on board. “Your [TOI] article brought in a potential licensee on board and helped take the technology to market. Absolute Cold director saw your story and reached out to us,” he said.The original IISc work involved making the foam using epoxidised fatty acids derived from non-edible oils and polyphenol-based materials derived from tea leaves.
The researchers also incorporated a chemical structure that allows the material to be reprocessed, rather than simply being discarded after use.Absolute Cold, which works in the cold-chain and temperature-controlled logistics sector, subsequently became interested in the technology. The company is now working towards translating the laboratory material into a product for applications where maintaining temperature during storage and transport is critical.
This could include packaging used to transport pharmaceuticals and other temperature-sensitive products. Such packaging needs to provide insulation while also being lightweight and strong enough to withstand handling and transportation. Its environmental impact after use is an increasing consideration as well.
The move is the latest step in Bose’s broader work on more sustainable polymeric materials. His research has included efforts to find ways of reusing or upcycling plastics that are otherwise difficult to recycle, with the aim of keeping materials in use for longer rather than sending them to waste.For IISc, the foam's progress also shows the less visible part of academic innovation: getting a material developed in a laboratory into a form that industry can manufacture and customers can use. The licensing and scale-up process can require changes to the formulation, manufacturing process and product design even after the underlying research has been demonstrated.The next test, therefore, is whether the foam can be produced at commercial scale while retaining the insulation, strength and durability demonstrated during development. Its performance in actual cold-chain applications will ultimately determine whether the IISc innovation can become a practical alternative to conventional foams.For a material conceived around the problem of what happens to foam after its useful life, that commercial journey is as important as the laboratory breakthrough itself.Also read: IISc-Bengaluru creates eco-friendly packaging foam
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Eight killed and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus
- Published
At least eight people have died and 18 others are still missing after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there has said.
Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus, said the ferry had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia on Sunday.
The ship's captain and seven crew members have been detained as part of an investigation into "how this tragedy occurred", Üstel wrote on social media.
Officials say the vast majority of those on board have been rescued. A search and rescue operation with Turkish authorities is under way.
The boat has now sunk, and the authorities are attempting to recover its black box recorder to establish what happened.
The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 local time (09:30 GMT).
Üstel said the boat had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday, but had been delayed due to poor weather conditions.
He told Turkish media outlet TRT that the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.
While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he told the outlet.
Helicopters and coastguard boats have been dispatched to the scene, while ambulances have been stationed on the beach ready to receive rescued passengers.
Üstel wrote on social media that the "priority right now is human life", adding that security forces, rescue teams and health officials were all on the scene.
He added the disaster will be thoroughly investigated and "even the slightest negligence will be uncovered".
"No one will be spared, regardless of who they are, who is found to be at fault or responsible," Üstel said.
Erhan Arikli, the transport minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media that 100 passengers had been taken to shore.
Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sent his condolences to Turkish Cypriots and said efforts to reach those who were still missing "continue uninterrupted".
"Immediately after the accident, we launched extensive search-and-rescue operations in co-operation with the authorities of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus," he said at a military ceremony on Sunday.
Mustafa Koc saved around 65 people with his boat after the vessel capsized. He told the BBC that he felt the crew should have waited until the sea was calm.
"It wasn't safe for them," he said. "The sea was quite choppy."
Koc added: "People died. It's not right."
He said the boat had arrived in Kyrenia on Saturday and "had some damage in the front".
The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.
Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".
A hotline has been set up to provide passengers' relatives with information. The nationalities of those who were aboard and the status of the injured are unclear.
Local television has broadcast images of the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its hull.
On Sunday evening, Arikli told TRT the ship had completely sunk.
The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.

'Too much, for too long': Senior US military commanders warn against continuing Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:46:21 UTC
01:46:21 KST

Senior commanders in the U.S. military have warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that large-scale operations against Iran cannot be sustained indefinitely, and that continuing to concentrate forces in the Middle East could undermine the U.S. military’s ability to respond to threats elsewhere in the world, including defending the United States itself, The Washington Post reported Sunday, citing officials familiar with a classified assessment prepared for the defense secretary.
The warnings were delivered to Hegseth by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, as well as the commanders of U.S. commands responsible for Europe, Asia and Latin America. They were included in the August 14 edition of the “Secretary of Defense Orders Book,” a classified document detailing the availability of U.S. ships, aircraft, troops and weapons systems around the world, and used by the Pentagon in decisions on force deployments.
The warning comes after about six months of fighting with Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump pressures Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept Washington’s terms for ending the conflict. Trump continues to make clear that all options remain on the table, including renewed strikes, and U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, has for months kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in case the president orders further military action.
According to the report, some of the forces deployed to the Middle East have already been ordered to remain in the region through September, while others are expected to stay into 2027. The Air Force is also preparing for a prolonged presence: According to two officials who saw the document, many of the units sent to the Middle East for bombing missions and around-the-clock operations are expected to remain in the region into 2027.
The possibility that the deployments could be extended again prompted several senior commanders to voice explicit objections. The commanders of U.S. European Command, Indo-Pacific Command and Southern Command, along with the Navy’s top officer, submitted what the Pentagon calls a “non-concur” — meaning they oppose the defense secretary’s decision to extend the allocation of their forces to the campaign, though they would carry out the order if it remains in effect.
The main reason for the opposition is that forces, ships, aircraft and equipment originally intended for operations in Europe, Asia and Latin America were transferred to the Middle East to support the campaign against Iran. According to the officials, that has reduced the commands’ ability to carry out missions and continue the training needed to maintain operational readiness.
One official familiar with the assessment described the overall message from the military leadership as “too much, for too long.” The official said discussions about the risks stemming from force deployments are routine, but this time the picture commanders presented to Hegseth was “bleaker” than usual — and several generals and admirals were especially direct and forceful in opposing the continued transfer of resources to the Middle East, with no clear indication of how or when the campaign will end.
Navy issues particularly stark warning
The most serious situation, according to the report, is in the U.S. Navy. Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations and the Navy’s highest-ranking officer, warned that the force cannot sustain its current level of support for the Iran campaign over the long term — particularly because there is no expected end date.
The Navy has been required to provide dozens of vessels for the campaign: initially for U.S. strikes and defense against Iranian counterattacks, and later to enforce Trump’s blockade of Iranian ports as part of efforts to force Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. As a result, the deployments of several ships and their crews have been extended by months.
Caudle warned Hegseth that only slightly more than a quarter of the U.S. destroyer fleet is now in a condition that allows it to deploy operationally — a sharp decline from the situation before the war. According to the assessment, if demands on the Navy remain at the same level, the impact on ship maintenance could jeopardize fleet availability in the event another conflict breaks out elsewhere in the world.
Caudle has also spoken publicly about the difficulty of extending deployments, saying at a recent event in Norfolk that the situation was “very challenging for sailors.” He said he generally opposes such extensions and “pushes back hard” against them, but added that ultimately “the enemy gets a vote too” on how long operational activity lasts.
The commanders of European Command and Southern Command also warned that the transfer of ships and intelligence and surveillance aircraft to Central Command has already harmed their ability to fulfill missions related to defense of the U.S. homeland. Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of Indo-Pacific Command, objected to the scale of support his command is being asked to continue providing to the campaign, including a carrier strike group and destroyers.
The cost is particularly evident in Asia. The aircraft carrier USS George Washington, permanently based in Japan and a central element in deterring China, was moved to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been on an extended deployment since November and is expected to complete more than 300 days at sea before returning to base.
At the same time, Washington’s allies in the region have expressed concern that the depletion of U.S. missile and interceptor stockpiles will hurt America’s ability to deter China and North Korea in the event of a regional crisis. The impact is no longer theoretical: Last week, the United States canceled an amphibious landing exercise with South Korea planned for September because of the strain the Iran campaign is placing on U.S. forces.
Interceptor, Tomahawk and drone stockpiles depleted
The heads of the Army and Air Force did not oppose the deployment extensions requested by Hegseth, but they too warned of the risks involved. About 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne Division, rushed to the region in March following the outbreak of the war, are expected to remain in the Middle East at least through September, and the Army assesses that their mission could be extended even further. The division is considered a key force in the event of a U.S. ground operation in Iran.
Units operating Patriot air defense systems also are expected to remain in the region beyond the original plan. Interceptor stockpiles for the systems were depleted during the war, after interceptors had already been transferred to Ukraine, and the shortage is limiting the Trump administration’s ability to escalate the fighting again because Iran still retains the capability to strike U.S. bases across the Middle East.
The war has also depleted stocks of THAAD interceptors and long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles. According to The Washington Post, about 25% of the Pentagon’s Reaper drone fleet was lost during the fighting, while U.S. bases in the region sustained billions of dollars in damage. The Trump administration, for its part, says reports of ammunition shortages are inaccurate.
The shortage has already caused tension at the highest levels of the administration. Earlier this month, the Post reported that Trump confronted Hegseth during a meeting at Camp David and demanded explanations for the severe shortage of ammunition and interceptors, which officials say is already limiting U.S. military options against Iran. According to the report, the president expressed frustration that the problem had still not been resolved after believing the Pentagon had already addressed it.
The scale of the fighting illustrates the extraordinary pressure on U.S. stockpiles. According to figures published this month by The Washington Post, between February 28 and April 7 alone, U.S. forces struck more than 13,000 targets in Iran while simultaneously confronting more than 8,500 missiles, drones and other threats launched at them. The Pentagon has since turned to defense manufacturers with demands to dramatically accelerate weapons production, but industry officials have warned that in some cases it will take years to replenish the stockpiles.
Tensions inside the Pentagon over the continuation of the campaign are not new. Even before the fighting began, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine warned the White House that the United States did not have enough munitions — or enough support from its allies — to wage a large-scale, prolonged campaign. This month it was also reported that European Command chief Gen. Alexus Grynkewich warned the Pentagon that he did not have enough naval forces to defend Israel and the United States simultaneously against missile attacks.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the Post that “decisions regarding the scale and duration of force allocations are made in accordance with the latest threat assessment, the priorities set by the president and the advice of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the various combatant commanders.”
“The Pentagon does not publicly discuss internal operational processes or the risk assessments presented by commanders,” he said.
Officials in Washington assess that Tehran is also well aware of the price the campaign is exacting from the United States. According to the Post, Iran’s leadership is aware of the war’s unpopularity among broad segments of the American public, as well as the depletion of the Pentagon’s weapons stockpiles — factors that could strengthen its resolve not to give in at this stage to Washington’s demands.

The Hugging Face deal would crown Nvidia king of AI
Unknown

16:43:49 UTC
01:43:49 KST

Nvidia Corp is not only tightening its grip on artificial intelligence (AI), it is also absorbing the companies fighting to keep the industry open and decentralized. On the same day the chip giant announced quarterly revenue that had doubled and would continue rising next year, sending its shares up 7 percent, news broke that it has reportedly agreed to spend US$13 billion on Hugging Face, a platform for open-weight AI models.
That name might sound familiar. It is the company that OpenAI’s rogue agents controversially breached during a recent security-testing exercise. Hugging Face handled that incident with diplomacy, as you would expect of a company that sits at the center of a broader open-source AI community. Founded by three French entrepreneurs, it hosts one of the world’s biggest collections of open-weight models, or AI systems that could be changed to suit a user’s needs, and it has long promoted the idea that AI development should be open to everyone and not centrally controlled.
So strongly did it believe in that credo that the start-up rejected a US$500 million investment from Nvidia last year that would have valued it at US$7 billion, on the grounds that it did not want a single dominant investor to sway decisions.
“I said it and will say it again: Concentration of power is the biggest risk in AI!” Hugging Face co-CEO Clem Delangue said in 2024.
Today’s apparent change of heart might be down to the higher price — and the fact that Hugging Face was reportedly being circled by other potential acquirers such as Salesforce Inc.
The deal would create a strange paradox. Nvidia wants open models to thrive, but for a more self-interested reason: to stop OpenAI and other large AI companies from threatening its chip business. OpenAI this week announced remarkably strong results for a custom AI chip called Jalapeno, with early tests suggesting it could outperform some of Nvidia’s most advanced versions.
Which makes the relationship between the two AI heavyweights ever more awkward. Nvidia is one of OpenAI’s biggest investors, an arrangement that has led to frequent accusations of “circular financing” on the chip giant’s part, but it also wants to keep the ChatGPT maker in its place. Owning Hugging Face could help it create a counterweight to closed-source AI developers such as OpenAI and Alphabet Inc’s Google, which are building chips to compete with its own. Developers using open models can choose which chips to run them on, and Nvidia wants a chance to sell them its hardware — rather than seeing them steered toward processors made by its competitors.
That helps explain the reported US$13 billion price tag. Hugging Face recently generated about US$150 million in annual revenue, which would mean Nvidia is paying a remarkably high sales multiple (about 86 times annualized revenue) for the start-up. However, Nvidia does not need much in the way of money. It has forecast chip sales to grow 70 percent in the next fiscal year and continues to enjoy gross margins of about 75 percent.
Instead, buying Hugging Face would give Nvidia a new strategic position in AI and greater influence over developers, thanks to the platform’s links to millions of coders at the point where they download and deploy models. That could rev up Nvidia’s cloud ambitions, giving it another way to rent computing power to AI makers.
There is a bigger irony here. Some supporters of Hugging Face, which now has hubs in Paris and New York, have been celebrating the reported sale as a win for European tech. However, it would also represent a sellout, not just for start-ups in Europe, which frequently capitulate to larger Silicon Valley buyers before they get a chance to build their own empires, but also for the open-source AI movement itself.
For all of Hugging Face’s efforts to make AI less centralized, it might help Nvidia protect its dominance. The potential acquirer controls an estimated 70 percent to 90 percent of AI chip sales, a market that Google has struggled to dent with its own processors. And Hugging Face’s famous neutrality would come into question if it provides the world’s dominant chipmaker with a new route to persuading developers to choose its hardware for their models.
However many makers of chatbot technology there may be, the infrastructure underpinning those services is still primarily controlled by one company. And one of the world’s biggest advocates for decentralizing AI power is about to hand Nvidia even more of it.

Deaths related to kidney disease rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:49 UTC
01:43:49 KST

The number of deaths, the mortality rate and the age-standardized mortality rate associated with kidney disease all increased in Taiwan last year, with healthcare providers warning of the growing challenges posed by multimorbidity as people take multiple medications or supplements that might harm their kidneys.
About 10,000 new patients go on dialysis every year, and although Taiwan’s overall age-standardized mortality rate last year was 3.7 percent lower than the previous year, the deaths, mortality rate and age-standardized mortality rate associated with kidney disease all increased, Ministry of Health and Welfare data showed.
Last year, 5,980 deaths were reported as associated with nephritis (kidney inflammation), nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder in which too much protein is released in urine) and nephropathy (kidney disease or damage), for a mortality rate of 25.6 deaths per 100,000 people and an age-standardized mortality rate of 10.6 deaths per 100,000, representing increases of 5.3 percent, 5.6 percent and 1.7 percent respectively from the previous year.
Photo courtesy of Ho Hao-chung
National Cheng Kung University Hospital Department of Internal Medicine deputy director Sung Chun-ming (宋俊明) yesterday said that standardized mortality rates for kidney disease have been rising in Japan and the US, a trend he linked to the increasing complexity of comorbidities among people with chronic kidney disease.
While the incidence and prevalence of dialysis in Taiwan are falling, the age of people on dialysis is rising and their comorbidities are increasing, so many physicians are seeing conditions becoming “increasingly severe,” he said.
“Many people have survived diseases that can be treated, but at the cost of damaging their kidneys,” Sung said.
Medical advances enable the treatment of many previously incurable diseases, but these therapies might impair renal function, he said.
These developments — coupled with an aging population, cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome and other comorbidities — are creating new challenges in Taiwan’s nephrology care, he added.
Kaohsiung Medical University Chung-Ho Memorial Hospital Division of Nephrology attending physician Hwang Shang-jyh (黃尚志) said that as medical care advances, more people are living long enough to develop kidney disease, which might be why kidney disease deaths are increasing.
However, a conclusion cannot be drawn from short-term data on changes in kidney disease mortality rates alone, and a slight increase in the mortality rates does not imply that past prevention and control efforts have failed, he said.
Clinically, patients often have multiple coexisting conditions, such as diabetes, liver cirrhosis, kidney failure and infections, Hwang said, adding that which condition is the primary cause of death can significantly influence statistical outcomes.
Kidney disease mortality rates among middle-aged adults have shown a slight upward trend over the past few years, ministry data showed.
Among people aged 45 to 64, the mortality rate associated with nephritis, nephrotic syndrome and nephropathy has ranged from 9.9 to 10.4 deaths per 100,000 people over the past five years, compared with a low of 9.2 deaths per 100,000 people in 2019.
Metabolic syndrome is occurring at younger ages, and the number of people with early-onset type 2 diabetes has increased, Sung said.
Middle-aged adults have poor adherence to medical advice for controlling the “three highs” — high levels of blood pressure, blood sugar and blood lipids, he said.
Moreover, many people purchase over-the-counter drugs or health supplements without consulting a doctor to “protect their kidneys,” but doing so can instead harm their kidneys, he said.
Public awareness of the importance of controlling the “three highs” should be improved, and the government should crack down on illegal advertisements for medicines and health supplements, and also consider requiring high-risk drugs to carry warning labels reminding people to consult a doctor before taking them, Sung said.
Federation of Taiwan Pharmacists Associations spokesman Huang Yen-ju (黃彥儒) said that as some painkillers can affect blood flow in the kidneys, a person’s medication use and medical history must be carefully evaluated before analgesics are prescribed.
People should also make a habit of asking a pharmacist before taking any new medicine, he said.
People should also not believe the myth that taking supplements will protect their kidneys, avoid purchasing drugs or health products from unknown sources and not take them long-term simply based on a friend’s or family member’s recommendation or online ads.

Vietnamese coffee farmers ride China’s durian wave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:47 UTC
01:43:47 KST

Vietnam’s Central Highlands produces around one-sixth of the world’s coffee, but farmers are switching their traditional crop for durian to cash in on surging Chinese demand for the pungent “king of fruits.”
“You can live okay with coffee, but it’s durian that makes you rich,” farmer Pham Xuan Lan said.
Blessed with a tropical climate and rich basalt soil, the lush Central Highlands produces vast quantities of robusta beans, and Vietnam trails only Brazil in coffee output.
Photo: AF
However, the area dedicated to durian has soared more than fivefold to 200,000 hectares nationwide over the past decade, the Vietnamese Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development said.
Vietnam only officially entered the Chinese durian market after a 2022 trade protocol, but last year became the country’s biggest supplier by volume, ending Thailand’s near two-decade dominance.
Lan was an early adopter, diversifying his crop two decades ago and now boasting 400 durian trees in Ea Knuec commune, part of Dak Lak Province.
They produce 60 tonnes of the sweet yet smelly fruit, which is driven in frozen containers thousands of kilometers north into China.
The 56-year-old expects to make US$76,000 this year — against US$10,000 had he stayed with just coffee.
“With durian, I bought a car, houses for my children and built a villa for my family,” he said, his affluence evident around him.
Other local farmers have followed suit, focusing on the premium Ri6, Musang King and Dona varieties.
During the August-October harvest, Dak Lak’s roads are packed with trucks loaded with the spiky fruit, and at a durian festival this month, 525 vehicles formed what the Guinness World Records declared the largest ever parade of fruit-carrying vehicles.
The boom is driven by demand from China, fueled by a combination of expanding supply and growing popularity on social media, particularly among young people.
On Douyin, China’s equivalent of TikTok, videos of users cracking open fruit with their bare hands have been watched billions of times.
“This tastes really sweet. It’s almost like it’s been coated in sugar,” Douyin influencer Liulianzi said in a clip liked more than 17,000 times.
Once a luxury food, increased competition between Thailand and Vietnam, and improved transport links have helped cut prices and make the fruit more affordable.
At a durian tasting event in Beijing last month, Ada Song said that she had spent almost 1,000 yuan (US$149) on the fruit in the past few weeks.
“I have tried nearly 20 different varieties,” Song said.
Durian “tastes just as sweet as cake, without the greasiness and heaviness,” she said.
China imported almost US$7.5 billion worth of fresh durian last year, a near 12-fold rise from 2015.
Beijing is seeking to boost its homegrown produce, with more than 3,000 hectares of plantations on the southern island province of Hainan, which has a similar climate to northern Vietnam.
However, “our Hainan durians will always be just a supplement to Southeast Asian durians,” said Feng Xuejie (馮學傑), a durian expert at the Hainan Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
“It’s not even a competition,” Feng said.
Vietnam’s durian exports are expected to reach US$4 billion this year, up from US$180 million in 2021 — 90 percent of them going to its northern neighbor.
However, in the Central Highlands there are concerns about the reliance on China, as well as the risks of oversupply as more farmers join the rush.
Many anxiously eyed a recent price crash in Malaysia, blamed on an unusually bumper harvest.
Many farmers there have also switched to durian, focusing on premium varieties and fresh fruit, although the country has only a small slice of the Chinese market.
The Vietnamese government earlier this month warned of the “risks of oversupply and loss of quality control as the planted area is increasing rapidly.”
Farmers warn durian is not a one-way bet, requiring a strict mix of humidity, water and fertilizers.
Lan likened growing it to “raising a child — I can give you all the tricks, but I cannot guarantee you similar success.”
He still grows coffee as his land is leased from a coffee company, allowing him to hedge his bets.
For some, the durian dream has already turned sour.
Hung, a farmer who gave only one name, switched entirely from coffee to durian five years ago, but switched back two years ago, admitting it was too hard to produce the quality required.
“I could not do it. I failed,” the 42-year-old said. “So, I would never go back to durian again.”

Coalition recycles fishing nets to make glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:47 UTC
01:43:47 KST

The Ocean Conservation Administration (OCA) is collaborating with the Marine Debris Recycling Coalition to repurpose marine waste, with plans to provide 2,000 pairs of protective glasses made from recycled seine nets to distant-water fishing crews.
The OCA announced the results of the collaboration at the 5th SDG Asia EXPO last week, highlighting how large purse seine nets collected from domestic fishing operators were recycled into pellets and repurposed to make protective glasses for fishing crews working across the three major oceans.
FCF Co and Ching Fa Fishing Implements Factory Co did the preliminary treatment of the recycled seine nets, which were pelletized by RebornPlas Composites Co and then repurposed into fishing glasses by Hwa Meei Optical Co, OCA Deputy Director-General Shih Yi-che (施義哲) said.
Photo courtesy of FCF Co
The straps were manufactured by Ecomax Textile Co, Shih said, adding the Plastics Industry Development Center assisted with the project’s matchmaking.
All the companies are members of the coalition, he said.
The effort marked a shift in the domestic seafood trading industry from one-way consumption to waste recycling and reuse, OCA Director-General Lu Hsiao-yun (陸曉筠) said.
The project integrates the expertise of coalition members from different fields to repurpose fishing nets into essential protective gear for fishing workers, which aligns with the OCA’s core values: upholding environmental, social and governance principles in marine conservation, she said.
FCF said it would give away 2,000 fishing glasses made from the recycled nets to distant-water fishing crews from next month.
The company would continue to engage in marine conservation projects to help promote ocean sustainability and marine debris repurposing, as well as facilitate the rights and benefits of fishing workers, it said.
In other fishing news, the Fisheries Agency last week reminded people that cannot sell their catch without a fishing license.
The agency imposed a NT$60,000 fine a person who sold fish caught from small private vessels — which are not licensed fishing vessels — through social media platforms.
Article 6 of the Fisheries Act (漁業法) stipulates that recreational fishers who sell their catches would face fines of up to NT$300,000, the agency said.
The definition of “recreational fishing” established in the act aligns with guidelines set by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, which specify that recreational fishers must not sell their catches, it said.
Recreational fishers are only allowed to bring their catches back for personal use, it agency said.
The agency has been developing a fishing apprenticeship program, to be implemented from next month, which would enable recreational fishers to safely and legally enter the commercial fishing trade, it said.
After four hours of training, a participant could apply for “trainee seafarer” status, which would permit them to sell catches captured while aboard licensed fishing vessels, it said.

Day traders abandoning S Korean leveraged ETFs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:43:46 UTC
01:43:46 KST

An onerous mock trading course is becoming an effective tool for South Korea to cool investor fervor over risky products that have turned the country’s US$4.3 trillion stock market extremely volatile.
Leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) targeting twice the daily returns of chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc have seen their trading value collapse to 4 percent of its June peak and are set for their first monthly outflow.
Key to sapping demand has been a series of regulatory tightening moves, most recently a rule to complete five-day simulated trading. Investors must download a Windows-only program on PCs and spend at least one hour a day learning the ropes — and the risks — of leveraged trading with virtual cash.
Photo: AP
Interviews with several South Korean retail investors suggested that the requirement, effective on Aug. 19, is too cumbersome to meet.
Gyeonggi Province resident Kim Jung-hoon said his first reaction to the mandatory mock trading was that he would not attempt it, as it was “too much of a hassle.”
“The hours sound long and you can only download the program on PCs,” Kim said. “My work computer can’t download external programs. It doesn’t sound easy to bring an extra laptop with me to work.”
The exercises add to a slew of regulatory curbs since last month to deter investors from trading the leveraged ETFs tied to Samsung and SK Hynix. Earlier measures included a higher minimum deposit.
The system gives investors a virtual cash deposit of 100 million won (US$72,560), offering a first-hand lesson on the perils of trading risky instruments. It lets them witness the so-called “volatility decay” — how returns can erode over time for leveraged products.
Another retail investor, Lee, who asked to be identified by his surname only, said he satisfied all the other prerequisites including the 30 million won minimum cash deposit, but stumbled over the mock trading course.
“You have to download a program and there were minimum time requirements,” Lee said, adding that he also had to create a new membership account. “So I didn’t proceed. I just turned off there.”
The single-stock ETFs tied to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have seen combined outflows of about US$1 billion so far this month, poised to experience their first monthly fund exodus, Bloomberg Intelligence data showed.
The ETFs’ combined assets under management shrank to US$5 billion as of Thursday, down from US$11.4 billion at their peak in late June.
While the rapid contraction in trading might frustrate investors hoping to cash out at higher levels, it has helped stabilize the market. The KOSPI’s volatility gauge has slid to a four month low of about 50, down from a peak of 97 in late June. The stock benchmark is up 61 percent so far this year, but remains 25 percent below its record high reached two months ago.

Nepal-Tibet flood and preparing for more climate-linked disasters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:41 UTC
01:43:41 KST

Thousands of people in Nepal and Tibet are in desperate need of emergency assistance following Wednesday’s disaster. With 360 people confirmed dead, more than 1,300 others are still missing as search and rescue operations continue. The precise sequence of events linking glacier collapse to flash floods is yet to be confirmed, but there is no doubting the enormous destructive power of the brown torrent that could be seen on video clips surging down the steeply sided Himalayan valleys, sweeping away everyone and everything in its path.
Testimony from survivors about terrifying near-escapes and losses is reminiscent of previous disasters, including the 2004 tsunami. With some of the worst-affected areas still cut off and accessible only by helicopter, there is a high level of uncertainty about the total number of people who have died or homes that have been destroyed. Medical, food, shelter and sanitation supplies would need to be replenished. Pledges of help for locally led relief efforts from foreign governments and agencies, following reports that hundreds of those missing were tourists or pilgrims, must lead to swift action. People need basics including electricity and clean water before they can start to rebuild and recover.
Satellite images of the glacier and affected rivers are among crucial pieces of evidence used by scientists to piece together an account of what happened. Initial reports of an earthquake were later discounted, with seismic activity instead attributed to the impact of the glacier collapse and ice-rock avalanche. Nepalese authorities have issued warnings about the high risk of further floods. Women and children who have been displaced are particularly vulnerable to further harm, including disease and trafficking.
As with other disasters that are widely recognized to be climate-related, it is unwise to jump too swiftly to conclusions. Tectonic movement, which leads glaciers to change their shape over time, is a natural process. However, already, multiple glaciologists and other earth scientists have pointed to global heating as a crucial destabilizing factor. Higher temperatures are well established to be altering mountain environments worldwide, with the Himalayas warming twice as fast as the global average.
As the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said, this puts the region and its people at heightened risk not only from avalanches, landslides and floods, but also from freshwater shortages caused by retreating glaciers.
The implications of this might seem overwhelming. While millions — and perhaps billions — of people around the world accept that greenhouse gas emissions have altered the Earth’s atmosphere, the impact of human activity on the geology of mountains is a less familiar idea. Once the immediate humanitarian crisis in Nepal has eased and survivors have been helped to safety, this is the reality that must be addressed.
Mitigation of the climate threat through the transition away from fossil fuels remains essential, but resilience and adaptation measures also offer vital protection, particularly to communities in exposed locations. As mountains become more dangerous, early-warning systems must be improved. Disaster preparedness should be prioritized at a national level and in aid budgets so that agencies are better equipped to react.
Governments must rally around the people of Nepal and Tibet, and prepare to support similarly afflicted parts of the world in future.

TSMC Q2 employee bonuses rise more than 50%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) has increased its second-quarter employee bonuses by more than 50 percent from a year earlier, as the world’s largest contract chipmaker posted record earnings in the three-month period.
TSMC distributed its second-quarter bonuses to employees on Friday.
Employee bonuses for the April-to-June period totaled NT$36 billion (US$1.14 billion), the chipmaker’s financial data showed.
Photo: I-Hwa Cheng, AFP
During the period, TSMC posted NT$706.56 billion in net profit, up 77.4 percent from a year earlier and 23.4 percent from a quarter earlier.
Second-quarter earnings per share (EPS) rose to NT$27.25, compared with NT$15.36 a year earlier and NT$22.08 in the first quarter, TSMC said.
The record quarterly net profit reflected strong global demand for high-performance computing devices, Internet of Things applications and consumer electronics products, it said.
Employee bonuses for the first half of this year totaled NT$70.35 billion, 54.3 percent higher than a year earlier, TSMC data showed.
In the first six months of this year, the chipmaker posted NT$1.28 trillion in net profit, up 68.3 percent from a year earlier, while EPS rose to NT$49.32 from NT$29.30 a year earlier.
With TSMC allocating more of its profits to enhance social sustainability as part of its efforts to give back to Taiwan, growth in employee bonuses lagged behind the increase in net profit during the six-month period. Nevertheless, the increase so far this year exceeded the about 30 percent growth recorded last year.
Sources said TSMC distributes half of its employee bonuses on a quarterly basis and pays the remaining half after the shareholders’ meeting the following year.

2026-08-30

Race leader Tadej Pogacar pulled out of the Vuelta a Espana on Saturday after suffering a fractured collarbone and other injuries from a fall 31km from the end of the eighth stage, with Spaniard Enric Mas inheriting the overall lead.
The stage was won by French sprinter Bryan Coquard, catching Danish rider Mads Pedersen right on the line at the beach resort of Xeraco with its protected wetlands.
Pogacar, who rarely falls heavily, has won five Tour de France titles and a Giro d’Italia and was hunting his first overall victory in the 21-day Spanish race.
Photo: AFP
Pogacar hit the road surface after swerving suddenly on an innocuous stretch of road, losing control, flying head-first over his handlebars and landing on his shoulder and face.
With his entire team stopping and waiting, the peloton at first slowed down but then carried on after the Slovenian rider tried to remount several minutes later, but cried out “no” and exhibited pain when he touched his bike.
He was led to an ambulance as his teammates set off up the broad and freshly-laid dual carriageway toward the finish line at Xeraco, near Valencia, with the look of a defeated army, nine minutes off the pace.
Pogacar had been leading Mas by 3:50. This is the first time the 27-year-old has failed to finish a Grand Tour.
His team confirmed he had sustained a displaced left clavicle fracture, a cervical fracture and a concussion.
“Fortunately, [he has suffered] no other major injuries and no neurological fallout,” UAE’s team medical director Adrian Rotunno said in a statement. “He will require clavicle surgery which will be delayed due to concussion precautions.”
“Tadej remains under the care of our medical team and we’ll provide further updates following the surgery,” he added.
Mas is 1:11 ahead of Austrian Felix Gall and former champion Primoz Roglic is third at 1:33.
In July, Pogacar joined a select group of five-time Tour de France winners with Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain.
He is the youngest rider to have won five Tours, more than a year younger than Merckx, and is the first person to finish on the podium seven years running.
He is also the only rider to have been on the podium in nine consecutive Grand Tours.

Low-pressure system to bring heavy rain to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

A low-pressure system over the South China Sea is expected to bring the heaviest rainfall of the coming week to Taiwan today and tomorrow, with southern and central areas as well as Taitung County potentially seeing extremely heavy rain, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
The low-pressure system could develop into a tropical depression as it approaches Taiwan, though it remains uncertain whether it will intensify into a tropical storm, CWA forecaster Wang Pin-hsiang (王品翔) said.
Taiwan will remain under the influence of a broad low- pressure belt throughout the week, resulting in unstable weather, he said.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
Southern Taiwan is expected to see localized heavy or extremely heavy rain today and tomorrow, while central areas and Taitung could see heavy rain or extremely heavy rainfall over short periods.
Afternoon thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall are forecast elsewhere.
An extremely heavy rain warning indicates accumulated rainfall of more than 200mm in 24 hours or 100mm within three hours, while a heavy rain alert means accumulated rainfall of more than 80mm in 24 hours or 40mm in one hour, according to the CWA.
Rainfall is expected to ease gradually from Wednesday through Saturday, although localized heavy rain will remain possible in southern Taiwan and mountainous areas on Wednesday. Elsewhere, afternoon thunderstorms are forecast, with isolated heavier downpours possible.
Daytime highs will remain around 33-34°C during the coming week, though conditions will remain hot and humid before rainfall begins, Wang said.
Separately, Wang said another tropical system east of the Philippines could strengthen into a tropical storm while moving toward the Ryukyu Islands, although its intensity and path remain uncertain.
Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Etau weakened into a tropical depression yesterday afternoon, while Tropical Storm Banlang continued moving northward. Neither system is expected to affect Taiwan, he said.

KMT planning campaign for referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) yesterday said it was planning 100 local events and launching a social media campaign to rally support for a referendum on whether to abolish the government’s policy to phase out nuclear power.
The Central Election Commission (CEC) on Friday reviewed three referendum proposals, passing one on whether to abolish the nation’s nuclear-free homeland policy and rejecting a referendum on using caning as punishment and another on using traffic fines to pay for road-safety improvements.
The rejected proposals did not meet the Referendum Act’s (公民投票法) requirement that referendums concern “the initiation or reconsideration of major policies,” CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
The KMT’s nuclear power referendum asks: “Do you agree that the government should abolish its ‘nuclear-free homeland’ energy policy to safeguard public health, ensure stable electricity supply and affordable electricity prices, enhance national defense resilience and support the development of the artificial intelligence [AI] industry?”
The referendum is an issue that affects Taiwan’s overall national competitiveness, KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Charles Chen (陳以信) said in a statement.
KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) has said that reliable electricity is essential to Taiwan’s competitiveness, as well as its high-tech and AI industries, he added.
The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) government has shut down nuclear power plants, forcing Taiwan to become reliant on natural gas and putting the nation’s energy security on a single source that is dependent on imports, Chen said.
The KMT would center its referendum campaign around the idea that energy is vital to national security, computing power is key to national strength and Taiwan must secure energy for AI, he said.
The party is calling for a stable power supply, a stronger economy and continued growth of the AI industry, he added.
The KMT would pursue three strategies: tying the referendum to elections, cooperation among opposition parties and promoting energy development, Chen said.
It plans to hold about 100 local events, coordinate with local candidates and use social media and other platforms to rally support for the referendum and overturn the DPP’s “misguided” non-nuclear energy policy, he said.
Meanwhile, environmental groups on Saturday said in a joint statement that the vague wording of the nuclear power referendum and one-sided explanatory statement do not provide voters with enough information.
The voter information booklet would only include the question and explanatory statement approved by the Legislative Yuan, with no views from other government agencies or civil society groups, the Taiwan Environmental Protection Union (TEPU) said in a statement.
That presents only the majority parties’ side of the argument, denying voters accurate, sufficient and comprehensive information, which contravenes the spirit of democracy, it said.
The referendum’s explanatory statement is riddled with false and misleading claims, most seriously asserting that the EU considers nuclear power to be green energy, it said.
The EU classifies nuclear power as a “transitional activity” to help achieve net zero emissions, it said.
The EU’s nuclear power policy requires concrete plans and funding for the disposal of nuclear waste, the group added.
As part of the global semiconductor supply chain, Taiwan needs green power, but also diverse, locally produced renewable energy to enhance its energy security, TEPU said, urging the government to continue developing renewable energy rather than abolish the non-nuclear homeland policy.
Typhoon Saudel has shown signs of weakening but is still expected to affect Taiwan when it comes closest to the nation on Friday, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said today. As of 8am, Typhoon Saudel was 980km east of Taipei, moving west-northwest at 18kph, it said.
